title: Too Much of a Good Thing
dek: How social media, online news, and the First Amendment are killing democracy.
excerpt: How social media, online news, and the First Amendment are killing democracy.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

Democracy was conceived under the assumption of informational scarcity.

When the Founders crafted the First Amendment, the primary threat to self-governance was state censorship: the silencing of dissenting voices by a central authority. The remedy was simple and elegant: protect the open marketplace of ideas. The premise was that truth, given a fair hearing alongside falsehood, would prevail.

What the architects of free speech could not anticipate was a world of radical informational abundance.

Today, democracy is not starving for information. It is choking on it.

The convergence of algorithmic social media, 24-hour online news, and near-absolute First Amendment protection has turned the public square into an echo chamber. Rather than creating an enlightened citizenry, the relentless torrent of targeted content, outrage-driven media, and instant digital connection is unraveling the social cohesion self-governance depends on.

This breakdown is not an accident of technology. It is what happens when a legal framework built for scarcity is applied to an era of abundance. Three shifts dismantled the guardrails of civic communication. _New York Times Co. v. Sullivan_ (1964) set an "actual malice" standard so demanding that it largely insulated publishers from defamation suits by public figures. The FCC's abolition of the Fairness Doctrine in 1987 ended the requirement for balanced political broadcasting and opened the door to hyper-partisan media. And Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act (1996) gave internet platforms near-total immunity for what their users post. Together, these removed accountability and turned information production into a low-liability, high-profit enterprise.

The legal shift coincided with an exploit of human biology. Human awareness prioritizes threat, conflict, and friction over calm consensus, and attention algorithms are engineered to capitalize on it. The business model is simple: in a hyper-competitive market for attention, anger and division keep people engaged far longer than nuance does. So platforms weaponize outrage to maximize screen time, and infinite streams of tailored content compress complex civic debates into rapid, hyperbolic triggers. Nuance needs time to process. The system rewards speed, drowns out deliberation, and locks citizens into tribal echo chambers.

The result is a collapse of accountability. Traditional editorial stewardship, once anchored by professional reputation and fact-checking, has been replaced by engagement metrics. Clicks, shares, and watch time now set the agenda. As expertise is democratized to the point of noise, the shared factual baseline self-governance requires dissolves. The volume of speech has grown exponentially; civic understanding has shrunk in proportion. We are drowning in information and starved for truth.

The First Amendment, designed to protect democratic debate, now shields the machinery destroying it. Legal doctrines forged in the age of the printing press block meaningful intervention against algorithmic amplification, foreign disinformation, and targeted radicalization. Speech has been decoupled from accountability, and amplification has replaced discourse.

The common currency of online media is deliberate shock and programmed outrage. Protected by the First Amendment, profit trumps reason. Civility has died.

Finding answers is not impossible. Scholars, technologists, and legal experts have put forward workable proposals: reforming platform liability, setting algorithmic transparency standards, teaching media literacy, and revitalizing public-interest media.

Enacting them in a society fragmented culturally, ethnically, linguistically, religiously, ideologically, and politically, and stitched together by technology, is probably impossible.

The crisis of the digital age is not a shortage of policy ideas. It is the breakdown of the collective trust needed to implement them.

In a nation fractured along every demographic and ideological fault line, any attempt to regulate the digital sphere is instantly weaponized as partisan suppression. When every faction sees the other not as a rival in debate but as an existential threat, the shared reality that compromise requires vanishes. Technology has provided the ultimate binding material for a vast, diverse population, but it binds by magnifying and straining every seam. We have built an information ecosystem that thrives on our divisions, protected by a constitutional framework that prevents its repair, and left a divided society unable to agree even on national survival.

I'd like to end on a note of optimism. I'm not sure that's realistic. In an open economy, profit usually outranks the public good. And at a time when the Constitution itself is held in diminished esteem, few will be moved by the reminder that James Madison, the First Amendment's author, was trying to protect the people from their government, not from each other.

In the end, public issues are like waves at sea. One by one, they break on the shore and dissipate. With how much force, and how much damage, is another story.

title: The Cosmic Ledger
dek: Why physics must trade abstract ghosts for concrete frontiers.
excerpt: Why physics must trade abstract ghosts for concrete frontiers.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

For a century, modern physics has been locked in a quiet existential crisis, drifting away from the tangible reality of things that are and into the speculative metaphysics of things that aren't. Popular science routinely tells a creation story that reads less like hard engineering and more like a secular myth dressed up in equations: the universe spontaneously popped into existence out of an absolute, zero-sized nothingness through a quantum tunneling event.

Strip away the mathematical veneer and the logic collapses. To argue that a universe can be "borrowed" into existence through the Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle requires a massive, unacknowledged leap of faith. It assumes that before space, time, or matter existed, the rules of the game (probability, quantum fields, mathematical logic) were already floating in a timeless limbo, waiting to enforce themselves. That is not creation from nothing. It is creation from a highly sophisticated, deeply structured something. It is quasi-mystical, self-inflating gibberish, and it violates the very definition of empirical science. Physics is supposed to be about what is, not what isn't.

Even the theories that predict how matter moves rest on shaky conceptual ground. General Relativity is a spectacularly accurate bookkeeper; your phone's GPS would drift by miles a day without its corrections. But accuracy is not the same as truth. GR replaces real physical forces with "spacetime," an oxymoronic fiction that welds a physical thing (space) to an abstract measure of duration (time) and calls the result an invisible fabric. To claim that a geometric abstraction can bend, twist, and push tangible matter treats the cosmos like a stage trick. The math works. The story told about the math is bunk.

Once we let the math stand in for physical reality, we're forced into absurd logical gymnastics. We spend immense human talent and billions in public treasure chasing mathematical ghosts: calculating what happened "before" time, hunting for unprovable parallel dimensions.

This institutional delusion feeds the multi-billion-dollar playgrounds of high-energy physics, above all CERN, the European Organization for Nuclear Research. There, humanity has buried a twenty-seven-kilometer ring of superconducting magnets, the Large Hadron Collider, largely to hunt for ever more obscure and hypothetical subatomic ghosts. We smash particles together at near-light speed to test abstract frameworks like supersymmetry, string theory, and colliding multi-dimensional "branes," none of which has delivered any practical, real-world payoff. The enterprise needs a good, stiff smacking. It has become an insular, self-perpetuating bureaucracy where physicists build bigger machines to justify bigger theories, a closed loop of academic indulgence that mistakes elegant chalkboard math for physical reality. Its most celebrated triumph, the Higgs boson, cost an estimated $13 billion to find: an astronomical sum for a fleeting particle that decays in a fraction of a second and has left daily life for the rest of humanity entirely unchanged.

Historically, the waste is tolerated because human endeavor is naturally prone to futility; if we weren't burning resources on abstract mathematics, we'd burn them in some other bureaucratic or geopolitical loop. And the wild-goose chases do throw off accidental benefits. Engineers building colliders have had to invent advanced computing networks, medical imaging technology, and new materials. The World Wide Web itself was invented at CERN, not as a goal, but as a utility so far-flung physicists could share their data. It is an indictment of modern science that its greatest practical breakthroughs are byproducts of chasing ghosts. If those billions and those elite minds were aimed directly at concrete physical problems from the start, rather than waiting for spillover from an academic fantasy camp, our rate of tangible progress would be unstoppable.

There is a more grounded way to break the cycle: stop chasing invisible cosmic origins and start conquering the physical space in front of us.

Reality is the ultimate proof of its own validity; whatever sparked the cosmos was reasonable precisely because it happened. Instead of looking backward into an unmeasurable past, humanity has far more to gain by looking outward. Space is a brutal frontier that ruthlessly weeds out abstract nonsense. A rocket engine either produces thrust or it explodes; a hull either holds pressure or it vents. Space does not care about equations that only work on paper. It demands real engineering and measurable results.

To turn that vision into infrastructure, humanity cannot rely on curiosity or national pride. History shows those motivations stall the moment the political winds shift. The most reliable engine of human progress is, and always has been, the profit motive.

The moment space shifts from an arena of exploration to one of economic exploitation, the same restless energy that feeds futility gets redirected into building. The incentives are staggering:

- **Asteroid mining.** A single metal-rich asteroid may hold more platinum-group and industrial metals than humanity has mined in its entire history. Even allowing for the price crash such a flood of supply would bring, the first operators stand to build the largest mining enterprises ever seen.
- **Orbital manufacturing.** In the microgravity of low Earth orbit, semiconductors, advanced fiber optics, and bio-printed tissue can be made with a purity impossible on Earth, opening entirely new markets.
- **Space-based solar power.** Orbital arrays harvesting unfiltered sunlight around the clock and beaming it to the surface could, once launch costs fall far enough, upend global energy markets on price per kilowatt-hour.

The shift is already underway. For decades, rocket technology stagnated under government monopolies. Once private enterprise stepped in, driven by the profit incentive to slash launch costs and capture the global telecommunications market, we got the engineering marvel of reusable rockets landing themselves on drone ships.

## A DOGE for space

What the space business needs now is DOGE: a hard-nosed efficiency audit of every space program the public pays for, combined. Not one agency at a time. All of them, at once.

The money is scattered across separate sets of books. NASA spends roughly $25 billion a year. The Space Force spends about $30 billion. The spy-satellite programs spend amounts that aren't even made public. The missions overlap, the contractors overlap, and nobody is paid to look at the whole.

An audit wouldn't have to dig far. NASA's own inspector general estimated that its return-to-the-Moon program would cost about $93 billion through 2025, and that each launch of its giant new rocket would cost around $4 billion. A private heavy-lift rocket launch is advertised for roughly $100 million. The James Webb Space Telescope was first pitched at a billion dollars or less and ended up close to ten. Those aren't rounding errors. They're the cost of a system with no one minding the till.

The original DOGE was wound down in late 2025, eight months ahead of schedule. The idea deserves a second flight, aimed at the one place where budgets are literally astronomical. One rule, though: nobody who sells rockets gets a seat at the table. The referee can't be a player.

By demanding that physics stay rooted in physical existence, and by tying our grandest ambitions to the relentless engine of commercial viability, we can stop staring into the void of what isn't. Conquering the frontier of what is will not only spark the next great economic gold rush; it will give our species' taste for futility something real to chew on, and help it build a tangible future among the stars.

title: Random Order
dek: Modern cosmology relies on a grand accounting trick. Look at all the motion at once, with nothing averaged away, and reality turns out to be one continuous fractal of noise. We are basking in the raw, un-averaged glow of an ongoing Big Bang.
excerpt: Modern cosmology relies on a grand accounting trick. Look at all the motion at once, with nothing averaged away, and reality turns out to be one continuous fractal of noise. We are basking in the raw, un-averaged glow of an ongoing Big Bang.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

## I. The Builders of Empires

Scientists lazily basking in the glow of the Big Bang, building little empires in the cosmos: that is the modern academic landscape. We are taught to look at the night sky and see harmony. Planets trace clean ellipses, stars orbit galactic cores in majestic spirals, and the cosmic web expands with predictable mathematical grace.

But that order is a product of human limits: our brief lifespans and our narrow instruments. To find it, the mainstream Brahmin has to act as a forgetful bookkeeper. He takes an instant of reality, a cloud of gas or a cluster of stars, and mathematically cancels the opposing motions. He crosses out the colliding particles, ignores the turbulent micro-tugs, and averages the noise until one clean arrow remains.

He calls that arrow "macro-order." But the noise never actually went anywhere.

In any real instant, every collision, every swirl, every thermal jiggle is happening at once. The universe does not pause its chaos to run an average. Refuse to abstract the data, look at all the motion of every piece of matter together, and the mirage of the clockwork universe evaporates.

## II. Basking in the Explosion

The foundational error of modern astrophysics is treating the Big Bang as something that happened: a distant genesis safely tucked away in the past.

It never stopped.

We are not living in the calm aftermath of a creation event. We are basking in the glowing, churning shrapnel of an explosion still in progress. Every atom of ordinary matter is a bullet still in flight. What we call "different scales" are just different sizes of the same turbulent eddies.

**At the micro-scale,** a hydrogen atom in a laboratory vibrates violently, driven by thermal and quantum agitation.

**At the macro-scale,** that same hydrogen atom, adrift in an intergalactic filament, is buffeted by supernova shockwaves and shifting gravitational fields.

The atom rides the same non-linear pinball machine wherever it sits. The laws of physics (gravity, electromagnetism, thermodynamics) do not exist to enforce geometric perfection or peace. They are the banks of a river. The water itself is a permanently churning rush.

## III. The Material Cosmos

Without invisible scaffolding like dark matter to force artificial stability onto our models, galaxies reveal their true nature. They are not permanent monuments of cosmic architecture. They are colossal, slow-motion illusions.

A spiral galaxy looks serene only because it takes hundreds of millions of years to turn. Speed up the clock to match its internal motion and the spiral loses its geometry. It bleeds, shears, and splatters like a drop of ink in a spinning glass of water: a vast storm of ordinary matter tearing at itself in freefall, following the same kinds of scaling patterns we see in a solar flare or a particle collision.

Order is not the baseline of the universe. Chaos is the architecture. The structures we admire are just the temporary shapes chaos takes when its own mass forces it to fold in on itself.

## IV. The Bookkeeper's Reply

The physicist has an answer, and it's a fair one. Averaging is how you get predictions that work. Nobody needs the path of every air molecule to forecast tomorrow's weather. Thermodynamics throws away almost all the detail and still runs every engine on Earth. The net arrow isn't a lie; it's useful.

Agreed. But useful is not the same as real. An average is a summary, and a summary describes the reader as much as the thing read. When the books stop balancing, as they do at the edges of galaxies, the honest move is to suspect the method of summary. Instead, cosmology adds new entries, dark matter and dark energy, until the ledger closes. The bookkeeper isn't wrong to average. He's wrong to forget that he did.

## V. Living in the Glow

So what's left when the clockwork goes? Not despair. A different kind of attention.

If order is a mirage produced by our short lives and slow instruments, then the patterns we prize, the elegant ellipse and the majestic spiral, are portraits of our own limits, drawn on a canvas that never holds still. That's no insult to science. It's an honest description of it: a short-lived species taking snapshots of a storm and calling them maps.

The universe isn't a machine we've nearly finished reverse-engineering. It's an explosion still under way, and we are part of the shrapnel: briefly warm, briefly coherent, briefly able to look around. The order we see is real the way a photograph of a breaking wave is real: the photograph is real, the stillness in it isn't. True for an instant, and ours.

We aren't living after the Big Bang. We're living in it. The least we can do is enjoy the light.

title: The Stuff Between the Stars
dek: What if space isn't empty, but the most common material there is?
excerpt: What if space isn't empty, but the most common material there is?
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

Ask a physicist what's between the stars and you'll get a strange answer. Not nothing, exactly. A vacuum, but a busy one: dozens of invisible fields overlapping in the same place, each ignoring the others, each producing its own particles as ripples. A particle is a ripple in a field; the field is defined by the particles it produces. Around and around it goes.

All of it sits on "spacetime," a fabric woven from space and time that bends near heavy objects and tells matter how to move. It's a superb calculating device. But a calculating device isn't a thing. Geometry can't push anything. Time is a measurement, not a material. Weld them together and you get an oxymoron with excellent predictive power.

So here's a simpler question. What if space isn't empty at all? What if it's the most common material there is?

## One stuff, many notes

Start with a single, continuous substance filling everything. Not a stage that matter sits on, but the stuff matter is made of. What physics calls separate fields would then be different motions of the same material: stresses, vibrations, currents. A pond can carry ripples, whirlpools, and sound waves at once without being three ponds. Maybe the universe is one pond.

Matter, in this picture, is a knot. A particle is a small region where the substance has wound itself tight and is vibrating hard, a tuning fork slapping against the medium around it. Its density is how tightly it's packed; its vibration is how hard it's ringing. Inertia, the stubbornness of objects to start or stop, stops being a mysterious built-in property. It's the resistance a tight, ringing knot meets when you try to drag it through the stuff it's tied in.

## Gravity as compression

If space is material, gravity needs no bent geometry. A star doesn't sit on space; it sits in it, displacing the substance around it and leaving a pressure slope. Anything nearby feels less push from the star's side than from the open side, and drifts inward. Not attraction. Compression.

The obvious objection: if planets move through a material, why don't they slow down and spiral in? They've circled the Sun for four and a half billion years. The answer may already be on the table. In this picture the medium doesn't resist motion; it resists change in motion. That's exactly what inertia is. A planet coasting in a steady orbit isn't fighting the medium. It's riding it.

## Galaxies as whirlpools

The outer stars of spiral galaxies orbit far too fast for the visible matter to hold them. Standard cosmology's fix is dark matter: an invisible substance, about five times more plentiful than the ordinary kind, that has never been directly detected despite decades of searching.

If space is material, there's another way to see it. A galaxy isn't a swarm of stars coasting through a void; it's a whirlpool in the medium. The core turns and drags the surrounding substance with it, and the outer stars are carried by the current like leaves in an eddy.

The idea isn't finished. Dark-matter defenders point to the way galaxy clusters bend light from behind them, and to the Bullet Cluster, where the mass and the visible matter seem to have parted company. A whirlpool needs an answer to both. But "we haven't explained this yet" is an honest place to stand. "There's an invisible substance we can't find" is a less comfortable one.

## Discovered, not collapsed

The same move clears up quantum mechanics' strangest claim: that a particle exists as a haze of possibilities until someone looks, and the act of looking collapses it into one answer.

If the universe is one material, there's no need for haze. The particle was somewhere all along; the wave function is a map of what we don't know yet. Measurement doesn't create the answer. It uncovers it.

This isn't fringe. Physicists have a respectable version of it, pilot-wave theory, in which particles always have real positions, guided by a wave. The price, as experiments since the 1980s have shown, is that the universe must be connected in ways that defy ordinary ideas of distance. For a picture in which everything is one continuous substance, that price may not be so steep.

## One camera, all scales

Modern physics runs on two rulebooks: quantum mechanics for the very small, general relativity for the very large. Push them together at the smallest scales and the math produces infinities. The usual excuse is that nature changes its rules depending on size.

The material view says otherwise. One substance, one set of mechanics, from the subatomic to the galactic. The cake stays the same; only the icing of scale changes how it looks. When equations blow up into infinities, that's not nature misbehaving. It's the equations running past the edge of what they were built to describe. The same goes for the Big Bang singularity: not an event, but the place where the math gives out.

## Plain words

Much of modern physics is written in a language that keeps outsiders out. That has its uses; precision matters. But when a theory can only be stated in jargon, it's worth asking whether the jargon is carrying the physics or hiding its absence. A material universe can be described in plain words: stuff, knots, pressure, whirlpools. That's not a weakness. It may be a sign the idea is pointing at something real.

None of this is proven. It's a question worth asking out loud: what if the stuff between the stars was never nothing, but everything?

title: The Accidental Eye
dek: Friction, form, and why the laws of physics may be ours, not the universe's.
excerpt: Friction, form, and why the laws of physics may be ours, not the universe's.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

Picture the universe's ground floor as a storm. A single material, everywhere, always moving, always grinding against itself. Not building anything. Not aiming at anything. Just churning.

Most of that churn leaves no trace. Motion meets resistance, swirls, and dissolves back into the background, over and over, across unimaginable stretches of space and time. Friction everywhere; form almost nowhere.

## How form happens

Every so often, by pure chance, the churn hits a pattern that holds. A swirl catches itself in a loop and keeps spinning instead of scattering. That's form: not the universe's goal, just a lucky knot that survives the current. Atoms, stars, galaxies: each is a whirlpool that happened to stabilize, a boundary where motion meets resistance and holds.

And because it's chance, the details could have been anything. Had one eddy turned a second later, billions of years ago, our galaxy might have been a ring of stars with spokes, a cosmic Ferris wheel. What chance can't change is the style. A fluid makes whirlpools, spirals, rings, and spheres, the way water makes snowflakes of endless variety that are all six-sided. The particulars are luck. The shapes belong to the medium.

## Time and decay

In a universe of constant grinding, time isn't a dimension. It's the counting system we invented to keep track of all that motion and wear. Its true name is entropy: the running tally of friction, resistance, and decay. Everything is slowing, smoothing, coming apart. The clock is just how we read it.

## Life: the knot that copies itself

Somewhere, around a hot vent on a young planet's sea floor, say, the churn produced a knot that did something new. It copied itself. Nothing in a uniform material forbids it. It's just very unlikely, and the universe is very big.

That changes everything, because a knot that copies itself has something to lose. Out there, the storm doesn't care. In here, a loop is trying to keep going. For the first time, randomness becomes a threat. Uncertainty isn't a feature of the universe; it's what randomness feels like to something that wants to survive.

So life builds walls. A cell membrane, a skin, a shell: structures that fence off a predictable "in here" from the chaos "out there."

## Consciousness: the scout

Consciousness, in this picture, is life's early-warning system: a scout sent out to watch the storm and report back before it can tear the loop apart.

It's a trillion-to-one fluke. But in a universe big enough, a trillion-to-one shot isn't rare. Somewhere, it's inevitable. You are the storm, by sheer accident, growing an eye.

And the eye has a problem. It can't take in the raw churn. Unfiltered, the chaos would overwhelm it. So it does what every survivor does: it builds shelter.

## Patterns govern the mind, not the world

Here's the turn. The laws of physics, geometry, fixed position, the steady tick of time: what if these aren't features of the universe at all? What if they're the shelter?

The mind needs a stable floor to stand on, so it stipulates one. It nails down "here" and "there" and measures how the storm pushes against them. Position isn't found in the universe; we assign it so we can work. The patterns are real, but they govern consciousness, not reality. They're the shape of the net, not the shape of the sea.

That's imagination's job: to take what consciousness sees and project order onto it. Stone walls, legal codes, scientific models. Each is a fence around a small, lit space in an endless dark.

## What it means to be

Flip the usual picture. Traditionally, things are solid and permanent, and change is what happens to them. Here, change is the ground and things are temporary interruptions. You are not a noun. You're an event, a whirlpool holding its spin for a while.

The self, the inner "I," may be nothing more mysterious than that: the feel of a whirlpool holding its own boundary against the current. Pushing back is what it's like to be someone.

Ask whether existence belongs to reality or to consciousness, and the answer is both. Reality supplies the storm; consciousness supplies the shape. Existence is where they meet.

## A brief, bright interruption

None of this makes life smaller. It makes it stranger. The universe didn't plan us, doesn't need us, and won't miss us. But for a moment, in a storm with no purpose, a knot of matter wound itself tight enough to look around and ask what it is.

Then the current carries it home. That's the deal. It's not a bad one.

title: Nouns Can't Do a Verb's Work
dek: Why breakthroughs happen by accident, and why institutions can't schedule them.
excerpt: Why breakthroughs happen by accident, and why institutions can't schedule them.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

In the summer of 1928, a Scottish doctor went on holiday and left a dirty dish in his London lab. When he came back, a mold had landed on it and killed the bacteria he'd been growing. That accident gave the world penicillin. Nobody planned it, nobody funded it, and nobody put it on a five-year schedule. It just happened.

That's not an exception. It's the rule. In 1964, two engineers in New Jersey couldn't get rid of a faint hiss in their radio antenna. They blamed pigeons, scrubbed out the droppings, and the hiss stayed. It turned out to be the afterglow of the birth of the universe. In 1895, a German professor noticed a screen glowing across his darkened lab when it had no business glowing. He'd found X-rays.

Breakthroughs don't arrive on schedule. They turn up in unexpected places, with unexpected people, usually while someone was looking for something else. Discovery is something that happens. And that's the whole trouble with how we organize science, because we've built a system that treats discovery as something you can own.

## The noun habit

Start with a quirk of language. We talk about the world as if it's made of things, nouns that sit there having properties. But most of what we name is something happening. And once we've given a happening a noun, we go looking for the thing.

Take "nothing." Put it at the front of a sentence ("nothing is dark," "nothing came first") and you've already turned it into a something with properties. A few years ago a bestselling book promised to explain how the universe came from nothing. A philosopher reviewing it pointed out that the author's "nothing" was a vacuum stuffed with energy and governed by laws. The hard question hadn't been answered. It had been renamed.

Take time. Nobody has ever measured time itself. We measure things moving: a pendulum swinging, the earth turning, a crystal vibrating. A clock is just a horse walking in circles. Take away all the motion and there's nothing left to measure. Time isn't a thing. It's our name for change.

Take matter, the most solid-sounding noun of all. Most of the weight of the particles in your body comes from the energy of their tiny parts racing around inside them. Solid stuff, looked at closely, is trapped motion.

And take a horse. You could catalog every molecule in it and still not know it's a horse, let alone whether it'll win on Saturday. A horse replaces most of its atoms over a few years and stays the same horse. The horse is the pattern, and the molecules just pass through. Anyone who buys horses knows you judge them by what they can do, not what they're made of.

That's the noun habit: freeze a happening into a thing, then spend a fortune hunting for the thing.

## Nouns built to hold still

Now look at the institutions that run science: the universities, the funding agencies, the giant labs. An institution is a noun. It's a fixed thing, built to hold still, to last, to keep doing tomorrow what it did today. That's its whole job.

So it does to discovery what language does to time. It turns it into a thing. Grant applications ask you to describe what you'll discover before you've discovered it. Five-year plans schedule breakthroughs. Progress reports count "deliverables," as if insight came by the crate.

The same habit shows up in the science itself. When the evidence doesn't fit, the reflex is to add a new noun rather than rethink the old ones. In the 1840s, the planet Uranus wobbled off course. Astronomers predicted an unseen planet pulling on it, and Neptune turned up right where they said. Triumph. So when Mercury wobbled too, they predicted another hidden planet and named it Vulcan. They searched for some sixty years. It wasn't there. The real fix came when a patent clerk rethought gravity itself, doing the homework on what was already on the table.

Today most of the universe is said to be made of two invisible things, "dark matter" and "dark energy," which nobody has ever caught. Maybe they're Neptunes. Maybe they're Vulcans. Either way, they're nouns, and the money follows the nouns.

## Scorn first, dependence later

Here's the contradiction at the heart of it. You can't ask a noun to do a verb's work. A thing built to hold still can't produce something that only happens. So the institution ends up living off the people who can, usually after doing its best to stop them.

A butcher's daughter from Hungary spent years in America trying to get funding for an idea about using genetic messages as medicine. She was turned down again and again and eventually demoted. Decades later, her work became the foundation of the vaccines that got the world out of lockdown. She won a Nobel Prize. The institution got the press release.

A blacksmith's son, apprenticed to a bookbinder, with almost no schooling, taught himself science from the books he was binding. He worked out how to make electricity from motion, which is how nearly every power station on earth still works. When he was put up for membership of Britain's top scientific society, his own patron, the most famous scientist of the day, opposed it.

A German weather scientist said the continents were slowly drifting apart. The geologists laughed at him for decades. He died on the Greenland ice in 1930. In the 1960s, they discovered he'd been right all along.

The pattern repeats like a pub argument on a Friday night. Working stiffs push the ball down the field. The posers scorn them, then collect the credit and the cash.

## Oddballs and natural selection

Nature figured this out long ago. Evolution only works if there's variation to select from: the odd mutation, the creature that doesn't fit, the one that tries something different. Wipe out the oddballs and you wipe out the future.

An institution that crushes its misfits is doing exactly that. It's removing the mutations it will someday need. And since nobody can tell the genius from the crank in advance, the only sane policy is to leave them alone and let time sort them out.

It doesn't even cost much. Real genius is cheap. The patent clerk who rethought gravity did it on a clerk's wage, in his spare time. The bookbinder's apprentice needed a lab bench and some wire. The horse dealer's son from Belfast, who set the terms of the deepest debate in modern physics, did it on the side of his day job. It's the institutions that are expensive.

## Last orders

So here's the modest proposal. Leave the geniuses alone. Don't scorn them, don't dismiss them, and don't make them fill in forms predicting what they'll find. Let insight come first and verification after, because that's the order it has always come in. They'll go on rescuing the makework careers anyway. They always have.

As for everyone else on the payroll: you can't catch a tiger with a brain wave, and you won't find the essence of existence chasing a boson around in circles. Get busy turning what we already know into something people can use. And stop dressing up guesses as facts. Every time science oversells a story, it spends trust it will need later.

Discovery is a verb. Institutions are nouns. You can't ask a noun to do a verb's work, and a contradiction never produced a lasting solution.

So, with apologies to the President: ask not what your knowledge can do for you. Ask what you can do with your knowledge.

title: False in One
dek: Putting the spokesmen of modern physics on trial.
excerpt: Putting the spokesmen of modern physics on trial.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

Criminals are law-abiding most of the time. They stop at red lights, pay for their groceries and return their library books. Nobody lets them off on that account.

The courts have an old rule for witnesses, and it has a Latin name: _falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus_. False in one thing, false in all. A witness caught deliberately lying about one point can be disbelieved on everything else. It doesn't matter how much of the rest of their story checks out. One tainted, all tainted.

I use a legal standard when I listen to modern physics, and I think you should too. Because modern physics, as it's sold to the public, is inconsistent with observable, confirmed evidence. And its defences are tainted.

## The charge sheet

Start with the evidence, not the excuses.

**Count one: the worst prediction in the history of science.** Quantum theory was asked how much energy sits in empty space. Its answer missed the measured value by a factor with about 120 zeros on the end. That isn't a rounding error. It's a theory pointing at the wrong universe.

**Count two: the universe can't agree on its own speed.** Two careful, well-funded methods of measuring how fast the universe is expanding give two different answers. For years the gap has refused to close, no matter how many times they check.

**Count three: the galaxies spin too fast.** There isn't enough visible matter in them to hold them together at the speed they turn. They should fly apart. They don't.

**Count four: the two pillars contradict each other.** Relativity rules the very large and quantum theory the very small. Each works beautifully in its own patch. Where they meet, at the birth of the universe or the heart of a black hole, they contradict each other flat out.

Modern physics leads to pristine local predictions. Beyond that, it's a failure. And success in one frame does not forgive failures in others.

## The willful part

The law is fair about this. False in one, false in all applies to deliberate falsehood, not honest mistakes. A witness who gets a date wrong keeps their credibility. A witness who knowingly dresses up a guess as a fact loses it.

So look at how the failures above get presented to the public.

The galaxies spin too fast? We're told, as plain fact, that most of the matter in the universe is invisible "dark matter." Nobody has ever caught a single particle of it. The expansion is speeding up? That's "dark energy," said to make up most of everything, with no idea what it is. The universe is suspiciously smooth? That's "inflation," a burst of expansion in the first instant that has never been directly confirmed. A bestseller promises a universe from nothing, and its nothing turns out to be full of energy and laws.

Those are patches, not discoveries. A philosopher of science named Imre Lakatos gave us the test. When a healthy theory hits trouble, it predicts something new that then checks out. When a dying theory hits trouble, it adds a patch that explains nothing new and just plugs the hole. Then the spokesmen call it settled science. Those are facts deployed to obfuscate the reality.

That's the willful part. It's task avoidance on a grand scale, dressed up as knowledge.

## The bystanders

Now the hard part, in fairness. Not all physicists are guilty of the crimes of their spokesmen.

Thousands of them spend their working lives at a bench or a computer, measuring things carefully and reporting what they find, including the inconvenient results. It was working physicists who measured the expansion rate twice and refused to fudge the gap. It was astronomers who clocked the galaxies spinning too fast. The evidence against the story comes from inside the field.

The witnesses in the dock are the ones who speak for physics: the bestseller authors, the lab press offices, the documentary presenters, the grant-winning names who turn every patch into a triumph. The rest are collateral damage, honest witnesses discredited by the people talking over them.

## Verdict

Where modern physics conflicts with confirmed observation, it has lost the right to call itself settled. The burden shifts to its defenders. And a defence that only patches the hole and predicts nothing new isn't evidence of truth. It's evidence of inertia and self-interest.

The spokesmen have been caught. False in one, false in all. Until they stop selling patches as discoveries, the public is entitled to disbelieve them on everything, and to keep listening to the honest witnesses at the bench, who were telling us the truth all along.

title: Cold Case
dek: Reopening cosmology's files: keep the evidence, throw out the ghosts.
excerpt: Reopening cosmology's files: keep the evidence, throw out the ghosts.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

When a detective reopens a cold case, the first thing to go is the old theory. The files stay. The fingerprints stay. The witness statements stay. But the story the first investigators told about them goes in the bin, because if it were right, the case wouldn't be cold.

Modern cosmology is a cold case. For fifty years its investigators have been unable to explain how galaxies hold together, why the universe is speeding up, or what most of it is made of. Their answer has been to name suspects nobody has ever seen: cosmic inflation, the cosmological constant, dark matter, dark energy. Those aren't discoveries. They're unproven mental conveniences, labels stuck on the holes in the story.

So let's do some cold case forensics. Throw out the theory, keep the evidence, and see where it points. Because the remarkable thing is this: there's already a better explanation on the table. We can all see the baby. We just need to find mom and dad.

## The evidence locker

Strip off the labels and here's what's actually been observed:

- Light from distant galaxies arrives stretched toward the red, and the most distant exploding stars look dimmer than they should.
- The faint afterglow of the early universe is almost perfectly even, with tiny ripples.
- Galaxies spin too fast for the matter we can see in them.
- Light bends around heavy objects more than the visible matter seems to account for.

That's the evidence. Everything else is somebody's story about it.

And the setting matters. The universe isn't a machine somebody designed. It's an enduring, stable system, worn down by entropy, traceable almost to its beginning. Random motion in it works like genetic mutation: accidents happen to stable systems, and the ones that hold become what we see. Keep that in mind, because a detective who understands the setting doesn't need ghosts.

## The fingerprint

Start with the crime that opened the case. Stars at the edges of galaxies move too fast. By the visible evidence, they should fly off into space. They don't.

The original suspect was dark matter: an invisible substance wrapped around every galaxy, holding it together. Fifty years of searching, with the most sensitive detectors ever built, and not one confirmed particle. No fingerprints, no witness, no body.

Then, in 2016, three astronomers lined up 153 galaxies of every size and shape. They found that the speed of the stars at every point could be worked out from the visible matter alone, by one simple rule. Big galaxies, small galaxies, crowded ones, sparse ones: the same rule, every time.

Think about what that means. If an invisible substance were doing the work, it would have to arrange itself in perfect lockstep with the visible matter in every single galaxy. That's like finding the same fingerprint at 153 crime scenes and still blaming a ghost.

The rule wasn't a surprise to everyone. An Israeli physicist predicted it in 1983, decades before the data arrived, with an idea called MOND: that gravity itself behaves differently where it's very weak. The rule kicks in only at the gentle outskirts of galaxies. And here's the second fingerprint. The strength at which the rule kicks in matches a number from the whole universe, its expansion rate multiplied by the speed of light. The same hand at the galaxy scene and the cosmic one. Nobody in the establishment has a settled explanation for why.

## Big mass, big resistance

So who's the better suspect? Not a ghost. The system itself.

Suppose space isn't empty. Suppose it's a material, a field of universal resistance filling everything. Matter would then be a knot in that material, and the more mass packed into the knot, the more the material pushes back. Big mass, big resistance. Little mass, less.

That's mechanical gravity, and it isn't new. A friend of Newton's proposed a version in the 1690s, and Newton was reportedly intrigued. It was shelved, not disproved.

And it solves a mystery the establishment has never explained. Physics has two kinds of mass. One is how hard a thing is to shove. The other is how hard gravity pulls on it. They've been measured to be equal to better than one part in a trillion, and nobody knows why. Newton accepted it as a fact. Einstein built his whole theory on it as a starting assumption. In a material universe, they're equal because they're the same thing: the medium's resistance to the knot. One mechanism, not a coincidence.

The old objection was drag: planets moving through a material should slow down. They don't, and they don't have to. A planet in orbit isn't plowing through the medium. It's carried along by the current, and what rides a current feels no drag.

A medium also explains the galaxy rule's threshold. Near a star, gravity is strong enough to overwhelm the medium's own character, the way a gale flattens water and hides its currents. Out at a galaxy's edge, the push is gentle, and the medium's character shows.

## The lens

Next piece of evidence: light bends as it passes heavy objects. That's measured, and it's the main tool astronomers use to "weigh" the dark matter they can't see.

But every civilian knows what bends light: a lens. Light bends going into a glass of water because the water slows it down. If mass thickens the medium around it, light passing nearby should slow down and bend in just the same way.

The clues fit. The astronomer who confirmed Einstein's light bending in 1919 also showed you could get the same answer by treating the space around the Sun as slightly denser glass. And in the 1960s, scientists bounced radar off Venus and Mercury. Signals that passed close to the Sun came back measurably late, as if they'd crossed thicker glass. The establishment calls that curved spacetime. It looks every bit as much like a medium thickened by mass. And where mass thickens the medium more widely than the visible matter suggests, the extra bending around galaxies is the same lens, only thicker than we counted.

## A witness for the defense

The prosecution's star witness is the Bullet Cluster: two great clusters of galaxies that smashed through each other.

Each cluster has two parts: its galaxies, and a huge cloud of hot gas that holds most of its visible mass. In the crash, the gas clouds slammed together and stalled in the middle. The galaxies sailed straight through, like bullets. Then astronomers mapped where light bends most, and it wasn't around the gas, where most of the visible mass sits. It was around the galaxies. So, they announced, invisible mass must be riding along with the galaxies. Case closed.

Not so fast. First, nobody photographs mass. The map is worked backward through a model from tiny distortions in background galaxies. Second, some studies found the collision too fast to happen at all in the establishment's own picture of the universe. Their own star witness is starting to waver.

And third, there's a simpler explanation. It's called good theory. Gas is widely diffused regardless of its mass. Solid matter presents solid surfaces that generate focused displacement. Mass alone isn't the whole story. How it's packed matters too.

You can prove it in a swimming pool. Drop a baseball and the same weight of fine sand into the water at the same moment. The ball punches a sharp, focused wake. The sand spreads into a cloud and barely stirs the water. Same mass, different displacement. That's the Bullet Cluster in your back garden.

It also squares with calm galaxies, where gas seems to count at full weight. The wake matters when things smash through each other at tremendous speed. When gas circles slowly and smoothly, everything gets counted.

That's a new prediction, one the establishment's theory doesn't make. Which is exactly what good theory is supposed to do. Cross-examined, the prosecution's star witness ends up testifying for the defense.

## Caught red-handed

Now the biggest story in cosmology: the universe is expanding. The evidence is redshift. Light from distant galaxies arrives stretched toward the red, and that's read as the galaxies racing away from us.

But a material space should change how light travels. In 1929 the astronomer Fritz Zwicky suggested light simply tires on a long journey, losing a little energy the way a ripple fades across a pond. Redshift would then measure distance traveled, not speed of retreat.

The establishment has a strong witness against that. Distant exploding stars flare and fade in slow motion, stretched in time by exactly as much as their light is reddened. A tiring journey doesn't do that. Slowing light on its way just delays it. A delayed train isn't a longer train.

But slowing at the source does stretch. Clocks near a heavy mass run slow, and their light comes out redder by the same amount. That's measured on GPS satellites every day. Now suppose the medium was thicker long ago and has been thinning ever since, worn down by entropy. Then the distant universe, which we see as it was long ago, really did run in slow motion. Its light arrives reddened and stretched, matched exactly, and nothing has to fly apart. In 2013 a German physicist showed that a version of this idea can fit the same data as an expanding universe.

And the old objection to a material space, that Earth should feel a "wind" as it moves through it, was answered more than a century ago. A Dutch physicist, Hendrik Lorentz, showed that motion through the medium hides its own wind, giving the same predictions as Einstein's theory. Physics chose Einstein's version largely on taste, not evidence.

If the redshift can be read this way, the expanding universe is an interpretation of the evidence, not the evidence. And the patches built on it, like dark energy, would need a fresh look.

## Explain yourselves

Lay the file on the table. One rule predicts how 153 galaxies spin from visible matter alone, and it was predicted decades before anyone checked. Its threshold matches the expansion of the whole universe. A material universe explains why the two kinds of mass are one, why light slows and bends near heavy objects, why a smash-up of galaxies looks the way it does, and how distant light can arrive reddened and stretched without the universe flying apart. Against that, the establishment offers four unseen suspects, none of them ever caught. The pieces were found by others over a century: a Swiss astronomer here, a Dutch physicist there, an Israeli, a German. What nobody had done was lay them side by side as one case. That's what we've done here, by asking civilian questions.

This isn't a finished theory. Nobody has worked the medium out in full, and the galaxy clusters still hold rooms nobody has searched. But a detective doesn't need a confession to know which suspect fits the evidence and which one needs an alibi for every scene.

The establishment has known about the galaxy rule since 1983 and seen the data since 2016. It has had the material-space idea since Newton's day. It owes the public an explanation of why it keeps paying to hunt ghosts while a better suspect sits in the interview room.

We can all see the baby. It's time to find mom and dad.

title: The Smart Insider's Trap
dek: Why powerful, intelligent people refuse to give up absurd endeavors.
excerpt: Why powerful, intelligent people refuse to give up absurd endeavors.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

Around the year 150, in Alexandria, an astronomer named Ptolemy wrote down how the heavens work. The Earth sat still at the center. The Sun, the Moon and the planets circled it. There was just one problem: the planets didn't behave. Mars would stop, back up for a few weeks, then carry on forward, as if it had forgotten something.

So Ptolemy gave each planet a second, smaller circle to ride on, a circle on a circle. He called it an epicycle. When that didn't quite fit, he moved the centers off to one side and added other devices. It worked. It predicted where the planets would be well enough to run calendars and cast horoscopes for the next fourteen hundred years.

Fourteen hundred years. Generation after generation of brilliant men, the finest minds of Greece, Persia, the Arab world and medieval Europe, kept tuning that machine. Whenever the sky disagreed, they adjusted the circles. Very few asked the obvious question: what if the Earth isn't in the middle at all?

Those men weren't fools. That's the point of this chapter. The most dangerous trap in science isn't stupidity. It's intelligence, organized.

## Monetized and weaponized

So here's the question this whole book keeps circling: why do powerful, intelligent people refuse to give up patently absurd endeavors?

Modern physics has its own epicycles. When galaxies spin too fast, add invisible matter. When the expansion speeds up, add invisible energy. When the early universe looks too smooth, add a burst of inflation nobody has seen. Each new wobble gets a new circle.

To understand why, you have to go back to 1942. Before the Second World War, physics was a small craft: a few thousand people in university labs, arguing over what reality is made of. Then came the Manhattan Project. Around 130,000 people, roughly $2 billion in 1940s money, and a weapon that ended a war. Physics was monetized and weaponized in the same stroke. It has never separated from either.

The money never left. The government built national laboratories, military research offices and federal science agencies, and physics became a permanent, fortune-making industry. The public pays. The players collect: contractors building the magnets and detectors, universities taking a cut of every grant, and careers that depend on the next big machine. It's profit to the players, not the funders.

The weapon never left either. The labs at Los Alamos and Livermore still design and maintain nuclear bombs. Under American law, nuclear weapons knowledge is "born secret," classified the moment it exists, even if a private citizen works it out alone. No other science lives under a rule like that. And when Robert Oppenheimer, the man who led the bomb project, opposed building the hydrogen bomb, he was stripped of his security clearance in 1954. Every physicist learned the lesson: questioning the establishment could cost you your career, not just your argument.

In his farewell address in 1961, President Eisenhower, a general who knew the machine from the inside, warned the country about the military-industrial complex. In the same speech he warned that a government contract could become a substitute for intellectual curiosity. He was describing physics.

## The seven springs of the trap

But money and bombs don't fully explain it. Plenty of the theories being protected, dark matter and inflation among them, live in cosmology, which is open, unclassified and has nothing to do with weapons. Something else is holding the circles in place. Call it the smart insider's trap: every individual acts rationally, and the system ends up absurd. It has seven springs.

**One: sunk cost.** After fifty years and billions of dollars, quitting means admitting the waste. Psychologists call it escalation of commitment. The more you've invested in a failing course, the harder you push it. Gamblers know it as chasing losses.

**Two: identity.** For a physicist, a theory isn't a job. It's a life's work. Giving it up means saying your life was spent on the wrong thing. That's why Max Planck, the father of quantum theory, said new ideas don't win by converting their opponents. They win because the opponents eventually die.

**Three: safety in numbers.** The economist John Maynard Keynes put it best: it's better for your reputation to fail conventionally than to succeed unconventionally. Wrong with the crowd is survivable. Right alone is career suicide.

**Four: no exit.** A theory is only abandoned when a better one is ready to replace it. But nobody funds the rival, so it's never ready. The trap closes itself.

**Five: the institution takes over.** Organizations outlive their purpose and end up run by people devoted to the organization itself. The machine needs the next machine. CERN is now pushing for a new collider about three times the size of its current one, at a first-stage price of around 15 billion Swiss francs, with no guaranteed discovery to justify it.

**Six: salaries.** The American writer Upton Sinclair said it's difficult to get a man to understand something when his salary depends on his not understanding it.

**Seven: intelligence makes it worse.** Smart people aren't better at changing their minds. They're better at defending what they already believe. Give a brilliant mind a bad idea and it will build the finest fortifications you've ever seen around it. Fourteen hundred years of epicycles prove it.

## Insiders in something

Watch these chaps long enough and you get the feeling they're all insiders in something. They are. It just isn't a secret society. It's a guild.

In 1935, a Polish doctor named Ludwik Fleck gave it a name: a thought collective. It's a group that shares a way of thinking so deeply that certain questions never occur to its members. Nobody has to suppress those questions. The members simply can't see them, the way you can't see your own glasses while you're wearing them.

The guild reproduces itself. In the 1970s, the sociologist Harriet Zuckerman studied America's Nobel Prize winners and found that more than half had trained under earlier Nobel winners. The same handful of universities train the top physicists. Those same insiders then review each other's papers, decide each other's grants and vote on each other's promotions. Same schools, same mentors, same reviewers, same way of seeing.

That's more damning than a conspiracy, because a conspiracy can be exposed and broken up. A guild can't. Nobody in it is doing anything wrong. They're just doing what everyone around them does, and the circles keep turning.

## Questions they should answer

Still, there are too many unexplained, nonsensical situations not to wonder about connections. I don't object to confidential arrangements. Governments have them. But the public that pays the bills is entitled to ask a few questions.

In 1993, the United States Congress killed its own giant particle collider in Texas. The Super Collider's cost estimate had roughly doubled, about fourteen miles of tunnel had already been dug, and the Soviet Union had collapsed two years earlier. Physics' blank check, it seems, had been tied to the Cold War. Four years later, the same country agreed to pay about $531 million toward Europe's collider at CERN, and American physicists became one of the largest national groups working there.

So why does a country that killed its own collider keep paying for Europe's? Why does the weapons wing of physics stay secret while its spokesmen sell the public cosmic ghosts? Why does every failed prediction lead to a bigger machine instead of a new idea?

There may be perfectly good answers. If so, let's hear them. The public has paid for every circle, every machine and every secret for eighty years. It's owed an explanation.

title: Secrecy Isn't the Problem
dek: Two farewell warnings, the race to get there first, and the trouble with pretending.
excerpt: Two farewell warnings, the race to get there first, and the trouble with pretending.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

In 1796, George Washington left office with a warning. Beware of faction, he told the young country, and beware of permanent entanglements abroad. Americans have been arguing about that speech for two centuries, mostly because he turned out to be right.

In January 1961, another general left the same office with another warning. Dwight Eisenhower, the man who had commanded the Allied armies in Europe, told the nation to guard against a permanent arms industry and its unwarranted influence. In the same speech he warned of something less famous: that public policy could become the captive of a scientific and technological elite.

Eisenhower's farewell may prove as prophetic as Washington's. The military-industrial complex wasn't a passing problem. It's still with us. And new generations of the Second World War and Cold War establishment are still highly influential in physics, the science that built the bomb. We do not know what their real goals are.

That isn't an accusation. It's the problem.

## The other guys first

To understand the secrecy, start with the fear. Policy makers deeply fear that somewhere along the research spectrum, at the most fundamental end or the most outlandish, lies something of decisive military advantage. And they don't want the other guys having it first.

That fear built the atomic bomb. In 1939, Albert Einstein signed a letter to President Roosevelt warning that Nazi Germany might build a uranium bomb. America raced to get there first. When Allied investigators reached Germany in 1945, they found the German program was far behind, nowhere near a bomb. The race had been run against a shadow.

The same fear ran the Cold War. When the Soviets launched Sputnik in 1957, Washington panicked. Within a year it had created NASA and a Pentagon research agency, and poured money into science education. In the 1960 election, John F. Kennedy campaigned on a "missile gap" with the Soviet Union. There was a gap, as it turned out, but it ran the other way. America was well ahead.

The fear reached the fringe, too. For more than twenty years, from the 1970s until 1995, the US government funded psychic spies, people trained to "remote view" distant targets with their minds. The program, eventually called Stargate, ran partly because officials believed the Soviets were doing it. When it was declassified, it had produced nothing of use.

And the fear is alive today. The United States and China are racing in quantum technology: computers that could break codes, and communication that can't be tapped. In 2016 China launched the first satellite built to test quantum communication from orbit. The physics of the very small has become a frontier of national security again.

Stanley Kubrick saw the absurdity in 1964. In Dr. Strangelove, as the world ends, American generals in the war room fret that the Soviets will get ahead in underground mineshafts for the survivors, and solemnly resolve that America must not allow a "mineshaft gap." Audiences laughed. Policy makers took notes.

## Cover stories

Where there's secret work, there are cover stories. Some of the clumsiest are now public record.

In 1947, something crashed on a ranch near Roswell, New Mexico. The Army Air Forces first announced it had recovered a "flying disc," then quickly said it was a weather balloon. It wasn't. It was Project Mogul, a top-secret program to fly microphones high in the atmosphere to listen for Soviet nuclear tests. The Air Force admitted it in 1994, nearly fifty years later. By then, the weather-balloon story had launched an entire UFO industry.

In the 1950s and '60s, the sky was full of UFO sightings. In 1997 the CIA published a history admitting that more than half of those reports were actually its secret U-2 and A-12 spy planes, flying higher than anyone believed aircraft could fly. Officials knew, and let the public go on wondering.

In 1974, the world was told that a huge new ship, the Glomar Explorer, was built by the billionaire Howard Hughes to mine the deep ocean floor. It was a CIA operation to raise a sunken Soviet submarine from three miles down.

None of those secrets were wrong to keep. The work was legitimate defense. What did lasting damage was the pretending. Seventy years after Roswell, millions of people still don't believe a word the government says about anything in the sky. Clumsy deception doesn't protect a secret. It poisons the well.

## Another Skunk Works

There's an honest way to do secret work, and America already knows how. In 1943, Lockheed set up a small, secretive engineering shop in California that came to be called the Skunk Works. It built the U-2 spy plane, the SR-71 Blackbird, and the first stealth fighter. Everyone knew the Skunk Works existed. Everyone knew its work was secret. Nobody pretended it was making crop dusters, and nobody felt lied to.

That's the whole difference. It's not what they're doing that's the problem. It's the clumsy deception.

If the secret work in physics, whatever it is, were openly placed under a Ministry of Defence, it would just be another Skunk Works. People would accept that some research is classified, as they always have. What they can't accept is being sold one story while something else is going on, and finding out fifty years later.

Kubrick saw that too. In Dr. Strangelove, the Soviets build a Doomsday Machine to deter any attack, then keep it secret, so nobody knows to be deterred. As Strangelove points out, the whole point of the machine is lost if nobody knows about it. Secrecy that defeats its own purpose: that's the absurdity at the heart of it all.

## What are the real goals?

Which brings us back to physics, and to the uneasy feeling so many of us have about it. The ghosts nobody can find. The bigger machines that never seem to need a reason. The two great theories that contradict each other, defended for a century by people too intelligent not to notice. The country that killed its own collider and then paid for Europe's.

Maybe there's nothing behind any of it but habit, money and a guild that can't see its own walls. Maybe some of it touches work that is legitimately secret. I don't know. Neither do you. That's exactly the point.

The public has paid for all of it, for eighty years, since the day physics was drafted into the war. It's entitled to know which parts are science and which parts are something else. Keep the secrets that need keeping. Just stop pretending.

Secrecy isn't the problem. Pretending is.

title: The Elephant and the Cat
dek: The Big Bang, black holes, and what the math is telling us when it gives up.
excerpt: The Big Bang, black holes, and what the math is telling us when it gives up.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

Forget the budgets and the guilds for a moment. This is about two things that were here long before anyone existed to fund them, hide them or argue about them. It's totally pre-human.

The first is the Big Bang, the beginning of everything we can see. The second is a black hole, a place where matter has been crushed so hard that nothing, not even light, comes back out. They're the two most extreme things in the universe, and they have something in common. In both, we understand up to a point. Then the math breaks and defaults to infinity.

That infinity has been treated as a mystery for a century. Maybe it's telling us something simpler.

## Where the math gives up

Every schoolchild learns one rule that never bends: you can't divide by zero. Try it on a calculator and you get an error. Push the math anyway and the answer runs off to infinity.

That's what happens at the Big Bang. Density is the amount of stuff divided by the amount of space it's in. Run Einstein's equations backward and the space shrinks, smaller and smaller, toward zero. Divide by zero, and the density comes out infinite.

So the infinity isn't measuring something unimaginably huge. It's the math reaching a place with no room left. There's nothing to measure, so there's nothing to detect. The great physicists Stephen Hawking and Roger Penrose described the singularity in almost those terms: not a very dense spot, but the place where space and time themselves come to an end.

It shouldn't surprise us. You can't describe nothing. Give something a description and it has properties, and things with properties aren't nothing. Ask the math to describe nothing and it divides by zero.

Physics has met these infinities before. Around 1900, the best theory of the day predicted that a hot oven should give off an infinite amount of energy. Ovens don't. Max Planck fixed the problem by proposing that energy comes in tiny packets, and quantum theory was born. Every time the math has gone to infinity, it has turned out to be the sign of an edge, the place where the map runs out. Whether there's simply nothing past this particular edge, or something no theory can yet see, is still the open question.

## Same wall, different animals

In the equations, the Big Bang and a black hole look like twins. Both are points where everything gets crushed and the numbers go to infinity. Same wall.

But look at the animals behind the wall. The Big Bang broke at a moment: the very beginning, everywhere at once. A black hole breaks at a spot: its very center, one place among billions, hidden behind a horizon nothing can see past. One wall is in time, the other in space.

And they behave like opposites. The Big Bang was astonishingly orderly. Its afterglow, which still fills the sky, is smooth to about one part in 100,000. Black holes are the most disordered objects known, the universe's great scrap heaps. In 1979 Roger Penrose pointed out how enormous that difference is, and argued that any theory treating the two as the same thing must be missing something.

They have a family resemblance, the way an elephant and a cat both have four legs and a tail. But one is an elephant and the other is a cat. The equations call them both "infinity." Nature says they're animals of very different size.

## The spacetime paradox

Here it gets stranger. In Einstein's picture, space and time are welded together into a single fabric called spacetime. Inside a black hole, his equations do something remarkable: they swap the two. Once you cross the horizon, the center stops being a place in front of you and becomes a moment in your future. You can't avoid it any more than you can avoid next Tuesday.

So in Einstein's universe, a place can turn into a time. That's not a discovery about nature. It's what you'd expect when you weld two different things together and call them one. Space is a place. Time is our name for motion and change. Spacetime, frankly, is an oxymoron, and the paradox is the welding showing through.

Picture space instead as a real material, the most common stuff there is. Then the paradox disappears. A place stays a place, and time is just things moving. The center of a black hole is simply where the material is compressed most. Nothing swaps.

## Everything compressed into one

What happens to the ordinary rules at those crush points? Maybe all forces and features compress to that point.

That isn't fringe thinking. It's close to what physicists already believe. The universe today runs on several separate forces: gravity, electromagnetism and two that work inside the atom. But the hotter and more crushed things get, the more those forces merge. Electromagnetism and one of the nuclear forces are known to become a single force at extreme temperatures, conditions that existed about a trillionth of a second after the beginning. Physicists suspect that, earlier still, all of them were one.

If space is a single material, that makes perfect sense. The separate forces would just be different behaviors of the same stuff: a compression here, a twist there. Crush it hard enough and the differences disappear, and it all becomes one thing again.

## Cats with little bangs

If everything gets compressed into one at the center of a black hole, what comes next? Here's a thought: a cat has a cosmologically tiny bang. An elephant has a vastly more resonant one.

That isn't as wild as it sounds. In 1992 the American physicist Lee Smolin proposed that every black hole gives birth to a new universe on the other side, a little bang of its own. And he took it further. Universes that happen to make lots of black holes would have lots of offspring, so over countless generations universes would evolve, the way animals do. He called it cosmological natural selection. Darwin, it turns out, may apply to the cosmos.

In fairness, Smolin's version stuck its neck out, and it got bruised. His idea predicted that neutron stars, the collapsed cores of dead stars, can never weigh more than about one and a half Suns. In 2010 astronomers found one weighing about two. But the broader idea, that a collapse might bounce back out instead of ending in infinity, is still very much alive. Several physicists are working on versions of it today.

If they're right, the night sky is full of cats, each one quietly having its own little bang, while we live inside the elephant's.

## The White Hats

And while the cats wait, they have a day job. Black holes are an environmental service function of the universe. They collect local space debris, compact it and atomize it for return to the space environment. They're not Black Holes. They're the White Hats.

The record backs the job description. Matter that spirals toward a black hole gets compressed and heated until it blazes, turning up to tens of percent of its mass into energy. The Sun's fusion manages less than one percent. Black holes are the most efficient recycling plants in the universe.

They give back, too. The giant black holes at the centers of galaxies blast out jets and winds that heat gas and drive it back into space, controlling how many new stars a galaxy can make. Astronomers have found that a black hole's mass closely tracks the size of its galaxy's central bulge. They grow together, like a forest and its soil.

And in the very long run, they atomize. In 1974 Stephen Hawking showed that black holes should slowly evaporate, returning everything they ever took as radiation, broken down finer than atoms. It takes unimaginably long, and nobody has seen it happen yet, but the theory says the White Hats eventually return the lot. Either way, a little bang on the other side or a slow return on this one, nothing is lost.

One correction to the popular picture: they aren't cosmic vacuum cleaners. A black hole pulls no harder than a star of the same weight. Debris falls in only when it loses its orbit, and most of the recycling happens just outside the edge. They're less like vacuum cleaners and more like the decomposers in a forest, the earthworms and fungi of the cosmos, quietly turning wreckage back into raw material.

## Up to a point

So here's where we stand. In both the elephant and the cat, we understand up to a point. Then the math divides by zero, defaults to infinity and goes quiet. Physics has spent a century treating that silence as a puzzle to be solved with ever more elaborate machinery.

Maybe it's simpler than that. Maybe the infinity is the math telling us honestly that it has reached the end of what can be described, a place compressed past anything our equations can describe. And maybe the elephant and the cat look alike only because the same tired equations are trying to describe two animals of very different size.

None of this needed us. It was all here long before anyone looked up. The least we can do is look carefully.

title: An Idea, Not a Discovery
dek: The collider, the brain scanner, the sequencer: three fields, one wall, and why no grant committee can buy the next Copernicus.
excerpt: The collider, the brain scanner, the sequencer: three fields, one wall, and why no grant committee can buy the next Copernicus.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

Here's a pattern I keep tripping over. Pick any of the big unsolved questions: what the universe is made of, how a lump of brain becomes a mind, how life comes up with new forms. In every one you find the same wall, and in front of it the same crowd, ordering a bigger hammer.

## Smash it smaller

For four hundred years science has trusted one method above all others. If you want to understand something, take it apart. The clock into gears, the body into cells, the cells into chemistry, the chemistry into particles. For the clock, it worked brilliantly.

The trouble starts when you use the smallest frame to answer the largest questions. Put a single pixel of your television under a microscope and you can learn everything about it: its chemistry, its exact shade of red. Stare at it for a lifetime and you will never see the movie. The movie lives in how the pixels relate, across time, from a distance.

This isn't only my complaint. In 1972 Philip Anderson, who went on to win the Nobel Prize in physics, wrote a short paper called “More Is Different.” His point: every level of nature has rules of its own, and you can't read them off the level below. Physicists still quote it with great respect. Then they go back to building smaller frames.

## Leg one: the collider

Physics' answer to every deep question is a bigger machine to smash things smaller. The Large Hadron Collider found the Higgs particle in 2012 and has found nothing new since. The proposed answer is a machine three times bigger.

Meanwhile, we're told most of the universe is made of dark matter and dark energy, two ingredients nobody has ever caught, despite about fifty years of looking. A placeholder is honest. A permanent placeholder is a fudge.

## Leg two: the brain scanner

Neuroscience has the same problem, wearing a lab coat instead of a hard hat. It can explain the logistics of a feeling, but not the content. Put a mathematician in a scanner while she works through a problem and you can watch exactly which parts of her brain light up. What you can't see is the “aha,” the moment she understands. You can't see the experience at all.
