And the deeper question isn't how a brain runs calculus. It's how a brain built for finding food and dodging lions invented calculus out of nothing in the first place. Nobody has an answer.

The insiders admit it. The philosopher David Chalmers named it the “hard problem” of consciousness in 1995: map every neuron in the brain and you still haven't explained why any of it feels like something from the inside. Thirty years on, there is still no workable description of consciousness, only maps of activity.

So neuroscience has its own placeholder. It's called “emergence”: put enough neurons together and a mind somehow appears. That's not an explanation. It's a label stuck on the gap, the brain's dark matter. And there's one question the scanners can't even approach: who is using it? Look for a pilot and you find wiring.

The instruments measure what happens. They never measure what it's like. Scanners show the tracks, not the traveller.

## Leg three: the sequencer

Biology made the same bet. Read the whole genetic code, the thinking went, and you'll understand the organism. The Human Genome Project finished in 2003 at a cost of around three billion dollars. Scientists had expected to find about 100,000 human genes. They found roughly 20,000, fewer than a grain of rice has.

Then came the placeholder. Height is about 80 percent inherited, yet the early gene studies could find only a small slice of the genes responsible. Bigger studies have since found much more for height, but for many other traits a good part is still missing. They call it “missing heritability,” and the answer, naturally, is to sequence more people.

Evolution has the same smallest-frame habit. The textbook engine is random copying mistakes plus survival of the fittest, one tiny typo at a time. But genes resist change. Most mutations are harmless or harmful, and the few beneficial ones mostly involve minor changes to existing forms.

Here's the twist: that's exactly where the big changes come from, just not the way the textbook tells it. Small changes to genetic switches can reshape a whole body. Stickleback fish in freshwater lakes lost the spines on their bellies when one switch turned off. Genes get copied by accident, and the spare copy drifts into a new job. Whole organisms merge: the power plants in every one of your cells were once free-living bacteria, swallowed and kept. Lynn Margulis, who argued that, was turned down by about fifteen journals before she was published in 1967. It's textbook fact now.

Switches, copies and mergers. That's the real story of how life changes, and the public has never heard it.

## Three fields, one wall

Line them up and they're the same story told three times. Each field bet the answer was in the smallest parts. Each found the parts don't add up. Each stuck a label on the gap: dark matter, emergence, missing heritability. And each one's answer is to buy a bigger instrument and stare harder.

But the instruments only ever see the after. If you are seeking before, don't waste your time on after.

## An idea, not a discovery

Copernicus didn't need a telescope. They hadn't been invented yet. He looked at the same sky everyone had stared at for thousands of years and had an idea: what if the Earth is the one that's moving? Einstein didn't need a laboratory. He was a patent clerk with a new way of looking at old facts.

To be fair, new ideas usually arrive when the old picture stops fitting the evidence. In all three of these fields, it stopped fitting years ago. The facts are already on the table. What's missing isn't a particle, a neuron or a gene. It's a new window.

The answer will be an Idea, not a Discovery.

And that is the institutional problem in one sentence. You can fund a discovery. A machine has contractors, a grant has a committee, a detector has a congressional district. You can't fund an idea. Breakthroughs are random, not bureaucratic. So the system keeps buying hammers, and the thinking starves.

No grant committee will ever buy the next Copernicus. The best we can do is stop crowding out the room he'd need to think in.

title: The Paradox of Science
dek: Something before the Bang, the safest grant in science, and the two sciences at war.
excerpt: Something before the Bang, the safest grant in science, and the two sciences at war.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

Start with something simple: nothing cannot exist. The moment you describe nothing, even as dark or empty or silent, you've given it properties, and things with properties aren't nothing. Philosophers have known this for 2,500 years. The Greek thinker Parmenides put it plainly: what is, is, and what is not, cannot be.

Now add a second idea. The universe is material, and it's a closed system. Nothing gets in and nothing gets out. Every bit of matter and energy it has, it keeps, changing form but never leaving the room.

But a closed system isn't the same as everything. A sealed jar is closed, and it still sits on a shelf in a room. So something could exist beyond the universe's boundaries. And since nothing cannot exist, whatever lies beyond, if anything does, can't be nothing.

Something, it turns out, has no opposite. That changes the oldest question in philosophy.

## Something before the bang

For centuries people have asked: why is there something rather than nothing? If nothing can't exist, the question falls apart. There was never an alternative. Nobody has to explain how something came from nothing, because it never did.

That leads somewhere the official story won't go. Something existed before the Big Bang. It had to. For there to be a bang, something had to exist. A bang is a happening, and a happening needs something to happen to. You can't have a bang without something to bang.

The official story actually concedes the point, quietly. Its leading account of the first instant needs an energy field and a vacuum already in place before anything can happen. It just doesn't call them "something before the Big Bang." It calls them the laws of physics, and asks no further questions.

What was that something? We can never know. If the universe is truly closed, no signal from beyond its edge, or from before its bang, can ever reach us. The honest answer is that we will never see it. In 1862 Herbert Spencer, the man who coined "survival of the fittest," called it the Unknowable: a reality we can be sure exists and can never grasp.

Something came before. We just can't see over the wall.

## Looking for what can't be found

Which raises an awkward question. Why are we looking for things we know we can't find?

In fairness, declaring something unknowable has a poor track record. In 1835 the French philosopher Auguste Comte announced that we could never know what the stars are made of. They were simply too far away. Within 25 years, two German scientists worked it out from starlight passed through a prism. Things that are merely hard to find are worth chasing.

But hard to find is not the same as impossible by definition. What lies beyond a closed system can't send us a signal, ever. That isn't a matter of better telescopes. It's built into what "closed" means. Yet physics keeps funding the search for what came before the Bang, and for other universes beyond ours, as if the answer were just around the corner.

There may be a reason those questions are so popular. A question that can never be answered can never be closed. It never fails and it never succeeds. It's the perfect permanent placeholder, and the funding never has to stop. The unknowable is the safest grant in science.

If the stated aim is answers and the real attraction is a question that never ends, then what's said isn't all that's being done. By the plain meaning of the word, that's perhaps a conspiracy. No plot required.

## Two sciences

To make sense of it, you have to see that the word "science" covers two very different things.

The first is a method. It's built to overturn its own ideas. The philosopher Karl Popper said a theory only counts as scientific if it could, in principle, be proven wrong. The method runs on curiosity and genius. It welcomes the oddball with a better idea, because the better idea is the whole point.

The second is an institution: the universities, agencies, laboratories and journals. Science as an entity is focused on survival. It's a human construct, like any other, and like any other, its first priority quietly becomes keeping itself going. For that mission, curiosity and genius are not essential. They're more likely threatening, because genius brings change, and change costs careers, budgets and reputations.

The record shows it. Grant reviewers, studied closely, give lower marks to the most original proposals. A biologist named Lynn Margulis had her paper on the origin of our cells rejected by about fifteen journals before it was published. It's now in every textbook. A weather scientist named Alfred Wegener was laughed at for fifty years for saying the continents move. They do.

The institution does make use of genius, eventually. It just prefers it safely famous. Living genius is a threat. Dead genius is a mascot.

The method is built to destroy ideas. The institution is built to survive them.

## The paradox

So here's the paradox of science. The institution that carries the name of curiosity is quietly afraid of it. It needs the method to justify its existence, and it needs to tame the method in order to survive. It funds the questions that can never close and starves the ideas that might actually change something. It honors the genius it once scorned, once the genius is safely gone.

None of that touches the method itself. The method is still the best tool humans ever invented for finding out what's true. It works in a garage, a patent office, a horse barn or a pub. It never needed the institution's permission, and it doesn't need it now.

If something existed before the Bang, we'll never see it. That's a limit of nature, and there's no shame in it. The shame is in pretending otherwise to keep the lights on.

The universe is a closed system. Science shouldn't be.

title: Two Sets of Books
dek: Secret science, CERN's industrial subsidy, and why the bookkeeping should match the rule.
excerpt: Secret science, CERN's industrial subsidy, and why the bookkeeping should match the rule.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

Everybody is in favor of cost-effective research. The trouble starts when you try to measure it. You can't judge whether something is good value until you know what it's for.

A giant machine that looks like a waste as physics might be excellent value as something else. Or it might just be a waste. From the outside, nobody can tell, and that's the problem. Government-funded stupid science may be obscuring that some of these projects contain elements of secret science.

Let me be clear about where I stand. I don't oppose secret science. Nations have secrets, and some of them are worth keeping. What I oppose is clumsy lies and wasted citizen dollars. And as long as the books are mixed, there's no way to tell the two apart.

## The rule on paper

Here's something most people don't know. America already has a sensible rule about this, and it's been on the books for forty years.

In 1985, President Reagan signed National Security Decision Directive 189. It says that federally funded basic research should stay open "to the maximum extent possible," and that where national security really requires control, the way to control it is classification, decided at the start. No half-measures, no quiet restrictions. Either it's secret, officially, or it's open.

The rule has been reaffirmed again and again: by Condoleezza Rice as National Security Advisor in 2001 and by the Pentagon in 2010, and the White House cited it again in 2021. On paper, it's exactly what we want: classify it or publish it.

The question isn't whether the rule is good. It's whether anyone outside the system can see that it's followed.

## Where the books blur

The line is clean on paper and smudged in practice. The great national laboratories, Los Alamos, Livermore and their sisters, do both kinds of work under the same roofs, with the same people, the same buildings and often the same machines.

Take the biggest laser in the world, at Livermore. It's presented to the public as fusion-energy research, and it does that. But its main mission is helping maintain the nation's nuclear weapons. That's not hidden; the government says so if you read far enough. But how the bill is split between the two missions is anything but clear to the taxpayer who funds both.

The same goes for the labs' giant supercomputers, built to simulate bomb tests after America stopped testing in 1992, and lent out between jobs to model climate and galaxies. When one building, one staff and one machine serve two masters, which master pays for what?

The country does know how to be honest about secret spending. Since 2007, it has published the total intelligence budget every year. It doesn't say what the money buys, only how much of it is secret. The sky hasn't fallen. The same plain honesty could be applied to science, lab by lab and machine by machine.

## The CERN puzzle

Which brings us to CERN, the great collider laboratory outside Geneva. Judged as physics, it looks like a monument to dogged stupidity. It found the Higgs particle in 2012, found nothing new since, and now wants a machine three times bigger. It's hard to believe that a couple of dozen governments keep paying for that unless there's an undisclosed purpose.

There is one. It just isn't secret. It's buried in the procurement rules.

CERN runs what it calls an industrial return policy. For every member country, it tracks the value of contracts that country's companies win, compared with the share of the budget that country pays. Countries whose companies get back less than they put in are classed as "poorly balanced," and their firms get preferential access to future contracts. Put plainly, the money a country sends to Geneva is designed to come home as orders for its own industry: magnets, cables, steel, electronics and engineering.

Add the diplomacy, since CERN was founded after the war partly to rebuild European science and keep its physicists from leaving for America, and the puzzle starts to make sense. CERN is an industrial and diplomatic program wearing a physics hat. America's share makes sense on the same terms: after killing its own collider in 1993, it bought a seat at Europe's for a fraction of the price.

None of this is hidden. You can read it on CERN's own procurement pages. But it isn't what the public is sold. The public is sold the secrets of the universe. What you say you're doing isn't all you're really doing.

## To what purpose?

So CERN works much like a big, semi-disclosed subsidy: public taxpayer money flowing to private businesses, by way of Geneva. To what purpose, might we ask? Here are three answers, from best documented to most speculative.

**Jobs and votes.** This one is stated openly. The return policy is meant to spread contracts and technology fairly among member countries, and it keeps the money coming. Every government that pays in gets orders for its own factories, so every parliament has local jobs riding on the budget. Small groups with a lot at stake always beat large groups with a little at stake. CERN isn't alone, either: the European Space Agency's founding rules contain the same "geographical return" principle.

**Keeping strategic industries warm.** CERN buys superconducting magnets, ultra-cold refrigeration, vacuum systems, precision engineering, radiation-proof electronics and massive computing. Every one of those is dual-use. They serve hospital scanners and fusion research, and they could just as easily serve defense and space. A steady stream of collider contracts keeps that know-how and those factories alive in peacetime, ready to be called on. Defense planners have a name for that: the industrial base. Whether anyone in Geneva thinks of it that way, I can't say. It's a question, not a finding.

**A quiet way around the subsidy rules.** European law tightly limits governments subsidizing their own companies. Money sent to an international laboratory, which then flows home as contracts to national firms, is a perfectly legal path for something that looks a great deal like a subsidy. Nobody I can find has documented that as the intent. Perhaps.

Any of those purposes could be perfectly legitimate, if it were declared. None of them is the secrets of the universe.

## Honest books

So here's the proposal. It doesn't ask anyone to give up a single secret. It asks for honest books.

**One: declare the secret share.** Any publicly funded science project with a classified side says so, and says roughly how much of the money goes to it. Not what the secret is. Just that it exists, and its size. That's exactly what the country already does for intelligence.

**Two: split the bill at shared labs.** Where one lab, one staff or one machine serves both open science and weapons work, publish how the costs are divided. If a laser is mostly a weapons tool, let the weapons budget carry it, and let the science budget answer only for the science.

**Three: judge the open part on its own merits.** Once the books are split, the public science has to justify itself as science. No more hiding behind a shadow mission, and no more blaming real science for costs it didn't run up.

**Four: name the other purposes.** Where a project also serves industry or diplomacy, as CERN does, say so up front. Industrial policy and diplomacy are legitimate. Selling them as the secrets of the universe isn't.

**Five: give the referee a clearance.** The independent auditor, call it a DOGE for science, includes people cleared to look at the secret side too. Then someone outside the guild can confirm the books are honest without telling the rest of us what's in them.

We had a referee once. In 1972 Congress created the Office of Technology Assessment, its own independent team of analysts, to advise it on science and technology without relying on the people asking for the money. In 1984 the office published a study, written by a young physicist named Ashton Carter, concluding that President Reagan's "Star Wars" missile shield was very unlikely ever to work as promised. Its supporters were furious. In 1995 Congress abolished the office to save about $20 million a year, a rounding error next to a single collider. The official reason was budget cuts. Nobody has proven the Star Wars report had anything to do with it.

But the pattern is hard to miss. The one independent referee that told Congress a weapons-physics program wouldn't work was eliminated, and never replaced. And here's the twist: that same Ashton Carter went on to become a senior Pentagon official, and eventually Secretary of Defense. In 2010 it was a memo from him that reaffirmed the rule from 1985: classify it or publish it. The referee was fired. The rule survived. No independent referee has been checking it since.

## The trap

The beauty of honest books is that there's no good reason to refuse them.

If nothing is hidden, honest books cost nothing. The science stands on its own, the labs publish a few extra numbers, and the suspicion goes away. If something is hidden, honest books are the only way the public can know what it's paying for, and the secret itself stays safe.

Either way, everyone wins except the people who've been hiding waste behind someone else's secret.

The rule has been on the books since 1985: classify it or publish it. All we're asking for is the bookkeeping to match. Secret science, fine. Secret bookkeeping, no.

title: Fewer Hammers, More Thinkers
dek: Five tried-and-tested ways to buy more discovery for less money.
excerpt: Five tried-and-tested ways to buy more discovery for less money.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

The last essay asked for honest books: say how much is secret, split the bill where labs serve two masters, and let open science stand on its own merits. Suppose we get them. Then comes the harder question. How do you spend the open money well?

The trouble is that nobody can pick a winner in advance. Nobody could have picked the patent clerk, the bookbinder's apprentice or the biologist rejected by fifteen journals. Breakthroughs are random, not bureaucratic. They turn up in unexpected places, with unexpected people.

So cost-effective research can't mean backing the right idea. Nobody knows which idea is right. It has to mean building a system that gives the right idea the best chance of turning up, at the lowest price. There are five ways to do that, and every one of them has been tried.

## Don't bet the farm on one horse

Anyone who deals horses knows the first rule. You don't put everything you own on one animal, however good it looks in the paddock. Horses go lame. Favorites lose. The trick is to spread your money so that when the long shot comes in, you're holding a ticket.

Big science does the opposite. It puts billions on a single horse, a collider, a telescope, a dark-matter detector, and when the horse loses, it doubles the bet on a bigger one. CERN's proposed next machine would cost around 15 billion Swiss francs for its first stage alone. For the same money, you could fund thousands of small research groups for a decade, every one of them a long shot, any one of which might change everything.

That isn't an argument against ever building big machines. Some questions really do need them. It's an argument against building nothing else. A sensible portfolio holds a few favorites and a lot of long shots. Physics today holds almost nothing but favorites.

## Pay for results, not promises

A grant pays for a promise. You describe what you'll discover, a committee likes the description, and the money arrives whether or not anything is discovered. A prize works the other way round. It names a problem, posts a reward, and pays nothing until someone solves it.

The British government tried it in 1714. Ships were being lost because sailors couldn't tell how far east or west they were, so Parliament offered a fortune to anyone who could find longitude at sea. The answer came from an unlikely place: a self-taught, Yorkshire-born carpenter named John Harrison, who built a clock accurate enough to do it. It took decades of argument before he was paid in full, but the method worked. It drew the answer out of nowhere anyone would have looked.

It still works. In 2004 a $10 million prize for the first private craft to reach space twice in two weeks drew about two dozen teams, which together spent around $100 million chasing it. The prize-givers got ten times their money's worth in effort, and private spaceflight was born.

Prizes don't suit every question. Nobody can post a reward for a discovery they can't yet describe. But wherever a problem can be named, a prize buys answers instead of promises, and costs nothing if nobody delivers.

## Fund people, not projects

Most research money is tied to a project: a plan, a timetable and a list of expected results. That rewards people who can predict what they'll find, which is to say people who aren't really looking for anything new.

There's another way, and it's been tested. The Howard Hughes Medical Institute, a private foundation, picks talented scientists and gives them steady money for years at a time, with freedom to change direction and tolerance for failure. In 2011, three economists compared Hughes scientists with similar scientists funded the usual way, project by project, by the government. The Hughes group produced far more breakthrough papers, and also more outright flops, which is exactly what you'd expect from people allowed to take real risks.

It's the oldest recipe there is. Bell Labs gave clever people room and a long leash, and got the transistor. Darwin paid his own way and took twenty years. Back the jockey, not the race card.

## Let chance help

Here's an idea that sounds mad until you think about it: draw lots.

Grant committees are supposed to pick the best proposals. In practice, studies show reviewers tend to mark down the most original ones, because original ideas look risky and unfamiliar. The committee doesn't filter out bad ideas so much as unusual ones.

Since 2013, New Zealand's main health research council has handed out some of its grants by lottery. Experts first weed out the unworkable proposals. Then, among everything that passes, the winners are drawn at random. Switzerland's national science fund now uses a lottery too, to break ties between equally rated applications.

It's cheaper, since less time goes into ranking, and it's fairer to the oddball, whose odd idea gets the same ticket as everyone else's safe one. When nobody can tell the genius from the crank in advance, chance is more honest than pretending you can.

## Put a clock on placeholders

Science is allowed to say "we don't know yet." Sometimes it has to invent a placeholder for something it can't see. In 1930, Wolfgang Pauli proposed an invisible particle, the neutrino, to balance the books on energy. It was found in 1956, twenty-six years later. That's how a placeholder is supposed to work.

Dark matter has had about fifty years. Every time a search comes up empty, the suspect is redefined as something harder to catch, and a bigger search is funded. A placeholder is honest. A permanent placeholder is a fudge.

So give every placeholder a clock. Any program hunting something unseen gets a review date: find it, show real progress, or explain to an independent referee why the hunt should go on. If the answer is good, fine, the clock resets. If it isn't, the money goes back into the pot for the long shots. Label it pending, keep moving, and don't stop the merry-go-round for everyone else.

## Fewer hammers, more thinkers

None of these ideas is radical. Every one has been tried, and every one is cheap next to a single giant machine. Spread the bets. Pay for answers. Back people. Let chance give the oddball a ticket. Put a clock on the ghosts.

What they have in common is that they take power away from the guild. Committees lose the right to decide in advance what's worth discovering. Big machines lose their automatic claim on the money. And the patent clerks, the bookbinders and the carpenters get a fair shot again.

Genius is cheap. It always has been. It's the institutions that are expensive. The cheapest way to buy the next great idea isn't a bigger hammer. It's more thinkers, and room for them to think.

Fewer hammers, more thinkers.

body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

In November 1095, in a field outside the French town of Clermont, Pope Urban II called on the knights of Europe to march east and take Jerusalem. The crowd answered with a roar that became the battle cry of the First Crusade: _Deus vult_. God wills it.

It's the oldest excuse in the world. Everyone wants to say it's God's will. Wars, conquests, missions and massacres have been launched in the name of one god or another for as long as there have been gods to name.

So it's tempting to blame the gods. That would be a mistake. The gods didn't command any of it. Humans did, and then signed the gods' names to the orders.

## The first value systems

Virtually every culture that has ever existed has had gods. That isn't a coincidence. The religions that grew up around them were humanity's first value systems: the rules about what's sacred, what's forbidden, who belongs and who doesn't.

The French sociologist Émile Durkheim argued more than a century ago that religion is really a community's shared values made sacred, a society binding itself together. More recently the psychologist Jonathan Haidt put it in four words: religion binds and blinds. It binds a group together, and it blinds the group to everyone else's point of view.

That binding is powerful. A value system distinguishes a community from its neighbors. It constrains behavior, so people can trust each other. It creates loyalty, and it gives a people coherence, a shared sense of who they are. One anthropologist, Richard Sosis, studied the utopian communes that sprang up across 19th-century America. The religious ones lasted far longer than the secular ones, and the stricter their rules, the longer they survived.

But every strong "we" makes a "they." And that's where the trouble starts.

## Fear first

The trouble starts in us, long before any god is consulted. In a primitive way, difference is seen as an intrinsic threat. The stranger at the edge of the firelight might be a trader, or he might be a raider, and for most of human history guessing wrong could get you killed. So fear is the first response. Aggression is the next. A hundred years ago the physiologist Walter Cannon gave the reflex its name: fight or flight.

The language remembers. "Xenophobia" comes from two Greek words, _xenos_ and _phobos_: fear of the stranger.

It takes almost nothing to switch it on. In the early 1970s the British psychologist Henri Tajfel split schoolboys into two groups on the flimsiest grounds imaginable, such as which of two abstract painters they preferred. Strangers until that moment, they immediately began favoring their own group and shortchanging the other. In a famous, though much debated, summer-camp experiment in Oklahoma in 1954, two groups of ordinary boys turned hostile within days. What calmed them down was being given shared problems that needed both groups to solve.

We still feel the same responses. The brain that flinches at a stranger's accent is the same brain that once flinched at a stranger's spear. The difference is that we should know better now. Religion didn't create the fear. It gave the fear a uniform, a banner and a commandment.

## The buffer instinct

A community that feels its values are threatened does something natural: it tries to make its neighbors more like itself. Convert them, conquer them or rule them, and the border is safer. Projecting your values onto others creates a buffer.

That instinct explains a great deal of history: crusades, missionary campaigns, empires that called their conquests civilization. And it explains the worst of all, the slave trade.

Slavery itself is almost instinctive. For most of history, the choice facing the defeated was blunt: be killed or be put to work. The sociologist Orlando Patterson found slavery in a large share of the world's societies, from ancient Greece and Rome to African and Arab kingdoms. Ireland wasn't spared either. St Patrick first came to Ireland in the 5th century as a slave, and Viking Dublin later ran one of Europe's biggest slave markets.

But slavery was local. The slave trade was global. It took one value system projecting itself across the world, with European ships, European demand and colonial laws that counted people as property, to turn local cruelty into an industry. Roughly 12.5 million Africans were shipped across the Atlantic. That was one local law crossing an ocean and exterminating another people's way of life.

## Same God, both sides

If the gods were the cause, you'd expect them to point one way. They don't.

The same Bible was used to defend the slave trade and to end it. Slave owners quoted scripture to justify what they did. And the movement that finally abolished the British slave trade was led largely by people of faith: Quakers, who refused to own slaves at all, and evangelical Christians like William Wilberforce, who spent twenty years pushing a ban through Parliament.

One god, two opposite commands. The only thing that changed between them was the humans doing the interpreting. Which tells you where the responsibility really lies.

Religion becomes a weapon not because gods demand it but because "God's will" is the most powerful banner a human being can carry. Nobody argues with a commandment. So everyone wants one.

## Evolution, not revolution

Notice how abolition actually happened in Britain. Not overnight, and not by force from outside. It took decades of sermons, pamphlets, boycotts and petitions, changing a culture from within until its own laws caught up. That's evolution. Slow, but sure.

Revolution is the opposite: fast, and temporary. In 1790, an Irishman named Edmund Burke watched the French Revolution and predicted it would end in terror and a dictator. Within a few years it had both, and by 1815 the monarchy was back. Russia's revolution of 1917 promised a new humanity and was gone by 1991. Egypt's revolution of 2011 was reversed by 2013.

The pattern holds because revolutions are utopian fantasies with an army attached. They try to replace a people's evolved values with a blueprint, all at once, and they have to crush everyone who doesn't fit the blueprint. The philosopher Karl Popper saw it plainly in 1945: the bigger the utopian plan, the more people it has to break. The utopian projects of the 20th century killed tens of millions.

And there's a deeper reason utopias always fail: reality is fiercely random. No blueprint can foresee what a whole society will actually do once the plan meets real people. In 1936 the American sociologist Robert Merton gave the problem its name: the unanticipated consequences of purposive action.

History is full of them. In 1958, Mao Zedong ordered the people of China to wipe out sparrows, which ate grain. Hundreds of millions of people banged pots and pans until the exhausted birds dropped from the sky. With the sparrows gone, the insects they used to eat swarmed the crops, and the plagues that followed helped deepen one of the worst famines in history. Half a century earlier, in 1902, the French rulers of Hanoi paid a bounty for every rat tail turned in. Enterprising residents cut off the tails, let the rats go to breed more tails, and some even started rat farms. The program was soon abandoned.

The planner always thinks he's dealing with a machine. He's actually dealing with a storm. Evolution works with the randomness, trying small changes and keeping what survives. Revolution bets everything on one prediction, and reality almost never cooperates.

Intolerance, conformity and utopia are the same disease in different clothes. Each insists that everyone must believe the same thing, and each is prepared to make them.

## Commerce, not crusade

Here's the big takeaway. Merging value systems, whatever the motive and whatever the rationalization, is always dangerous. A crusade merges them by the sword. A revolution merges them by decree. A missionary merges them one soul at a time. The result, too often, is a community that has lost its own coherence and hasn't really gained anyone else's.

But there is one force that mixes peoples without wrecking them: commerce. In 1748 the French philosopher Montesquieu observed that wherever there is trade, manners grow gentler. Traders don't need you to share their god. They need you to pay your bill. Commerce is an equalizer. It lets two peoples deal with each other for centuries while each keeps its own values, and whatever crosses over does so slowly and voluntarily.

That's the difference between evolution and revolution again. Trade lets cultures influence each other at their own pace. Crusades force the pace, and blame God for the wreckage.

## Only local law

All value systems evolved locally. Each grew out of a particular place, a particular history and a particular people's experience of what helps them survive together. That's why there's no universal law for humanity, only local ones.

Europe learned this the hard way. The Thirty Years' War, fought largely over religion, killed millions across central Europe. It ended in 1648 with the Peace of Westphalia, which settled on a simple rule: each ruler decides the religion of his own realm, and the others stay out. It was the birth of the idea that nations shouldn't meddle in each other's beliefs.

Three centuries later, the world tried the opposite. In 1948 the United Nations adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. It sounds grand. But it's a resolution, not a treaty, and nothing in it can be enforced. Even on the day it passed, eight countries abstained, among them the Soviet bloc and Saudi Arabia, which objected in part to its articles on changing one's religion and on marriage. Local value systems were refusing the "universal" one from the very start.

Universal declarations are neither universal nor serious. They're a pious, timid way of saying God wills it, with the God taken out and the will left in. The English philosopher Jeremy Bentham called natural rights "nonsense upon stilts" back in the 1790s. In 1981 the moral philosopher Alasdair MacIntyre went further, comparing belief in universal human rights to belief in witches and unicorns.

That raises the hardest question this essay has to face. What about the horrors? Should cultures be left in place no matter how horrid we find them? In 1994, the world stood by while about 800,000 people were slaughtered in Rwanda, and most people now call that a failure. It's a fair challenge, and it deserves an honest answer.

Here's mine. Universal truths may well exist. Cruelty may be wrong everywhere. But nobody has the right to enforce their version of the truth on everyone else, because every crusader in history believed he had the truth. The record of outside powers remaking other peoples by force is mostly a record of new horrors replacing old ones. The cure that lasts is the one that grows from inside, as abolition did in Britain. It's slower. It's surer.

There's a difference, though, between stopping a massacre and remaking a people. In 2000, British troops went into Sierra Leone, a former colony, helped end a brutal civil war, and then pulled their combat troops out. They didn't stay to rule, convert or rebuild the country in Britain's image. A brief police action that stops the killing and leaves the culture to run itself is a very different thing from a crusade or a colony. The first can be a mercy. The second is the old disease again.

## An equal opportunity employer

So don't blame the gods. They never sent a single ship across the Atlantic, lit a single heretic's fire or drew a single map of a utopia. Humans did all of that, and signed the gods' names at the bottom.

Blame what deserves the blame: the old fear of difference that we all still carry, the urge to make everyone else believe what we believe, and the stupidity of thinking it can be done by force without breaking something precious on both sides.

Every people's values are local, hard-won and imperfect. None was handed down to rule the rest. Reality doesn't play favorites. It treats every culture the same way, rewarding what works and punishing what doesn't, slowly, in its own time.

We still feel the fear. We just should know better now. Reality is an equal opportunity employer. It's not gods' fault we keep trying to fire the other applicants.

title: The Unfortunate Mutation
dek: Hunters and farmers, the farmer's sky, and the hunter we keep trying to bury.
excerpt: Hunters and farmers, the farmer's sky, and the hunter we keep trying to bury.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

There's a story in the Book of Genesis about two brothers and a bowl of stew. Esau, the elder, "was a cunning hunter, a man of the field." Jacob, the younger, "was a plain man, dwelling in tents." One day Esau comes in from the field, starving, and Jacob, who has been cooking, makes him an offer: the stew in exchange for Esau's birthright. Esau takes the deal. The settled brother ends up with everything.

It's one of the oldest stories we have, and it's still being played out inside every one of us. There's a permanent psychological tension between nature's laws and group laws, between instinct and conformity. Between the hunter and the farmer.

## Two laws

For almost all of human history, there was only one law: nature's. You followed the herds, read the weather, trusted your instinct and took your chances. The world was wild, and every day was different.

Then, about 12,000 years ago, in the hills of the Middle East, people began to plant seeds and stay put. Farming needed things hunting never had: fences, calendars, property, storehouses, and neighbors who all did the same thing at the same time. Instinct was traded for conformity. Nature's laws gave way to group laws.

That trade has never settled. Every one of us still carries both men inside: the hunter who wants to roam and the farmer who wants to fence. The farmer keeps trying to bury him. No luck so far.

## The unfortunate mutation

We usually tell the story as progress. The hunter was the primitive, the farmer was the future. But look at it from Reality's side and the picture flips. It's the farmer who, in Reality's eye, is the unfortunate mutation.

Our species has been around for about 300,000 years. We've farmed for about 12,000 of them, roughly 4 percent. For the other 96 percent, the hunter was simply what a human being was. The hunter is who we are: meat-eating hunters, subjugated by mutants.

And the first farmers paid dearly for the change. Their skeletons are shorter than those of the hunters before them, with more tooth decay and more signs of disease and hunger. Living crowded together with their animals brought new plagues; measles, for one, jumped to us from a cattle virus. In southern Mesopotamia, centuries of irrigation slowly salted the soil until the wheat failed and only tougher barley would grow. In 1987 the American scientist Jared Diamond called farming "the worst mistake in the history of the human race."

In Ireland, the takeover is written in the bones. Ancient DNA shows that nearly 6,000 years ago, the island's native hunters were largely replaced by incoming farming people whose ancestors had set out from what is now Turkey. And the mutation is literal. Being able to digest milk as an adult is a genetic mutation that spread across Europe with dairy farming, and Ireland has one of the highest rates of it in the world.

The obvious comeback is that the farmer feeds 8 billion people, where the hunters numbered only a few million. Some mistake! But success isn't permanence. The dinosaurs ruled for well over 100 million years. A mutation can spread like wildfire and still be a dead end. The farmer counts his harvests and thinks he's won. Reality is still keeping score.

## Memorialized in every mythology

It's a foundational conflict, memorialized in every mythology. The farmers won, and then they wrote the stories, and the stories read like a guilty conscience.

In Eden, Adam is thrown out of a garden where food simply grew, and sentenced to farm: "In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread." Farming is the punishment. His son Cain, "a tiller of the ground," murders his brother Abel, "a keeper of sheep," and then goes on to build the first city. In the oldest great story of all, the Epic of Gilgamesh, the wild man Enkidu runs with the gazelles until a temple woman civilizes him. After that the animals flee from him, and on his deathbed he curses her for it, before relenting.

Rome was founded when Romulus ploughed a furrow to mark the city's boundary and killed his brother Remus for leaping over the wall. In Ireland's own myths, after the Second Battle of Mag Tuired, the defeated king Bres buys his life by teaching the victors when to plough, when to sow and when to reap. Farming is the ransom. And the Greek poet Hesiod described a Golden Age, when the earth fed people without anyone working it.

Over and over, the farmer wins, and the hunter is cheated, tamed or killed. Then the farmer builds him a monument and tells the story.

## The wheel

The farmer didn't just want order. He wanted repetition: the same seasons, the same planting, the same harvest, year after year. His time was a wheel. The historian of religion Mircea Eliade called it "the myth of the eternal return." Early farming peoples saw time as a cycle that comes round forever.

The hunter lived in one-offs. Every chase was different. Nothing came round again.

And the wheel needed a sky to turn it. A farmer plants by the seasons, so he needs the heavens to be predictable. That's why Newgrange was built, in Ireland's Boyne Valley more than 5,000 years ago, older than Stonehenge and the Pyramids. Once a year, around the winter solstice, the rising sun shines down its long stone passage and lights the chamber at the end. It's a stone promise that the sun will come back.

## Pretending to be permanent

There's something else about Newgrange. It's a tomb.

We know that we are transitory, but we pretend to be permanent. The ancients watched the dead decompose. The modern hid them in urns and graves.

The great tombs, the mounds and the pyramids came with farming. Egypt, the great grain civilization, spent fortunes keeping its corpses from rotting. Elsewhere people still watch the dead go: Tibetan sky burial leaves the body to the vultures, and Zoroastrians built "towers of silence" for the same purpose. Even in medieval Europe, some wealthy men had their tombs carved showing their own corpses rotting, as a reminder to the living.

In 1973 the American writer Ernest Becker published _The Denial of Death_, which won a Pulitzer Prize the following year. He argued that much of human culture is an elaborate defense against knowing we will die. Psychologists later ran experiments suggesting that reminders of death make people cling harder to their own group's beliefs and turn colder toward outsiders, though some large recent attempts to repeat them have come up short. Perhaps.

## The farmer's sky

So the farmer projected his wishes upward: order, repetition and permanence. The sky became the farmer's field.

Aristotle taught that the heavens were "incorruptible," made of a fifth element that never decays or changes. Almost literally, a sky that doesn't rot, because we do. For 2,000 years the planets had to move in perfect circles, the shape that repeats forever, and when they didn't, astronomers added more circles to the circles.

Then the hunter's sky broke through. In 1572 the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe watched a brand-new star blaze up where none had been, and proved it lay far beyond the Moon, out in the unchanging heavens. In 1609 Johannes Kepler admitted, against his own wishes, that the orbits were ellipses, not circles.

The farmer never gave up. In 1917 Einstein added a fudge factor to his equations to keep the universe from moving. In 1948 Fred Hoyle and two colleagues proposed a "steady state" universe that never changes and goes on forever, the purest wheel of all. The evidence sank it in 1965.

Today's cosmology rests on an assumption called the cosmological principle: on the largest scales, the universe is the same everywhere and in every direction. Nobody measured that first. It's repetition projected across all of space, the farmer's field stretched to the edge of the universe. Astronomers keep finding structures, like the "Giant Arc" spotted in 2021, that some argue are too big for a universe that's the same everywhere. That one is still pending. And every one-off that won't fit gets a fence of its own: dark matter, dark energy, inflation.

## Made for the marketplace

The farmer's main tool for fencing the sky is mathematics. And math was made for the marketplace.

The oldest known writing and numbers, from Sumer about 5,000 years ago, are accounts: clay tablets counting grain, beer and sheep. The word "geometry" means "earth measuring." The Greek historian Herodotus said it began with Egyptian surveyors re-marking field boundaries after the Nile flooded. Math is the farmer's bookkeeping.

Is it even relevant to the heavens? To be fair, it works astonishingly well up there. In 1960 the physicist Eugene Wigner called it "the unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics." But notice where it works and where it doesn't. Math is the language of repetition. It's brilliant at whatever happens again and again: orbits, tides and seasons. And it breaks down at exactly the one-offs, the Big Bang and the heart of a black hole, where it divides by zero and gives up. The farmer's tool works on the farmer's sky. It fails on the hunter's.

## Projection or observation?

Which raises the question underneath all the others. Is our entire framework a projection or an observation? Can we ever know?

The framework is projection. Observation is what it attaches to. We see what is; we project what we wish.

The sunrise at Newgrange is observation. The promise built around it is projection. Tycho's new star was observation. The incorruptible heavens were projection. The farmer never stopped seeing what was there. He just kept hanging his wishes on it.

## The buried hunter

The farmer keeps trying to bury the hunter, but he won't stay buried. He lives in antisocial expression.

By antisocial I don't mean criminal. I mean unconventional in some material respect, someone who won't live entirely by the group's rules. I consider oddballs antisocial, like me.

In 1930 Sigmund Freud argued in _Civilization and Its Discontents_ that civilization runs on bottled-up instinct, and bottled-up instinct always comes back out as discontent. Sometimes it comes out as rebellion, risk and recklessness. Sometimes it comes out on a Saturday afternoon: the zoologist Desmond Morris argued that football is a ritual hunt, a pack chasing a target across open ground.

And sometimes it comes out as genius. Tycho, Kepler, and the weather scientist Alfred Wegener, who was laughed at for saying the continents move, each looked at a sky or a world everyone else had tidied, and saw what was actually there. Every crack in the farmer's sky was made by an oddball. The institution calls him antisocial while he's alive, and a genius once he's safely dead.

## Sadly unsettled

So what's the lingering consequence of this inner turmoil?

Part of it is in the body. Scientists call it mismatch: an animal built for one life, living another. Short sight, for one, has soared as children spend their days indoors; in some East Asian cities most young adults now need glasses. Part of it is in the mind: Freud's discontent, a restlessness that never quite goes away.

And part of it is in the sky. We look up with the farmer's eyes and the hunter's hunger. The hunger sends us out looking; the eyes fence in whatever we find. The turmoil inside us shows up as anomalies up there.

The tension is also the engine. Every breakthrough is the hunter breaking out of the fence. A species that finally settled the fight, whichever side won, would stop moving.

But it comes at a price. It's a dichotomy that keeps the species sadly unsettled by its own creations. The farmer built the fields, the cities, the calendars, the institutions and the tidy sky, and none of them ever quite feels like home. Reality, meanwhile, has never stopped being the hunter's world: wild, random and indifferent. Five times it has wiped out most of the species on Earth, and one day the Sun will make this planet too hot for life as we know it. Is life an accident of Reality awaiting removal? Perhaps. But this accident has hung on for more than three and a half billion years.

The farmer keeps trying to bury the hunter. No luck so far. And no peace either.

title: Two Maybes
dek: Postcards from inside the envelope, the threshold, and the humble understanding.
excerpt: Postcards from inside the envelope, the threshold, and the humble understanding.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

Anyone who has sailed out of a harbour knows the moment. Inside the bay you know everything: every rock, every buoy, every current, which pub on the quay has the best view. Then you pass the headland, and in a single stroke you know nothing. The water changes colour, the swell changes rhythm, and the chart in your lap is suddenly a lot less use. When you sail from the bay to the sea, you go from knowing everything to knowing nothing at the moment of the threshold.

Humanity has spent its whole history in the bay, looking out at the sea of the cosmos. And we keep telling ourselves we know what's out there.

## Postcards

Here's the first problem. Looking out from inside the envelope, we can only experience what we observe in miniature: still images on pages or screens. Nobody has ever felt the extent of cosmic time or distance. We've seen pictures of it.

The Webb space telescope's first deep image, packed with thousands of galaxies, covered a patch of sky about the size of a grain of sand held at arm's length. Thousands of galaxies, each with billions of stars, and we look at them on a phone.

The pictures aren't even what an eye would see. Webb sees infrared light, which no human eye can, so its images are translated into colours chosen to make them readable. They're beautiful, and partly made up for our benefit.

And every one of them is an old photograph. The light from the Andromeda galaxy, our nearest big neighbour, set out about 2.5 million years ago, long before our species existed. We look at a still of the distant past and call it the sky.

Even home shrinks to nothing. In 1990 the Voyager 1 probe looked back from beyond the outer planets, and Earth came out as a speck smaller than a single pixel.

## Too small for the numbers

The second problem is in our heads. Our minds were built for dozens, maybe hundreds: a herd, a tribe, a day's walk. Ask young children to place numbers along a line and they squash the big ones together at the far end. We learn to space them properly on paper, but the feeling never catches up.

A million and a billion sound like neighbours. They aren't. A million seconds is under twelve days. A billion seconds is nearly 32 years. And the cosmos deals in numbers that make a billion look small. We can write them down. We can't feel them.

Almost nobody has even left the bay. A few hundred people have been to space, and only 24, the Apollo crews, have travelled far enough to see the whole Earth hanging in the dark. Many came back changed by it; the writer Frank White called it the "overview effect." Yet even they only reached the harbour mouth. The Moon is a little over one light-second away. The nearest star is more than four light-years off.

We are too isolated, and all our interpretations are imagined.

## Past the Pillars

The ancients knew all about thresholds. At the Strait of Gibraltar stood the Pillars of Hercules, said to carry a warning: _Non plus ultra_, "nothing further beyond." The Mediterranean was the bay. Past the Pillars lay the open ocean, where the charts ran out. When Spain's sailors went through anyway, the king dropped the "Non" and took _Plus ultra_, "further beyond," as his motto. It's still on the Spanish flag. Ireland has its own threshold sailor: St Brendan, who in the old tale took a leather boat out into the open Atlantic looking for the Promised Land.

The cosmos has its own Pillars. The farthest edge of the observable universe is a threshold no telescope will ever cross, because beyond it no light can ever reach us. That isn't a matter of better instruments. It's the shape of the bay.

And there are thresholds much closer to home. Our rules of gravity, Newton's and Einstein's, were tested in the bay: inside the solar system, where the pull is strong. Out at the edges of galaxies, the pull is far weaker than anything we've ever measured at home, and that's exactly where the rules stop working. The stars there move too fast. In 1983 the Israeli physicist Mordehai Milgrom showed that the trouble starts at one particular, very weak level of pull. That's the threshold.

The humble response would have been: we've sailed past the chart. Instead, cosmology drew invisible dark matter across the open sea so the bay's rules could keep working out there. Perhaps the sea really is full of something invisible. Perhaps the chart simply ends at the headland. The honest answer is: maybe.

## The boy on the seashore

The greatest scientists have always known this. Near the end of his life, Isaac Newton said that he seemed to have been "only like a boy playing on the sea-shore," pleased now and then to find a smoother pebble or a prettier shell, "whilst the great ocean of truth lay all undiscovered before me." The man who worked out the laws of motion and gravity saw himself standing in the bay.

He was in good company. Socrates, as Plato tells it, said he was wiser than other men only because he didn't think he knew what he didn't know. The French essayist Montaigne took as his motto _Que sais-je?_, "What do I know?" And in a lecture in 1964 the American physicist Richard Feynman said, "I think I can safely say that nobody understands quantum mechanics."

Humility used to be the mark of greatness. Somewhere along the way the institution swapped it for certainty, perhaps because nobody ever won a grant by writing "maybe" on the application.

So here's the humble understanding. Given our limitations, everything we know, we can't really "know." That isn't despair. A horseman doesn't need to know a horse down to the molecule to ride it well. We can use what works, the GPS, the medicine, the bridge, without pretending we've understood the sea.

Someone will fire back: if you can't know anything, how do you know that? Fair enough. It isn't a claim of knowledge. It's a posture: the posture of a sailor at the headland, eyes open, chart held lightly.

## Two maybes

Which brings us to the distant horizon.

Take people first. When two sides are each certain they're right, the only way forward is for one to beat the other. Every crusade, every war fought because God wills it, began with two rights. Two people who each say "maybe" can sit at the same table and talk.

Now take physics. Its two great theories, relativity for the very large and quantum mechanics for the very small, are each called right, and each has been brilliantly tested in its own bay. But push them together, at the centre of a black hole or the first instant of the Big Bang, and they contradict each other. For nearly a century, physicists have tried to force them into one, and failed. Two rights, one wrong. Treat them as two maybes, and you're free to look past both.

The hunter understood this long before the physicist. The farmer deals in rights: rules, boundaries, fixed seasons, certainties written down. The hunter deals in maybes: a track, a scent, a shift in the wind, never sure of anything until the end. Maybe that's what the hunter has known all along.

We're still in the bay, looking at postcards of the sea. The honest thing isn't to pretend we've sailed it. It's to stand on the shore like Newton, look out at the ocean, and say: maybe.

Two rights always create a wrong. Two maybes don't.

title: Past the Headland
dek: A commencement address: one story, one picture, two words.
excerpt: A commencement address: one story, one picture, two words.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

Thank you. And congratulations.

I should tell you straight away who's talking to you, because you may be wondering. I'm not a scientist. I'm not a professor. I'm a Welsh and Irish descendant who breeds sporthorses as a retirement hobby and writes essays that annoy experts. In the language of this building, I'm what you'd call an outsider. In the language of the pub, an oddball.

Commencement speakers are supposed to give advice, and graduates are supposed to forget it by lunchtime. So I'll make it easy. I'm going to give you one story, one picture and two words. If you remember any one of them, I'll count it a good day.

The story is about two brothers. It's in the Book of Genesis, and it's one of the oldest stories we have. Esau "was a cunning hunter, a man of the field." Jacob "was a plain man, dwelling in tents." One day Esau comes in from the field, starving, and Jacob, who has been cooking, offers him a deal: a bowl of stew in exchange for his birthright. Esau takes it. The settled brother ends up with everything.

That story is still being played out, inside every one of us. For about 300,000 years, human beings were hunters. We followed the herds, read the weather, trusted our instincts and took our chances. Then, about 12,000 years ago, we started farming. And farming needed things hunting never had: fences, calendars, property, rules, and neighbours who all did the same thing at the same time. Instinct was traded for conformity.

The farmer won. He built the fields, the cities, the laws, and, if you'll forgive me, the universities. But the hunter never went away. He's still in there, in every one of you: the part that wants to roam, to try something nobody's tried, to look at the thing everyone else has learned not to see.

The farmer keeps trying to bury him. No luck so far.

And here's the uncomfortable part. For the last several years, you have lived in the most carefully tended field there is. Timetables. Syllabuses. Grading rubrics. Deadlines. Somebody told you what to plant, when to plant it, and what the harvest should look like. You've done it brilliantly; that's why you're wearing those gowns. But today the gate opens.

Which brings me to the picture.

Anyone who has sailed out of a harbour knows the moment. Inside the bay you know everything: every rock, every buoy, every current. Then you pass the headland, and in a single stroke you know nothing. The swell changes, the water changes colour, and the chart in your lap is suddenly a lot less use. When you sail from the bay to the sea, you go from knowing everything to knowing nothing at the moment of the threshold.

This morning, you are at the headland.

Nobody will tell you this, so I will: the feeling you're about to have, of not knowing, isn't failure. It's the sea. It's what the open water feels like. Everybody who ever discovered anything felt it.

Near the end of his life, Isaac Newton, the man who worked out the laws of motion and gravity, said he seemed to have been "only like a boy playing on the sea-shore," pleased now and then to find a smoother pebble or a prettier shell, "whilst the great ocean of truth lay all undiscovered before me." The greatest scientist who ever lived thought of himself as a boy standing in the bay.

So don't be frightened of the sea. Be frightened of the people who tell you they've already charted it.

Out there, you'll meet Jacob. Many times.

He'll be holding a bowl of stew. It'll look like a good salary, a safe title, a pension, a seat at the right table. And the price will be a little piece of your birthright: your curiosity, your instinct, your willingness to say the odd thing out loud.

I'm not going to tell you never to take the stew. Everybody has to eat. I've taken it myself. Just know what you're trading, every time, and don't sell the whole birthright for one bowl.

And know this about the institutions you'll join. They are built to hold still. That's their job. So they will often scorn the very people they later depend on.

A blacksmith's son from London, apprenticed to a bookbinder, with almost no schooling, taught himself science from the books he was binding. Michael Faraday worked out how to make electricity from motion, which is how nearly every power station on earth still works. When he was put up for Britain's top scientific society, his own boss opposed it.

A German weather scientist named Alfred Wegener said the continents were drifting apart. The experts laughed at him for decades. He died on the Greenland ice in 1930, and in the 1960s they found out he'd been right.

A butcher's daughter from Hungary, Katalin Karikó, spent years in America chasing an idea nobody would fund. She was turned down again and again, and demoted. Her work became the basis of the vaccines that got the world out of lockdown. In 2023 she won the Nobel Prize.

Each of them was, in the true sense of the word, antisocial. I don't mean criminal. I mean unconventional in some material respect: unwilling to live entirely by the group's rules. Oddballs. The institution calls you antisocial while you're alive and a genius once you're safely dead. My advice is to be just a little antisocial anyway. The world has always depended on it.

Now, the two words. You'll like them, because they're short.

The farmer deals in rights: rules, boundaries, certainties written down. The hunter deals in maybes: a track, a scent, a shift in the wind, never sure of anything until the end.

The world you're walking into is full of people who are certain they're right. Watch what happens when two of them meet. The only way forward is for one to beat the other. Every crusade in history, every war fought because God wills it, started with two people who were sure.

The same thing happens in science. Physics has two great theories, one for the very large and one for the very small. Each is called right. Each works beautifully in its own bay. Put them together at the edge of things, and they contradict each other. For nearly a century the best minds in the world have tried to force them into one, and failed.

So here are your two words, and a rule to go with them.

Two rights always create a wrong. Two maybes don't.

Two people who each say "maybe" can sit at the same table and talk. They can learn something. They can change their minds without losing face. "Maybe" is the most underrated word in the language. It isn't weakness. It's what the boy on the seashore says, looking at the ocean.

Let me leave you at the Strait of Gibraltar.

According to an old legend, the Pillars of Hercules, on either side of it, carried a warning: _Non plus ultra_. "Nothing further beyond." Inside was the Mediterranean, the known world, the bay. Outside was the open ocean, where the charts ran out.

Then sailors went through anyway. And the king of Spain did something I've always loved. He didn't change the motto. He just knocked off the first word. _Plus ultra._ "Further beyond." It's still on the Spanish flag today.

That's my whole speech, really. Somebody, somewhere along the way, has carved _Non plus ultra_ over the gate of your life: this far and no further, this is how it's done, this is what's known. Your job is to knock off the "Non."

So: one story, one picture, two words.

Keep the hunter alive; the farmer will keep trying to bury him, so don't let him have any luck. When you pass the headland and suddenly know nothing, smile, because that's the sea. And when somebody tells you they're certain, be kind, and say: maybe.

Plus ultra. Further beyond.

Congratulations, and good luck out there.

title: Enrich or Enslave?
dek: The hurdles before the starting line, the reform carousel, and a modest proposal.
excerpt: The hurdles before the starting line, the reform carousel, and a modest proposal.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

In 2002 a group of British scientists showed eight-year-olds two sets of picture cards. One set showed common British wildlife: oak trees, badgers, beetles. The other showed Pokémon, the made-up creatures from a video game. The children named about 78 percent of the Pokémon and only about 53 percent of the oaks and badgers.

Nothing was wrong with those children's memories. They had soaked up hundreds of imaginary creatures, each with its own name, powers and weaknesses, without a single lesson. Before they ever set foot in a school, they had learned an entire language the same way.

Kids have a tremendous capacity to absorb information, unless they're bored to death. It's easy to educate people. We just refuse to do it.

## Free men and servants

So what is school for? Is it to enrich, or to enslave? The question is older than you'd think. It's built into the words.

"School" comes from the Greek _scholē_, which meant leisure: the free man's time. The "liberal arts" were the arts fit for a free person. The other kind were called the "servile" arts, for slaves and labourers. From the start there were two educations: one to free you, and one to fit you for your place.

Frederick Douglass, born into slavery in Maryland, was being taught his letters when his master found out and put a stop to it, warning that reading would make him unfit to be a slave. Douglass later wrote that from that moment, he understood "the pathway from slavery to freedom." Several slave states made it a crime to teach enslaved people to read. The masters knew exactly what education was for.

So did the Prussians. After Napoleon crushed Prussia in 1806, it built the first great state school system to turn out loyal citizens and soldiers. The philosopher Johann Fichte said it plainly in 1808: education should "fashion" a pupil "in such a way that he simply cannot will otherwise than you wish him to will." In 1843 the American reformer Horace Mann toured the Prussian schools, came home impressed, and helped bring the model to Massachusetts, which made schooling compulsory in 1852. Bells, rows of desks, children batched by age and moved along on schedule. The farmer invented school to make more farmers.

Enrich or enslave? It depends who holds the chalk. And before a child can learn anything at all, he has to clear a set of hurdles that would stop a racehorse.

## Bored to death

The first hurdle is the oldest. Is it better to be instructive or interesting? Schools usually choose instructive. The science chooses interesting.

In 2014 a team of brain researchers found that when people were curious about a question, they remembered the answer far better. They even remembered unrelated faces flashed at them while they were curious. Curiosity opens the gate. The Greek writer Plutarch said it nearly 2,000 years ago: the mind doesn't need filling like a bottle, it needs kindling like wood.

And interesting doesn't just get them in the door. It keeps them in the building. In a 2006 survey of young Americans who had dropped out of school, 47 percent said a major reason was that classes weren't interesting. Not too hard. Not interesting. Gallup found that about three-quarters of fifth graders feel engaged at school. By twelfth grade it's about a third. The building keeps their bodies and loses their minds, one year at a time.

## Duress and choice

The second hurdle is format. Kids open books under duress. They live on smartphones by choice.

American teenagers average more than eight hours a day of screen time for entertainment. Meanwhile the share of thirteen-year-olds who read for fun almost every day has fallen from about a third in the 1980s to 14 percent in 2023. School gets the duress. The phone gets the devotion.

This isn't new. Every format has been feared. Socrates, as Plato tells it, warned that writing would ruin people's memories. The printed book was once the dangerous new gadget. And it cuts both ways: studies keep finding that people understand long, serious texts better on paper than on a screen. The phone is good for the spark and weak at the slow burn.

The real trouble is who owns the phone. It's engineered to hold attention for profit, and it's very good at it. The hunter lives in the phone, but the phone is someone else's farm.

## Nothing to grow up for

The third hurdle is the strangest. Kids need to want to grow up. In our bad-news-choked society, that's nuts, and they know it.

In 2021, a survey of 10,000 young people aged 16 to 25 in ten countries found that three-quarters called the future frightening and more than half thought humanity was doomed. In America, the share of high-school students reporting persistent sadness or hopelessness rose from 28 percent in 2011 to 42 percent in 2021.

The news business has learned that fear sells. A 2023 study of over 100,000 headlines found that every extra negative word made people more likely to click. So the feed fills up with doom, and what it leaves out never makes the screen: since 1990, the share of the world living in extreme poverty and the number of children dying before age five have both fallen dramatically. The Swedish doctor Hans Rosling spent his last years trying to tell people this, and found that most of them, experts included, guessed the world was getting worse.

We ask children to climb toward the future while telling them, every hour of the day, that it's on fire. Nobody climbs a ladder toward a burning house.

## Feet of clay

The fourth hurdle: kids need heroes. How hard is that in today's environment?

The hunger hasn't gone anywhere. The Marvel superhero films have taken in around $30 billion worldwide, more than any film series in history. Children haven't stopped needing heroes. They've just been handed invented ones, because the real ones get torn down so fast.

It matters, because children become what they admire. In the 1960s the psychologist Albert Bandura showed that children learn largely by copying the people they look up to. In 2019 a survey asked children aged eight to twelve what they'd most like to be. In America and Britain, 29 percent said a YouTuber and 11 percent an astronaut. In China, 56 percent said an astronaut.

For centuries, the standard way to raise a young person was a book called Plutarch's _Lives_: real heroes, faults and all, read as examples. The phrase "feet of clay" comes from the Book of Daniel, where a great statue of gold and silver stands on feet of iron mixed with clay. Every real hero has them. The old way was to admire the gold and know about the clay. Ours is to point at the clay and stop there.

The real heroes are still available. A blacksmith's son who taught himself science from the books he was binding and gave the world electric power. A Hungarian butcher's daughter, demoted for an idea nobody would fund, who won the Nobel Prize for it. A slave boy who taught himself to read. They beat any comic book. Somebody just has to tell the children.

## The bookends

The fifth hurdle stands at home, at both ends of the shelf: broken homes at one end, success-obsessed push parents at the other.

In 2019 the Pew Research Center found that the United States has the highest share of children living with a single parent of any country it studied, about 23 percent. In fairness, plenty of single parents raise children superbly; the research points less to any one family shape than to instability, the ground shifting under a child's feet.

At the other end is the parent who never lets the ground move at all. In 2011 a Yale law professor's memoir, _Battle Hymn of the Tiger Mother_, made push parenting a household phrase. A 2013 study of Chinese-American families found that "tiger" parenting went with lower grades and more depression than supportive parenting. In 2018 a major American health foundation listed "excessive pressure to excel" as a risk to children, alongside poverty and trauma. And in 2019 the college-admissions bribery scandal showed wealthy parents paying to cheat their children into elite universities.

One bookend leaves the child with no fence and no guide. The other builds an iron fence and drives him round it. In 1953 the English paediatrician Donald Winnicott offered the sane alternative: the "good enough" parent. Not perfect. Steady enough for a child to grow.

## The reform carousel

And the last hurdle, at least in America: meaningful reform is out of the question. Not because nobody has tried. Because everybody has.

In the 1960s it was "New Math," which left a generation of parents unable to help with homework. In 1983 a federal report called _A Nation at Risk_ warned of "a rising tide of mediocrity." In 2009 came Race to the Top. In 2010 came the Common Core standards, adopted by most states and then renamed, revised or dropped by many of them.

But the masterpiece was No Child Left Behind. In 2002 Congress passed a law requiring every child in America to be proficient in reading and maths by 2014. Every child. By law. When 2014 arrived and the children hadn't complied, Washington quietly replaced the law in 2015. It was utopia by statute: pass a law that reality must improve by a set date, then act surprised.

Two historians of education, David Tyack and Larry Cuban, called their book on all this _Tinkering Toward Utopia_. The reforms come round like painted horses on a fairground ride. The music plays, the politicians wave, and the classroom stays where it was.

Part of the trouble is that there's no one to steer. America has more than 13,000 school districts, each a little kingdom with its own board. Washington pays only about a tenth of the bill, so it can make speeches but not decisions. And the results speak for themselves. The country spends more per pupil than most rich nations and scores below the developed-world average in maths. In 2022 the national tests recorded the steepest drops in maths scores ever measured.

This isn't the fault of teachers, parents or pupils. It fails all of them. It's a system so tangled that nobody in it can fix it, and everybody in it gets the blame.

## Saved by the land

So how does a country this careless with its children stay rich? Luck, mostly. Geography.

Around the time of the First World War, the French ambassador to Washington, Jules Jusserand, is said to have summed it up: America has a weak neighbour to the north, a weak neighbour to the south, and to the east and the west, fish. Add the Mississippi river system, which drains about 40 percent of the lower 48 states through some of the richest farmland on earth, and an energy supply that has made the United States the world's biggest oil producer since 2018. A country could get a great deal wrong and still eat well.

There's an old line, often credited to Bismarck, probably wrongly: "God has a special providence for fools, drunkards and the United States of America." That nobody can pin down who said it only makes it truer.

This country is saved by the land under our feet. And who is it saved from? Us! The cartoonist Walt Kelly put it into the mouth of Pogo the possum in 1970: "We have met the enemy and he is us."

## A modest proposal

In 1729 an Irishman named Jonathan Swift published _A Modest Proposal_, solemnly suggesting that the poor of Ireland sell their babies to the rich as food. He wasn't mocking the poor. He was mocking the people who let them starve. In that tradition, here is a modest proposal for American schools.

Since reform is impossible, let Congress simply pass the Boredom Abolition Act, requiring every classroom in America to be interesting by 2040. It worked so well last time.

Failing that, there's a cheaper plan, and it's been tested for a few thousand years.

First, fix the books. Real reform starts with interesting, relaxed and attractive books and other teaching aids. Any book that can't be understood and enjoyed by all is a bad book.

It has been done. In 1954 the novelist John Hersey complained in _Life_ magazine that children were bogging down on dull primers about Dick and Jane, and asked why schools didn't hire real artists to make reading books, naming Dr. Seuss among them. A publisher took up the idea and challenged Seuss to write a first reader using only a short list of words a beginner would know. In 1957 he delivered _The Cat in the Hat_, built from just 236 different words. Children have been reading it for fun ever since.
