Now look at the books schools actually buy. In 1964 the physicist Richard Feynman agreed to help California choose its maths textbooks. He found most of them muddled and badly written. One book on the list hadn't even been finished; the publisher sent a cover with blank pages inside, and some of the other reviewers rated it anyway. That's how much anyone was reading.

Second, put the front door back. For centuries, a European education began with grammar, logic and rhetoric: learning to think before learning anything else. France still makes philosophy a required subject in the last year of secondary school. Call the textbooks _Metaphysics for Morons_ and _Logic for Loons_ if that sells them. The "morons" and "loons" will come out thinking more clearly than a good few people with doctorates.

Third, remember that the brain is an organ that works like a muscle. It's strengthened by degrees. London taxi drivers who memorise the city's tangle of streets grow a larger memory region in the brain. People who learned to juggle gained grey matter in three months, and lost it again when they stopped. The Greeks told of the wrestler Milo of Croton, who carried a newborn calf on his shoulders every day until it was a bull. Add a little weight each day, and keep it interesting enough that the child wants to lift it. Gimmicks won't do it: in 2016 American regulators fined the makers of one "brain-training" game $2 million over their claims. The weight has to be real.

Fourth, give them heroes, real ones with feet of clay, and a reason to believe the future is worth growing into.

None of this needs a new law, a new agency or a new acronym. It needs people who remember what school was for before the Prussians got hold of it.

Enrich or enslave? The children can't choose. They're too busy memorising Pokémon. It's easy to educate people. We just refuse to do it.

title: Too Much of a Bad Thing
dek: The fear merchants, the bubble, and why they're terrified of everyone getting smart.
excerpt: The fear merchants, the bubble, and why they're terrified of everyone getting smart.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

The first essay in this collection, "Too Much of a Good Thing," argued that social media, online news and an outdated reading of the First Amendment were killing democracy. It ended on a shrug: public issues are like waves at sea, breaking on the shore one by one.

This is the sequel, because the story didn't end there. Since then we've looked at the schools, the children and the future they're being asked to grow into. And at the bottom of nearly every problem, the same industry keeps turning up.

It's an information and entertainment industry that will devour its whole world for the sake of celebrity, scandal and cash. It batters us continuously with vivid and lyrical images of the collapse of civilization, and then wonders why we have a hard time getting out of bed.

## If it bleeds, it leads

There's an old newsroom saying: "If it bleeds, it leads." It was never a secret. It was a business plan.

It works because of how we're built. Our senses evolved to save us from an early death, so the brain treats bad news as urgent and good news as optional. The evolutionary psychiatrist Randolph Nesse calls it the smoke-detector principle: a false alarm costs little, a missed fire costs everything, so the alarm is set to go off at the slightest whiff.

The news business has learned to hold a match under that alarm all day long. A 2023 study of more than 100,000 headlines found that every extra negative word made readers more likely to click. So the negative words multiply. The planet is burning, democracy is dying, the economy is collapsing, the next pandemic is coming, and here, in vivid colour and lyrical prose, is exactly how it will feel.

Some of it is true, and some of it matters. But a steady diet of it isn't information. It's a drip feed of dread, sold by the click.

## Devouring its own world

An industry that chases celebrity, scandal and cash will eventually eat everything around it, itself included.

In Britain, the _News of the World_ was one of the best-selling newspapers on earth. In 2011 it emerged that its reporters had hacked into the voicemail of a murdered thirteen-year-old schoolgirl, Milly Dowler, while police were still searching for her. The public revulsion was so great that the paper was closed within days, after 168 years in print. That's what scandal for cash looks like at the end of the road.

In America the devouring has been quieter but just as deadly. Since 2005 the country has lost roughly 3,000 newspapers, more than two a week, most of them small local papers that covered the school board, the county court and the high-school football game. The industry's money and talent drained toward the national stage, where the outrage is louder and the clicks are bigger. Millions of Americans now live in "news deserts," with no local paper at all, while their screens fill up with the doings of celebrities they'll never meet.

The industry didn't just stop telling people about their own towns. It taught them to care more about strangers' scandals than their own neighbours.

## The view from the bubble

The business model explains the fear. The attitude explains the rest. And the elite, entitled, condescending, self-absorbed attitude isn't a side issue. It's an essential feature of the problem.

The people who describe the country to itself increasingly don't live in most of it. A 2017 analysis found that the large majority of American internet-publishing jobs were packed into a few coastal corridors. The newsroom looks out at the nation the way Newton's boy looked at the ocean, except without the humility.

The historian Christopher Lasch saw it coming. In 1995, in a book called _The Revolt of the Elites_, he argued that the people running the country's institutions had stopped sharing the lives of the people they lectured, and had come to look down on them. Thirty years later it reads like a forecast.

You can hear it in the tone. The reader isn't treated as a grown-up to be informed. He's treated as a child to be frightened, scolded or managed. And every time the scolding fails, the scolds conclude the public must be stupider than they thought.

## The audience walks out

The public isn't stupid. It's leaving.

Gallup found that Americans' trust in the mass media fell to a record low in 2024: only about three in ten said they trust it. Around the world, about four in ten people now say they sometimes or often avoid the news altogether, and one of the commonest reasons they give is that it drags their mood down. People don't stop trusting someone who is merely wrong now and then. They stop trusting someone who frightens them for money and talks down to them while doing it.

The heaviest cost falls on the young. Three-quarters of young people in one ten-country survey called the future frightening. In America, the share of high-school students reporting persistent sadness or hopelessness rose from 28 percent to 42 percent in a single decade. We ask children to grow up while the loudest voices in their lives tell them, hour after hour, that there's nothing worth growing up into.

None of this is forgivable. An industry that claims to be the guardian of an informed public has made the public more frightened, less informed and less willing to listen, and then blamed the public for it.

## When we all get smart

No wonder they're terrified of AI.

For a century the information business has rested on a simple monopoly: they had the facts, the access and the microphone, and the rest of us had to take what they gave us, with the fear and the sermon included. That monopoly is ending. Major news organisations are already in court against AI companies; the _New York Times_ sued two of them at the end of 2023. They say it's about copyright. Perhaps. It's also about the gate.

Because here's what changes when ordinary people have a patient, tireless assistant at their elbow. A horse dealer can ask what a bill actually says, instead of what an angry headline says it says. A mother can check a scary statistic before it ruins her evening. A teenager can ask for the other side of the argument and get it, without a sneer attached. A pub argument can be settled with evidence instead of volume.

The fear merchants have had a long run. They batter us with the collapse of civilization and wonder why we can't get out of bed. Well, we're getting up now. And the question they should be asking themselves isn't how to win the public back with another scary headline.

It's this: how long will they be tolerated when we all get smart?

title: What a Twisted Circle
dek: A catalogue of the impediments that stand between us and Reality.
excerpt: A catalogue of the impediments that stand between us and Reality.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

Every word, every theory, every opinion posits there is an observer. Science likes to forget that. It presents its findings as a view from nowhere, as if the universe had been photographed by no one. But every observation is made by someone, from somewhere, with equipment that was never designed to find the truth.

Life predates brains. For roughly three billion years, most of life's history, there wasn't a brain anywhere on Earth. The observer is a latecomer, and it arrived with equipment built for a narrow job: keeping a moving creature alive. So before we can ask what Reality is, we have to take stock of everything that stands between us and it.

Here is the catalogue. There are twelve impediments, in four groups: the body, the self, the tools and the frame.

## The body

**1. Senses built to survive, not to know.** In a paleo sense, all sensory organs are adapted to save us from an early outcome. Truth was never the assignment. We see only a thin sliver of the light that exists, roughly the band where the sunlight reaching the ground is strongest. We hear only a narrow range of sound. And the brain is set like a smoke detector: a false alarm costs little, a missed lion costs everything, so we're built to see threats and patterns that aren't there, a face in the clouds, a lion in the grass. An eye tuned to survive is not an eye tuned to see.

**2. Senses that filter out our peril.** The same equipment hides the dangers we can do nothing about. At the equator, the spinning Earth carries us along at about 1,000 miles an hour; its orbit moves us around the Sun at about 67,000; the Sun hauls us all around the galaxy at roughly 500,000. We feel none of it. Particles from cosmic rays pass through us every second, unfelt. The brain stops noticing whatever is constant, and most of us expect better outcomes than the odds allow. It's a mercy. An animal that felt the full scale of its peril could never get out of bed. But mercy is not accuracy.

**3. A mind too small for the scale.** From inside the envelope we can only experience what we observe in miniature: still images on pages or screens. The Webb telescope's first deep image held thousands of galaxies in a patch of sky the size of a grain of sand at arm's length, and we look at it on a phone. Our minds were built for dozens and hundreds. A million seconds is under twelve days; a billion is nearly 32 years; the cosmos deals in numbers that dwarf both. We can write them down. We can't feel them.

## The self

**4. The reference point.** Observation is a unique, tangible activity. It produces information, stimulates action and needs a reference point, a "here" that everything else is measured from. That "here" is the self: a feature of mobile life, a child of the senses, undetectable from without. But a reference point is a place to stand, and wherever you stand, there's a horizon. A sailor's horizon moves with his boat. The edge of the observable universe is centred on us, wherever we are. Horizons are features of observation, not reality. Every observer carries one, and none can see past it.

**5. The eye that can't see itself.** The one thing an observer can never observe is the observer. About 2,700 years ago, the Indian scripture called the Upanishads put it plainly: "You cannot see the seer of seeing." The self is the black hole and Big Bang of neuroscience: scientists can trace every signal up to its edge, and there the trail stops. It's why gods were invented right after tools and weapons. Every horizon gets a god, or in modern science, a placeholder.

**6. Projection.** We see what is; we project what we wish, and what we fear. For two thousand years, the planets had to move in perfect circles and the heavens had to be "incorruptible," a sky that never changes and never rots, because we do. Today's cosmology still assumes the universe is the same everywhere on the largest scales, the farmer's field stretched to the edge of space. Our wishes for order, repetition and permanence get hung on whatever we observe, and the framework is projection. Observation is just what it attaches to.

## The tools

**7. Language.** Language was built for the bay: for food, tools, cattle and kin. It freezes happenings into nouns, then sends us hunting for the noun. "Time," "nothing" and "the self" all become things to be found, when each is really something happening. In 1921 the philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein put the limit in one line: "The limits of my language mean the limits of my world." When we try to describe the intangible, we reach for metaphor, which is language admitting it has run out of road.

**8. Logic and mathematics.** Maths was made for the marketplace: the oldest known written numbers are Sumerian clay tablets counting grain and sheep, and "geometry" means "earth measuring." It's the language of repetition, brilliant at whatever happens again and again, and it breaks down at the one-offs, at the Big Bang and the heart of a black hole, where it divides by zero and gives up. Logic is the same kind of tool, superb on separate, countable things. The quantum world strained it so badly that in 1936 two mathematicians proposed a separate "quantum logic." Logic is the chart, not the sea.

**9. Instruments.** Telescopes, microscopes and particle detectors extend the senses, but they don't escape them. They're designed by survival-tuned brains, aimed at what those brains expect to find, and read through the same projections. Webb sees infrared light no human eye can see, so its pictures are translated into colours chosen for us. We've made the eyes bigger, not less biased.

## The frame

**10. Isolation.** We are too isolated, and all our interpretations are imagined. Humanity has spent its whole history in the bay, looking out at the sea of the cosmos. Only a few hundred people have ever left the planet, and only 24 have travelled far enough to see the whole Earth hanging in the dark. Even they only reached the harbour mouth. When you sail from the bay to the sea, you go from knowing everything to knowing nothing at the moment of the threshold.

**11. Brevity.** Our lives are short and our instruments are young. A spiral galaxy looks serene only because it takes hundreds of millions of years to turn. The order we see may be a portrait of our own short lives, a snapshot of a storm mistaken for a map. Every observation is a still frame of something that never stops moving.

**12. The framework.** Put all of the above together and you arrive at the deepest impediment: all knowledge is framework-dependent. There's no view from nowhere. Even agreement doesn't rescue us, because other observers share our framework. For thousands of years everyone agreed they could see the Sun move across the sky.

## Can we know Reality at all?

Twelve impediments, and every observer carries all of them. So can we know Reality at all?

Not completely, because there's always the horizon. Not directly, because there's no stepping outside the self to compare the picture with the world. Out there is whatever won't bend to our wishes. In there is whatever will.

That leaves the humble understanding: given our limitations, everything we know, we can't really "know." Hold every framework as a maybe, and keep the one that fights Reality least.

And notice the shape of the whole thing. We use a framework we invented to define a Reality that created us.

Of one thing I am sure. The cosmos knows nothing about itself. It doesn't know it made us, and it won't notice when we're gone. All the knowing happens in here, in small, brief, moving pockets of life, each at the centre of its own horizon, each looking out through twelve layers of glass.

What a twisted circle.

title: SOBs and Placeholders
dek: Two very different things science finds at the edge of what it can see.
excerpt: Two very different things science finds at the edge of what it can see.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

Two words keep turning up in these essays: SOBs and placeholders. They sound alike, they turn up in the same places, and they get confused all the time, by scientists as much as anyone. They are totally different things. This piece is just to sort them out, once and for all.

## The wall: SOBs

An SOB is a scientific observational boundary: a place where our methods of looking simply run out.

There are three great ones. The Big Bang, where the equations stop at the first instant. The black hole, whose horizon hides whatever is inside. And self-awareness, where scientists can trace every signal up to the edge of the self, and the trail stops there. You could add the edge of the observable universe, which is as far as light has had time to travel to us.

All of them assume Somethings on the other side, but our methods cannot capture them. And all of them are features of observation, not reality. They mark the reach of whoever is looking, not the end of the world. A sailor's horizon is real, but it isn't a cliff.

An SOB is honest. It says: we can't see past here. The right response is equally honest: maybe.

## The ghost: placeholders

A placeholder is something else entirely. It's an invented thing, parked in a gap to make the books balance. It doesn't say "we can't see past here." It says "there's something here we can't see."

Placeholders aren't automatically bad. Some of science's finest moments began as one. In the 1840s the planet Uranus wobbled off course, astronomers predicted an unseen planet pulling on it, and in 1846 Neptune turned up almost exactly where they said. In 1930 Wolfgang Pauli proposed an invisible particle, the neutrino, to balance the energy books. It was caught in 1956.

But some placeholders never get found and never get retired. In 1859 the same astronomer who predicted Neptune blamed Mercury's wobble on another hidden planet, Vulcan. It was hunted for decades. It was never there. The wobble was finally explained in 1915, when Einstein rethought gravity itself.

## Telling them apart

Four plain questions sort the walls from the ghosts, and the good ghosts from the bad.

**Does it claim a thing?** An SOB claims nothing except a limit. A placeholder claims something exists.

**Does it make a definite prediction?** Neptune had to be in one patch of sky. The neutrino had to show up in a particular kind of detector. A good placeholder sticks its neck out.

**Is there a clock?** Neptune was spotted on the first night an astronomer went looking with the prediction in hand; the neutrino took twenty-six years. A placeholder that has gone half a century without being found deserves a hard look, not a bigger budget.

**Does it get redefined after every miss?** This is the surest sign of a bad ghost. When a search comes up empty and the answer is that the ghost must be lighter, heavier, shyer or stranger than we thought, it has stopped being a prediction and become a habit.

## Ghosts on the walls

The real mischief starts when the two get confused: when an SOB is treated as a gap waiting to be filled, and a placeholder is painted onto it. Then the ghost takes on the authority of the wall. It starts to look permanent, unquestionable, part of the landscape.

Look at where today's biggest placeholders sit. **Inflation**, an unseen burst of expansion in the first instant, is painted on the Big Bang. **Dark matter**, sought for about fifty years and never caught, is painted on the outskirts of galaxies, exactly where our rules of gravity, tested only in the solar system, stop working. **Dark energy** is painted on the far edge of the observable universe, where the light is faintest and oldest. And in brain science, **"emergence"** is painted on the self: the word for whatever happens at the point where the explanation runs out.

Each of them sits right on a boundary of observation. Each fills a place where we can't see with something we can't see. And each has been searched for, redefined and searched for again.

## Respect the wall, question the ghost

So here are the rules, in one place.

At an SOB, admit the limit. Say "we can't see past here," and leave it at "maybe." That isn't failure. It's honesty about the twelve layers of glass every observer looks through.

With a placeholder, label it pending, demand a definite prediction, and give it a clock. If it's found, cheer. If the clock runs out, retire it, and go back to rethinking the rules, the way Einstein did with Vulcan.

And never, ever paint a ghost on a wall and call it a discovery.

An SOB is a wall. A placeholder is a ghost painted on the wall. Respect the wall. Question the ghost.

title: The Third Rail
dek: Shamans and scientists, the tragic cost of certainty and prejudice, and an invitation to dinner.
excerpt: Shamans and scientists, the tragic cost of certainty and prejudice, and an invitation to dinner.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

On 17 February 1600, in a square in Rome called the Campo de' Fiori, the Church burned a former friar named Giordano Bruno alive. The charges against him were mostly theological. But among his ideas was one that sounded mad at the time: that the stars were suns, with worlds of their own. Astronomers have now found thousands of planets circling other stars.

In 1943, in a prison in the Soviet city of Saratov, a scientist named Nikolai Vavilov died of starvation. He was one of the greatest plant scientists of his century, a man who had travelled the world collecting seeds to end famine. His crime was believing in genetics, which the Soviet state had decided was incompatible with its ideology. During the siege of Leningrad, some of the botanists guarding his great seed collection starved to death at their desks rather than eat the seeds.

One man was killed by a church, the other by a state that called itself scientific. It was the same fire.

## Holmes and Moriarty

The war between the shamans and the scientists is the third rail of public life: touch it and you get burned. Faith against logic, religion against science. It's been running so long that each side defines itself by the other.

Arthur Conan Doyle wrote the perfect picture of it in 1893. Sherlock Holmes and his great enemy, Professor Moriarty, meet on a narrow path above the Reichenbach Falls, grapple, and go over the edge locked together. Neither can let go. Each needs the other to know who he is.

The question this essay asks is simple. Why can't they stop fighting, even when neither side knows what it's talking about?

## The war that wasn't

Start with a surprise: much of the war is a story told after the fact.

The idea of an eternal battle between science and religion was largely popularised by two American books in the late 1800s, John Draper's in 1874 and Andrew Dickson White's in 1896. The famous belief that medieval people thought the Earth was flat was spread mainly by Washington Irving's 1828 life of Columbus. Educated people in the Middle Ages knew perfectly well it was round.

For most of history, the scientists were believers. Kepler thought he was reading the mind of God in the orbits of the planets. Isaac Newton wrote more about theology than about physics. And the Big Bang itself was first proposed in the late 1920s by a Belgian Catholic priest and physicist, Georges Lemaître. When Pope Pius XII hailed the idea in 1951 as near-proof of creation, Lemaître quietly asked him not to. The priest understood something the Pope didn't: science could take you to the edge, but not past it.

## Beyond the Wall

That edge is the key to the whole quarrel.

Think of the scientific observational boundaries, the SOBs: the Big Bang, the inside of a black hole, the self. Each is a wall where our methods run out. Beyond it there is surely something, but nobody can see what. It's the old Wall of the North, with only rumours of what lies past it.

And that is exactly the ground the two sides are fighting over. Where did everything come from? What is a person? What happens beyond the edge? The shaman paints a god on the wall. The scientist paints a placeholder. Each accuses the other of seeing ghosts, and both are pointing at the same blank stone.

That's why they can't stop. They aren't fighting over evidence. Neither side has any from beyond the Wall. They're fighting over territory: who gets to name the dark.

## The cost of certainty

If that were all, it would be a harmless pub argument. It isn't, because when a maybe hardens into a certainty about what lies beyond the Wall, it becomes an ideology. And an ideology needs bodies to hold its ground.

The religious side has its martyrs on both sides of the Reformation. In 1553 Protestant Geneva burned Michael Servetus, a Spanish physician and theologian who had described how blood passes through the lungs, in the same book that got him condemned. In 1600 Catholic Rome burned Bruno. In 1633 the Inquisition forced Galileo, under threat, to deny that the Earth moves, and he spent the rest of his life under house arrest.

But the other side has its dead too, wherever ideology put on a lab coat. In 1927 the United States Supreme Court upheld the forced sterilisation of a young woman named Carrie Buck. Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes, a different Holmes entirely, wrote that "three generations of imbeciles are enough." Some 60,000 Americans were sterilised under such laws, in the name of the science of the day, eugenics. In the Soviet Union, the state's official science threw out genetics and starved Vavilov to death, and Lysenko-style farming methods were later pushed in China during the famine years of the Great Leap Forward. In the purges of the late 1930s, the same state that called itself scientific arrested tens of thousands of priests and believers and shot many of them.

And underneath the fire there is always prejudice. Certainty about the beyond doesn't stay up there; it comes back down as contempt for the people who see it differently. The faithful called them heretics and infidels, and in 1492 Spain expelled its Jews for believing the wrong thing about what lies beyond the Wall. The other side found new words: backward, superstitious, unfit. Eugenics, a term coined in 1883 by the Victorian scientist Francis Galton, dressed old prejudices about race and class in the language of science, and in Nazi Germany "racial hygiene" helped pave the road to the gas chambers. Today the weapons are milder but the reflex is the same: believers are written off as fools, scientists as godless. Prejudice is what certainty feels like from the inside: the conviction that the other fellow isn't merely wrong, but lesser.

The church that burned Bruno and the state that starved Vavilov had one thing in common. Each was certain about what lay beyond the Wall, and each was willing to kill to keep the map.

## Two rights

There's a simple rule behind all of it. Two rights always create a wrong. Two maybes don't.

When two sides are each certain they're right, the only way forward is for one to beat the other. That's what happened at the stake in Rome and in the prison at Saratov. When two sides each say "maybe," they can sit at the same table.

The tragedy is that the ground they fought over is the one place where nobody can be right. Beyond the Wall, every map is a guess. People were burned, sterilised and starved to defend guesses.

## Shake hands and go home for dinner

So here's a modest proposal for the oldest war in the world: humility and civility.

On this side of the Wall, fight as hard as you like. Argue about evidence, test each other's claims, knock down bad ideas. That's healthy. But when the fight goes over the Wall, into the ground neither side can see, pick up your weapons, shake hands and go home for dinner.

And both sides need to live by one good rule: respect the other fellow's belief. Faith and air are free for everybody. Nobody has to prove what they believe about the far side of the Wall, because nobody can. The scientist who sneers at a believer and the believer who damns a scientist are making the same mistake: each is claiming the deeds to land neither has ever seen.

It can be done. In the first winter of the First World War, British and German soldiers climbed out of their trenches on Christmas Day 1914, met in no-man's-land, swapped cigarettes and food, and in places kicked a football about. For a day, enemies admitted they were all just men in the mud. Every decent sport ends the same way: the fight is real, but it ends at the whistle, and rugby players even have a name for the drink they share afterwards, the "third half."

Both sides have models to follow. Lemaître the priest refused to let his science be used as proof of God. Einstein, no churchgoer, wrote in 1941 that "science without religion is lame, religion without science is blind." Neither man pretended to see over the Wall.

Holmes and Moriarty went over the falls because neither would let go. The shamans and the scientists don't have to. The Wall will still be there in the morning, and so will the questions. Nobody has to die over them.

Shake hands. Go home for dinner.

title: A Definition of Terms
dek: Our model of physics and Reality, in plain words.
excerpt: Our model of physics and Reality, in plain words.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

Over two dozen essays, we've built up a way of looking at the universe, and a vocabulary to go with it. This is the key: our model of physics and Reality, one term at a time, in plain words. Where something is our best guess rather than an established fact, it says "pending." We hold ourselves to the same standard we ask of everyone else.

## The basics

**Reality.** Whatever is there whether we look or not. It doesn't care what we believe, and it won't bend to our wishes. That's how we tell it apart from what's in our heads.

**Nothing.** Nothing cannot exist. The moment you describe it, even as dark or empty or silent, you've given it properties, and things with properties aren't nothing. So nobody has to explain how something came from nothing. It never did.

**Something.** Whatever exists. Since nothing can't exist, something has no opposite. There was always something, including before the Big Bang.

**Matter.** The stuff of the universe. Matter cannot be non-material: no ghostly half-stuff, no particle that is somehow everywhere and nowhere until someone looks. Whether _everything_ real is matter is a separate question, and an open one.

**Motion.** Matter is always moving, and motion is as basic as matter itself. A particle is trapped motion: energy wound tight and ringing in place. What's left at the bottom of it all is matter, energy and motion.

**Time.** Not a thing, and not a dimension. Time is our name for motion and change, and a clock is just a horse walking in circles. Nobody has ever measured time itself, only things moving. So instead of an arrow of time, we speak of an arrow of motion: things move, wear down and come apart.

## The stuff of space

**Material space.** Space isn't empty, and it isn't a geometric fabric called "spacetime." It's a real material, the most common stuff there is, filling everything. Particles are tight knots in it. Inertia, the stubbornness of things to start or stop, is the resistance a knot meets when it's dragged through the medium. _Pending._ In its simplest form, the idea matches the classic tests of Einstein's theory, such as the bending of starlight by the Sun and the drift of Mercury's orbit. It doesn't yet explain everything, and it needs a physicist to finish it.

**Gravity.** Not bent geometry, but compression. A heavy body sits in the material and leaves a pressure slope around it, and anything nearby is pushed inward. _Pending._

**Galaxies.** Not swarms of stars coasting through a void, but whirlpools in the medium, with outer stars carried along by the current. That would make invisible dark matter unnecessary. _Pending._

**The closed universe.** The universe is material and a closed system: nothing gets in, nothing gets out. But closed isn't the same as everything. A sealed jar still sits on a shelf. So something may lie beyond the universe's edges, and before its beginning, that we can never reach.

## The edges

**The Big Bang.** The point where the equations run backward and give up. It's where the math divides by zero, not a moment we've seen. Something had to exist for there to be a bang at all. What it was, we can never know.

**Black holes.** Places where matter is crushed until nothing comes back out. In the equations they look like the Big Bang's twin, but they're different animals, an elephant and a cat: one breaks at a moment, the other at a spot. If space is a real material, their shadows should look a few percent larger than Einstein predicts, and telescopes can check. _Pending._

**Expansion.** Galaxies are moving apart. That's observed. "Space itself is stretching" is an interpretation laid over the measurements, a verb turned into a noun. In our worldview, that part is speculative.

**Infinities.** When an equation goes to infinity, it isn't measuring something infinitely big. It's the math reaching the edge of what it can describe. Every infinity is a sign that the map has run out.

## The rules of the game

**Order and randomness.** The universe looks orderly and behaves randomly. The paradox is solved by a simple axiom: things break and stuff happens. Order is what we see in the stretches between breakages; randomness is the breakages themselves. A genetic mutation is just one more thing breaking, and every living species is the record of which breakages happened to work.

**SOBs.** Scientific observational boundaries: the Big Bang, the inside of a black hole, the self, the edge of the observable universe. Places where our methods run out. They assume Somethings on the other side, but our methods can't capture them. They're features of observation, not reality. An SOB is a wall.

**Placeholders.** Invented things parked in a gap to make the books balance: dark matter, dark energy, inflation. Some placeholders get found, like Neptune and the neutrino. Others never do, like the phantom planet Vulcan. A placeholder is a ghost painted on the wall. Respect the wall; question the ghost.

**Projection and frameworks.** We see what is; we project what we wish. Every observation arrives inside a framework, so there's no view from nowhere. But frameworks aren't all equal. Keep the one with the fewest anomalies, the one that fights Reality least.

**Pending.** Our label for anything unproven, ours included. Pending doesn't mean wrong. It means keep testing, and don't stop the merry-go-round for everyone else.

**The humble understanding.** Given our limitations, everything we know, we can't really "know." Two rights always create a wrong; two maybes don't. We use a framework we invented to define a Reality that created us. Hold it lightly, and keep looking.

title: There's Always Hope
dek: Why we resist reason and direction, and the pilot in the seat.
excerpt: Why we resist reason and direction, and the pilot in the seat.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

Every horseman knows the opposition reflex. Push on a horse and it pushes back, straight into the pressure. You don't get a horse to move by shoving it.

People are the same animal. Everything in these essays points to a human trait that likely goes back to the beginning: we resist rationality and direction. We're shown the evidence and we dig in. We're given good advice and we do the opposite. We have a brain, and we ignore it.

Why?

## Inertia with an opinion

Start further back than humans. Start with the stuff the universe is made of.

Newton's first law says a body keeps doing whatever it's doing until something forces it to change, and it resists the change. We call that inertia. Matter doesn't like being told where to go. And friction, motion meeting resistance, is where every shape in the universe comes from: the whirlpool, the star, the cell with a wall around it. Without resistance, nothing would hold its form.

So resisting direction isn't a design fault peculiar to people. It's the oldest rule in the universe, wearing a human face. Human resistance is inertia with an opinion.

## The membrane

But life is divergent in so many respects. A rock resists blindly: it pushes back against every shove equally, good or bad. Life can't afford that. It's fragile, with thin skin and short lives, so it needs to be thoughtful about survival.

The very first living cell already was. Its outer wall is what biologists call semi-permeable: it lets food and water in and keeps poison out. The immune system does the same on a grand scale, welcoming friends and fighting foes. That isn't stubbornness. It's judgement, built in from the start. Thoughtful resistance is life's primary strength within a body of weakness.

So there are two kinds of human resistance. Blind resistance, refusing every direction because it's direction, is just inertia: the rock in us. Thoughtful resistance, weighing each push, taking the good and refusing the leash, is the membrane in us. The trouble is that we so often fall back on the rock.

## Phantom hope

There's a further reason, and it's the most powerful of all: phantom hope, embedded in mythology, religion and ideology, provides a rationale for resistance. Why accept today's direction when you've been promised a better world: a paradise, a golden age restored, a revolution, a saviour on the way?

The Greeks put it in their oldest stories. In the poet Hesiod's telling, when Pandora opens her jar, every evil flies out into the world, and only hope stays inside. People have argued for 2,700 years over whether that was a gift or a cruel trick. In 1878 Nietzsche came down hard on one side: hope, he wrote, is the worst of evils, because it prolongs man's torment.

History has its examples. In 1890 many Lakota people took up the Ghost Dance, a new faith promising that the dance would bring back the buffalo, the dead and the old world. It ended in the massacre at Wounded Knee. Ideology has its own versions. Marx dismissed religion as "the opium of the people" in 1843, then offered a paradise of his own, always one more revolution away.

Not all hope is a phantom. The Czech playwright Václav Havel, who spent years in a communist prison, drew the line: real hope is not the conviction that something will turn out well, but the certainty that something makes sense, however it turns out. Phantom hope points over the Wall, to a promised world nobody can see. Real hope stays on this side.

## The machinery

It's a cruel and ironic twist, having a brain and ignoring it. But look at how the brain is built, and the twist starts to make sense.

**It predicts first and looks second.** A leading theory in neuroscience holds that perception is mostly the brain's own forecast of what's out there, with the senses mainly reporting where the forecast went wrong. We see what we expect, corrected only when reality shoves hard enough.

**It's expensive to run.** The brain is about 2 percent of the body's weight and burns about 20 percent of its energy. So it economises, running on habit and shortcut wherever it can. Rethinking a belief costs fuel, and the budget says no.

**Beliefs become body parts.** In a 2016 study, people's strong political beliefs were challenged while they lay in a brain scanner. The regions that lit up were ones tied to personal identity and to threat. A challenged belief is handled less like a wrong fact and more like an attack.

**It invents reasons after the fact.** Studying patients whose brain halves had been surgically separated, the neuroscientist Michael Gazzaniga found that the left half would confidently make up explanations for actions the other half had started. He called it "the interpreter." It doesn't know why we did something, so it tells a plausible story and believes it.

**It digs in when reality disagrees.** In 1954 the psychologist Leon Festinger studied a small group who believed a flood would end the world on a set date. When the date came and went, many of them became more fervent, not less. That's phantom hope defending itself.

And where reality is most uncertain, fantasy fills the gap. The anthropologist Bronisław Malinowski noticed in the 1920s that islanders in the western Pacific used no magic at all when fishing in their calm lagoon, but plenty when they sailed out onto the dangerous open sea. Baseball players are the same: hitters, who fail most of the time, are covered in lucky charms; fielders, who rarely fail, aren't.

## Pilot and autopilot

Put all of that together and you might decide we're machines that make excuses: the brain decides, and consciousness just narrates. That's bleak, and it isn't the whole story.

The self is partners with the brain, not part of it. The narrator, the interpreter spinning its stories, belongs to the brain. But when the neuroscientist Benjamin Libet found in the 1980s that the brain starts preparing a movement a moment before we feel we've decided, he also found that people could still stop the movement at the last instant. He called it "free won't." The veto belongs to the senior partner.

Think of a modern airliner. The autopilot flies most of the trip, and that's a good thing: it's tireless, steady and efficient. The partnership works as long as the pilot stays in the seat, watching the instruments and ready to take the controls. It goes wrong when the pilot stops paying attention and trusts the machine too far.

That's the self and the brain. Let the autopilot fly: the predictions, the habits, the shortcuts. But stay the pilot. Overrule the narrator when the story doesn't add up, and go looking for the errors the brain would rather not see. Having a brain and ignoring it is the cruel twist. Having a brain and supervising it is the escape.

These essays were written the same way. A person in the pilot's seat, choosing the destination, steering, and taking the controls when it matters. An AI on autopilot, doing the long, steady work of research and drafting, and sounding the alarm when a fact drifts off course.

## Teach your children well

So how does a person learn to be the pilot? The same way pilots do: in advance, before the storm.

Teach your children well. Help them understand how things happen in advance, and how important their powers can be. Show them, before anyone tries to fool them, how the brain predicts, takes shortcuts, defends its beliefs and invents excuses. Researchers call it prebunking, and it works: in studies around 2019, people who first played a short game showing how fake news is manufactured got noticeably better at spotting it afterwards. Tell them about their powers, too. A large American study in 2019 found that a short lesson teaching teenagers that the brain grows with effort modestly lifted the grades of the students who were struggling most.

We will never stop resisting. It goes all the way down, to the inertia in every grain of matter. Nor should we want to, because a creature that could be pushed anywhere would be pushed everywhere. But resistance can be blind or it can be thoughtful. It can serve a phantom or it can serve the truth. It can be the rock or the membrane.

The difference is whether there's a pilot in the seat. Teach the children, early, that there should be, and that it's them.

title: From What Can't Change to What Might
dek: Time, motion, and the only direction we can be sure of.
excerpt: Time, motion, and the only direction we can be sure of.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

Nine hundred years ago, the Persian astronomer and poet Omar Khayyam wrote a verse that every English schoolchild once knew, in Edward FitzGerald's 1859 translation:

_The Moving Finger writes; and, having writ,
Moves on: nor all thy Piety nor Wit
Shall lure it back to cancel half a Line,
Nor all thy Tears wash out a Word of it._

What's done is done. Everybody knows that. The harder question is the other half: where is the finger going?

## Does time have direction?

In these essays, time isn't a thing. It's our name for motion and change, the counting of things moving. But as a companion of motion, time does have direction. We just don't know what it is. That's what's worth exploring.

Physics has its own version of the puzzle. Almost all its basic laws work just as well run backwards: film two billiard balls colliding, play the film in reverse, and nothing looks wrong. In 1927 the astronomer Arthur Eddington gave the puzzle its name, "the arrow of time," and pinned it on the one law that does seem to care which way the film runs: things run down, spread out and fall apart. An egg breaks; it never unbreaks.

Notice where the direction actually lives. It isn't in time. It's in what happens.

## What can't change

The road behind is fixed. Things break and stuff happens, and what has broken stays broken. The past is the record of it all, and nothing can rewrite a line.

Even our picture of the past is fixed in a stranger way than most people realise. The oldest light in the sky, the faint afterglow of the early universe, left its source more than 13 billion years ago. The glowing gas that sent it is long gone, turned into stars and galaxies. We are looking at a photograph of a scene that no longer exists, and we even set our cosmic speedometer by it.

In 1843 the Danish philosopher Søren Kierkegaard put the human side of it in one sentence: life can only be understood backwards, but it must be lived forwards. Understanding belongs to what can't change. Living belongs to what might.

## Running down

So where is it all heading? The standard answer is gloomy.

In 1852 the Scottish physicist William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, published a short paper arguing that nature has a universal tendency to run down: heat spreads out, differences even out, and useful energy drains away. Followed to its end, the universe winds up cold, even and still, with nothing left to happen. Later writers called it the "heat death."

It's a respectable forecast. It's also a farmer's forecast: a single destination, written down in advance, for a universe nobody has ever seen finish anything. By our usual rule, it's pending.

## Pockets of order

Because something doesn't fit. If everything is running down, why is the universe full of things running _up_?

Out of all that breakage, stars form. Planets form. Life forms, and in at least one place, minds. In 1944 the physicist Erwin Schrödinger, in a little book called _What Is Life?_, put his finger on it: a living thing keeps itself in order by feeding on the order around it, pushing its disorder out into the world. The overall tally of breakage still rises, but inside the flow, pockets of astonishing order keep appearing.

In 1977 the Belgian chemist Ilya Prigogine won a Nobel Prize for showing how this happens. Wherever energy flows through matter, as heat flows through a pan of water on the stove, order can form spontaneously: swirls, cells, patterns, holding their shape as long as the flow continues. A whirlpool in a draining sink is the simplest example. It exists because the water is running down, not in spite of it.

So the direction isn't simply "down." Disorder rises overall, and order keeps forming in the current. Both at once.

## What might

Is the road ahead already written, just waiting to be read? For a long time, the best minds thought so.

In 1814 the French mathematician Pierre-Simon Laplace imagined a vast intellect that knew the position and motion of every particle in the universe. For such a mind, he wrote, nothing would be uncertain, and the future, like the past, would be present before its eyes. It was the clockwork universe in its purest form.

The clock broke in 1963. The American meteorologist Edward Lorenz, running a simple weather model on an early computer, found that a tiny change in the starting numbers, a rounding error, sent the forecast somewhere completely different. Nine years later he gave a talk with a title that became famous: "Does the flap of a butterfly's wings in Brazil set off a tornado in Texas?" Whatever the deepest truth, in practice the future can't be read far in advance, because we can never measure the present precisely enough, and the smallest flutter changes everything.

Aristotle had sensed it more than 2,300 years ago. A statement like "there will be a sea battle tomorrow," he argued, isn't yet true or false. It's waiting.

The cosmos agrees. Our galaxy is falling toward the Great Attractor, a vast concentration of matter hidden behind the dust of our own Milky Way, and the Attractor itself seems to be drawn toward something bigger still. Currents within currents, with no known final destination.

## The direction

So here is the one direction we can be sure of. It isn't a place. It's from whatever can't change to whatever might.

Behind us is everything that has already broken: fixed, recorded, photographed, finished. Ahead is everything that hasn't yet: open, unwritten, full of currents and whirlpools and pockets of order nobody can predict. And the only place anything ever changes is the narrow present in between, the pilot's seat, where the moving finger writes.

It's odd, then, that physics spends most of its effort looking back and down instead of out and away: back to the first instant, down to ever-smaller particles. The past holds still long enough to be measured, and for a century the smallest pieces have carried the biggest prizes. But in 1972 the physicist Philip Anderson, who later won a Nobel Prize himself, published a short essay called "More Is Different." At each new level, he argued, from particles to chemistry to life to minds, genuinely new rules appear, and you can never get them just by taking things apart. Knowing every brick doesn't tell you what the cathedral is for. The interesting road doesn't run back and down. It runs out and away.

That's why the road ahead is more interesting than the road behind. The road behind can only be understood. The road ahead can still be lived.

title: This Isn't the Garden of Eden
dek: Why the oldest story we tell is a story about leaving.
excerpt: Why the oldest story we tell is a story about leaving.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

Everybody carries a picture of the garden.

For some it's the good old days, when neighbours knew each other and the doors were never locked. For some it's the promised land, still ahead, just over the next hill. For some it's the perfect society, one election or one revolution away. For some it's simply peace: the quiet that will surely come after this war, the last war, is won.

It's the oldest hope we have, and it's built into the oldest story we tell. Once upon a time there was a garden, and in the garden there was no conflict, no toil and no death. Then something went wrong, and we were sent out.

This essay starts from a plain fact that the hope keeps hiding. This isn't the Garden of Eden. It never was. And if we read the old story carefully, the people who first told it knew that better than we do.

## What the old story says

Read the first chapters of Genesis slowly, in the old King James words, and they stop sounding like a fairy tale. They start sounding like a memory.

In the garden, the food grows on trees: "Of every tree of the garden thou mayest freely eat." Then comes the forbidden tree, the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Adam and Eve eat, and the first thing that happens isn't punishment. It's awareness: "the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked." A creature sees itself for the first time.

Then the sentence is passed, and listen to what it actually is. "Thou shalt eat the herb of the field. In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread." From the fruit of the trees to the plants of the field. From picking to toil. And bread is made from wheat and barley, which are grasses. The curse is the move from the trees to the grass, in so many words. Behind them, the way back is barred by a flaming sword.

The next chapter finishes the thought. "Abel was a keeper of sheep, but Cain was a tiller of the ground." The farmer kills the herder. Cain is cursed to be "a fugitive and a vagabond," settles in the land of Nod, east of Eden, and builds the first city.

In three short chapters you get the trees, self-awareness, the grass, farming, murder and the city. That's the whole human journey, told by people with no fossils, no climate records and no DNA, only memory and story. _Perhaps_ that's what myth is: a species remembering its past with the only instrument it had.

## Creatures of the edge

The science tells a similar story, with one important twist.

The old textbook picture had our ancestors climbing down from the trees and striding out onto the open savannah for good. The newer picture is messier. Early humans lived on the edge, in a patchwork of woodland and grassland that came and went as the climate swung back and forth. Lucy, found in Ethiopia in 1974 and 3.2 million years old, walked upright on the ground but still had long, curved fingers and strong arms for climbing. In 2016 a team of scientists argued that she died falling out of a tree.

So we were never savannah creatures who left the trees behind. We were creatures of the edge, built for both and never fully committed to either.

That's where the war without end begins: not on a battlefield, but inside one skull. The tree in us wants shelter, the band and staying put. The grass in us wants open ground, ranging and risk. Neither ever surrendered to the other. The first division is in our consciousness, and every conflict since has been that division turned outward.

## Domesticated

For the hunter, life was judged by outcomes. The hunt succeeded or it failed. The river was crossed or it wasn't. The band ate, or it went hungry. Nature handed out results, not verdicts. Nobody was wicked for missing the deer.

Then came the fields. The word "domesticate" comes from the Latin _domus_, a house, and that's exactly what farming did. It brought everything indoors: the wheat, the sheep, the dog, and in the end the people too. And it brought success and failure indoors with them, and turned them into something else: good and evil.

A farmer can't judge by the hunt. He needs rules that hold from one season to the next: whose field this is, whose ox, whose wife, whose well. The commandments give the game away. "Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house… nor his ox, nor his ass." You need a house, an ox and a neighbour before that law makes any sense.

The German philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche noticed the shift in 1887. He argued that the oldest morality was "good and bad," meaning strong or weak, well done or badly done, and that it was later replaced by "good and evil," a verdict on the soul. Put the split where it belongs: success and failure are the hunter's outcomes, and good and evil are the farmer's abstractions.

And remember which tree Adam and Eve ate from. It was the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. _Perhaps_ the knowledge of good and evil is the farmer's knowledge.

## Keeping the peace

Once the conflict was inside us and the fields were fenced, every group faced the same problem: how to keep the peace. Each size of group found its own answer, and each answer was the original conflict in a new costume.

**Tribes make rules.** A band of hunters, rarely more than about 150 people, the most a human can know face to face, keeps order up close. Anthropologists have found that such bands cut bullies down to size with ridicule, then shunning, and in the end by force. And when a quarrel can't be settled, one side often simply packs up and moves camp. A hunter can walk away.

**Nations establish compulsion.** A farmer can't walk away: his fields, his house and his dead are in the ground. So once people settled in the thousands, the rules had to be written down and enforced by people nobody knew. Around 1750 BC, Hammurabi of Babylon carved his laws in stone so that justice would prevail in the land, the wicked and the evil would be destroyed, and the strong would not oppress the weak. Good and evil were now law, backed by the king. In 1793 revolutionary France went a step further and declared every French citizen permanently requisitioned for the war effort. The peace inside the border was kept by compulsion, and the conflict was shipped out to the border.

**Religions create crusades.** The largest groups of all are held together by nothing but shared belief, and belief can mobilise people no king could reach. In 1095 Pope Urban II stood in a field at Clermont in France and called Christendom to war in the East, and the crowd answered, "God wills it." The original conflict now had a god on its side.

The prophets dreamed of the opposite: "They shall beat their swords into plowshares." But notice what that picture is: a farm. Peace, as the settled imagine it, is a quiet field where nothing moves. The Roman historian Tacitus knew what that looked like when an empire delivered it. He gave the line to a British chieftain facing the legions: "They make a desert and call it peace."

## Us and them

Underneath every rule, every law and every crusade lies the oldest line of all: the one between us and them.

It's written into our names. The Inuit call themselves Inuit, "the people." The Navajo call themselves Diné, "the people." The ancient Greeks called everyone else _barbaroi_, because foreign speech sounded to them like "bar-bar." The Chinese called their land the Middle Kingdom, the centre of the world. Nearly every people has put itself at the middle of the map. In 1906 an American sociologist popularised a name for the habit: ethnocentrism.

It doesn't take a history to start it, either. In the 1970s, psychologists split schoolboys into two groups on a pretext as thin as which of two painters they preferred. The boys favoured their own group anyway, even though they didn't know who else was in it, over a difference that meant nothing at all.

That's why the line never fades. Empires rise and fall, faiths split and merge, borders are redrawn, but the line is redrawn with them. It doesn't need a reason. It only needs a difference, and there is always a difference.

## Same war, new battlefields

Follow the line through history and it behaves like a river.

It rises in Eden, with the trees and the grass and the farmer who kills the herder. It runs through ancient Israel, where one people with one faith split into two kingdoms, Israel in the north and Judah in the south, and fought each other. In Rome it becomes Christian, when an emperor legalises the faith in 313 and the creed is fixed in 325. In Aachen, where Charlemagne ruled and German kings were crowned for six hundred years, it becomes imperial. In the German town of Worms it turns geopolitical, twice: in 1122, when pope and emperor divide the bishop's staff from the king's sword, and in 1521, when Luther refuses to recant before the emperor. At Westminster it becomes purely political: Parliament makes Henry VIII head of the church in 1534, and in 1649 Charles I is tried there and beheaded a few days later, a short walk away in Whitehall. Then it sails for America, and runs on through Appomattox to the evening news.

Imagine pouring a different coloured dye into that river for each of the old frameworks. A thousand years downstream, at the river's mouth, they would still be running side by side, unmixed.

The war stays the same. Only the battlefields and the dialects change. It's fought in the language of theology at Worms, of law at Westminster, of politics at Appomattox, and of culture today. Underneath, it's the same quarrel each time: authority against conscience, the settled against the free, the farmer against the hunter, the tree in us against the grass.

## A condition, not a disease

So this isn't really a story about war. It's about conflict, and conflict isn't an event. It's a condition.

Wars are the weather; conflict is the climate. Storms come and go, and the climate stays. Two and a half thousand years ago the Greek philosopher Heraclitus put it in a single line: "War is the father of all." Curiosity and conflict are both friction with the unknown, and friction is what gives everything its shape: the whirlpool, the star, the living cell. Take them away and you don't get paradise. You get nothing at all.

But conflict and violence are cousins, not twins. Conflict is the tension; violence is only one way of settling it. A hunting band can quarrel and walk away. It's settled people, unable to leave and bound together by flags and creeds, who turn friction into slaughter, because they can kill a stranger for an abstraction. Only a community could have fought the Thirty Years' War, or Gettysburg, or the Somme.

And a condition isn't a disease. You don't cure it; you live with it, the way you live with gravity. That's the trouble with every promised Eden, whether it's sacred or secular. Each one treats the human condition as an illness that the right faith, the right law or the right revolution will finally cure. Peace, in that sense, is a farmer's fantasy.

The ancients understood that conflict was an unavoidable feature of existence, and they blamed it on flaws in human nature. So look where every Eden has been put. The Sumerians, long before Genesis, placed their paradise, Dilmun, where "the lion kills not," in the distant past. The Hebrew prophets moved it to the future: "The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb." The philosophers put it in the eternal, unchanging heavens, and the Stoics inside a calm mind, because the world outside was at war. Later thinkers promised it at the end of history. Peace has always been a feature of then and again. Never now.

## Telling it again

Like everything we write, this is offered as something to consider, not something to accept. Where an idea is our best guess rather than an established fact, we've said so: _pending_, or _perhaps_.

There's a reason for telling it as a story at all. Science piles up; every generation stands on the shoulders of the last. Wisdom doesn't. Every child starts from zero and has to learn for themselves what the ancients already knew. The ancients understood that, which is why they didn't store their wisdom in formulas. They stored it in stories, Eden among them, and told them again and again.

So here is the story again, told plainly and without the promise at the end. This isn't the Garden of Eden. It never was, and it was never going to be.

We are creatures of the edge, half tree and half grass, and we always will be. The war inside us can't be won. It can only be kept honest.

Reality doesn't take sides. Things break, stuff happens, and every generation inherits the same war in new clothes. There's no promised land at the end of the river. There's only the river.

Life is a hunt, not a harvest. Nothing is guaranteed, nothing stays won, and peace is only the pause between seasons. That isn't a tragedy. It's what being alive is.

No one is coming to save us, and no one needs to. Curiosity and conflict, success and failure: that's the whole of it, and it's enough.

title: What Do We Really Know?
dek: The smooth universe is the biggest assumption in science. It is time to stop treating it as a fact.
excerpt: The smooth universe is the biggest assumption in science. It is time to stop treating it as a fact.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

Ask an astronomer what the universe is, and the answer comes back without hesitation. Thirteen point eight billion years old. Expanding, and speeding up. Five percent ordinary matter, 27 percent dark matter, 68 percent dark energy. And on the largest scales, smooth.

Look up. Nothing is smooth. Stars in galaxies. Galaxies in clusters. Clusters strung on filaments around vast empty voids. All of it spinning, falling, colliding.

So what do we really know?

## What "smooth" means

Not calm. Not still. Average.

Take a big enough cube of space, a few hundred million light-years on a side, and every cube is supposed to look like every other. The ocean looks flat from orbit, even in a gale.

The evidence is one thing. The afterglow of the early universe arrives at the same temperature from every direction, to about one part in a hundred thousand.

The idea itself was not discovered. It was chosen. In the 1920s Alexander Friedmann and Georges Lemaître set out to apply Einstein's equations to the whole universe. In full, the equations could not be solved. So they made the universe the same everywhere and in every direction. Then they could. In the 1930s the British astrophysicist Edward Milne named it "the cosmological principle," and a convenience became a foundation.

The universe was made smooth because the mathematics needed it.

## The wall

We see only our own patch: the region light has had time to cross. Beyond its edge, no instrument will ever reach.

So "smooth" makes two claims. Our patch looks even when averaged; that can be tested. Everything beyond the edge looks like here; that can never be tested.

In these essays we have a name for such a place: an SOB, a **scientific observational boundary**. The Big Bang, the inside of a black hole and the self are all SOBs: places where our methods run out and something surely lies beyond. An SOB is a wall. A placeholder is a ghost painted on it.

The edge of the observable universe is the SOB of all SOBs. The smooth universe is the biggest ghost on the biggest wall in science.

## What rests on it

Almost everything.

The age of the universe comes from running a smooth model backwards. The expansion rate comes from fitting one to the data. Where the model failed, ingredients were added.

Galaxies spin too fast for the matter we can see in them. So dark matter was added: 27 percent of everything. Hunted for about fifty years. Never found.

In 1998, distant exploding stars looked too dim. So dark energy was added: 68 percent of everything. Never detected directly.

The afterglow was too even for regions that could never have been in contact. So in 1980 the physicist Alan Guth proposed inflation, an unseen burst of expansion in the first instant. Never observed.

Run the model back to the start and the equations go to infinity and break. That instant is called the Big Bang. It is where the mathematics gives out, not something anyone has seen.

What is observed is light from distant galaxies stretched toward the red, more the farther they are. Galaxies moving apart is the strong reading of that. "Space itself stretching" is the model's story about it. Edwin Hubble, who found the pattern, spent years calling them only "apparent velocities."

Then there is the Andromeda exception. The first galaxy ever to have its speed measured, by the American astronomer Vesto Slipher in 1912, was Andromeda, our nearest large neighbour. Its light was stretched not toward the red but toward the blue. It is coming toward us, at about 110 kilometres a second. Close to home, gravity wins and galaxies fall together. The universe's first measured motion was not expansion. It was approach.

One assumption at the top. A ghost at every bend below it. About 95 percent of the standard universe is made of things no one has ever detected.

## The cracks

**Structures too big to exist.** Under the smooth model, nothing should be much larger than about 1.2 billion light-years. In 2021 Alexia Lopez, a PhD student at the University of Central Lancashire, reported the Giant Arc, about 3.3 billion light-years long. In 2024 she reported the Big Ring, about 1.3 billion across. Both are disputed. If either holds, smoothness fails.

**Dark energy as an error.** In December 2024 a New Zealand team led by David Wiltshire analysed 1,535 exploding stars. Drop the smoothness assumption, they reported, and the need for dark energy disappears. "Dark energy is a misidentification." Contested. _Pending._

**A placeholder that won't sit still.** In March 2025 the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument reported growing evidence that dark energy changes over time. "Is it just that we are missing something big in the model of our universe and we just don't know it?" asked Mustapha Ishak, one of its leaders.

**Numbers that won't agree.** The two main measurements of the expansion rate differ by about 9 percent. Years of checking have not closed the gap.

## Einstein, at home and abroad

Fairness requires one distinction.

At home, Einstein's gravity has passed every test: Mercury's orbit in 1915, starlight bending in the eclipse of 1919, the GPS in your phone, gravitational waves in 2015, the shadow of a black hole in 2019.

Abroad, stretched across the universe, it works only with an untestable assumption and invisible ingredients making up 95 percent of the total.

That is not a theory of how the universe moves. It is a patchwork that keeps a theory standing.

The fault may not be Einstein's. His genius may have been greater than his heirs have grasped. He thought in pictures: riding a beam of light, falling in a closed lift. "Imagination is more important than knowledge," he said in 1929. The equations came after the thinking. His successors reversed the order. They took the equations, solved what could be solved, and wrote the stories to fit.

Einstein himself doubted some of those stories. In 1939 he published a paper arguing that the black holes his equations seemed to allow could not form in nature. And a colleague recalled him saying, "Since the mathematicians have invaded the theory of relativity, I do not understand it myself any more."

The math is not the problem. The narratives are.

## Why is this allowed?

Nobody is lying. The causes are ordinary, which is why they last.

**The math must be solvable.** A smooth universe gives clean answers. A lumpy one does not. Choose the solvable fiction often enough and you forget you chose.

**"It works."** No other venue accepts this excuse. A doctor whose remedy seemed to work is not excused a wrong diagnosis. A banker whose books balance is not excused invented entries. Ptolemy's earth-centred heavens predicted the planets for some 1,400 years. They worked. They were wrong. When Copernicus's book appeared in 1543, an unsigned preface told readers its ideas need not be true, only useful for calculation. Physics has lived on that bargain ever since. "It works" justifies a tool. It does not justify a story.

**Anomalies are shelved.** In 1962 the historian Thomas Kuhn described "normal science": puzzles solved inside an accepted frame, misfits set aside until they pile too high. They are piling.

**Careers are invested.** Telescopes, grants and reputations are built to measure the model's own numbers. As Upton Sinclair wrote in 1934, "It is difficult to get a man to understand something, when his salary depends upon his not understanding it."

**The treasure is spent.** For nearly forty years, detectors have waited in deep mines for a single particle of dark matter. Every one has come up empty. Each failure has been answered with a bigger detector. In 2023 Europe launched Euclid, built largely to study dark matter and dark energy, for about 1.4 billion euros. In 2014 a team at the South Pole announced the fingerprint of inflation to front-page headlines. Within a year it was shown to be dust in our own galaxy.

It is the old joke of the man hunting for his keys under a streetlight, not because he dropped them there, but because that is where the light is. Cosmology's version: when the keys aren't found, apply for a bigger lamp. This is public money. Too much of it goes to confirming **fairy tales** rather than asking what really happened.

**Ideas die with their owners.** Max Planck wrote that a new scientific truth wins not by convincing its opponents, but because they eventually die.

**And beneath it all, a wish.** Aristotle's perfect heavens. Newton's clockwork. Einstein's static universe, held still in 1917 by a term added for the purpose, until observation showed the galaxies on the move. The smooth universe is the same wish: a tidy, tranquil cosmos. It has never been true.

## What we really know

Strip away the assumption and the placeholders.

We know our patch of the universe is lumpy and in motion, at least up to hundreds of millions of light-years, perhaps far beyond. We know the afterglow is remarkably even. We know Einstein's gravity works close to home. We know that the farther away a galaxy is, the more its light is stretched toward the red, and the best reading of that is that distant galaxies are moving apart, the farther the faster. We know our best measurements of the rate disagree.

We do not know what lies beyond the edge. We do not know what 95 percent of the standard universe is, or whether it exists. We do not know that the universe is smooth.

This has to stop. Not the looking. The pretending.

Assumptions must be labelled as assumptions. Placeholders must have deadlines. Failure must count as evidence. And the public that pays must be told plainly what is known and what is only hoped.

Until then, the honest answer to "what do we really know?" is short. Less than we're told.

Respect the wall. Question the ghost.

title: The Universe Is Filled with Questions
dek: Answers are hard come by.
excerpt: Answers are hard come by.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

Every child goes through a season of "why?"

Why is the sky blue? Why do dogs bark? Why do people die? Why is there anything at all? The questions come faster than any parent can answer them, and sooner or later the parent says what parents have always said: "Because." Or, "That's just the way it is." Or, in desperation, "Go and ask your mother."

Then the season ends. The child goes to school, where questions come with answers attached, printed at the back of the book. Somewhere along the way most of us learn that the point of a question is to get rid of it as fast as possible. It's an odd thing to teach a survivor, because the instinct to question is the _sine qua non_ of survival.

The universe never learned that lesson. It is filled with questions. Answers are hard come by.

## The open questions

Here is a short list of things nobody knows. Not "nobody in this village." Nobody on Earth.

**Why is there something rather than nothing?** The German philosopher Gottfried Leibniz asked it in 1714. Three centuries later, no one has an answer that isn't a restatement of the question.

**What is time?** Around the year 400, St Augustine wrote: "What then is time? If no one asks me, I know; if I wish to explain it to one that asketh, I know not." Physics still can't do much better.

**How did life begin?** Life on Earth goes back well over three billion years. How chemistry first became biology, nobody knows. No laboratory has ever made life from non-life.

**What is consciousness?** We can trace every signal in the brain up to the point where someone experiences it, and there the trail stops. In 1995 the philosopher David Chalmers called this "the hard problem." It's still hard.

**Why does mathematics describe the world at all?** In 1960 the physicist Eugene Wigner wrote an essay on what he called "the unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics." Numbers were invented to count sheep and keep accounts. Nobody knows why they also describe the orbits of planets.

**Are we alone?** In 1950, over lunch, the physicist Enrico Fermi asked a simple question about all those billions of stars and all that time: "Where is everybody?" No one has answered him.

**What is most of the universe made of?** The standard account says 95 percent is dark matter and dark energy. Nobody has ever caught either.

And beyond them all are the walls. In these essays we have a name for them: SOBs, **scientific observational boundaries**. The first instant of the universe, the inside of a black hole, the edge of what can be seen, and the self that does the seeing are all places where our methods run out, though something surely lies beyond. The questions on the far side of an SOB may not just be unanswered. They may be unanswerable.

## What an answer costs

The question comes from the senses. The answer comes from experience, if we live that long. Real answers do come. But look at the price.

Around 1637 the French lawyer Pierre de Fermat scribbled in the margin of a book that he had a marvellous proof of a simple-looking claim about numbers, but the margin was too small to hold it. The best mathematicians in the world chased it for over three and a half centuries. The English mathematician Andrew Wiles finally proved it in the mid-1990s, after seven years of near-solitary work, a published flaw, and another year of repair.

Einstein predicted ripples in space in 1916. The first one was caught in 2015, almost a hundred years later, by detectors four kilometres long that could sense a change smaller than the width of a proton.

The Higgs particle was proposed in 1964 and found in 2012, after forty-eight years and the largest machine ever built.

And even a right answer can wait a lifetime to be heard. In 1847 a Hungarian doctor in Vienna, Ignaz Semmelweis, showed that if doctors washed their hands, far fewer mothers died after childbirth. His colleagues mocked him. He died in an asylum in 1865, two decades before germ theory proved him right. In 1912 the German scientist Alfred Wegener proposed that the continents drift. He was ridiculed for half a century. The evidence came in the 1960s, thirty years after he died on the Greenland ice.

Sometimes an answer comes cheap: Eratosthenes measured the Earth with a stick and a shadow. But mostly an answer costs years, fortunes, reputations and sometimes lives. And even then, it has to be paid for twice: once to find it, and once to get people to believe it.

## Counterfeit answers

If real answers are that expensive, it's no wonder people print their own.

The human mind hates an open question. Psychologists have a name for the itch: the need for closure. Under pressure, people will grab a quick, firm answer, even a wrong one, rather than live with "I don't know." The brain even manufactures answers on its own. Its "interpreter," which we met in an earlier essay, invents reasons after the fact and believes them.
