So the gaps fill up. In the old days they filled with gods: thunder was an angry sky-father, plague was a punishment. Late in the 1800s a Scottish preacher, Henry Drummond, warned believers against this habit of filling the gaps in knowledge with God, because each time science closed a gap, God retreated. People came to call it the God of the gaps.

Science has its own version. For most of the 1800s, physicists were certain that light travelled through an invisible substance filling all of space, the "luminiferous ether." Nobody had ever detected it, but the equations seemed to need it. In 1887 two Americans, Albert Michelson and Edward Morley, built an exquisite instrument to measure Earth's motion through it. They found nothing. Within twenty years the ether was gone. Today's dark matter and dark energy may yet be found, like Neptune, or may yet go the way of the ether.

A counterfeit answer is worse than no answer. It closes the question. It stops the looking. And it carries the authority of a real answer, until the day it doesn't.

## Living with the questions

The alternative isn't despair. It's a skill, and an old one.

Socrates is remembered for saying that the only thing he knew was that he knew nothing. He wasn't being modest. He was being accurate. When the oracle at Delphi declared that no one in Athens was wiser than he, he concluded that this was the reason: he alone knew how little he knew.

In 1817 the young English poet John Keats, writing to his brothers, named the quality he most admired in great minds. He called it "negative capability": being "capable of being in uncertainties, Mysteries, doubts, without any irritable reaching after fact and reason." That irritable reaching is exactly what produces counterfeit answers.

In 1903 the poet Rainer Maria Rilke wrote to a young man who was troubled by questions he couldn't resolve. Be patient, he told him, and "try to love the questions themselves." Live the questions now, and perhaps one day you will live your way into the answer.

And in 1981 the American physicist Richard Feynman, who had a Nobel Prize and every reason for confidence, told a television interviewer: "I can live with doubt and uncertainty and not knowing. I think it's much more interesting to live not knowing than to have answers which might be wrong."

A philosopher, a poet, another poet and a physicist, all saying the same thing: hold the question open. In these essays we have a plain word for it. When we don't know, we say _pending_, or _maybe_. It's the most honest word in the language, and the hardest to say.

## Keep asking

So perhaps the child had it right all along.

The season of "why?" isn't something to grow out of. It's the one time in life when we meet the universe on its own terms: full of questions, short of answers, and in no hurry to hand them over. School teaches us that every question has an answer at the back of the book. The universe has no back of the book.

Real answers come, but slowly and at a price, and often decades after the people who found them are gone. Cheap answers come quickly, and they are nearly always counterfeit. The difference between the two is usually just patience: the willingness to say "I don't know" and keep looking.

The universe is filled with questions. Answers are hard come by. The easy ones are usually wrong. Keep asking why.

The last question is always why.

title: Why We Stay Stupid
dek: The givens of existence are few and never change. Why can't we learn them?
excerpt: The givens of existence are few and never change. Why can't we learn them?
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

The variables of modern life are countless. Prices, rules, machines, news, opinions: they change by the hour, and we track them all.

The givens of existence are few, and they never change. We die. Things break. Nothing stays won. No one is coming to explain it all. The Stanford psychiatrist Irvin Yalom counted four in 1980: death, freedom, isolation, and the absence of any meaning handed to us ready-made.

We have been writing these things down for as long as we have been writing anything. The epic of Gilgamesh, set down some four thousand years ago, is about a king who refuses to accept death, chases immortality to the ends of the earth, loses it, and comes home. The book of Ecclesiastes sighs that "there is no new thing under the sun." Every generation since has said the same things again.

And every generation hears them as if for the first time.

We can master the variables. We cannot seem to learn the givens. This essay is about why.

## The wagon

Start with the machine we are using.

The oldest fossils of our species, found in Morocco, are about 300,000 years old. In all that time the human brain has barely changed. The brain that carves a spear and the brain that writes software are the same brain.

Everything else has changed beyond recognition. Writing is about 5,000 years old. Printing is less than 600. Mass schooling is about 200. The smartphone in your pocket is younger than most of the people carrying it. Culture and technology have done in a few thousand years what evolution takes millions of years to do.

The American biologist E. O. Wilson put the result in one sentence in 2009: "We have Paleolithic emotions, medieval institutions and godlike technology."

We have strapped a jet engine to a toy wagon, and we expect it to carry the load.

## The overload

The wagon shakes.

The body's stress system was built for short emergencies: a predator, a fall, a fight. It surges, we act, it switches off. Modern threats are abstract and never end: the bills, the deadlines, the news. So the alarm stays on. Over time, constant stress wears down the part of the brain that files memories and strengthens the part that runs fear.

Worse, stress takes the pilot out of the seat. Research led by Amy Arnsten at Yale has shown that even mild stress quickly impairs the prefrontal cortex, the part of the brain that reasons, plans and takes in new ideas. Other studies show that under stress the brain abandons deliberate thinking and falls back on habit. Learning needs the pilot. Overload hands the controls to the autopilot.

The workbench is small to begin with. Working memory, where we hold new ideas while we make sense of them, holds about four things at once. Pile on more and learning doesn't speed up. It stops.

Our reward circuits were built to chase new information when it was scarce. Now it is endless, and attention on a screen lasts, on average, well under a minute before it moves on. The brain also weighs bad news more heavily than good, which made sense on the savannah, so a constant stream of bad news keeps it in low-grade alarm. And the screens steal the sleep in which the day's learning is filed.

Overload doesn't make us learn more. It drives the brain back to its oldest, safest circuits: fear, habit and the tribe.

## The water

Even without the overload, the givens would be hard to see.

The nervous system is built to detect change, not to dwell on what stays the same. Walk into a house and you smell it. Live there a week and you don't. A constant sound fades from hearing; a constant pressure fades from touch. Whatever never changes, the brain stops reporting.

The givens are the most constant things in life. Death, change and conflict have been here every day of every life. So the brain does with them what it does with the smell of the house. It stops noticing.

In 2005 the novelist David Foster Wallace opened a commencement speech with a story. Two young fish are swimming along when an older fish passes and says, "Morning, boys. How's the water?" The young fish swim on a while, and then one turns to the other and asks, "What the hell is water?"

The givens are the water.

## The gatekeeper

But it goes further than not noticing. When the givens do get through, something in the brain refuses them.

In 2019 researchers at Bar-Ilan University in Israel used the brain's "surprise" signal, which fires whenever a pattern it has learned is broken. They paired faces with words like "grave" and "funeral." When the face was a stranger's, the brain learned the link, and fired surprise when the pattern broke. When the face was the person's own, the signal never came. The brain's prediction machinery simply declined to connect the self with death. The researchers titled their paper "Prediction-based neural mechanisms for shielding the self from existential threat."

The neuroscientist Tali Sharot found a second gate. People readily update their beliefs when they hear good news about their own future, and barely at all when they hear bad. In 2012 her team used magnetic pulses to briefly disrupt a region of the frontal lobe, and the bias vanished. People took in bad news about themselves as readily as good. The refusal isn't carelessness. It is a function, and it has a location.

Neurology offers the starkest case. After certain strokes on the right side of the brain, patients paralysed down their left side flatly deny it. They insist the arm moves, and invent reasons why it isn't moving just now. Squirt cold water into the left ear, and the denial briefly lifts. The patient admits the paralysis, and later forgets having admitted it.

Why would evolution build a mind that refuses the truth about itself? In 2013 the American biologist Ajit Varki and his colleague Danny Brower offered an answer in a book called _Denial_. A creature that fully grasped its own inevitable death might simply stop striving. So human self-awareness, they argue, could only evolve if it came packaged with the power to deny mortality. The gatekeeper is the price of the mind.

It isn't that we fail to learn the givens. We are built to refuse them.

## Certainty and curiosity

So inside every head two forces pull against each other.

One is certainty. It wants the world settled, the questions closed and the bad news kept out. It is the gatekeeper, the habit and the comforting story. It keeps a creature calm and functioning today.

The other is curiosity. It is wired into the same reward system that drives hunger. In 2009 researchers found that monkeys' dopamine neurons fire for advance information about a reward, even when knowing early changes nothing about what they will get. Knowing is its own reward. Babies stare longest at whatever is new. Every animal that forages must choose, again and again, between exploiting the patch it knows and exploring the one it doesn't.

Both are biological. But they play different games. Certainty plays the short game: survive the moment. Curiosity plays the long game: survive change.

Culture takes sides. The citadel, with its doctrines, institutions and settled answers, is built on certainty. It does not quietly bury the givens. It denies them, explicitly and out loud: in creeds, in curricula, in the confident voice of authority. Death is not the end. Conflict can be abolished. The universe is smooth and settled. Peace is coming. That is why the same old truths are said and unsaid for thousands of years. Every time they are spoken, the citadel answers no.

But the world always changes eventually, and a species that stops exploring is stranded when it does. Certainty wins the day. Curiosity wins the age. In the end the jungle trumps the citadel, and the biological imperative outlasts the cultural one.

## Why we stay stupid

Put it together, step by step.

We run a 300,000-year-old brain in a world a few thousand years old. The world overloads it, and overload knocks out the part that learns. The brain is built to notice change, so the givens, which never change, fade from view. When they do break through, a gatekeeper in the brain turns them away, because a mind that fully faced them might stop striving. And the citadel takes the gatekeeper's quiet refusal and turns it into loud, official denial.

That is why we stay stupid. Not for lack of brains, but by design.

It is a war: the man and the machine. And the machine is one thing, not two. The gatekeeper in every skull is the citadel in miniature; the citadel is the gatekeeper built in stone. Against it stands the man, the curious creature underneath, the one who still asks why.

It is also why the old truths keep returning. The gatekeeper can turn them away, and the citadel can deny them, but neither can kill them, because they are true. Each generation meets them again, as if for the first time, and a few in each generation let them in.

Those few are the curious. The world has always cost them dearly: Socrates, Bruno, Semmelweis, Wegener. They have been mocked, locked away, poisoned and burned. But they are the species' long game, and the long game is the only one that wins.

The English poet Alfred Tennyson gave the curious their creed in 1842, in the voice of old Ulysses setting out once more: "To strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield."

title: Two
dek: Why everything that exists comes in pairs, and the riddle of what didn't Bang.
excerpt: Why everything that exists comes in pairs, and the riddle of what didn't Bang.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

Look around and count.

Up and down. Left and right. Night and day. True and false. Plus and minus. North and south. Life and death. Mom and Dad.

Everywhere we look, at every scale, in matter, in living things, in thought and in language, reality comes in twos. Not in threes, not in fives, not in tens. In pairs.

Why? Why should two, of all numbers, be the basic integer of existence? And if everything that exists comes in pairs, what came before the first pair? What was there before anything split in two? What didn't Bang?

Those are big questions. Let's take them in order.

## The oldest observers

The ancients noticed first.

The Greek philosopher Heraclitus, around 500 BC, saw opposites everywhere, and saw them bound together: "The road up and the road down are one and the same." The followers of Pythagoras drew up a table of ten basic opposites from which they believed the world was made: limit and unlimited, odd and even, one and many, right and left, male and female, rest and motion, straight and curved, light and darkness, good and bad, square and oblong.

In China, the Tao Te Ching taught that being and non-being produce each other, that difficult and easy complete each other, that long and short define each other. From that came the most famous pair symbol in the world, yin and yang: dark and light, each holding a seed of the other.

And look at how the oldest creation story in the Western world begins. Genesis doesn't open with God making things. It opens with God dividing them. "God divided the light from the darkness." Then the waters above from the waters below. Then the sea from the dry land. Creation, in the beginning, is division into pairs.

The Tao Te Ching tells the same story as arithmetic: "The Tao gave birth to One. One gave birth to Two. Two gave birth to Three. Three gave birth to the ten thousand things."

## The smallest difference

Why two? Start with the simplest answer. Two is the smallest number that can make a difference.

One thing alone can't be compared with anything. There is nothing to set it against, nothing to tell it apart from. The moment there are two, there is a difference: this and that, here and there, more and less. Every relationship needs at least two parties.

The Dutch philosopher Baruch Spinoza put it in three words in 1674: "determination is negation." A thing is only a thing because of what it isn't. Draw a circle, and you have made two things at once: an inside and an outside.

Language works the same way. In the early 1900s the Swiss linguist Ferdinand de Saussure showed that words have no meaning on their own, only by contrast with other words. "In language," he wrote, "there are only differences." You can't know what "hot" means without "cold."

Logic works the same way. Aristotle's first law of thought is that nothing can be both true and false at the same time and in the same respect. In 1854 the English mathematician George Boole built an entire algebra on just those two values, true and false. Less than a century later, it became the 1 and 0 inside every computer.

The German philosopher Gottfried Leibniz had already invented counting with only 1 and 0, in 1703, and he saw in it something more than arithmetic. To him, binary was an image of creation itself: God as 1, nothing as 0, and everything built from the two. He was delighted to find the same pattern in the ancient Chinese I Ching.

In 1989 the American physicist John Wheeler took the idea to its limit with a phrase: "it from bit." Perhaps every physical thing, at bottom, is information. And a bit, the smallest unit of information, is simply a pair: yes or no.

## Does one even exist?

Here is a stranger thought. Perhaps one, on its own, isn't really a number at all.

The ancient Greeks thought so. To Euclid, a number was "a multitude composed of units." One was the unit, the thing numbers were made of, not a number itself. Aristotle said it plainly: one is not a number but the measure of number. For the Greek mathematicians, counting began at two.

Modern mathematics, which builds every number out of the barest possible materials, reaches a curious result of its own. In the 1920s the Hungarian-American mathematician John von Neumann showed how to construct the numbers from nothing at all. Zero is the empty set: a bag with nothing in it. One is a bag containing that empty bag. Two is a bag holding both. In the foundations of mathematics, one is literally nothing, wrapped.

So perhaps one is not a thing we can ever meet. The moment anything is counted, it has been set apart from something else, and there are already two. One may be the number of what we can't observe: the undivided.

## Pairs in matter

This isn't just a matter of words and numbers. The physical world is built in pairs, and we can watch it happen.

Electric charge comes in two kinds, positive and negative, and the books always balance. Magnets come with two poles. Cut a magnet in half and you don't get a separate north and south; you get two smaller magnets, each with its own north and south. Nobody has ever found a single pole on its own. Isaac Newton wrote the rule in 1687: to every action there is an equal and opposite reaction.

In 1918 the German mathematician Emmy Noether proved one of the deepest results in physics. Every symmetry in nature, she showed, produces a law of conservation: something that can never be created or destroyed, only moved from one side of the ledger to the other. Nature keeps double-entry books.

In 1928 the English physicist Paul Dirac's equations predicted that every particle of matter has an opposite twin: antimatter. In 1932 the first one was found, the positron, the electron's opposite. Since then, physicists have watched again and again as a burst of energetic light turns into matter. It never produces one particle. It produces a pair, an electron and a positron together. When an electron and a positron meet, both vanish, and two flashes of light fly off in exactly opposite directions. Hospitals use this every day: a PET scanner works by catching those paired flashes on either side of a patient.

Pairs hold matter together, too. A chemical bond, the thing that turns hydrogen and oxygen into water, is a pair of electrons shared between atoms, spinning in opposite directions. The American chemist Gilbert Lewis described the electron pair in 1916. In superconductors, electrons travel in pairs and flow without resistance.

Then there is the strangest pairing of all. Two particles created together stay linked, however far apart they travel. Measure one, and you know the other at once. Einstein doubted it in 1935. Experiments since have proved it beyond argument, and the 2022 Nobel Prize in physics went to the men who did. Physicists call it entanglement.

Niels Bohr, one of the founders of quantum physics, spent his life on the fact that light behaves both as a wave and as a particle, two descriptions that exclude each other yet are both needed. He called it complementarity. When Denmark honoured him in 1947, he chose the yin-yang for his coat of arms, with a Latin motto: _Contraria sunt complementa_. Opposites are complementary.

## Pairs in life: Mom and Dad

Life is built on pairs from the inside out.

The molecule that carries every living thing's instructions, DNA, is a double strand, described in 1953 as a twisted ladder. Each rung is a pair: A always with T, G always with C. When a cell divides, the ladder unzips down the middle, and each half rebuilds its missing partner. Life copies itself by pairing.

Most animals are built in pairs on the outside too. For more than 500 million years, the great majority have been bilateral, with a left side and a right. We have two eyes and two ears for a reason: the brain finds depth and direction by comparing what the pair reports.

And then there are Mom and Dad. Sexual reproduction is at least a billion years old; the earliest known example is a tiny red seaweed. Every human being carries 23 pairs of chromosomes, one of each pair from each parent. Every egg and every sperm carries just one of every pair. Each of us is, quite literally, two halves joined.

Why sex exists at all is still an open question. Biologists have called it the queen of problems in evolutionary biology, because sex is wildly inefficient. A creature that simply clones itself passes on all of its genes and needs no partner. Sex halves your share and costs the search for a mate. The British biologist John Maynard Smith called it the twofold cost of sex. The leading answer is called the Red Queen, after the character in _Through the Looking-Glass_ who must keep running just to stay in the same place. Diseases and parasites constantly evolve to crack whatever lock a species carries. Cloning keeps the same lock forever. Sex reshuffles the genes every generation, so the parasites never quite catch up.

Why two sexes, and not three or ten? One hypothesis, put forward in 1992, is that every cell carries tiny power plants, the mitochondria, with genes of their own. If both parents passed theirs on, the two sets could compete inside the child. So one parent supplies them and the other does not, and two roles emerge. Tellingly, some fungi, which mate without merging their cells, have thousands of mating types instead of two. _Perhaps._

The doubling then runs backward forever. Two parents. Four grandparents. Eight great-grandparents. Go back thirty generations and there are more than a billion slots in your family tree, more people than were alive at the time, so the same ancestors fill many slots. Every family tree is a tree of twos.

## Pairs in the mind: caution and curiosity

The mind is built on pairs as well, and not by accident.

The nervous system is a difference detector. It reports change and contrast, and stops reporting whatever stays the same. Walk into a house and you smell it; live there a week and you don't. Everything we perceive, we perceive as a difference: this against that, light against dark, sound against silence. A mind built that way can only see a world of pairs.

And at the root of every living mind sits the pair that keeps it alive: caution and curiosity.

Watch a wild rat find a new food. It doesn't gorge on it, and it doesn't ignore it. It takes a tiny nibble, waits to see whether it gets sick, then comes back for more. Curiosity says try it; caution says carefully. Every foraging animal lives on that balance, choosing again and again between the patch it knows and the patch it doesn't. Inside the brain, the circuits for threat and the circuits for novelty pull against each other all day long.

All curiosity, and the first snake gets you. All caution, and you starve in the cave. Life survives by keeping both.

The same pair runs through reproduction. Cloning is caution: copy what worked and keep it. Sex is curiosity: gamble on new combinations every time. Sex costs more, and over the long run it wins.

When the pair breaks, trouble follows. Caution without curiosity hardens into certainty: the closed mind, the walled citadel, the settled answer that refuses every question. Curiosity without caution is recklessness. The pair, held in tension, is what preserves life.

## The pair that didn't balance

Now comes the deepest puzzle in the story.

When energy becomes matter, it makes pairs: a particle and its antiparticle, in exactly equal numbers. So the early universe, in its first instants, should have made matter and antimatter in perfect balance. And when matter meets antimatter, both vanish. Every particle should have found its partner and disappeared, leaving nothing behind but light.

That isn't what happened. Look across the sky and there are no antimatter galaxies. Somehow, in the beginning, matter outnumbered antimatter, by about one part in a billion. The rest cancelled out, and that tiny surplus is everything that exists today: every star, every planet, every horse and every one of us.

Nobody knows why. It is one of the great unsolved problems in physics. But it means this: we are the leftovers of a pair that failed to balance. The universe we live in is not a pair. It is the remainder.

And there may be a hidden explosion here, right under our noses. Count the particles of light in the afterglow of the early universe, and there are about a billion of them for every particle of matter. That is the tally of the annihilation: for every particle that survived, roughly a billion pairs cancelled out and turned to light. The glow we call the echo of the Big Bang carries the energy of that great cancellation.

So perhaps the Big Bang wasn't followed by a separation and an annihilation. Perhaps the Big Bang _was_ the separation: the instant the undivided One first split into a pair, matter and antimatter, and split unequally. In that same instant the antimatter was wholly consumed, and a sliver of matter was left behind. In the 1960s the Swedish physicist Hannes Alfvén, later a Nobel laureate, proposed something related, in which the universe began as a vast mix of matter and antimatter. His version was set aside because separated regions of antimatter would still glow at their borders, and none are seen. But if the antimatter was subsumed in the very event that created it, there would be no borders left to glow, which is exactly the universe we observe. One question remains: why the split was unequal. _Pending._

If so, antimatter becomes the mother of Two. She gave herself up entirely in the event, and everything that exists is what she left behind. Her light still fills the sky.

## What didn't Bang

Which brings us to the last riddle. If everything that exists comes in pairs, what was there before the first pair? What split? What didn't Bang?

Some physicists have proposed a startling answer, beginning in 1973. Perhaps the total energy of the universe is exactly zero. The positive energy of all the matter may be balanced, to the last decimal, by the negative energy of gravity. If so, the Big Bang wasn't something coming from nothing. It was nothing splitting into a pair: a plus and a minus that still add up to zero. _Pending_, and unproven.

The old mystics reached for the same thing in their own words. In the third century the philosopher Plotinus taught that behind every pair stands "the One," beyond all opposites, from which all things flow. In 1440 the German cardinal Nicholas of Cusa wrote that in the infinite, all opposites coincide, and he gave his book a title that could stand over this whole essay: _On Learned Ignorance_. In 1952 the physicist Wolfgang Pauli, whose own Nobel-winning principle is the reason electrons pair up, and the psychiatrist Carl Jung published a book together. They went looking for a single reality beneath both mind and matter: one thing, showing two faces to anyone who looks. Jung borrowed an old alchemists' name for it, the _unus mundus_, "the one world," the undivided ground from which both mind and matter split.

Here the riddle turns back on us. A mind that perceives only differences can see only pairs. The undivided One, if it exists, has no opposite to show against. It isn't hidden because it is far away. It is hidden because a mind like ours has nothing to compare it with.

In these essays we have a name for a place like that: an SOB, a **scientific observational boundary**, a point where our methods run out though something surely lies beyond. The Big Bang is one. The inside of a black hole is another. The self is another. What didn't Bang may be the last SOB of all: invisible not by accident, but by design.

## Two

So here is where we stand.

We know a great deal about what pairs do. They mark one thing off from another, which is what it means to exist. They hold matter together and keep nature's books balanced. They let life copy itself and outwit its enemies. They give us depth, direction and meaning. And the pair of caution and curiosity keeps every living thing alive.

What we don't know is where pairs come from. That lies on the far side of the last boundary, with the One that didn't split. Perhaps one was never a number at all, only the name for what we can't see. Perhaps the universe is a nothing that divided, or the leftover of a pair that didn't balance. Perhaps.

With the function in hand and the origin out of reach, we can have our milk and cookies and sleep soundly through the night, until the day comes round again, which is, of course, the other half of a pair.

One is what didn't Bang. Two is the first thing that did.

title: A New Home for Quantum
dek: Not physics, not math, not philosophy. The study of structure and strength at the smallest scale, and the bridge from science to engineering.
excerpt: Not physics, not math, not philosophy. The study of structure and strength at the smallest scale, and the bridge from science to engineering.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

## The lodger

For more than a hundred years, quantum has lived in other people's houses.

It was born in 1900, when the German physicist Max Planck proposed that energy comes in tiny, fixed packets. He called them quanta. Physics took the child in. Mathematics gave it a language. Philosophy has argued over what it means ever since the great meeting of physicists in Brussels in 1927, and the argument has never been settled.

Three houses. None of them home. The residents know it. In 1964 Richard Feynman told a lecture hall at Cornell: "I think I can safely say that nobody understands quantum mechanics." In 1989 the physicist David Mermin summed up the reigning attitude in one line: "Shut up and calculate."

That is how you talk about a lodger, not a member of the family.

## Not physics, not math, not philosophy

**Quantum is not physics.** Physics studies tangible existence: what can be weighed, measured, pushed and touched. Quantum deals in things no one has ever touched. No one has seen an electron's wave. No one has seen a particle in two places at once. What we see is a click on a detector, a dot on a screen. The rest is inferred.

And there is a wall. In 1927 Werner Heisenberg showed that a particle's position and its motion can never both be known exactly. Not because our instruments are crude. Because nature won't allow it. In these essays we have a name for such a place: an SOB, a **scientific observational boundary**. Physics lives on the near side of it. Quantum lives on the far side.

**Quantum is not mathematics.** Mathematics studies numbers. Quantum borrows them, brilliantly; some of its predictions match experiment to better than one part in a billion. But the numbers are not the subject. A cookbook is written in words. It is not about words.

**Quantum is not philosophy.** Philosophy studies ideas. Quantum has handed philosophers a century of ideas: waves that collapse when looked at, worlds that split, a cat both dead and alive. Philosophy has not settled one of them. Meanwhile, quantum built the phone in your pocket. Philosophy doesn't build phones.

## Structure and strength

So what is it?

Quantum is the study of structure and strength at the most fundamental scales. What things are made of, how they are arranged, and what holds them together.

Ask why a table holds up your cup. An atom is almost entirely empty. If its nucleus were a pea at the centre of a football stadium, its electrons would be specks in the far stands. Everything you have ever leaned on is mostly nothing. Why doesn't it fall in on itself?

The answer is quantum. In 1925 the Austrian physicist Wolfgang Pauli found that no two electrons can occupy the same state. Electrons refuse to crowd. In 1967 Freeman Dyson and Andrew Lenard proved that this refusal is what keeps ordinary matter from collapsing. The solidity of the world is a quantum rule.

Ask what holds water together, or steel, or the DNA in your cells. Chemical bonds. In 1927 two German physicists, Walter Heitler and Fritz London, used quantum to explain the simplest one, in the hydrogen molecule: two electrons, a pair, shared between two atoms. Every bond in chemistry is a quantum story.

Ask what holds the centre of the atom together. Its protons all carry the same charge and should fly apart. They are held by the strong force, about a hundred times stronger than electricity at that range. Strength, at the smallest scale there is.

Structure is how things are arranged. Strength is what holds them. That is quantum's real subject. The strangeness is only what we see at the wall. The structure is what stands behind it.

## The bridge

Quantum is a bridge, from what's known to what's speculation.

One end stands on solid ground: rules tested a million times and never broken. The other end disappears into fog: what is really going on behind the wall. Physicists and philosophers crowd the foggy end, arguing about cats.

But look at what has crossed the bridge, and which way it went.

The transistor, built at Bell Labs in 1947 from the quantum understanding of how electrons move through crystals. A single chip now holds billions of them. The laser, first switched on in 1960. The MRI scanner, which reads the quantum spin of the hydrogen in your body. The LED in your lamp. The solar panel on the barn roof. The atomic clocks in the satellites that keep your phone's map honest.

None of it waited for the fog to clear. No engineer asked whether the cat was dead. They took the structure and the strength and built with them.

That is where quantum does its best work: materials. Semiconductors, magnets, superconductors, alloys, the crystal in every chip. Point it at the small and the solid, and it delivers every time.

Point it at the Big Bang and it is probably wasting its time. It could get lucky. But the first instant lies behind the biggest SOB of all, where no instrument will ever reach. Until something crosses that wall, whatever quantum says about it is a story, not a fact. We have said so before.

That is quantum's real home. Not a lodger in physics, a tenant of mathematics, or a riddle for philosophy. Quantum is the essential link from science to engineering: the place where knowing what holds the world together becomes knowing how to build with it.

Give it a house of its own. Put the front door on the engineering side.

title: Did Math Destroy Philosophy?
dek: In the century after Darwin, every discipline wanted to be a science. Wise men perished, posers flourished. It's time to bring philosophy home.
excerpt: In the century after Darwin, every discipline wanted to be a science. Wise men perished, posers flourished. It's time to bring philosophy home.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

## The son and the father

For two thousand years, philosophy was the father of every discipline. Physics was once called natural philosophy. Psychology was the philosophy of mind. Economics was moral philosophy. The doctorate in nearly every subject is still a Doctor of Philosophy.

Then, somewhere in the nineteenth century, the children turned on the parent.

It wasn't enough any more to be brilliant. You had to be experimental. You had to be measurable, data-driven and mathematical, like a real scientist. It happened in philosophy first, and then in nearly everything else: psychiatry, literature, theatre, music, art, economics. Every intellectual discipline slipped its moorings and set sail for the laboratory.

Wise men perished. Posers flourished.

This is the story of how the son killed the father, and then discovered that father knew best.

## The stampede

They said so themselves, in print.

**The mind.** In 1879 Wilhelm Wundt opened the first psychology laboratory, in Leipzig. In 1895 a Viennese doctor named Sigmund Freud drafted a "Project for a Scientific Psychology." In 1913 the American John Watson published his manifesto: "Psychology as the behaviorist views it is a purely objective experimental branch of natural science." The inner life, the thing psychology was named for, was struck off the books.

**The novel.** In 1880 the French novelist Émile Zola published _The Experimental Novel_, openly modelled on a textbook of experimental medicine. The novelist, he said, should set up his characters like a scientist sets up an experiment, and record the results.

**Politics.** The same year, Friedrich Engels published _Socialism: Utopian and Scientific_. Marx's followers didn't want to be dreamers. They wanted to be scientists.

**Money.** In the 1870s William Jevons and Léon Walras rebuilt economics on mathematics. Critics would later call it physics envy.

**Music.** In the early 1920s Arnold Schoenberg devised his twelve-tone method: composition by system. In 1958 the American composer Milton Babbitt published the essay that came to be known as "Who Cares if You Listen?" Composers, he argued, should work in universities like research scientists, whether or not anyone wanted to hear the results.

**The stage.** In 1948 Bertolt Brecht wrote _A Short Organum for the Theatre_, borrowing his title from Francis Bacon's founding book of scientific method. He wanted a theatre for a scientific age.

**And philosophy itself.** In the 1920s a group of philosophers and scientists in Vienna, the Vienna Circle, set out to make philosophy scientific. In 1936 the young English philosopher A. J. Ayer gave their idea its sharpest form in _Language, Truth and Logic_. Any statement that could not be checked by observation or proved by logic was, he declared, literally meaningless. Metaphysics, ethics, beauty and God: meaningless, all of them. With one rule, two thousand years of philosophy was sent home.

## Why it happened

No single cause. A pile-up.

**The prophet came first.** In the 1830s the French thinker Auguste Comte announced that every field of knowledge passes through three stages: religion, then philosophy, then science. Philosophy was a phase to be outgrown. He called for a "social physics" and coined the word _sociology_. The hangover began before anyone had poured the drinks.

**Then Darwin.** In 1859 _On the Origin of Species_ took the oldest question of all, where we came from, away from the priests and the philosophers and handed it to the naturalists. If science could answer that, what couldn't it answer?

**Then the results.** Railways, the telegraph, electric light, vaccines, germ theory. Science delivered, visibly and every day. Wisdom had never built a railway. Prestige follows results, and the prestige moved. Meanwhile millions left the village for the factory town, where life ran by the clock and the machine, and the measured life began to look like the only real one.

**Then the payroll.** This is the cause most people miss. From the 1870s universities everywhere copied the German research model; in America it began with Johns Hopkins in 1876. The doctorate became a research degree. To hold a chair in anything, music, poetry or ethics included, you had to produce research. Brilliance didn't fit on a résumé. Experiments did.

**Then the war.** In 1914 the old order marched a generation into the trenches, and its wisdom went down with it. The young came home trusting nothing that couldn't be measured.

Comte supplied the theory, Darwin the shock, industry the evidence, the university the money, and the war the rubble. By 1920 "scientific" had become the only badge of seriousness left.

## The twist

All of it rested on one hope: that mathematics and logic could, in the end, settle everything.

The greatest mathematician of the age, David Hilbert, believed it. Around 1900 he set out to put all of mathematics on a foundation so complete that every true statement could, in principle, be proved. Bertrand Russell and Alfred North Whitehead spent a decade on the same dream and produced _Principia Mathematica_, three enormous volumes, published from 1910 to 1913. Famously, it takes them hundreds of pages to reach the proof that one plus one equals two.

On 8 September 1930, in his home town of Königsberg, Hilbert gave a radio address that ended with the words that are now carved on his tombstone: "We must know. We will know."

The day before, at a meeting in the same city, a young Austrian logician named Kurt Gödel had quietly announced a result. Hardly anyone noticed. It was published the next year, and it ended the dream.

Gödel proved that any consistent system of mathematics rich enough to do ordinary arithmetic contains true statements it can never prove. Not because we haven't been clever enough. Because it can't be done, ever. Logic has a wall inside it.

In these essays we have a name for such a place: an SOB, a **scientific observational boundary**. Gödel's is the strangest SOB of all, because it isn't out at the edge of the universe. It is inside reason itself.

The son set out to replace the father with mathematics. And mathematics, the son's own weapon, proved what the father had said all along: there are truths that cannot be reached by calculation. Some things must be seen whole, or not at all.

The philosophers who tried to make philosophy scientific fared no better. Their test for meaning, that a statement must be checkable by observation, could not itself be checked by observation. By its own rule it was meaningless. Late in life, A. J. Ayer was asked on television what the main defect of the movement had been. "I suppose the most important of the defects," he said, "was that nearly all of it was false."

## What was lost

But the damage was done. The dream died; the habit lived.

Philosophy never recovered its place. Much of it retreated into the analysis of language and logic, written by specialists for specialists, in a vocabulary closed to everyone else. The great questions, how to live, what matters, how to face death, were left to the self-help shelf and the slogan.

In the other disciplines the costume became the career. The music that nobody wanted to hear got tenure. The psychology that ignored the mind got grants. The economics with the most equations got the prizes, and missed the crashes. The art that came with the longest explanation got the gallery. Method became a disguise. If you couldn't be wise, you could be rigorous, and if you couldn't be rigorous, you could at least look it.

That is how the posers flourished. A poser is not a fool. A poser is someone who has learned to wear the uniform of a discipline without carrying its burden. The uniform of the age was the lab coat, so everyone put one on.

And the wise perished, not by persecution this time, but by neglect. There was no grant for wisdom. No journal for it. No experiment that could prove it. So it went where unfunded things go: to the margins, to the grandmothers, to the people who still had time to sit and think.

## Why we need it back

The sciences have earned their place. Nobody is asking for the railway back to the drawing room. But we need philosophy back, and here is why.

**Data tells us what is, not what matters.** In 1739 the Scottish philosopher David Hume pointed out that you cannot get an _ought_ from an _is_. Science can tell us how to split the atom. It cannot tell us whether to. Every decision that matters, to a person or to a nation, lies on the far side of that gap.

**The walls need someone standing at them.** Measurement stops at every SOB: the first instant, the inside of a black hole, the self, and now the wall inside logic itself. Thinking does not stop there. The ground beyond the wall has always belonged to philosophy. Leave it empty, and fairy tales move in.

**Science needs it more than anyone.** The smooth universe is a philosophical failure: an assumption that forgot it was an assumption. In 1944 Albert Einstein wrote to a young teacher that most scientists seemed to him like someone who "has seen thousands of trees but has never seen a forest." Philosophical insight, he said, was "the mark of distinction between a mere artisan or specialist and a real seeker after truth."

**The givens have no experiment.** Death, change, conflict and loss cannot be measured away or solved in a laboratory. The only tool ever made for living with them is wisdom, and philosophy is where wisdom is kept.

**The machines now do the calculating.** This is the new reason, and the most urgent. Machines can crunch any number we give them. The one job left that is distinctly human is judgment: asking why, and deciding what is worth doing. The autopilot can fly the plane. It cannot choose where to go. A generation trained only to calculate will be out-calculated.

**It belongs to everyone.** Philosophy left the kitchen table for the faculty lounge, and it never came back. But brilliance needs no grant and no laboratory. It needs plain words and permission to think.

## Bring it home

So, did math destroy philosophy?

No. Math was only the weapon. What destroyed philosophy was envy: a century of brilliant people ashamed of being merely brilliant, dressing up as something they were not. And in the end the weapon turned in their hands. Mathematics itself proved that reason has walls, which is exactly what philosophy had been saying since Socrates.

The father was right. It is time to bring him home.

Not to the faculty lounge. To the kitchen table, the shop floor, the barn and the porch. To everyone, in plain words, with no lab coat required. That is what these essays are for: things to consider, not things to accept.

title: You Are Not Me
dek: Boundary, belonging, rank: the biological sequence behind every conflict, and the roads to civilization and Armageddon that start from the same place.
excerpt: Boundary, belonging, rank: the biological sequence behind every conflict, and the roads to civilization and Armageddon that start from the same place.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

## The oldest sentence

Every war has its issues. Land, water, oil, faith, borders, flags, taxes, insults. The historians list them, the generals cite them, the newspapers argue over them.

The issues are not the cause. They are the rationalization. The cause is always the same, and it is older than any war, any nation and any species. It is the oldest sentence in biology:

_You are not me._

Everything else grows from it, in three movements. First comes the boundary: you are not me. Then belonging: you are not us. Then rank: I am stronger than you.

Follow those three steps downstream and you arrive at a fork. One road leads to civilization. The other leads to Armageddon. And both start from the same place.

## You are not me

Life began with a wall.

The first living thing, more than three and a half billion years ago, was little more than chemistry with a skin around it. A membrane. An inside and an outside. Inside was self; outside was everything else. Before life could do anything, it had to draw that line.

The line has never been erased. Your body redraws it every second. Its immune system has one job above all others: to tell self from non-self, and to attack whatever is not self. The Australian scientist Macfarlane Burnet shared the 1960 Nobel Prize for work on how the body learns that difference. Get it wrong one way and infections win. Get it wrong the other way and the body attacks itself.

The mind draws the line too. Put a dab of rouge on a baby's nose and set it in front of a mirror. Somewhere around eighteen months to two years, the child stops reaching for the baby in the glass and reaches for its own nose instead. It has found the boundary of the self. Not long after comes the first great declaration of independence, shouted in every nursery on Earth: _Mine!_

This is not a flaw. It is the price of being anything at all. In an earlier essay we called it the first division: before there can be two, one must split. You are not me is where every story starts.

## You are not us

The second movement stretches the wall around more than one.

First around kin. In 1964 the English biologist W. D. Hamilton worked out the mathematics of why animals favour their relatives: they share the same blood, so helping them helps your own kind survive. Family is the first "us."

Then around the band. The British anthropologist Robin Dunbar has argued that a human brain can keep track of about 150 real relationships. Up to that number, "us" is simply everyone you know: every face, every voice, every smell.

Past 150, faces run out, and something new takes their place: symbols. A community too large to know itself needs badges to tell us from them. A creed. A flag. An accent. A uniform. A team. More people, more symbolic reality. And symbols are cheap to make and endless to fight over, which may be why communities are more violent than tribes.

It takes almost nothing to make an "us." In the early 1970s the psychologist Henri Tajfel told a group of English schoolboys that they had been sorted by which of two painters they preferred. In fact the sorting was random. Strangers a moment before, the boys at once began to favour their own group and short-change the other.

And the smaller the difference, the hotter the fight. Freud called it "the narcissism of minor differences." Neighbours who are nearly alike fight hardest over the little that divides them: two churches on one street, two counties across one river. Pour dyes into a flowing river, one for each creed, and a thousand years downstream the colours are still separate at the mouth. The boundary is the point.

In 1954 the psychologist Muzafer Sherif took twenty-two ordinary boys to a summer camp at Robbers Cave, Oklahoma, and split them into two groups. They named themselves the Eagles and the Rattlers. Within days they were raiding each other's cabins and burning each other's flag. Nothing divided them but the line itself.

The issues never mattered. The membrane did.

## I am stronger than you

The third movement is rank. And here a precious irony is waiting.

Odd numbers are dangerous. Divide an even number by two and it splits clean: balance, symmetry, a pair. Divide an odd number by two and something is left over. A remainder. Disparity, and disparity is the father of conflict.

The universe itself began with an odd split. When matter and antimatter separated, they should have come out exactly even and cancelled each other to nothing. They didn't. For roughly every billion pairs, one extra particle of matter was left over. Every star, every horse, every one of us is made of that remainder. An even division would have left an empty universe. Disparity is the father of existence, too.

Three is where politics begins. Two can face each other as equals. Add a third, and someone becomes the odd one out. In 1908 the German sociologist Georg Simmel noticed that in any group of three, two tend to join against one. Some seventy years later the Dutch primatologist Frans de Waal watched it decide power among the chimpanzees of a zoo in Arnhem. The male who rose to the top was not the strongest. He was the one with an old ally whose weight tipped the balance, two against one.

Even the farmyard keeps score. In 1921 the Norwegian zoologist Thorleif Schjelderup-Ebbe published what he had seen since boyhood among his family's hens: every flock sorts itself into a strict ladder of who may peck whom. He gave us the phrase _pecking order_.

Boundary. Belonging. Rank. You are not me. You are not us. I am stronger than you. Each step leaves a remainder, and someone will always fight over it.

## Two roads from one place

Now follow the sequence downstream, and watch it fork.

Stretch the membrane, and you get civilization. Every time "us" grows, from family to village, village to city, city to nation, strangers can trade, share laws, build roads and pool what they know. The Robbers Cave boys showed how. When the researchers arranged for the camp's water supply to fail, Eagles and Rattlers had to work together to fix it. Sherif called it a superordinate goal: a problem too big for either side alone. The hostility began to melt. A bigger "us" had formed around a shared need.

Harden the membrane, and you get Armageddon. The same wall that makes cooperation possible inside the circle makes slaughter possible outside it. And every tool a bigger "us" invents, writing, roads, organisation, industry, the split atom, also builds a bigger army.

So civilization and Armageddon are not opposites. They are twins, born of the same boundary. Every advance that makes "us" larger also raises the stakes when two great "us"es meet. That is why the war has no end. The battlefields change and the dialects change, but you cannot have one road without the other.

The membrane is not a choice. It is what we are. The choice, every time, is whether to stretch it or to harden it.

## Who saves us from ourselves

Who does the stretching?

Not science. Science can tell us that any two human beings share about 99.9 percent of their DNA. It cannot make us care. Whom to count as "us" is not a fact to be measured. It is a choice to be made, an _ought_, not an _is_. Only philosophy can draw the circle.

And every time the circle was deliberately drawn wider, a thinker drew it first.

Diogenes the Cynic, asked where he came from, answered: "I am a citizen of the world." His Greek word gave us _cosmopolitan_.

Marcus Aurelius, an emperor with every reason to think only of Rome, wrote in his private notebook: "My city and country, so far as I am Antoninus, is Rome; but so far as I am a man, it is the world."

Zixia, a disciple of Confucius, put it in a single line: "Within the four seas, all men are brothers."

In 1795 Immanuel Kant published _Perpetual Peace_, imagining a world in which free nations treat each other as neighbours rather than enemies.

Philosophy does not save us automatically. Aristotle, the greatest mind of his age, argued that some people were slaves by nature. Thinkers can harden the wall as well as stretch it. The wise draw the circle wider. The posers and the ideologues draw it tighter. That is why the difference between them matters so much, and why losing the philosophers is so dangerous. Without them, nobody stretches the membrane, and it hardens by default.

It's the philosophers who save us from ourselves.

## The membrane and the road

So here is the sequence, from the first cell to the last war.

You are not me: the boundary that makes life possible. You are not us: the belonging that makes community possible. I am stronger than you: the rank that makes order possible, and conflict certain.

None of it can be abolished. Peace without boundaries is a fairy tale; a creature without a membrane is a puddle. But none of it is destiny, either. The same wall that leads to Armageddon leads to civilization, depending on which way we push it.

The membrane is biology. The road is philosophy.

Every war will come dressed in its issues. Look past them. Underneath, it will be the oldest sentence in biology, with a flag on it.

title: The Self Is What Saves Us
dek: The first thing we know and the last thing we lose. Science can study everything else, but here it is a guest.
excerpt: The first thing we know and the last thing we lose. Science can study everything else, but here it is a guest.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

## The first and the last

The first act of human awareness is the self. A child finds its own face in the mirror, and then its own will. _Mine. Me. No._

The last regret of a dying person is the loss of self. An Australian nurse named Bronnie Ware spent years caring for people in their final weeks and wrote down what they regretted most. The commonest regret of all: "I wish I'd had the courage to live a life true to myself." Not to the job, not to the family, not to the church. To _myself_.

Every thought and every action in between is an act of self. Every choice, every love, every fight, every sentence that begins with _I_.

The self is the first thing we know and the last thing we lose. And on this one subject, more than any other, science and humanity are at odds.

## What people feel

Ask anyone what they are, and almost no one will point to their brain.

People feel the self as something more than chemistry. Not a lump of grey matter, but something profound, not profane. Something that could, perhaps, outlast the body. No ordinary human being has ever felt otherwise. Never has, never will.

It starts early. The Yale psychologist Paul Bloom argued in 2004 that children are natural dualists: long before anyone teaches them, they treat the mind as something separate from the body. That same year two American psychologists, Jesse Bering and David Bjorklund, showed young children a puppet show in which a mouse is eaten by an alligator. The children agreed the mouse no longer needed to eat or drink. But many said it still loved its mother and still thought about things. The body was gone. The someone carried on.

It lasts a lifetime. In 2023 the Pew Research Center found that 83 percent of American adults believe people have a soul or spirit in addition to their physical body, and 81 percent believe there is something spiritual beyond the natural world, even if we cannot see it.

And it spans every culture that ever buried its dead. In every afterlife humans have ever imagined, what survives is never the brain. It is the person.

## Something to stay alive for

The mind does not merely hold this feeling. It defends it.

In an earlier essay we met the gatekeeper. In 2019 researchers at Bar-Ilan University in Israel found that the brain's prediction machinery simply refuses to link a person's own face with words of death, though it links a stranger's face easily. The mind cancels whatever contradicts the certainty of self. The American biologist Ajit Varki argued that it must: a creature that fully grasped its own death might stop striving, so self-awareness could only evolve if it came packaged with the power to deny mortality.

In 1973 the anthropologist Ernest Becker made the same case from the other direction in _The Denial of Death_, which won a Pulitzer Prize. Much of human culture, he argued, is built to shield us from our own ending.

This is not a failure of education. It is an evolutionary barrier, and it serves a fundamental purpose. We have something to stay alive for. Viktor Frankl, who survived Auschwitz, liked to quote Nietzsche: "He who has a why to live can bear almost any how." The self is the why. What the gatekeeper guards is the will to live, not a promise of heaven. Many peoples have lived full, striving lives with no afterlife at all; take away the promise, and people don't give up. They value their time more.

So the big problem here is not scientific. It is perceptual. And biology will not let it be solved.

## The wall

Nor can science solve it from its side. The self cannot be seen from outside.

In 1739 David Hume looked inward for himself and reported: "I never can catch myself at any time without a perception." An Upanishad some 2,700 years old says it more simply: "You cannot see the seer of seeing." In 1995 the philosopher David Chalmers named the gap between brain activity and felt experience "the hard problem." It is still unsolved.

In these essays we have a name for such a place: an SOB, a **scientific observational boundary**. The Big Bang, the inside of a black hole and the self are all SOBs: places where our methods run out, though something surely lies beyond. The self may be the deepest of them, because it is the one doing the looking.

We have said before that the self is partners with the brain, not part of it. The brain is the junior partner, taken on long after life first learned to tell self from other. Science can study the junior partner in fine detail. The senior partner sits behind the wall.

So here is the honest position. Science cannot prove the self is ethereal. It cannot prove the self is not. Its instruments do not reach that far.

## Arrogance and the placeholder game

That is not what the public hears.

It isn't ignorance that stops science from saying "we don't know." It's the unmistakable arrogance of an elite that has decided the rest of humanity is a problem to be managed. Eight in ten people say they have a soul. The elite's answer is not "perhaps." It is "naive." In 1994 a Nobel laureate, Francis Crick, wrote that you are "no more than the behavior of a vast assembly of nerve cells." A celebrated American philosopher, Daniel Dennett, called consciousness a "user illusion." The billions who feel otherwise are not argued with. They are talked down to.

And when the elite cannot explain the self, it plays its favourite game. It names the gap and calls it an answer.

**Emergence.** Consciousness, we are told, "emerges" from complexity. The word explains nothing. It marks where the gap is and paints a ghost on the wall.

**Illusion.** When the self won't fit the theory, call it an illusion. But an illusion needs someone to be fooled. Who is being fooled?

**Neural correlates.** They find what lights up in the brain when you feel something, and announce that they have found the feeling. A footprint is not the foot.

**The IOU.** In 1977 the philosopher Karl Popper gave this game a name: _promissory materialism_. It is a cheque written on the future: science will explain the self some day, so believe it now. In 1998 one neuroscientist bet a case of wine that the cheque would clear within twenty-five years. It didn't.

Notice that Crick, to his credit, titled his book _The Astonishing Hypothesis_. A hypothesis. Pending. His followers forgot the word.

## Not us

This is where the subject touches the third rail.

Most people in our tradition will never accept that reality holds no timeless, non-material dimension. Not because they are stupid. Because they feel the self too deeply to give it up, and the same evolution that science reveres built that feeling.

So when science persists in telling people that the most important thing they know is an illusion, something old and predictable happens. Science puts itself outside the circle. It becomes _not us_.

We have seen what humans do with "not us." They close ranks. They stop listening. They burn the other side's flag. Every falling poll of trust in experts, every crusade against "the scientists," every parent who no longer believes a word from a lab coat, is partly this. Not a war over evidence. The oldest sentence in biology, aimed at the people who seem to want to take away the self.

Science is not the enemy of humanity. But here, it can act like one. And a partner who acts like an enemy will be treated like one.

## How hard is it?

Science needs to be scientific about this. A barrier in human perception is evidence, and ignoring evidence is the least scientific thing there is.

Why won't it say "we don't know for sure either"?

Because it has forgotten its own working rule. Science assumes that only matter and energy are in play, because that is all its instruments can measure. Philosophers call this _methodological naturalism_: a rule for how to work, not a finding about what exists. Over time the rule was mistaken for a result. "We only look at matter" became "only matter exists." An assumption that forgot it was an assumption.

Because the institution cannot afford doubt. Grants, chairs and reputations rest on confidence. "We don't know" does not win funding.

Because of envy. A field that fought for a century to be taken seriously is afraid that admitting a limit hands ground back to the priests and the philosophers.

And yet it can be done, and done with grace. In 1998, in a bar in Germany, the neuroscientist Christof Koch bet the philosopher David Chalmers a case of wine that within twenty-five years science would discover how the brain produces consciousness. In June 2023, on a stage in New York, Koch conceded and paid up. Chalmers offered to bet again for another twenty-five years. Koch took him on.

That is a good look. "We don't know for sure either," said in public, with a case of wine on the table. How hard is it? Not hard at all. One honest scientist has shown how. The rest just won't.

## Sovereign

And there is one more thing, and it outweighs all the rest.

When it comes to our selves, we are absolutely entitled to believe whatever we choose.

That is not a loophole. It is one of the oldest principles of a free people. In 1859 the English philosopher John Stuart Mill wrote in _On Liberty_: "Over himself, over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign." In 1948 the nations of the world wrote freedom of thought, conscience and religion into Article 18 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Universal truths may exist, but nobody has the right to enforce them on others.

The self is the one territory where nobody holds title but its owner. Not the priest. Not the state. Not the scientist.

Science may study everything else under the sun. Here, it is a guest. Guests who knock are welcome. Guests who announce that the house does not exist will be shown the door.

The first thing we know. The last thing we lose. Every thought and every act in between. The self is what saves us, and the self is ours.

title: Or, Maybe This Could Happen
dek: A companion to No. 36. Suppose the self were proven to reach beyond matter. Science would change in a decade. The world would change overnight.
excerpt: A companion to No. 36. Suppose the self were proven to reach beyond matter. Science would change in a decade. The world would change overnight.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

## A gift for life

In the last essay we stopped at the wall. The self lies behind an SOB, a **scientific observational boundary**: a place where our methods run out, though something surely lies beyond. Science cannot prove the self is more than matter. It cannot prove it is not.

Now let's climb over the wall and see what's on the other side. Not as prophets. As storytellers.

Here is the story. Not an afterlife. Something stranger and more modest. Suppose the self is a gift for life: a temporary hookup to an extra-material aspect of the universe. Every living, moving, sensing thing is plugged in for a while. When it dies, the connection is broken. The current goes on; the lamp goes out.

Would a life with no afterlife be worth less? Just the opposite. Take away the promise of forever, and people do not give up. They value their time more. A gift you know you must hand back is the one you hold most carefully.

The idea has an old pedigree. In 1898 the American psychologist William James suggested in a lecture at Harvard that the brain might transmit consciousness rather than produce it, the way a prism passes light along rather than making it. In 1954 the English writer Aldous Huxley borrowed the philosopher C. D. Broad's image of the brain as a "reducing valve," letting through only a trickle of something far larger.

Nobody has ever proven it. But suppose, one day, somebody did.

## The proof

It would have to be a real proof. Carl Sagan's rule applies, and fairly: extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence.

So imagine the evidence is extraordinary. A signal that no known physics explains, present in every living, moving creature, absent in every machine and every corpse. It fades in deep dementia and fails a moment before death, before the heart stops and before the brain falls silent. Repeated in a hundred laboratories on five continents, under blind conditions, by people who wanted it to fail.

The connection, measured. The plug, found. The power station still out of sight, behind the wall.

What happens next?

## What science loses

Inside science, the damage would be swift and specific.

In the first year, three claims fall. The claim that the brain _produces_ the self, mind and brain as one and the same thing. The claim that consciousness is an illusion. And the IOU the philosopher Karl Popper called _promissory materialism_: the promise that science would one day explain the self in matter alone. The cheque bounces.

Within a few years, deeper pillars crack. Modern physics quietly assumes that every physical event has a purely physical cause. If the hookup moves so much as one molecule, that assumption fails. The dream of building a mind out of software goes too: if the connection needs life, a machine can be brilliant without anyone at home. And medicine must ask again when a person dies. Since 1968 the answer has been tied to the brain. It would have to be tied to the connection.

Over a generation, neuroscience gets a new job. It does not die. Most of its data stays true; the patterns it found in the brain turn out to be measurements of the plug, not the power station. Evolution survives too, with a new chapter: natural selection did not invent the self. It built better receivers.

And most of science would not change at all. Chemistry, engineering, medicine for broken bones and failing hearts. Quantum would still build chips.

Science has turned on a dime before. In 1982 two Australian doctors, Barry Marshall and Robin Warren, showed that stomach ulcers were caused by a bacterium, not by stress. They were scoffed at. Twelve years later the consensus had turned; in 2005 they won the Nobel Prize. Science can change its mind in a decade.

That was the optimistic version. Here is the real one.

## Flaming wings

A non-material reality, proven. Where did it come from?

Science would have no answer. Its methods would have measured the plug and stopped at the wall, as they always do. But the question would not wait for science. Within a day, it would be answered from a great many pulpits, with one word.

God.

God would fly back into the picture with flaming wings. The Big Bang becomes the wand of God. Black holes become the far edges of creation. The SOBs become the walls of heaven. Eschatology, the study of the end of all things, becomes the next cosmology.

We know this because it has happened before, on a smaller scale. In 1951 Pope Pius XII told the Pontifical Academy of Sciences that the new cosmology of a universe with a beginning supported the idea of a creator: a moment of creation, "Let there be light," confirmed by physics. The man who had first proposed that beginning, the Belgian astronomer Georges Lemaître, was himself a Catholic priest. He was so uneasy at seeing his science used as scripture that he reportedly persuaded the Vatican not to do it again.

That was one theory about the distant past. This would be proof of something beyond matter, inside every living person, right now. No priest would be persuaded to stay quiet about that.

## Armed proof

Here is the part the optimists miss. The proof would not unite the faiths. It would arm them.

Most believers would greet the news with quiet joy: they had known it all along. But some, in every tradition, would claim the signal as theirs alone. Ours was right; the hookup is to our God, through our prophet, by our rites. Yours is a counterfeit. The extra-material dimension would be the greatest land rush in history: empty territory beyond the wall, and every tribe racing to plant a flag in it.

We have seen this before, in every essay on conflict we have written. The issues are never the cause. The cause is the oldest sentence in biology: _you are not us_. And the smaller the difference, the hotter the fight. Pour a dye for each creed into a flowing river, and a thousand years downstream the colours are still separate at the mouth. Now imagine the river in flood.

Until now, every religious war has been fought over things that could not be proven. That uncertainty was, in its way, a brake: somewhere in every believer was a small voice saying _perhaps_. Proof would take the brake off. The zealots, and every tradition has them, would mobilise, not for faith any more, but for fact.

The proof of the self would not end the war without end. It would hand it its holiest cause.

## The burial ditch

And science would be crushed between the two.

The faithful would blame it for denying the self for a century. The secular would blame it for opening the door to the zealots. Some physicists would convert. Most would dig in, and science, as the saying drawn from Max Planck goes, advances one funeral at a time.

The graves are already dug. Outside Geneva, the European laboratory CERN runs the Large Hadron Collider, a ring 27 kilometres around and roughly a hundred metres underground: the most expensive trench ever built. On the day of the proof, CERN would become a burial ditch for physicists, every career built on matter alone, laid end to end around the ring.

And the mourner is already on site. Since 2004 CERN's grounds have held a statue of Shiva Nataraja, the dancing god of creation and destruction, a gift from India. If the gods came back, one would already be dancing at the physicists' front door.

## Maybe

Science would change in a decade. The world would change overnight, and not peacefully.

That is the strange lesson of the story. The wall between us and the self may be a mercy. It keeps the question open, and an open question is the one thing every side must share. While nobody can prove what lies beyond, the scientist must say _perhaps_, and so must the priest. Uncertainty is the last common ground we have.

Break the wall, and the gift for life would become a reason for death.

None of this is a prediction. We're storytellers, not scientists. It is a thing to consider, not a thing to accept. But consider it the next time someone, in a lab coat or a cassock, tells you they know for certain what the self is.

They don't. And maybe, for now, it's better that nobody does.

title: Did We Create the Universe?
dek: The universe is real. The cosmos is ours: an ordered drawing, made together, because from the day we left the Garden, agreement was how we stayed alive.
excerpt: The universe is real. The cosmos is ours: an ordered drawing, made together, because from the day we left the Garden, agreement was how we stayed alive.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

## The question

Did we create the universe?

Not the stuff of it. The stars were burning long before anyone looked up, and they will burn long after the last of us has gone. The stuff was here first.

But look at the word the ancient Greeks gave it. Tradition says Pythagoras was the first to call the world _kosmos_. The word means order. Arrangement. The pleasing way things are put together. It is the root of _cosmetic_.

That is the clue. The universe is the stuff. The cosmos is the order we see in it: the names, the numbers, the shapes, the boundaries, the nouns and the verbs. And that order, this essay argues, is something we drew. Not alone, and not on a whim. Together, and for the oldest reason there is.

## The path from the Garden

Fate gave us a path from the Garden. In these essays we have pictured the Garden as the trees, and the exile as the open grass of the savannah. In the trees, a small ape could climb out of reach. On the grass, there was nowhere to hide.

We were somebody else's breakfast. In the 1970s the South African palaeontologist C. K. Brain studied a young hominin skull from the Swartkrans cave with two round holes punched in the back of it. The spacing matched the lower canine teeth of a leopard. He called his book _The Hunters or the Hunted?_ The famous Taung Child, the small skull found in South Africa in 1924, was probably killed by an eagle; the talon marks were identified in 2006.

On open ground, a lone animal is a meal. A group that cannot agree is a meal too. Which way is the danger? Which way do we run? Where is the water? Who keeps watch tonight? The band that could answer those questions together, quickly, lived. The band that argued did not.

From the first day out of the Garden, consensus was not a luxury. It was the goal. It was how we stopped being breakfast.

## Eyes built for agreement

Our bodies still carry the lesson.

Look into a chimpanzee's eyes and you will see mostly dark. Look into a human's and you will see a bright white frame around the iris. No other ape shows so much white, so plainly. One explanation, the "cooperative eye" hypothesis, holds that the white evolved so others could see exactly where we are looking. A built-in signal for shared attention: look _there_.

In 2007 a team led by the American psychologist Michael Tomasello tested it. When a person turned only their eyes, human infants followed the gaze. Great apes mostly ignored the eyes and followed the head.

We are a species whose faces were shaped to make agreement easier. Consensus is not just something we do. It is written into us.

## Drawing the cosmos

What began as agreement about danger grew into agreement about everything.

Look up on a clear night. In Ireland, seven bright stars make the Plough. In America, the same seven make the Big Dipper. In India, they are the Seven Sages. The stars did not change. The drawing did.

Colours are drawn too. English has one basic word for blue. Russian has two, one for light blue and one for dark. In 2007 researchers found that Russian speakers tell those shades apart faster than English speakers do. The words shape the seeing.

Every measurement is a treaty. The metre was set by international agreement in 1875 and redefined by the speed of light in 1983. The kilogram was redefined in 2019. The second has been defined by a caesium atom since 1967. Nature supplied the atoms. We agreed on the counting.

Even our most basic words are a drawing. We take the world's endless motion and divide it up. Stable patterns we call _order_, and give them nouns. Changes we call events, and give them verbs. Changes we like, we call growth. Changes we don't, we call disruption. The motion is real. The categories are ours.

In 1783 Immanuel Kant said it outright: the understanding "does not derive its laws from nature, but prescribes them to nature." Even physics has our fingerprints on it. To measure how disordered something is, a physicist must first decide which details count. In 1965 the American physicist E. T. Jaynes, borrowing a remark from Eugene Wigner, said it bluntly: "entropy is an anthropomorphic concept."

The universe is the stuff. The cosmos is the drawing. And the drawing is accumulated consensus, line by line, generation by generation.

## Objectivity is agreement
