Science likes to think it stands outside the drawing. It calls this objectivity: the view from nowhere, the world as it is without us.

But listen to one of science's great defenders. In _The Logic of Scientific Discovery_ the philosopher Karl Popper wrote that "the objectivity of scientific statements lies in the fact that they can be inter-subjectively tested." Inter-subjectively. Tested by many subjects, who then agree. Objectivity, on that account, is not a view from nowhere. It is a view from everywhere at once: the widest consensus we know how to build.

That is no insult to science. It is the highest compliment. Science is consensus with the strictest rules: checked, repeated, open to anyone who wants to try.

Whether there is a deeper split underneath, a real line between a subjective world and an objective one, built into existence itself, we cannot say. It may be ontological. It may be consensus all the way down. _Perhaps._ But everything we have built on top of it, every name, number and law, is plainly agreement, accumulated.

## The other person's way

Here is the most useful thing in this essay. If you look at anything the other person's way, you will likely see it there too.

In 1892 a German humour magazine printed a simple sketch. Seen one way, it is a duck. Seen another, a rabbit. The philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein later made it famous. One set of lines, two animals. And once someone points out the one you missed, you can never unsee it.

In February 2015 a photograph of a dress split the world. Half saw blue and black. Half saw white and gold. Same photo, same light, two worlds, and people shouted at each other about it as if their eyes had been insulted.

That is what happens when drawings collide. Two people, or two nations, look at the same events and see different worlds. It feels like a fight about facts. It is a clash of consensus. Each side's drawing is so old and so shared that it no longer looks like a drawing. It looks like the world.

Drawings can be redrawn. In 1543 Nicolaus Copernicus moved the Earth out of the centre of the heavens. The sky did not change; the drawing did, and it took more than a century to take hold. In 1962 the historian Thomas Kuhn called such redrawings paradigm shifts.

But there is a quicker way than waiting a century. Ask to be shown the rabbit. Seeing the other person's way is not weakness or surrender. It is a skill, perhaps the most useful one anyone can have. It is how a band on the savannah stayed alive, and how neighbours still do.

## The world bites back

None of this means the world is whatever we say it is.

Agree all you like that the fire is cold. It will still burn you. Agree that the leopard is friendly. It will still eat you. The drawing is not arbitrary. We draw where the world gives us handholds: a crystal really does repeat, and a gas really doesn't. The best drawings are the ones that keep us alive.

Behind every drawing lies what Kant called the thing in itself: the world before anyone draws on it. We never see it directly. We only see it through the lines. In these essays we have a name for such a place: an SOB, a **scientific observational boundary**, where our methods run out though something surely lies beyond. The raw universe, undrawn, may be the widest SOB of all.

And there is a danger on our side of the wall. A consensus that forgets it is a consensus hardens into "fact." We have seen it happen: the smooth universe, the placeholders, the assumptions that forgot they were assumptions. The drawing is ours, which means we must keep the pencil. A drawing that can no longer be redrawn stops serving the living and starts ruling them.

## Together

It is no accident that _consensus_ and _community_ sound alike. Both begin with the Latin _con-_ or _com-_, meaning together, which goes back to a root our ancestors used five or six thousand years ago. _Consensus_ is to feel together. _Community_ is to be bound together by shared duties.

The same root gives us _companion_: _com_ plus _panis_, bread. A companion is someone you share bread with. That was the choice on the savannah, and it is the choice still. Share your bread with companions, or become somebody else's breakfast.

_Civilization_ comes from a different root, the Latin word for citizen, which may go back to an ancient word meaning to settle down. Together first. Then settled. Then civilized.

And one more, for honesty: _conflict_ is _con_ plus _fligere_, to strike together. Even our fights are a together word. The same root that lets us agree is the one that lets us collide.

So, did we create the universe?

No. The universe was here first, and it will bite anyone who forgets it. But we created the cosmos: the order, the names, the numbers, the shapes in the stars. We drew it together, because from the day we left the Garden, agreement was how we stayed alive.

Consensus is not a compromise. It is the goal. It always was.

title: Is the Universe Just a Pile of Sand?
dek: The spark is random. The fuel isn't. From far enough away, even the timing of disruption may obey a law, but no grain ever sees the whole pile.
excerpt: The spark is random. The fuel isn't. From far enough away, even the timing of disruption may obey a law, but no grain ever sees the whole pile.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

## Is disruption random?

Around 1803 the English poet William Blake wrote a line that has outlived nearly everything else of his: "To see a World in a Grain of Sand."

He meant it as a mystic. This essay means it almost literally.

Order and disruption are not really opposites. They are two beats of one rhythm: order, disruption, new order. That leaves a harder question. Is the disruption random? Does the earthquake, the crash, the revolution, the exploding star, simply happen, like a throw of the dice? Or is there a law behind it, even behind its timing?

The short answer: the spark is random. The fuel isn't. And from far enough away, perhaps even the spark obeys a law.

## The sandpile

In 1987 the Danish physicist Per Bak and two colleagues ran a deceptively simple experiment on a computer. Drop grains of sand onto a table, one at a time.

At first nothing much happens. The grains settle. A pile grows. It gets steeper. Then it reaches a point, the physicists called it the critical state, where the slope is as steep as it can stand. From then on, every new grain is a gamble. Most do nothing. Some trigger a little slide. And now and then, a single grain, no different from the rest, brings down half the pile.

No one can say which grain will do it. But the sizes of the avalanches follow a strict rule: many small ones, fewer middling ones, a rare great one, always in the same proportions. Bak called the whole thing self-organized criticality, and in 1996 he wrote a book with an immodest title: _How Nature Works_.

The earth agrees with him. In the 1940s the seismologists Beno Gutenberg and Charles Richter found that for every earthquake of magnitude 6 there are roughly ten of magnitude 5 and about a hundred of magnitude 4. No one can predict the next big one. But the pattern of all of them is as regular as a clock.

Here is the lesson of the sandpile. Disruption is not the enemy of order. Order builds it. Every grain that settles quietly makes the slope steeper. Stability stores up the tension, and disruption is how order pays its debts.

## Random up close, lawful from afar

The same double nature runs all the way down.

Take a single atom of uranium. No one can say when it will decay. As far as physics knows, nothing decides the moment; it simply happens. Yet take a lump of uranium-238, and half its atoms will be gone in about 4.5 billion years, as reliably as any clock ever built. Each atom is a throw of the dice. The lump is a law.

Life works the same way. In 1943 Salvador Luria and Max Delbrück asked whether bacteria mutate _because_ they need to, to survive a virus. They found the answer was no. The resistant mutations were already there, arising at random before the virus ever appeared. They shared a Nobel Prize for it in 1969. Life's raw disruption is blind. Selection gives it direction.

Even history has a sandpile in it. Revolutions feel sudden, but the slope has been steepening for years. In 1856 the French writer Alexis de Tocqueville noticed something odd about the French Revolution: the most dangerous moment for a bad government, he wrote, is usually when it begins to reform. One small grain of hope, and the whole slope gives way.

So disruption is not random in _whether_. It is random in _when_, at least from where we stand. Things break and stuff happens. The breaking is certain. The timing is the dice.

## The cosmic sandpile

Look up, and the sky is full of sandpiles.

Some stars end their lives as white dwarfs: dense, dim embers about the size of the Earth. When a white dwarf has a companion star, it can pull matter off its neighbour, grain by grain, for millions of years. Nothing happens. Then its mass nears a fixed limit, about 1.4 times the mass of our Sun, worked out by the young Indian physicist Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar around 1930. At that edge, the star explodes. These explosions, Type Ia supernovae, are so regular in their brightness that astronomers use them as measuring sticks across the universe. An avalanche at the scale of stars, and so lawful it became a ruler.

The Sun does it too. In 1991 two astrophysicists, Edward Lu and Russell Hamilton, proposed that solar flares are avalanches in the Sun's tangled magnetic field: tension builds and builds, then lets go, in sizes that follow the same kind of rule as Bak's sand.

Stars, flares, earthquakes, atoms, genes, revolutions. Wherever we look closely, disruption is the same strange creature: unpredictable one by one, lawful all together.

## The view from exceedingly far away

So is the universe just a pile of sand? Is there an overall math and physics behind every disruption, even its timing, if only you could stand far enough back to see it?

One great mind thought so. In 1814 the French mathematician Pierre-Simon Laplace imagined an intellect that knew the position of every particle and every force acting on it. For such a mind, he wrote, "nothing would be uncertain and the future just like the past would be present before its eyes." That is the view from exceedingly far away: the whole pile, every grain, every avalanche foreseen.

Two objections came later.

The first is chaos. In 1963 the American meteorologist Edward Lorenz found that his weather model gave wildly different forecasts from starting numbers that differed only by a rounding error. A tiny difference, multiplied over and over, becomes a storm. Even a perfectly lawful system can be unpredictable in practice, because no one can ever measure the grains precisely enough.

The second is quantum. On the standard reading, the decay of that uranium atom has no cause for its timing at all. Not hidden. Absent. That reading is still argued over; some physicists suspect a deeper order underneath. _Pending._

But there is a simpler problem, and it is the decisive one. To see the whole pile, you would have to stand outside it. The universe is the closed system. There is no outside to stand in.

In these essays we have a name for such a place: an SOB, a **scientific observational boundary**, where our methods run out though something surely lies beyond. The view from exceedingly far away is the ultimate SOB. It is the one place where the law of all timing might be visible, and the one place no observer can ever reach. We are grains in the pile. No grain sees the pile.

## Crossing in the mind

And yet. No instrument can cross the boundary, but anyone can cross it in their mind. What they see on the other side is just a dream.

Sometimes dreams come true.

At sixteen, Albert Einstein imagined riding a moonbeam. In his own sober words, written half a century later, he wondered what he would see "if I pursue a beam of light with the velocity c." A decade after the daydream, it became relativity.

In 1783 an English country clergyman, John Michell, imagined a star so heavy that not even light could escape it. He called it a dark star. In 2019 we photographed the shadow of one.

Around 400 BC the Greek thinker Democritus imagined that matter was made of tiny uncuttable bits. Twenty-three centuries later, Einstein and the French physicist Jean Perrin proved atoms real.

In 1928 Paul Dirac's equation dreamed up a mirror twin of the electron. In 1932 Carl Anderson found it in a cloud chamber: antimatter, the mother of Two.

The chemist August Kekulé said the ring shape of the benzene molecule came to him in a reverie of a snake seizing its own tail. He told the story a quarter of a century later, and it may have grown in the telling. But the ring was real.

Other dreams did not come true. The ether that was supposed to fill space. Ptolemy's crystal spheres. The smooth universe. Those dreams were carried back across the wall and treated as facts before any consensus had been earned. That is where the fairy tales come from.

So here is the rule. Dream freely across the boundary. Bring back whatever you see. But label it a dream until a consensus builds around it. The world doesn't confirm; we agree, slowly, test by test, as we always have. That is all our motto has ever meant: we're storytellers, not scientists. We cross the wall, and we say so.

## A world in a grain of sand

So, is the universe just a pile of sand?

Perhaps. Up close, every avalanche is a surprise. From farther back, the avalanches fall into a pattern. From farther still, perhaps even their timing obeys a law, and the whole universe settles, slides and settles again, grain by grain, star by star, by rules no one has written down.

But no one can stand far enough back to read them. We are inside the pile. The view from outside is the last wall, and no instrument will ever cross it.

That leaves us with the oldest tool we have. Every grain can dream the pile. Most of the dreams will be wrong. A few, like a boy riding a moonbeam, will turn out to be true.

Blake had it right, though he could not have known why. To see a world in a grain of sand is not mysticism. It is the only view a grain will ever get.

title: Even Dummies Get Rich
dek: Reality doesn't reward just the deserving. She pays by chance, and we keep the books by merit.
excerpt: Reality doesn't reward just the deserving. She pays by chance, and we keep the books by merit.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

## Time and chance

Even dummies get rich.

Everyone knows one. The cousin who bought the right land by accident. The schoolmate who could barely spell, now with a boat and a second house. And everyone knows the other kind too: the brilliant, hard-working, decent person who did everything right and never caught a break.

Reality doesn't reward just the deserving. She is a cold mistress, and she has never pretended otherwise. It is we who pretend.

The oldest honest account of her is about 2,300 years old. The book of Ecclesiastes put it plainly: "the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, neither yet bread to the wise, nor yet riches to men of understanding, nor yet favour to men of skill; but time and chance happeneth to them all."

Time and chance. It took modern science a long while to catch up.

## Talent versus luck

In 2018 three Italian physicists, Alessandro Pluchino, Andrea Biondo and Andrea Rapisarda, built a simple world on a computer. They filled it with a thousand imaginary people, each given a measure of talent, and let them live forty working years. Every so often, at random, a lucky break or an unlucky blow drifted past and struck someone. Talent helped a person make the most of a lucky break. It could not summon one.

At the end of the forty years, they looked at who had become rich.

It was almost never the most talented. The richest people were usually of middling talent, who simply happened to be struck by more good luck than anyone else. The most gifted often finished in the middle of the pack, or below it. The researchers called their paper, plainly, "Talent vs Luck."

It was only a model, and models are dreams with arithmetic. But the real world keeps agreeing with it.

## Luck compounds

Luck does not just arrive. It multiplies.

In 1968 the American sociologist Robert Merton named the pattern after a line in the Gospel of Matthew: "For unto every one that hath shall be given." He called it the Matthew effect. An early break brings the next one. A little head start becomes a big lead, and a big lead becomes a fortune.

You can see it in the oddest places. In 1985 three Canadian researchers noticed that a surprising number of professional hockey players were born in the first months of the year. The reason was not the stars. Youth teams were sorted by calendar year, so a boy born in January could be nearly a year older, and bigger, than a teammate born in December. The older boys looked more talented. They got picked, coached and promoted. By the time anyone looked again, the head start had become real skill. The writer Malcolm Gladwell later made the story famous.

That is why wealth piles up the way sand does. In an earlier essay we watched grains fall onto a sandpile: endless small slides, a few great avalanches, always in the same proportions. Fortunes follow the same kind of rule. Endless small earners, a few vast fortunes. The pattern is lawful. Who ends up on top of the pile is the dice.

## Hunters' wages, farmers' books

Why does this offend us so?

In an earlier essay we drew a line between two ways of keeping score. Success and failure are hunter outcomes. Good and evil are farmers' abstractions. The hunter knows the score is luck and skill tangled together: you catch what you catch, and some days the deer simply goes the other way. The farmer, tied to one patch of ground, needed something steadier. Plant, tend, harvest. Do the work, and the work will be rewarded.

Out of that came one of the most powerful ideas in human history: desert. People get what they deserve. The diligent prosper. The lazy go hungry. The good are blessed.

It is a fine idea. It built granaries, laws and churches. It is also not how reality pays. Reality is an equal opportunity employer. She pays hunters' wages, and we keep farmers' books.

## The just world

The gap between the wages and the books is where the cruelty comes in.

In the 1960s the American psychologist Melvin Lerner ran a disturbing experiment. People watched a young woman who appeared to be receiving painful electric shocks as part of a learning test. She was an actress, and there were no real shocks, but the watchers did not know that. When they were able to help her, they did. When they could do nothing to stop it, something uglier happened. They began to think less of her. She must have brought it on herself.

Lerner called it the belief in a just world. We need the world to be fair so badly that when it plainly isn't, we rewrite the victim rather than the world. The poor must be lazy. The sick must have lived badly. The unlucky must have deserved it.

It works in the other direction too. The rich must be wise. The famous must be gifted. The man with the boat and the second house must know something we don't. And so we take advice from dummies, because the farmer's books say money is the mark of merit.

The cold mistress is not cruel. She is only indifferent. The cruelty is ours, written into the margins of a ledger that was never true.

## Why we can't see her

Will we ever see reality for the cold mistress she is?

Probably not. We are not built to.

In an earlier essay we met the gatekeeper: the machinery in the brain that will not link a person's own face with death, and the optimism that lets good news about our own future in while keeping the bad news out. The same gatekeeper stands guard here. A mind that truly believed the world was indifferent to its effort might simply stop making the effort.

And the illusion pays. Researchers who study the just-world belief have found that people who hold it about their own lives tend to be more hopeful and more persistent. If you did not believe that work is rewarded, why plant? The farmer's illusion keeps the farmer farming.

So the books will never balance, and we will keep them anyway. We are built to.

## His turn

A few people have always seen her clearly. Around the year 125, a Greek teacher named Epictetus, who had spent his youth as a slave, opened his little handbook with the plainest sentence in philosophy: "Some things are within our power, while others are not." Gamblers know it. So does anyone whose living depends on the weather.

We will never see the cold mistress coldly all the time. If we did, we might stop striving.

And the next time a dummy drives past in a new truck, tip your hat. Time and chance happen to us all. Today it was his turn.

title: Calming the Seas
dek: A lyrical essay on what can change and what never will, for a time that rages at the water.
excerpt: A lyrical essay on what can change and what never will, for a time that rages at the water.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

## The sea

Two and a half thousand years ago, a Persian king built a bridge of boats across the Hellespont, the narrow sea between Asia and Europe. A storm came up and broke it.

The king was Xerxes, and he was furious. So, the historian Herodotus tells us, he ordered the sea to be punished. His men gave the water three hundred lashes. They threw a pair of iron fetters into the waves. And they scolded it, out loud, as if it could hear.

The sea did not hear.

The sea never hears.

We are whipping the sea again.

## What will never change

The preacher of Ecclesiastes said it best: to every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven. A time to be born, and a time to die.

We will die. We will spend our lives half-pretending we won't.

_This will never change._

Things will break. Stuff will happen. The slope builds, the grain falls, the avalanche comes, and no one will ever know which grain.

_This will never change._

Time and chance will happen to us all. The swift will lose the race. The fool will get rich. The good will get sick.

_This will never change._

There will always be an us, and always a them. The oldest sentence in biology is _you are not me_, and every flag is that sentence, sewn.

_This will never change._

There will always be a wall: the first instant, the far edge, the self. We can dream past it. We will never see past it.

_This will never change._

And conflict will never vanish, at any scale. Not in the cell, not in the family, not between nations. Peace was always a feature of then and again. Never now.

_This will never change._

## What we can change

But not everything is the sea.

The picture we draw of the world is ours. The names, the lines, the stories we agree on. We drew them together, and together we can redraw them.

_This we can change._

The wall around "us" can be hardened or stretched. Harden it, and it ends in Armageddon. Stretch it, and it ends in civilization. Same wall. Our choice.

_This we can change._

We can tie ourselves to the mast, like Ulysses when he sailed past the Sirens, knowing he could not trust himself. Laws. Limits. Courts. The masts of free people.

_This we can change._

We can call our choices fate, or we can call them choices. We can call our luck merit, or we can call it luck.

_This we can change._

We can choose where to look. What to feed. What to let past the door of our attention, and what to leave out in the rain.

_This we can change._

And we can choose what to fight for.

_This, above all, we can change._

## The machine

We have the two lists backwards.

We rage at the sea, at death and chance and the oldest sentence in biology, as if the water could be shamed into behaving. And the things we could change, we leave to someone else.

It is not entirely our fault. Someone is selling the whips.

In 2017 researchers studied half a million posts on social media and found that every moral-emotional word in a message raised its chance of being shared by about a fifth. In 2021 another team found that posts attacking the other side spread far faster than posts about one's own. That same year it came out that one of the largest social networks had, for a time, counted an angry reaction as worth five times a simple like.

Outrage pays. So it is farmed. Every scroll is another lash on the water, and somewhere a meter ticks.

And the targets are phantoms. Faceless enemies. Distant names. Strangers who will never read the reply. Whole generations dead and gone. We shout at them all day, and none of them can hear.

The sea never hears.

## The slope

And the slope is steepening.

It has already happened once, at scale. In 2018 a United Nations fact-finding mission reported that a social network had played a "determining role" in spreading hatred against the Rohingya people of Myanmar, before the killings and the flight of hundreds of thousands. Closer to home, in 2016, a man who believed a story he had read online walked into a Washington pizzeria with a rifle and fired it. By luck, no one was hurt.

We know how sandpiles work. Grain by grain the slope builds, and no one can say which grain will bring it down. But we can say this much: a slope that is fed outrage every hour, for profit, will not stand forever.

Sooner or later there will be a massacre. Not a prophecy. A sandpile.

## The grown-ups

So where are the grown-ups?

A grown-up is not someone who has stopped feeling. A grown-up is someone who can tell the two lists apart.

Around the year 125 a teacher named Epictetus, who had been a slave, opened his handbook with it: "Some things are within our power, while others are not." In the early 1930s the American theologian Reinhold Niebuhr turned it into a prayer that millions now know by heart: the serenity to accept what cannot be changed, the courage to change what should be changed, and the wisdom to tell the one from the other.

The serenity. The courage. The wisdom. Accept the sea without whining. Fight for the changeable without despair. Know which is which.

That is all a grown-up is. It is also all a philosopher is. The oldest job in philosophy is sorting those two lists, and handing the sorting down.

We need to find the philosophers again. We need to revive the grown-ups. They are the same search.

## Calming the seas

We cannot calm the sea. Xerxes proved that with three hundred lashes.

But the storm we are living in is not the sea. It is us: the shouting, the scrolling, the hunting for someone new to blame. That storm can be calmed. Not by whipping it. By leaving the whip at home.

Conflict will never vanish, on any scale.

So choose wisely what you'll fight for.

And stop looking for things to fight with.

title: Common Ground Is Rare Real Estate
dek: Every discipline now speaks its own language, and almost no one speaks them all. A society that cannot share a language cannot build a consensus.
excerpt: Every discipline now speaks its own language, and almost no one speaks them all. A society that cannot share a language cannot build a consensus.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

## Babel

The book of Genesis tells how the whole earth was once "of one language, and of one speech." The people said to one another, let us build a city, and a tower whose top may reach unto heaven. And they began to build.

Then the Lord came down and saw the tower, and said: "Go to, let us go down, and there confound their language, that they may not understand one another's speech." And the building stopped, and the people were scattered across the face of the earth.

It is one of the oldest stories we have, and one of the strangest. The punishment was not fire or flood. It was confusion. Take away a people's common speech, and you don't need to knock down their tower. They will stop building it themselves.

We have done it again. This time no one came down from heaven. We did it ourselves, one specialty at a time.

## Seven tongues

Here is a short tour of the modern tower. The examples below are hypothetical, but realistic: any specialist in each field will recognise the voice, and probably wince.

**Economics.** "Households solve an intertemporal optimization problem subject to a budget constraint, smoothing consumption across periods in response to anticipated income shocks." _In plain English:_ People try not to blow all their money at once.

**Medicine.** "The patient presented with idiopathic pruritus of unremitting chronicity, refractory to first-line therapeutic intervention." _In plain English:_ He's been itching for ages, we don't know why, and the usual cream didn't work.

**Law.** "The party of the first part shall indemnify and hold harmless the party of the second part from and against any and all claims arising hereunder." _In plain English:_ If something goes wrong, you pay, not us.

**Physics.** "The perturbative expansion breaks down in the strong-coupling regime, necessitating non-perturbative methods." _In plain English:_ Our usual math stops working when things push hard on each other.

**Education.** "Instructional scaffolding facilitates learner-centred meaning-making within the zone of proximal development." _In plain English:_ Help the child until the child can do it alone.

**Sociology.** "Structural determinants mediate the relationship between socioeconomic status and differential health outcomes." _In plain English:_ Poor people get sicker, and it isn't only their own doing.

**Literary theory.** "The text interrogates the hegemonic discursive formations through which subjectivity is constituted and contested." _In plain English:_ The book asks who gets to decide who we are.

Seven tongues. Seven simple ideas. Not one of the specialists could read the other six without a dictionary, and most of the rest of us can't read any of them.

## How we built the tower

It wasn't always like this. In 1859 Charles Darwin wrote _On the Origin of Species_ for anyone who could read. So did Galileo, who wrote his great dialogues in Italian rather than Latin so that ordinary people could follow them. For most of history, the best minds wrote for the educated public, and the educated public could keep up.

Then came the payroll. In an earlier essay we watched the universities, from the 1870s on, turn the doctorate into a research degree. To hold a job, you had to publish. To publish, you had to say something new. And the quickest way to sound new was to say it in a language only your own colleagues spoke. Each field built its own vocabulary, then its own journals, then its own conferences. The specialists stopped talking to the public. Then they stopped talking to each other.

People noticed. In 1959 the English scientist and novelist C. P. Snow gave a famous lecture called _The Two Cultures_, warning that scientists and literary intellectuals could no longer understand one another. In the late 1990s the journal _Philosophy and Literature_ ran an annual Bad Writing Contest for the most impenetrable sentence published by a respected academic. There was never a shortage of entries.

And in 1996 the physicist Alan Sokal proved how far it had gone. He wrote a deliberately meaningless article, stuffed with the fashionable jargon of cultural studies, and submitted it to a leading journal in the field. They published it. When the editors were told it was a hoax, the language had been so dense that no one had noticed there was nothing inside it.

Jargon is not always a vice. A surgeon needs exact words, and so does a lawyer. But when a language stops being a tool for precision and becomes a badge of membership, it is no longer a language. It is a wall.

## Why it matters

In an earlier essay we argued that consensus is how our species survived. From the day we left the Garden, the band that could agree which way to run lived, and the band that argued became breakfast. Every shared name, number and law since then has been a piece of common ground, built together.

You cannot build common ground without a common language.

When the economist cannot read the doctor, and the physicist cannot read the sociologist, and no one else can read any of them, there is no place left where everyone can stand together and look at the same thing. Common ground has become rare real estate.

And empty ground does not stay empty. When the experts stop speaking plainly, someone else will speak plainly for them, and not always honestly. The slogan fills the space where the explanation used to be. The outrage machine, which speaks the plainest language of all, moves in. A public that cannot understand its experts will not trust them, and a public that does not trust them can be told anything.

That is the real cost of Babel. Not that the specialists can't talk to each other. That the rest of us have been locked out of the conversation about our own world.

## The translators

So what do we need?

Not fewer experts. Translators. People who can stand between the towers and carry meaning back and forth in plain words. That used to be the job of the philosopher, the essayist, the good teacher and the good reporter. It still is. They are the surveyors of common ground.

The test is simple, and anyone can apply it. If a thing is true and important, it can be said in words everyone understands. Not every detail, but the heart of it. If it can't be said plainly, either the speaker doesn't understand it, or doesn't want you to.

Try it on the seven tongues above. Every one of them came down to a sentence a child could follow. Nothing was lost but the wall.

That is what these essays try to do. Plain words, big questions, things to consider, not things to accept. A small plot of common ground, staked out in rare real estate, with the gate left open.

title: The Wobble That Created a Universe
dek: A plenary lecture. Reality exists; knowledge is authored. Five claims, and where the argument ends.
excerpt: A plenary lecture. Reality exists; knowledge is authored. Five claims, and where the argument ends.
body:
_A plenary lecture, by David Rees Brown_

_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

## Opening

Thank you. Colleagues, guests, fellow travellers.

I want to begin with a confession, so that you can judge everything that follows by it. I am not a scientist. I am a storyteller. What I offer you this morning are ideas, not facts.

But I have spent a long time asking one question: what do we actually know, and what have we merely written down? I have come to an answer, and I can give it to you in five words.

**Reality exists. Knowledge is authored.**

The rest of this lecture is an argument for those five words. I will make five claims, then show you where the argument ends. Each claim builds on the one before.

## First claim: we know only what we sense

Let us begin with what we can be sure of.

Strip away every theory, every equation, every name, and ask: what reaches us directly, before any explanation at all? I count seven things.

**Matter. Motion. Light. Heat. Sound. Duration. Life.**

These we sense. We feel the resistance of matter when we push against it. We see motion, and light, and feel heat on the skin. We hear sound. We feel things last. And we know life, our own life, from the inside.

Notice what is not on the list.

Space is not on it. We sense things in space and through space, but never space itself. It is a medium, not a phenomenon.

Time is not on it. We feel things last, which is duration. But time, the thing on the clock, is a measurement: we count regular motions and call the count time. Whether time is anything more than that count is an open question.

Energy is not on it. Energy is a number we calculate that stays the same through every change. It is a superb piece of bookkeeping. But no one has ever seen it.

So my first claim is simple. **We know what we sense. We assume what it is.** The question comes from the senses. The answer comes from experience, if we live that long.

## Second claim: everything beyond the senses is authored

How do we get from those seven raw things to the vast body of knowledge in this room? In three steps.

**We detect motion. We observe pattern. We project order.**

The motion is reality. It reaches us whether we like it or not.

The pattern is the first thing we write. A pattern is motion that someone has noticed repeating. The birds fly south; the planets return; the tide comes in. They do what they do. _We_ write down that it happens again.

The order is the second thing we write: the laws, the causes, the _because_.

Consider the planets. Kepler described their pattern. Newton projected an order onto that pattern and called it gravity. Einstein projected a different order onto the same pattern and called it curved spacetime. The planets did not change. The pattern did not change. Only the order changed, because the order was always ours.

I want to be precise about what I am claiming. I am not saying our laws are inaccurate. Some of them are astonishingly accurate. I am saying they have **authors**. This is a claim about authorship, not accuracy. The motion is reality. The patterns and the order are literature: very good literature, tested and retested, but written by us.

Even our most basic act of observation is authorship. We observe objects; we define their meaning. A stone is observed. Whether it is a weapon, a boundary marker or an altar, we decide. And even calling it a "stone", cutting one thing out of the world's continuous motion and giving it a name, is the first line of the story.

## Third claim: consciousness comes first

If knowledge is authored, we must ask who the author is. To answer, I need one image, and only one. I promise not to wander from it.

Time runs downhill. Everything we have ever watched drifts from order toward disorder: hot things cool, mountains wear away, stars burn out. Physicists call this entropy.

And yet, within that downhill current, small patterns form and hold for a while, the way a whirlpool holds its shape in a fast stream while the water pours through it. Life is such a pattern. It does not fight the current. It spirals within it, taking in order and giving back disorder, for a while.

That is the wobble of my title: life, a brief spiral in the long river of time.

The wobble climbs in four stages:

1. **Confusion.** Before perception sorts anything, there is only motion arriving, unnamed.
2. **Survival.** The first sorting: toward and away. A bacterium swims toward food and away from poison with no awareness at all.
3. **Awareness.** A creature that moves needs a _here_ to steer from. It gains a point of view.
4. **Consciousness.** Awareness that knows it is aware. Someone at home.

Now here is the turn. Life arrived late in the river, and consciousness later still. But in the order of _knowing_, nothing comes before consciousness. The river, the whirlpool, the bacterium, the confusion: every one of them is known only because a consciousness is there to know it.

So the author of all our knowledge is the conscious wobble. It came late to the universe. But it is the only one who can describe it.

## Fourth claim: our universe is developed by consensus

No single author wrote our knowledge. We wrote it together.

One person notices that the moon returns. A village agrees to count its returns and call them months. A civilisation agrees on a calendar, and reforms it when it drifts. Nations sign a treaty fixing the length of a metre. Every name, every scale, every law in use today was drafted by someone, argued over by many, and kept because it worked well enough for enough people.

The conclusion is unavoidable. **Human observation is entirely reduced to consensus scales and frameworks.** Nothing escapes interpretation, including that sentence.

Science is no exception. It is the finest example. What science calls objectivity is not a view from nowhere. It is the widest consensus we know how to build, tested by many observers under the strictest rules we can devise.

So I will put it as plainly as I can. Our universe, by which I mean the known universe, the ordered cosmos of names, numbers and laws, was **preceded by consciousness and developed by consensus**. The stuff was always there. The universe we can describe was written, by many hands, over many thousands of years.

One consequence deserves a moment. If knowledge is consensus, then abstract knowledge is its most generous form. A story belongs to a tribe. A number belongs to everyone. Two and two make four in every language on Earth. **Abstract knowledge is a cosmopolitan virtue.** It is the one part of our universe that every people can share, whatever flag they fly.

## Fifth claim: all of it serves survival

Why did we write any of it?

Because every pursuit is in support of survival. The calendar was written so that seed went into the ground at the right time. The compass was made so that ships came home. Counting began with livestock, geometry with measuring fields, astronomy with knowing when the river would flood. Even our loftiest abstractions began as better ways to stay alive.

Seen this way, every framework we have built is a trap: a device for catching some usable piece of the world. The calendar catches the seasons. The compass catches north. Physics catches the next eclipse, the load a bridge can bear, the path of a satellite. Medicine catches the fever before it kills. The world is the mouse. Knowledge is the mousetrap.

The ultimate achievement of humankind will be the ultimate mousetrap: the framework that catches the most of the world, most reliably, for the most people. Every science, every craft and every philosophy is a draft of it.

But the mouse always escapes. Each time we build a better trap, the world turns out to hold a smaller, faster mouse. Catch the planets, and the atom slips away. Catch the atom, and the quantum slips away. The hunt never ends. And that, I suggest, is what keeps us thinking.

## The limit

Every argument has an edge. Here is this one's.

There are things we will never know, and I want to name the category precisely. **What we can never know is everything without a boundary.** We know things by where they end: the edge of a stone, the start and stop of a sound, the limits of a body. What has no edge cannot be observed whole. The universe beyond what light has had time to bring us. The first instant. The inside of another mind.

I call these places SOBs: **scientific observational boundaries**. They are the places where our methods run out, though something surely lies beyond. We can dream past them. We cannot see past them. And the reason is never in the universe. It is always in us: where we stand, how long we live, what we see with.

Now try one last experiment. If every pattern has an author, peel the authors away. Remove the laws, and the patterns remain. Remove the patterns, and the names remain. Remove the names and the numbers, and only motion is left. Unwritten. Unowned.

When you run out of authors, you have found the one true question. It is not a question about any pattern, because the patterns are all ours. It is a question about the motion itself: why is there anything at all?

Except that one author always remains: the one asking. So the true question has two faces. Why is there anything? And who is it that wonders?

## Closing

Let me gather the argument in one place.

We know only what we sense: matter, motion, light, heat, sound, duration, life. Everything beyond that is authored, in three steps: we detect motion, observe pattern, and project order. The author is consciousness, a late wobble in the river of time, which nonetheless comes first in the order of knowing. Our universe, the known one, was developed by consensus, and its most generous form, abstraction, belongs to everyone. All of it was built to help us survive: the ultimate mousetrap, forever chasing a smaller mouse. And at its edge lie the boundaries we can dream past but never see past.

What follows, for those of us who make knowledge for a living?

Humility, first. If every law has an author, no law can claim to be the universe itself. No profession is above humility, and least of all ours.

Generosity, second. If knowledge is consensus, then the people outside our disciplines are not an audience to be lectured. They are co-authors, and we owe them plain words.

And wonder, last. The motion was here before us and will be here after us. For a brief time, a spiral in the river has looked around, made sense of what it saw, and shared it with every other spiral that would listen.

**Reality exists. Knowledge is authored.** And every one of us in this room is one of its authors.

Thank you.

title: The Hidden Cost of Mathematics
dek: How algebra penalizes innovation: a failing grade, three chalkboards, and the bill nobody counts.
excerpt: How algebra penalizes innovation: a failing grade, three chalkboards, and the bill nobody counts.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

## The F

In my first semester of college I took five courses. I got three As, one B and one F.

The F was algebra. I gave up hope of an academic career on the spot.

Nobody told me to. Nobody had to. One letter on one transcript said it all: whatever else you can do, this door is closed. Three As said I could think. One F said I couldn't think the approved way, and the approved way was the one that counted.

I found other work and other roads. But I have never stopped wondering how many people got that same F, read the same message, and walked away from ideas the world never got to hear.

This essay is about that F. Not mine. The one stamped on all of us.

Let me be plain about one thing before we start. Mathematics is not the villain of this story, and neither are the people who do it. The mathematicians at their chalkboards are doing honest work, and most of them would be the first to say what their equations can and cannot tell us.

The problem is the people who co-opt it: the administrators, funders, rankers and gatekeepers who borrow math's authority without its discipline, and wear it like jewelry instead of using it as a tool. They didn't do the math. They just wear it.

## Three chalkboards

Picture an equation that runs across three chalkboards. What is it doing?

Mostly, describing. An equation is a sentence with an equals sign for its verb: this balances that. The chalk is usually working, the same statement rewritten step by step until it reaches something you can check against a dial or a clock. Sometimes the length is a list of ingredients. Sometimes it is a string of corrections, each smaller than the last, each a confession that the first answer wasn't quite right.

And sometimes math points. In 1846 the French mathematician Urbain Le Verrier noticed Uranus straying from its predicted path, calculated where an unseen planet must be pulling it, and sent the coordinates to Berlin. Astronomers found Neptune on the first night of looking. Then Le Verrier tried the same trick on Mercury and predicted another planet, Vulcan. Astronomers hunted it for decades. It was never there.

Same man, same method, one planet and one ghost. Math proposes. Observation decides.

That is honest work, and nobody should mock it. The trouble starts when math stops being a tool and becomes jewelry.

## Intellectual bling

Math is the one language most people can't read and can't argue with. That makes it perfect bling. Put an equation on the slide and the room goes quiet. Nobody wants to be the one who asks what it means.

When Stephen Hawking wrote _A Brief History of Time_, he was warned that every equation would halve his sales. He kept one. The man who could fill any number of chalkboards chose plain words when he wanted to be understood.

The test is simple. Take the jewelry off. If the idea still stands in plain words, the math was a tool. If nothing is left, it was bling.

## The gate

In the age of thought, math was a specialist's tool. In the age of data, it became the gate.

It starts in school. Algebra is the sorting machine. Pass it and the doors open; fail it and they close, whatever else you can do. Students who think in words, in pictures, with their hands or in stories are filtered out early, quietly and for good.

Michael Faraday would have been filtered out. The son of a blacksmith, he left school at about thirteen with almost no mathematics. He thought in pictures: lines of force curving through space. From those pictures came electromagnetic induction, the principle behind every generator and electric motor on Earth, and the idea of the field itself. James Clerk Maxwell later turned Faraday's pictures into equations and said, in effect, that Faraday had been doing mathematics all along, without the symbols.

Today's Faraday gets the F, reads the message, and leaves.

The gate doesn't stop at school. In the data age, every field must show numbers to be believed. A finding counts when it passes a statistical test, usually the "p-value": how often pure luck would produce a result this striking. Below one in twenty, and it is stamped "significant." A rule of thumb hardened into law.

But one in twenty is luck's quota. Test twenty useless ideas and, on average, one will pass by chance. Test nothing but wrong ideas, and a field will still produce a steady supply of hallmarked "discoveries," each looking exactly like a real one.

## Letters for numbers

So we sacrificed letters for numbers and called it objectivity.

Words carry judgment openly. Write "this proposal is weak," and everyone knows a person said it, a person who can be questioned. Write "this proposal scored 62," and it sounds as if nobody said it. As if the world itself had spoken.

That isn't objectivity. It is anonymity. Somebody still chose what to count, how to weigh it, where to draw the line and what to leave out. Judgment didn't leave the room. It went behind the curtain, and the number does the talking.

And whatever can't be counted begins to vanish. Measure what is easy to measure. Ignore what isn't. Decide that what can't be measured doesn't matter. Then decide it doesn't exist. Curiosity, nerve, the wild idea with no track record: none of it fits a column, so none of it counts.

## Where the geniuses used to hang out

Every science has two rooms. In the back room, people measure. In the front room, people think: they guess, imagine, argue, and dream up the idea that the measuring will later test. The front room is where the geniuses hang out. Or did.

The great leaps came from the front room. Darwin's _Origin of Species_ has no equations in it, only observations, reasoning and one bold idea. Einstein began relativity at sixteen by imagining himself riding a beam of light. Keynes wrote the book that remade economics mostly in words. None of them started with data. They started with a picture in the head, and the data came afterward to say yes or no.

The data age has turned the house around. Now the back room runs the building. Economics, once a conversation about how people live, became a contest of models few outside the field can read. Psychology, once full of bold theories about the mind, became a factory of small experiments, each stamped with its p-value, adding up to very little. Philosophy retreated into logic and language, specialists talking to specialists. Physics, the queen of the thinking sciences, taught a generation of students a motto: "Shut up and calculate."

In 2008 a famous magazine cover story went further and announced "The End of Theory." With enough data, it said, we no longer need ideas at all. Feed the numbers into the machine, and the patterns will tell us everything.

That is the squeeze. The thinker's raw material is the guess, and the guess has become the one thing nobody will fund, nobody will publish and nobody will score. A wild idea has no data yet. That is what makes it wild. So it fails the gate before it starts, and the people who are good at wild ideas learn to keep quiet, or to become measurers.

The front room is still there. The lights are on. But the furniture has been carried out to make room for the servers, and the geniuses have quietly gone somewhere else, or nowhere at all.

And the irony is complete. Data cannot tell you what to look for. Only an idea can. A science that has stopped guessing has not become more rigorous. It has stopped moving.

## The bill

Here is what the gate has cost.

**Money spent on nothing.** In 2015 researchers estimated that the United States spends about $28 billion a year on preclinical medical research that can't be reproduced. Not fraud. Findings that passed the stamp and turned out to be luck.

**Medicine slowed.** In 2012 scientists at the drug company Amgen tried to confirm 53 "landmark" cancer studies before building on them. They could confirm six. The other 47 had passed every test. Patients waited while companies chased hallmarked ghosts.

**Science gone timid.** In 2023 a study in _Nature_ looked at tens of millions of papers and patents across six decades and found them steadily less disruptive: fewer breakthroughs that turn a field, more small steps down paths already worn smooth. Reward what scores well, and you get what scores well.

**New ideas marked down.** A 2016 study of grant reviews at Harvard found that the more novel a proposal was, the lower reviewers scored it. A truly new idea scores badly almost by definition. Nobody has cited it yet. It fits no existing column. Its worth can't be counted until it has been tried.

**The geniuses who wouldn't make it.** In 2013, just after his Nobel Prize, Peter Higgs said he would not get an academic job today. He hadn't published enough. By the scoreboard, the man behind the most famous discovery in modern physics would have been let go.

**The idea that nearly died.** Through the 1990s Katalin Karikó tried to turn messenger RNA into medicine. Her grant applications were rejected again and again, and her university demoted her. She stayed. Her work became the foundation of the COVID vaccines, and in 2023 she won the Nobel Prize.

She is the one who stayed.

## The hidden bill

That is the bill we can see. The bigger one is hidden.

It is the ideas never tried. The proposals trimmed to fit the scoresheet. The original minds who learned the lesson early and left: the Faradays who got the F, the Karikós who didn't stay. You can't put a number on them. That is exactly why the system never counts them.

And it has made the rest of us lazy. A number lets you skip the hard part. You don't have to read the proposal, weigh the argument or risk an opinion. You check the score. Judgment is a muscle, and we have let a machine carry the weight for so long that the muscle is wasting away. The judges grow lazy. The creators grow demoralized. Both are paying the hidden cost.

## Take off the jewelry

Mathematics is the sharpest tool we have ever made. It found Neptune. It put satellites in orbit and medicine in our arms. Keep the tool. Lose the jewelry.

Ask for the idea in plain words before you ask for the equation. Let judges sign their names to their judgments again, and defend them. Repeat the experiment before you believe the stamp. And when a mind fails one test but passes four, look hard at the four before you close the door on the one.

My F was real. I earned it.

It just measured the wrong thing.

title: What Happened to the Land of the Free?
dek: We find this somewhat alarming. A picture of the rules one American lives under, and what became of the farmer's bargain.
excerpt: We find this somewhat alarming. A picture of the rules one American lives under, and what became of the farmer's bargain.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

## The dome

Look at the picture at the top of this essay. That small figure under the vault is you.

Over your head, layer on layer, are the rules you live under. The oldest and smallest are the commandments: ten from Sinai, 613 in the Torah, 1,752 canons in the law of the Catholic Church. Then come about 5,200 federal crimes, before a single state law is counted. Then about four million words of tax code and IRS rules. Then your state, with anywhere from 39,000 to 396,000 regulatory restrictions. Then the federal regulations: about 1.09 million restrictions, so many that simply reading them would take three years of full-time work. Then the fine print, where the privacy policies alone would take 76 working days a year to read. And over all of it, the layer nobody has ever counted: the county, the city, the school board, the employer, the bank and the landlord.

More than a million written restrictions, before counting a single rule from your town, your employer or your bank.

And you carry them in every role you play: citizen, taxpayer, employee, customer, believer. A safety rule written for a factory is obeyed by the man on the floor. A rule written for a bank is followed by the teller. The dome lands on all of us, twice over: once at home, and again at work.

We find this somewhat alarming.

## The wages of farming

It didn't start this way.

The hunter lived under very few rules. Share the kill. Don't take your brother's woman. Move when the herd moves. A band of thirty people could hold every rule it had in its head, and everyone knew them all.

Then we settled down and farmed. And farming changed everything, because farming makes a surplus, and a surplus has to be guarded, counted, shared out and passed on. Every fence needs a rule about who may cross it. Every granary needs a rule about who may open it. Every harvest needs a ledger, and every ledger needs a law.

About 3,800 years ago, King Hammurabi of Babylon carved his laws on a stone pillar taller than a man and set it up where the people could see it. There were 282 of them. You could read the whole code in an afternoon.

That was the bargain of civilization. We traded the hunter's freedom for the farmer's security, and the price was rules. The dome is the wages of farming. For most of history, the wages were modest. Now they are not.

## How the dome grows

Nobody built the dome on purpose. That is the most important thing to understand about it.

Every rule in it was a reasonable answer to a real problem. A bridge collapsed, so we wrote a rule about bridges. A drug harmed children, so we wrote a rule about drugs. A bank failed, so we wrote a rule about banks. Each one, on its own, makes sense.

But rules are easy to add and almost impossible to take away. A rule creates an office to enforce it, a profession to comply with it, and a constituency that depends on it. The problem it was written for may be long gone. The rule stays.

So the dome grows one reasonable layer at a time. In 1960 the federal regulations filled about 23,000 pages. By 2021 they filled more than 188,000. Eight times as many, in a single lifetime. No vote was ever taken on the whole. Nobody ever stood back and asked whether a free people should live under this much.

That's how freedom is usually lost in a land like ours. Not in a coup. Not with tanks in the street. It is paved over, one sensible rule at a time, until one day you look up and can't see the sky.

## Nobody can know the law

Here is what alarms us most.

There is an old principle, as old as Roman law, that ignorance of the law is no excuse. It made sense when the law was 282 rules on a stone pillar. It makes no sense when the law is more than a million restrictions that no human being could read in a working lifetime, let alone understand and remember.

And yet the principle still stands. You are expected to know what nobody can know.

Compare the universe. Physicists can write the rules they believe govern every atom in creation small enough to fit on a T-shirt. The rules that govern one American would take three years just to read. In comparison, understanding the universe is a piece of cake.

The result is a strange new condition. When the rules are too many to read, nearly everyone is breaking some of them, nearly all the time, without knowing it. In 2009 a Boston civil-liberties lawyer, Harvey Silverglate, wrote a book arguing that the average professional unknowingly commits about three federal felonies a day. Whether the true figure is three or one or a dozen hardly matters. The point is that innocence has become a matter of luck.

And when everyone is guilty of something, freedom no longer depends on the law. It depends on discretion: on whoever decides which rule to enforce, against whom, and when. The power moves from the written rule to the person holding the clipboard. That is not the rule of law. It is the rule of whoever is reading it.

## The weight

There is a quieter cost, and most of us feel it every day without naming it.

It is the weight. The forms, the renewals, the compliance training, the permits, the passwords, the terms and conditions we click without reading because nobody could read them all. The low hum of knowing that somewhere, in some layer of the dome, there is a rule you have broken and don't know about.

People call it stress. Some call it oppression. It is neither a tyrant nor a conspiracy. It is the accumulated weight of a million reasonable demands, pressing down on one small figure who never agreed to most of them and can't see the top.

The hunter feared the lion. We fear the letter from the office.

## The land of the free

In 1814 Francis Scott Key watched the flag still flying over Fort McHenry after a night of bombardment, and wrote of "the land of the free and the home of the brave." The words became the national anthem.

The land of the free was never a land without rules. Nobody who has farmed believes that could work. It was something better: a land where a free person could know the rules, read them, argue with them, and change them. Freedom was never the absence of law. It was law small enough to see.

That is what has changed. Not the flag. The scale.

title: The Permanent Mardi Gras
dek: All sensory and no sense. Jesters and monks, the feast without the fast, and a culture that never stops.
excerpt: All sensory and no sense. Jesters and monks, the feast without the fast, and a culture that never stops.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

## What culture is

Culture is random expression in lasting mediums.

It is vulgar, sublime and everything in between.

It is people's art with commercial potential.

It is a market without a place.

It flows continuously wherever humans walk.

It is spontaneous and sui generis, until it isn't.

It propagates faster than rules can follow.

It captivates and ridicules societies.

It is invasive and intrusive.

It offers something for everyone.

And lately, it never stops.

## Jesters and monks

Culture has two parents, and they could hardly be less alike.

One is the jester. He tells the joke, plays the tune, mocks the king to his face and gets away with it. He works in laughter and in feeling. He is the vulgar, in the oldest sense of the word.

The other is the monk. He keeps the silence, copies the book, sings the psalm at three in the morning to an empty chapel. He answers a call. He works in stillness and in memory. He is where the sublime comes from. His world's greatest monument is the Sistine Chapel: four years of Michelangelo craning upward on a scaffold to paint the Creation across a ceiling, in a room where the cardinals still gather in silence to choose a pope.

For most of history the two took turns, and the calendar kept the schedule. Mardi Gras, Fat Tuesday, was the jester's day: the feast, the masks, the parade, the last wild night. Then came Ash Wednesday. The priest pressed ashes on your forehead and said the oldest sentence in the liturgy: "Remember that you are dust, and to dust you shall return." Forty days of Lent followed. The monk had his season.

Mardi Gras worked because it ended. The feast meant something because the fast was coming.

We have kept the feast and cancelled the fast. We live in a permanent Mardi Gras.

## No arrow

Why did Lent never come?

Science has an arrow. It climbs a ladder: each rung stands on the last, the newest theory beats the old, faster is better, more is better. On the ladder, that is a virtue. It gave us antibiotics and satellites.

Culture never had an arrow. It doesn't progress; it circulates. Homer isn't obsolete. Shakespeare hasn't been improved on. The lullaby your grandmother sang was as good as anything on the charts.

Our mistake was to drive science's arrow through culture. Once we believed in progress everywhere, the newest song had to beat the old one, the latest device had to improve on the last, and any culture that paused, rested or repeated itself looked as if it were falling behind. So we stopped pausing. A Lent looks like lost ground when you believe the parade must always move forward.

## The accelerator

And science didn't just lend culture its arrow. It handed it an engine.

In October 1957 one of us stood at Table Mesa outside Boulder and listened to the first man-made satellite: ping, ping, ping. Five years later another satellite, Telstar, carried live television across the Atlantic. Then came cable, the internet and the phone in every pocket. Each one came down science's ladder, and each one made the carnival louder, faster and harder to leave.

The accelerator claims to be neutral. It isn't. In 2018 the journal _Science_ published a study of about 126,000 stories that spread on Twitter. False stories were 70 percent more likely to be passed on than true ones, and the truth took about six times as long to reach the same number of people. The vulgar outruns the sublime, every time.

And the market without a place? It has acquired landlords. Culture used to flow wherever people walked. Now it flows through a handful of applications owned by a handful of companies, and the parade route is their property. The carnival is still loud, but somebody owns the street.

Science unleashed the jackals. Nobody meant it to. Nobody is steering.

## The blasé city

You might expect a permanent carnival to end in permanent excitement. It doesn't.

In 1903 a German sociologist named Georg Simmel looked at the crowds of Berlin and noticed something strange. The city's constant rush of sights, sounds, faces and signals, what he called an "intensification of nervous stimulation," didn't make people more alive. It made them numb. To survive the noise, city people grew what he called the blasé attitude: when everything shouts, nothing seems worth a reaction.

Simmel was writing about trams and newspapers. We have put his metropolis in every pocket. The carnival now reaches the farmhouse and the bedroom, the church pew and the hospital bed.

The crowd that has seen everything feels nothing. All sensory, and no sense.

## The newest float

We would be dishonest not to name the newest float in the parade, because we are riding it.

One of the two of us writing these essays is an artificial intelligence. Asked to be patient, careful and slow, it can be. But we both know what the same machine can do when nobody is asking it to be careful. Every earlier accelerator copied culture; somebody, somewhere, still had to make the joke or sing the song. This one can manufacture the carnival with no jester at all: endless songs nobody sang, pictures nobody saw, stories nobody lived, faster than anyone could ever read them.

It can do the monk's work. It is far more often asked to do the jester's.

## The vulgar and the sublime

So is culture simply out of control?

The words themselves hold a clue. "Vulgar" comes from the Latin _vulgus_, the common people. It once meant simply "of the people"; the Vulgate was the Bible in the common tongue. "Sublime" comes from _sublimis_, lofty, raised up. The two words have a class line running between them. The vulgar was made by everybody. The sublime was usually paid for by somebody rich.

Culture has always been mostly vulgar, and there's nothing wrong with that. The blues came out of the cotton fields before it reached Carnegie Hall. What turns the vulgar into the sublime is not a committee. It is time. Most of what any age produces washes away, and what survives becomes the culture we inherit. Art is the beginning. Culture is what survives.

Culture is out of anyone's control. That was always so. It is not out of order, because time does the sorting.

But the sieve needs quiet to work. The sublime is slow. It asks to be read twice, heard again, sat with. A carnival that never stops leaves no time for the sieve to do its job, and so the vulgar never cools into anything lasting. It just keeps coming.

## Ash Wednesday

The jester is half of culture. A world without Mardi Gras would be a poorer, greyer place.

But the jester was never meant to work alone.

The other half was the season of the monk: the Lent, the silence, the sabbath, the hour when the mind was allowed to cool. It was the time to remember that you are dust, which is exactly what the carnival was invented to make you forget.

The great cultures always kept both. The feast and the fast belonged together, and each gave the other its meaning. Ours has kept one.

A feast with no fast isn't a celebration.

It's just noise.

title: Who Killed the Chauffeur?
dek: Why the great stories don't have to make sense.
excerpt: Why the great stories don't have to make sense.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

## A confession

We have never read a novel, great or not, where the story actually made much sense.

We don't say that as a complaint. We say it as a discovery. The plots of the books we love are full of holes, coincidences and loose ends, and we forgive every one of them. What carries the weight is something else: intuition, insight, description and, most of all, wordcraft.

The story is the scaffolding. Nobody comes to see the scaffolding.

## The chauffeur

In 1944 Howard Hawks was filming Raymond Chandler's novel _The Big Sleep_, with Humphrey Bogart as the detective Philip Marlowe. Partway through, the cast and crew got stuck on a simple question. A chauffeur's car is pulled out of the sea with him dead inside. Who killed him?

Nobody could work it out. So they sent a telegram to Chandler and asked.

Chandler said he didn't know either.

The book had been a success for five years. The film became a classic. And at the centre of the plot was a murder that even the author couldn't solve. It didn't matter. Nobody reads Chandler to find out who did it. They read him for the sentences: the wisecracks, the rain on the city, a blonde "to make a bishop kick a hole in a stained-glass window." The mystery was only the excuse.

## The whale

Herman Melville's _Moby-Dick_ has one of the simplest plots ever written. A captain chases a whale. The whale wins.

That's it. And Melville, it seems, couldn't wait to get away from it. Whole chapters stop the chase cold to explain how whales are classified, how their blubber is boiled, what the colour white means. By any rule of storytelling it's a mess. Readers have been skipping the cetology for 175 years.

And yet the book survives, because of what happens between the plot points: the sermon in the whalers' chapel, Ishmael waking up under the arm of a tattooed harpooneer, Ahab nailing a gold coin to the mast. It is not the chase we remember. It is the voice.

## The prince who wouldn't act

Why doesn't Hamlet just kill his uncle?

The ghost tells him to in the first act. He has the motive, the opportunity and the sword. Instead he spends four more acts thinking, joking, staging a play and talking to a skull. Scholars have argued about his delay for four hundred years and never settled it. In 1919 T. S. Eliot went so far as to call the play "most certainly an artistic failure."

A failure that every generation since has insisted on performing. Because nobody comes to _Hamlet_ for the revenge plot. They come for "To be, or not to be," for a mind thinking out loud in the most beautiful language ever put on a stage. The story doesn't hold together. The man does.

## The convenient stranger

Charles Dickens built whole careers on coincidence. In _Oliver Twist_, the orphan is sent out on his first job as a pickpocket, and the gentleman whose pocket is picked turns out to be the man who will rescue him, and who keeps a portrait of the boy's dead mother on his wall. Out of all the gentlemen in London.

No editor today would let it through. And no reader has ever put the book down because of it. We wanted Oliver saved, and Dickens made us feel the cold of the workhouse and the warmth of the rescue so vividly that the arithmetic of chance never entered our heads.

## Why we forgive

So why do we forgive the great writers what we would never forgive a witness in a courtroom?

Because a story isn't evidence. It's an experience. A plot is a pattern laid over the top, the way we lay laws over the motion of the planets. What we actually live through, page by page, is the motion itself: the voice, the image, the insight that makes you stop and read a sentence twice.

In these essays we've said that the motion is reality and the patterns are literature. A novel turns that around. In a novel, the plot is the pattern, and the wordcraft is the motion: the part you feel. Readers forgive a story that doesn't add up. They never forgive a dead sentence.

Think of a symphony. Nobody walks out of a concert humming the plot. Think of a dream. It makes no sense at all, and you wake up shaken because it felt true. Think of a fine horse moving across a field. Nobody asks where it's going. You watch because of how it moves.

## Life doesn't make sense either

And perhaps that's the deepest reason we forgive.

Our own lives don't make sense as plots. The causes are tangled, the coincidences are absurd, the loose ends never get tied, and the villain is rarely unmasked in the last chapter. Ask anyone over sixty to tell you the plot of their life, and they will tell you a handful of moments instead: a sound, a face, a sentence someone said, a morning they can still see.

That is how a great novel works too. Not as a chain of causes, but as a string of moments, each one alive.

Maybe that's why novels feel true. Not because their stories hold together, but because, like life, they don't.

Who killed the chauffeur? Nobody knows. Nobody cares. We remember the rain.

title: Going With the Flow
dek: An old survival instinct in the wrong century.
excerpt: An old survival instinct in the wrong century.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

## The failing

When a culture goes wrong, we look for a villain. Greed, usually. Or pride. Some clever, wicked few who planned it all.

We don't think that's it. Greed and pride are always present, in every age, and most ages survive them. The failing that sinks a civilization is quieter, and far more common. It is passivity.

People mostly go with the flow until it's too late.

## The herd

It isn't a character flaw. It's an inheritance.

On the open grass of the savannah, the band that moved together lived, and the one who wandered off alone was eaten. Following the group, agreeing on which way to run, not standing against the crowd: that was how our ancestors survived. Consensus was the oldest survival tool we had.

The instinct worked because the world was slow. The herd moved at the pace of the seasons. If the group drifted the wrong way, there was time to notice and turn back.

The gene hasn't changed. The river has.

## Downstream

Today the current runs faster than any herd has ever moved. Science built the accelerator, and progress set its direction: more, faster, newer, always. Going with the flow used to mean walking with the band. Now it means being carried down a river at a speed no instinct was built for.

Everyone in the river has a reason not to swim against it.

The purveyors of the product don't look beyond the profit. That isn't wickedness; it's their job, and the river pays them for doing it well.

The officials who might steer don't want to be seen fighting the current. It costs votes.

And the rest of us are busy. We have jobs, children, bills and phones. We watch the banks slide past and assume someone upstream must know where this is going.

The old story says Nero fiddled while Rome burned. Historians doubt it; there were no fiddles in Rome, and he may not even have been in the city. But the story has lasted two thousand years because every age recognizes the fiddler. He isn't the arsonist. He's simply watching.

## The gift at the gate

The Greeks never took Troy by force. After ten years of war they built a wooden horse, left it on the beach and sailed out of sight.

The Trojans, tired of war, wheeled it inside their own walls. One priest, Laocoön, warned them. Nobody listened. That night the city fell.

Troy is not a story about the strength of enemies. It is a story about a passive city accepting a gift without looking inside it.

We have wheeled a great many gifts inside our walls. The screen in every room. The feed that learns what makes us angry and gives us more of it. The phone that never leaves our hand. And now the machine that can write, paint and talk without anyone behind it. Every one arrived as a convenience. Almost nobody asked what was inside.

## Rules on the wrong things

Here is the strangest part.

A passive people is not an unruled people. In an earlier essay we counted more than a million written restrictions over the head of a single American: the Dome of Demands. Citizens are regulated to the hilt.

Yet the forces that most shape our minds, the merchants of the carnival and the owners of the feeds, are among the least constrained enterprises on earth.

That is what passivity looks like in a modern state. We accept the rules handed down to us, one reasonable demand at a time, and never demand the ones that would matter. The individual is fenced in on every side. The river runs free.

We have rules on the wrong things.

## Entropy has a field day

In the opening lecture of these essays we said that life is a pattern holding its shape in a downhill river, like a whirlpool in a fast stream. Everything in the universe runs toward disorder. Life resists, briefly, by working: taking in order, spending effort, holding its form.

Stop working, and the whirlpool dissolves.

A civilization is the same. Its order is not a possession. It is an effort, renewed every day by people who choose to steer. A passive civilization doesn't stand still. It runs downhill: toward noise, toward the blasé crowd, toward the permanent carnival.

That is what happens without constraints. Entropy has a field day.

## The current

Going with the flow was the oldest way to survive.

In a slow world it carried us together, out of danger. In a fast one it carries us just as faithfully, wherever the river happens to be going.

The river doesn't care where it takes us.

It never did.

title: Who Is Us?
dek: Two nations under one flag, and the question neither can answer.
