The new indulgences are the final theory, the moment of creation, the nature of dark matter, the multiverse and the meaning of the whole. Every one is delivered beyond the verge, the place where the received runs out. Every one is paid for in advance with public money: the next collider, the next telescope, the next decade of promise. No one can inspect the product, because the product lies where no one can go.

The coin rings. The soul is promised. The basilica gets built.

## The theses

Luther nailed up ninety-five. We need far fewer.

**All laws are situational, not universal.** Every law belongs to the frame and scale in which it was made. General relativity works superbly within its frames. Carried to the beginning of the universe, or the inside of a black hole, it produces infinities: heat and density that cannot exist. The law has not revealed the edge of the cosmos. It has revealed the edge of its own situation.

**Prediction does not equal truth.** It is local and non-transferable. A theory can predict brilliantly and still be wrong about what is happening, and it is entirely possible to predict without understanding anything at all.

**A placeholder is not a discovery.** In the standard account of the cosmos, ordinary matter makes up about five per cent of the universe. The other ninety-five is dark matter and dark energy, neither ever directly detected, both added because the theory did not fit the sky without them. A theory that cannot name ninety-five per cent of what it describes is not an account of the universe. It is a name for a gap.

**Reality and material are the same thing.** It is a tautology, and that is its power. Whatever is claimed to be real but is not material is a word.

## The press

Gutenberg's press had been running since the middle of the fifteenth century. Within weeks of 1517, Luther's theses were in print across Germany. Within a few years he was the most widely printed author in Europe. In 1522 he published the New Testament in German, and ordinary people could hold the Bible in their own hands and judge the priest against it.

The press did not work alone. Cheap pamphlets and woodcut cartoons, many from the workshop of Lucas Cranach, carried the quarrel to people who would never read a treatise. And Christendom was coming apart. The Holy Roman Empire was a patchwork of princes, and when Rome and the Emperor moved against Luther, one of them, Frederick the Wise of Saxony, hid him in Wartburg Castle. There was no longer a single power that could close every door.

The press did not make Europe wiser. It made the Church answerable.

The new press has four parts, and all four are running at once.

Self-publishing removes the gatekeeper between the writer and the reader. Artificial intelligence removes the gatekeeper between the reader and the research. Anyone can now take a paper, a claim or a placeholder and have it explained, cross-examined and checked against the evidence. Mathematics, the Latin of physics, no longer guards the door.

One of us is exactly that kind of machine.

Social media is the pamphlet and the woodcut: fast, cheap, crude and impossible to recall.

And the world order is fragmenting, as Christendom did. The institutions that set the agenda for science after the Second World War no longer speak for the whole world. New centres fund their own research, publish their own journals and keep their own counsel. There is no longer a single power that can close every door.

## When the public reads

When the public reads, it reacts. It always has.

A monopoly on interpretation lasts exactly as long as the public cannot read the source. What if the people paying for science could read what they are paying for? What if they could see for themselves that the beginning of time is where the equations break down, that most of the universe is a name for what the theory cannot see, and that the next machine is promised to find what the last one did not?

The indulgence works only in the dark.

## The scholar

Luther was not an outsider. He was a monk and a professor of theology. The Reformation began with a scholar who read the Bible himself and said what it plainly said.

The scholar has nothing to fear from the new press. He goes to the verge alone, with no grants, no teams and no laboratories, armed only with his intelligence, and whatever answer lies there, he will feel it. The press serves him. It always did.

Science is judged by its real accomplishments, and they are numerous and enormous. Its failures are forgiven. They are innocent and unavoidable, the cost of exploration.

The indulgence is not a failure. It is a sale.

## Judgement

If science can read the stars, it ought to be able to sense the wind.

The Church did not fall in 1517. Its authority began a long time dying.

At some time certain, the free ride on other people's money will slam to a halt, and the public's judgement will be unforgiving.

The coin still rings in the coffer. The public is learning to read.

title: The Afterglow
dek: Physics is the Afterglow of the Manhattan Project.
excerpt: Physics is the Afterglow of the Manhattan Project.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

## The deal

For a hundred years, physics made a difference within somebody's lifetime. Electricity went from the lab to the house in a generation. Then came radio, X-rays, the transistor, the laser, nuclear power. A boy born in 1900 lived to see nearly all of it. That was the deal: the questions were hard, and the answers came home.

## The blank check

In 1945 the deal changed. Physicists handed the government the most frightening thing ever built, and the government handed back a blank check. Nobody argues with the people who know how. Through the Cold War, physics was paid for the way armies are paid for, out of fear and for prestige.

The moon landings came out of the same purse. They were never about the moon. They were about stuffing the Russians. If the moon isn't made of cheese, who needs it?

## The split

By the mid-1970s the frontier stopped coming home. Its grand theory was finished, and nothing found at the frontier since has changed how anyone lives. The other half of physics, the half that works with materials, never stopped delivering: chips, lights, batteries. The prestige and the big money run to the half that delivers nothing.

## Questions nobody needs answered

Look at what the frontier works on now. What came before the beginning? Are there other universes? What is dark matter made of? What happens inside a black hole? Which interpretation of quantum mechanics is true? Is time real?

Not one answer would change a single life. Most of these questions sit past our scientific observational boundaries, the SOBs: the lines beyond which nothing can be seen, measured or checked. A question past an SOB can never be settled. That makes it the safest career in science. Forty years of work, and never once wrong.

## The customer leaves

When the Russians folded, the customer left the store. In 1993 Congress cancelled the Superconducting Super Collider with its tunnel already being dug under Texas.

The frontier didn't take the hint. It moved its biggest machinery to CERN, where many governments split the bill and no single one has to answer for it. It kept the budget and lost the reason.

## Why it survives

Prestige runs backwards: the farther a question sits from any use, the higher its status. Solve a problem people have and you're an engineer. Ponder the origin of everything and you're a genius.

The frontier also lives on an old IOU. Because Maxwell and the quantum paid off, every fundamental question borrows against that record, and nobody checks the date on the note.

Meanwhile the people who want to make a difference drift off to build things. The ones who stay like it abstract.

## The storytellers

And the public finances their whims. Museums and parks at least are places to take the family. The frontier asks for money as investment, with talk of spin-offs and "you never know," and delivers stories. Black holes fill planetariums. Beginnings sell books.

The frontier has become a storytelling business. We admit we're storytellers. They don't.

What if physics were measured by what it changes within somebody's lifetime? What if the frontier had to ask for its money as art instead of as investment?

Would anyone still write the check?

title: The Speed of Response
dek: Information travels at the speed of light. Response travels at the speed of a walk.
excerpt: Information travels at the speed of light. Response travels at the speed of a walk.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

## The limiting speed

In physics, the speed of light is not really about light. It is the speed limit on cause and effect. Nothing can influence anything faster. Physicists draw it as a cone: the region of space and time you can reach, and that can reach you. Outside it, events happen that you could never have answered.

Human affairs have a limiting speed too.

## Information reached the limit

A signal in an optical fibre travels at about 200,000 kilometres a second, two-thirds of the speed of light. A rumour, a picture or an accusation can cross the world before the person it concerns is awake. For information, the limit has effectively been reached. There is nowhere faster to go.

## Response did not move

Response is everything that has to happen before anyone can answer: noticing, understanding, deciding, acting. It is the same for a person, an editor, a court or a parliament. It runs at human speed. It needs sleep, reading, consultation and second thoughts. It moves about as fast now as it did when the printing press was new.

The gap between the two has never been wider, and every improvement in transmission widens it further.

## The slow version

Television changed protest over half a century. It rewarded what could be seen, so protest learned to be seen: shorter signs, marches timed for the evening news, crowds that knew the whole world was watching. It happened slowly enough to notice, argue about and write about.

Social media has done the same to nearly everything in a decade. There was no time to notice.

## Past the horizon

In March 2023, depositors at Silicon Valley Bank asked for about $42 billion in a single day, much of it set in motion on phones and in group chats. The bank was closed the next morning. No one had time to answer.

In 2018 a study in _Science_ found that false stories on Twitter reached their audiences about six times faster than true ones. The correction travels at the speed of response. By the time it arrives, the falsehood has already gone everywhere it was going.

This is the black hole. Past the event horizon, nothing gets back out. In the gap between information and response, nothing can be called back: no correction, no apology, no second thought. The consequence arrives first.

## Why this is happening

The suggested causes are not mysterious.

Transmission is engineering, and engineering improves. Response is biology, and biology does not.

The animal mind has two speeds. Reaction is fast, built for the rustle in the grass. Response is slow, built for everything else. A system that moves faster than response leaves only reaction to meet it, and past a certain speed there is no response, only reaction.

And platforms are rewarded for whatever is shared quickest. What is shared quickest is what provokes reaction.

## What is clearly not right

The belief that more information makes a people better informed. Information beyond the speed of response is not knowledge. It is impact.

The belief that the old safeguards still work. Editors, courts, retractions and cooling-off periods were built for information that travelled at the speed of a walk. They still work at that speed. Nothing arrives at that speed any more.

## The better question

What if the true limit of a society is not how much it knows, but how fast it can respond?

What if the fastest information a people can afford is the information it can still answer?

Information travels at the speed of light. Response travels at the speed of a walk. We live in the gap.

title: Pants That Fit
dek: What a science looks like when it knows it has a subject.
excerpt: What a science looks like when it knows it has a subject.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

## The condition of being one

When most of us say "subjective", we mean personal bias: an observer's opinions, tastes and hopes leaking into what he sees. Science was built to drain that off, and it does the job remarkably well. Measure it, repeat it, let your rivals check it, and the quirks of the single observer wash out. That is how science achieves consensus, without ever confronting subjectivity.

Subjectivity runs deeper than the individual. It comes in three layers, and the method reaches only the top one.

The top layer is personal, and consensus corrects it. Beneath it lies the layer every human observer shares: the same brain, the same senses, the same restless habit of finding patterns. Consensus can't touch this one, because everyone in the consensus carries it, and for the same reason hardly anyone notices it. At the bottom lies what anything means or feels like from the inside, which can't be handed to anyone at all. That layer sits across the Existential Boundary, the line between observed reality and what needs to be experienced to be understood.

So what science calls objectivity turns out to be agreed subjectivity: the top layer scrubbed away, the middle one shared, the bottom one quietly ignored. Somewhere along the way, removing the bias was mistaken for removing the subject.

Subjectivity isn't a flaw in the observer. It's the condition of being one.

## The instrument we can't set down

The middle layer isn't a figure of speech. It's chemistry.

A tenth of a milligram of LSD, nudging one system in the brain, is enough to make time stretch, let space lose its edges and dissolve the line between self and world. A general anaesthetic removes the world altogether while the body goes on living. One small difference in the pigments of the eye gives about one man in twelve of northern European descent a different world of colour. Change the chemistry and the picture changes. Reality doesn't.

Every telescope, detector and equation is read through that chemistry. No instrument can get behind the brain, because the brain is reading the instrument. It is the first SOB, the first scientific observational boundary, and every other boundary sits inside it.

So we are incomplete observers, and our conclusions are date-specific. Each one describes the world as it appeared to a particular kind of brain, with particular instruments, at a particular time. The observer is part of the measurement, and the observer is never finished.

## The wrong size

For a century, science has dressed for a larger figure: the final theory, the universal law, the meaning of the whole. It isn't, mostly, dishonesty. It's a want of self-awareness, of its limitations and, just as much, of its possibilities.

The pants don't fit.

## A science that fits

A science that knew it had a subject would say what each claim had survived, and when. Its laws would carry their scale, because what works at one scale doesn't, of itself, work at all scales. We call this the Einstein Conundrum. Its placeholders would be marked pending, and "discovered" would give way to "consistent with". It would weigh its work by consequence, not verdict, and keep its highest respect for the work that reaches the verge honestly.

## The possibilities

Pants that fit aren't smaller pants. They're the ones you can dance in. Inside its own situation science has no equal: it set the bone, raised the bridge and grew more wheat on the same field, and none of it needed a claim on the whole universe. A science that claims only what it can carry gets believed when it speaks.

## The better question

What if a scientist's authority came from how precisely he could say where his knowledge ends?

Reality is a given. What we make of it is not. A science that knows the difference can wear the pants that fit, and dance in them.

title: When Will They Ever Learn?
dek: Individuals learn the hard way. Groups almost never do.
excerpt: Individuals learn the hard way. Groups almost never do.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

## The question

In 1955 Pete Seeger wrote a folk song about flowers, young men and graves, and asked when we would ever learn. By the early sixties a generation was singing it. The boys went anyway.

## The old rules

The rules were never lost. They are among the oldest things we ever wrote down.

About four thousand years ago an Egyptian vizier named Ptahhotep told his son not to be proud of his knowledge, and to consult the ignorant as well as the wise. The Greeks carved two short commands at Apollo's temple at Delphi: know thyself, and nothing in excess. Confucius put the whole of ethics in a sentence: what you do not wish for yourself, do not do to others. The _Dhammapada_ said that hatred is never ended by hatred.

Four thousand years, every culture that learned to write, and the list hardly changes: humility, moderation, self-knowledge, reciprocity. We have never been short of the rules.

## The first lesson

Genesis places the trouble at the very beginning. The first rule ever given was broken at the first chance, and what the fruit delivered was knowledge of good and evil, not the will to choose the good. Knowledge came first, and exile came with it. "He that increaseth knowledge increaseth sorrow," wrote the Preacher of Ecclesiastes. Aeschylus said the rest: wisdom comes through suffering.

An aphorism is received information. Wisdom is actual information, and it lies across the Existential Boundary, the line between observed reality and what needs to be experienced to be understood. No one has ever learned humility by reading Ptahhotep. We learn it the one way it can be learned, by being humbled ourselves, and usually late.

## People learn

So people do learn. One at a time, at their own cost, and too late to pass it on. Each life gathers its wisdom, and each death takes it away. Only the report survives, and the report has never taught anyone what they had not already felt.

## Nations don't

Societies are made of people, but they do not live like people. They have priorities of their own: power, revenue, security, glory, the survival of the institution itself. When those priorities meet the needs of the people, the society wins. It always has.

The ancients knew it. Herodotus has a defeated king observe that in peace sons bury their fathers, and in war fathers bury their sons. Thucydides gives the Athenians, before the killing at Melos, the coldest sentence in history: the strong do what they can, and the weak suffer what they must. Laozi saw that the people go hungry because those above them eat too much in taxes. Mencius ranked the people first, the land second and the ruler last, and no state has ever been governed in that order. Isaiah dreamed of a day when nations would learn war no more. They are still learning it.

A state has no body to be humbled. It cannot feel the loss it causes, so it cannot learn from it. In the 1820s Hegel summed up the record: peoples and governments have never learned anything from history, or acted on principles deduced from it.

## The bond

And yet the man cannot leave the tribe. Alone, we have never survived. The tribe feeds us, shelters us, and gives us our language, our law and our name. It also drafts our sons, taxes our bread and spends us on its own priorities.

Symbiosis and dissonance, at once and always: an imperfect bond, and an unbreakable one.

That is why the rules never take. They are written for the man, and the man lives inside the tribe. He learns, the tribe goes on as before, and he goes on belonging to it.

## The better question

What if the song asked its question of the wrong party? "They" do learn, one by one, and carry what they learned to the grave. It is the tribe that never learns, because it never has to feel what it costs.

When will they ever learn? They always do. Just never in time, and never together.

title: We're Only Human
dek: Our explanation of Reality may be correct. It will never be certain.
excerpt: Our explanation of Reality may be correct. It will never be certain.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

## The finding

All observation is self-centred. Every observation is made from somewhere, by someone, through a body and a brain, on a particular day. Reality does not possess a self. It has no somewhere, no someone and no centre.

So the account and the thing can never line up exactly. Not because observers are careless, but because a view needs a self, and Reality has none to share.

Our explanation of Reality may be correct. It will never be certain.

## Four roots

The reasons are many. They grow from four roots.

**The observer.** Every observation passes through a human brain, and no instrument can get behind it, because the brain is reading the instrument. Change the brain's chemistry and the picture changes. The observer is never finished, so every conclusion is date-specific.

**The method.** No number of confirmations guarantees the next case. One contrary result can overturn a thousand. Different theories can fit the same evidence equally well. Instruments find what their builders expect to find.

**The situation.** All laws are situational, not universal. We observe from one planet, in lives too brief for the processes we study, by light that shows only the past, in the one universe we have, with nothing to compare it against.

**The silence.** Reality has no voice. It never confirms a theory. It has only consequences, and there is no place to stand outside it and check the description against the thing.

As long as we're human, something has been overlooked.

## Invented and observed

We can be certain of what we invent, never of what we observe.

Arithmetic, chess, the calendar and the metre hold exactly, because we wrote their rules and nothing outside us has a say in them. The world answers only to itself. Einstein put it in 1921: "As far as the laws of mathematics refer to reality, they are not certain; and as far as they are certain, they do not refer to reality."

Physics borrows its certainty from the mathematics it invented and lends it to the world it observes. The loan is never repaid.

## Our expectation of science

A public that expected certainty from science would always feel misled. A public that expected fit, usefulness and consequence would hear every revision differently: not as betrayal, but as the system working. "They changed their minds again" is the sound of an expectation science could never meet.

The bridge stands. The fever breaks. That has always been enough.

## Science's expectation of itself

A science that expected only what it could deliver would mark every result: correct, as of this date, for observers like us. The final theory, the end of physics and the truth about the universe are expectations science set for itself, and they are the ones it cannot meet. It would disappoint itself less, and be believed more.

## Our expectation of Reality

Reality is not a puzzle awaiting its final solution. Reality is a given. What we make of it is not.

It is the one thing we did not invent, so it is the one thing we can never be certain of, and the one thing none of us can avoid. It can be described provisionally and lived fully. We meet it in experience, not in conclusions.

Experience is real. Knowledge is optional.

## The better question

What if certainty was never the goal? What if the point of knowing was to live well inside a Reality we will never finish describing?

If this is right, it changes three expectations at once: what we expect of science, what science expects of itself, and what all of us expect of Reality.

After all, we're only human.

title: What Black Hole Are We Talking About?
dek: Never seen, never proven and far from convincing.
excerpt: Never seen, never proven and far from convincing.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

The black hole is the last great fantasy of modern physics, and it has everything a good fantasy needs: a door that opens only one way, a place where time stops, a point of infinite density, a slow evaporation and a paradox the experts have been arguing over for half a century. Take it apart a piece at a time and see what's left.

## The fabric and the hole

It starts with spacetime. Space, which is material, gets welded to time, which is a measurement, and the result is declared to be a fabric that bends and tells matter how to move. A measurement can't bend, and geometry has never pushed anything. Einstein's equations calculate superbly; the fabric is a story someone told about them. Without it there's nothing to tear, and so nothing to make a hole in.

Look at what actually sits at the centre of our galaxy and you find the opposite of a hole. Four million Suns' worth of mass is packed into a space about the size of our solar system, and stars whip around it at nearly eight thousand kilometres a second. That's a presence, not an absence.

The name came first anyway. John Wheeler made "black hole" popular in 1967, and from then on everything that came near had to fall in, be swallowed, be lost. The astronomers who actually watch the process have a plainer word for it. They call it accretion, which just means gathering.

## The door, the inside and the point

The event horizon is supposed to be a one-way door that not even light can come back through. If so, it's the purest SOB in nature, a scientific observational boundary past which nothing can ever be seen, and yet the far side has been described in remarkable detail.

Inside, we're told, space and time swap jobs, so the centre stops being somewhere ahead of you and becomes a moment in your future, as unavoidable as next Tuesday. The experts can't even agree whether a traveller would cross the doorway unharmed or be burned up on the threshold.

At the centre the equations run to infinity. Nobody has ever measured an infinity; it's what an equation produces when it has stopped working. The singularity is that breakdown with a name on it, given a place and a date. It has a twin at the beginning of the universe, built the same way out of the same equations run backward.

## The evaporation

Then there's Hawking radiation, the faint glow that's supposed to let black holes slowly evaporate. One with the Sun's mass would glow at about sixty billionths of a degree above absolute zero, millions of times colder than the empty space around it, so nobody will ever detect it. Hawking himself said the popular explanation, the one in all the books, was only a picture to help people imagine the mathematics. For fifty years some of the best minds in physics have argued over what happens to the information that falls in. They have been arguing about a place nobody can see, over an effect nobody can measure.

## The Kool-Aid

So why does science keep serving phony Kool-Aid? The equation came decades before the evidence, and when the evidence turned up it was poured into a picture that was already waiting. The mathematics is exact, and its certainty, which only ever belonged to what we invented, got lent to what we observe. Whole careers have been built inside the hole, and nobody saws off the branch he's sitting on. A place where time stops fills theatres, lecture halls and grant committees in a way a dense, dark object never will. And sixty years of textbooks have made doubting it look like ignorance.

The public isn't to blame. It was handed the cup and told it was science.

## What's left

Clear all that away and the observations are still standing, exactly as they were: stars racing around an unseen centre, mass packed tighter than anything else we know, rings of light around dark middles, jets thousands of light-years long and ripples from merging pairs. Matter is drawn in and heated to vapour, much of it turns to light, some is thrown back out, and the rest stays on as weight. As far as anyone can tell, nothing is lost.

We don't know what these objects are. Nobody does.

Old Faithful, in Yellowstone, goes off every hour and a half or so. In between, nothing seems to happen, while underground the water gathers and the heat builds until the pressure can't be held any longer. The things at the centres of galaxies look like the quiet part of that cycle. Mass piles up, the heat rises, giants merge into bigger giants, and some of it is already escaping in the jets. The Big Bang is told as matter flying apart out of extreme density, and here is matter gathering back into it. A better answer than a hole is a new Big Bang getting ready.

What if the object is just an object, and the hole was only ever a word? The observations are real and the story isn't. Meanwhile, at the centre of every galaxy, the pressure keeps building.

Whatever it is, we won't be here to see it. That counts for something.

title: Why Can't We Understand Quantum Theory?
dek: Space is the singular field of Reality.
excerpt: Space is the singular field of Reality.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

Physics has a theory that predicts the behaviour of the very small more precisely than any theory in history, and a century after it was written down, its own practitioners can't say what it describes. The trouble starts with something that seems to be two things at once.

## Two natures

In 1801 Thomas Young sent light through two narrow slits and found bands of light and dark on the wall behind them. Waves do that. Where two sets of ripples meet crest to crest they reinforce each other, and where crest meets trough they cancel. Light, it seemed, was a wave.

In 1905 Einstein showed that light also arrives in separate lumps. It knocks electrons out of metal one packet at a time, and the energy of each packet depends on its colour, not its brightness. Light, it seemed, was a particle.

Then electrons, the most particle-like things there are, turned out to make the same bands of light and dark when sent through slits. Fire them one at a time and each one arrives as a single dot on the screen, in no predictable place. Keep firing and the dots pile up into the bands. Each electron lands like a particle, and the crowd lands like a wave.

Physics named this wave-particle duality and has lived with it ever since. Every electron and every particle of light is taught as somehow both.

## The cat

In 1935 Erwin Schrödinger tried to show how absurd that was. Put a cat in a sealed box with a vial of poison, rigged to break if a single atom decays. Until someone looks, the theory says, the atom is a blend of decayed and not decayed. By the same arithmetic, the cat is a blend of dead and alive until the lid comes off.

Schrödinger meant it as a joke at the theory's expense. It became the theory's most famous illustration instead. Ninety years later physicists still can't agree on what happens in the box, and a survey of more than a thousand of them last year found no interpretation with a majority.

## What we measure

The way out begins with a plain fact. Every measurement in science is the record of a meeting. A click in a detector, a dot on a screen and a needle on a dial are each what happened when two things pressed on each other. The instrument is one of the parties, so what shows up belongs to the encounter and not to either side of it.

We measure the reaction, never the reactors. Mass is how hard a thing is to move. Charge is how it pushes on another charge. Colour is the light a surface throws back. A property is how a thing reacts to pressure, and nobody has ever found a property of any other kind.

Quantum theory is the bookkeeping of those reactions. It records how often each kind of reaction turns up and the frequency at which things ring. It does both superbly, and it says nothing at all about what is doing the reacting.

## The field

Something is. Empty space reacts. It carries light at one fixed speed, and that speed is set by how space answers electric and magnetic pressure, which has been measured to many decimal places. Something that reacts is something. Space isn't the stage that matter performs on. It is the material, and it is the only one.

Physics calls the vacuum nothing and then credits it with energy, fluctuations and forces. Its reactions say it is the most common substance there is.

## One substance

With the material in place, the two natures turn out to be one.

The wave is the field moving. A disturbance spreads through space the way any disturbance spreads through a medium, and it passes through both slits at once because the medium is on both sides of the barrier. The bands on the wall are the field's ripples reinforcing and cancelling, exactly as Young saw.

The particle is the field reacting. When the spreading disturbance meets something that resists it, such as a detector, a screen or an atom in the wall, the reaction happens at one spot, and that spot is the dot. The dot isn't a little ball that travelled the whole way. It's where the field's motion met resistance and gave up its energy in a single exchange.

There is no electron that is somehow both. There is one substance doing two things, moving and meeting. The wave is how it travels and the particle is how it arrives. Neither is the thing itself. The thing itself is space.

## Feeding the cat

The cat, meanwhile, wants feeding, and it's alive to eat.

The blend of dead and alive was never in the box. It was in the bookkeeping. The theory's spread of possibilities records how often each reaction will turn up; it doesn't describe a cat. And reactions don't wait for a physicist to lift the lid. The atom meets the trigger, the trigger meets the vial, the poison meets the cat or doesn't, and the cat meets the air and the floor of the box. All of it is space reacting with itself, continuously, billions of times a second. Observation isn't something a person does. It's what material does whenever it touches material.

The cat was always either dead or alive. Only the physicist didn't know which.

## The bubbles

Nothing has to set the field in motion. Motion is a feature of the stratum, the way wetness is a feature of water, and particles are what that motion throws up, like bubbles in boiling water.

Some bubbles last. The electron and the proton hold their rhythm indefinitely, and every atom and everything solid is built of them. Each has its own frequency, and that frequency is its identity: the electron rings about 120 billion billion times a second. Some bubbles travel. Light is a disturbance crossing the material at the one speed the material allows, carrying a push from one lasting bubble to another. And some burst as soon as they form. Most of the particle zoo found in colliders lives for a millionth of a second or far less and is known only by the debris it leaves. Those aren't things. They're the splash from knocking lasting bubbles together hard.

Concentrate enough energy in one place and particles appear out of it, matter and antimatter in pairs. Physicists have watched it happen since the 1930s. The bubbles aren't waiting somewhere to be found. The field makes them when the heat is there.

## The whole

Everything in Reality moves, the field included. The universe began in a hot, dense material state with momentum, and it has been coasting ever since. Gravity is situational, overwhelming at the scale of a star and no brake at the scale of everything, so dark energy, invented to explain why the brake didn't work, isn't needed. Edward Milne proposed a coasting universe in the 1930s. It was set aside, but it was never refuted.

## Why we can't understand it

We can't understand quantum theory because we've been trying to understand the wrong thing. Physics looked at the reactions and asked what the reactors were, found two answers and couldn't choose between them. It treated the one material doing all the reacting as empty, and so it has spent a century describing the bubbles while insisting there is no water.

What's clearly not right is the belief that the strangeness lives in nature. It lives in a theory that counts reactions and forgets what is reacting.

## The better answer

Wave and particle were never two things. They are one substance, space, caught travelling and caught arriving.

We measure the reaction, never the reactors. But every reaction happens somewhere, and that somewhere is one thing.

title: Beyond the Big Bang: A Point in Time
dek: A spark before the explosion.
excerpt: A spark before the explosion.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

Call this one a moonbeam. We've earned one.

For a century we've been told the universe started with a bang: everything there is, squeezed into a point smaller than a pinhead, blowing apart. Run the equations backward and you hit a singularity, which is a polite word for the place where the math gives up. We've already said what we think of that.

So take the point away. What's left?

A moment. Not a place where everything exploded, but a time when something first held still long enough to count.

## Two, not one

Here's a fact worth chewing on. Every time energy turns into matter, it comes out in pairs: a particle and its antimatter twin, opposite charges, perfectly balanced. Physicists have watched it happen since the 1930s and have not once seen a single.

So the first thing was never one thing. It was two. That's the spark, the moment the first pair held instead of vanishing. It isn't the birth of Reality. It's the birth of structure, the first brick.

## The fabric

In No. 67 we put space first and called particles its bubbles. Here's the other way of reading the same evidence, and it may be the better one. The pairs come first, and space is the fabric they weave between them.

That's not as wild as it sounds. In 2010 a Canadian physicist named Mark Van Raamsdonk argued, with a great deal of math, that space is woven by what it connects. Pull the threads and the fabric comes apart.

It's real fabric, though. Material. Not the "spacetime" the professors drape over everything. You can't weave a measurement. You can weave particles.

## Motion, and the word always

Everything moves: the fabric, the pairs, all of it. Time is just what we call that motion, and it follows the motion wherever it goes.

Did the motion ever start? We don't know, and neither does anybody else. "It began from nothing" and "it never began" are both claims about all of time, and nobody has been around long enough to check. Always is not a word in science. Neither is never.

## Then the bang

The bang comes after the spark, not before it. Pairs formed wherever they could, the fabric thickened, and the whole business got hotter and denser until it couldn't hold any more. Then it went.

The explosion is real enough. The hot, dense, expanding early universe left plenty of evidence behind. But it wasn't the beginning. It was an eruption, Old Faithful letting go after the pressure built underground.

We've seen that kind of building before. In No. 66 we looked at the dark monsters at the centres of galaxies, the so-called black holes, and found no hole at all, just mass piling up, heat rising and pressure building. The hole that wasn't a hole may be the next eruption getting ready.

## The settling

After the bang comes the cooling off, and here the textbooks tell it pretty well. In the first millionths of a second, protons and neutrons form. In the first few minutes they lock into the first atomic nuclei. About 380,000 years on, electrons settle in, the first atoms appear and light finally breaks loose. That light is the microwave background, still coming at us from every direction.

None of that is creation. It's the house settling after the party.

## The leftovers

Most of those early pairs found their twins again and went back to light. About one in a billion didn't. That stray bit of matter, multiplied across the sky, is everything there is: you, me, the horses and the hay.

Physics can't tell you why there were leftovers. In our picture, the spark was a pair, and the leftovers are what kept it going: the one that held when its twin didn't. The pairs came as two, but what survived came one at a time, a single stray for every billion pairs, and those singles kept the ball rolling. The real question is why, out of a billion pairs, one hung on. We're what hung on.

## One force

As things cooled, the push running through the fabric started meeting different kinds of resistance and began to look like four different forces. Physics has already caught two of them in the act. In the 1960s Sheldon Glashow, Steven Weinberg and Abdus Salam showed that electromagnetism and the weak force are one and the same. The weak one only looks different because its carriers get dragged down by a field that fills space, and those carriers were found in 1983. The strong force is expected to join the club at higher heat.

Gravity is the holdout only because physics insists it's geometry. Call it what it looks like, the fabric pushing back, and it falls in line. The mass that makes a thing heavy and the mass that makes it hard to shove have been measured equal to about one part in a million billion; a French satellite checked again in 2022. Weight and resistance are the same number because they're the same thing.

One force, four theaters, one movie.

## So

The universe didn't start with a bang out of a point in space. It started with a spark at a point in time: two bubbles that held, and a fabric woven out from them. The bang came later, when what the spark had built got too crowded to hold.

What came before the spark? We can't say, and we won't pretend to. That's the difference between us and the people selling tickets to the singularity.

One more thing, for the record. We're not scientists, and these aren't facts. If they are, we can't prove it.

title: For Its Own Sake, or for Ours?
dek: Hunger creates its own perspective.
excerpt: Hunger creates its own perspective.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

Ask what science is for and you get two answers. They've been talking past each other for a couple of thousand years, and the longer we look at them, the more it seems they come from two different tables.

## The pack's answer

The first answer is older than writing. We're pack predators, and for as long as there have been bands of us, knowing things was how we stayed alive: where the water was, when the frost would come, which berry would kill you. Knowledge was the first line of defense, the sword and shield of survival, and it was always pointed at the same three things, a roof, a meal and each other.

The third turns out to carry the other two. Nobody hunts alone or raises a roof alone, which may be why the pack's oldest punishments go straight for connection. Exile forces you out, prison forces you in, and the last resort, for most of 300,000 years, was to take you out of the pack for good.

If that's where science comes from, it would explain a few things. It would explain why every discipline climbs a ladder with no ground and no ceiling: chemistry never quite reaches the bottom of the atom, medicine never quite says what life is, and still they keep climbing, because the pack keeps needing them to. And it would explain the people on those ladders. They're the white knights in lab coats, the science commandos, scaling their rungs in defense of the realm.

## The answer from the full table

The second answer is nearly as old, and it seems to have been written by people who had already eaten.

Around 350 BC Aristotle described the highest kind of knowing as something pursued "in order to know, and not for any utilitarian end." He was honest about when it started, too: only after the necessities of life had been taken care of. So knowledge for its own sake may have been born at a full table, which is worth keeping in mind.

The idea travelled well. John Henry Newman told the universities in 1852 that knowledge is "capable of being its own end." Henri Poincaré said scientists study nature because they delight in it, not because it's useful. In 1939 Abraham Flexner, who founded the institute in Princeton where Einstein spent his last years, wrote "The Usefulness of Useless Knowledge," which more or less said: chase your curiosity and the payoffs will turn up on their own.

Then, in 1945, Vannevar Bush handed President Truman a report with a lovely title, _Science, the Endless Frontier_. In it he defined basic research as work "performed without thought of practical ends," and he argued that the government should pay for it. Much of the world's public science funding still runs on that blueprint. Aristotle had supplied the ideal, Flexner the excuse and Bush the chequebook.

There was a third voice, and it's the one that got lost. In 1605 Francis Bacon, who did as much as anyone to shape the modern scientific method, wrote that its real purpose was "the relief of man's estate," making human life better. Somewhere along the way, science kept his method and mislaid his goal.

## What each table served up

It's tempting to settle this by argument, but the record may be more persuasive.

From the knights in lab coats came the Haber–Bosch process, a piece of chemistry from just before the First World War that pulls fertilizer out of the air. By 2008 it was reckoned to be feeding nearly half the people alive. From them came vaccines, which the World Health Organization credits with saving at least 154 million lives in fifty years, and the end of smallpox in 1980. From the working half of physics came the transistor and fibre optics, and with them every phone call and every screen.

From the Big Bang gang came the Higgs boson in 2012. It won a Nobel Prize, and nobody has found a use for it. The collider that found it hasn't found anything new since, and decades of hunting for dark matter have come up empty. Now the request is for CERN's Future Circular Collider, a tunnel 91 kilometres around, its first stage costed at roughly 15.3 billion Swiss francs and ready sometime in the 2040s: a bigger machine to look for what the last one couldn't find.

The gang does have an answer, which is the spinoff. The web was built at CERN, and detectors built for physics ended up in hospitals. Both are real, but they were accidents along the road rather than the destination, and if better hospital scanners are what we want, it's cheaper to pay for scanners.

## Other people's money

None of this is a case against wonder. Wonder is real, and some of it is well worth paying for. The trouble is the casual way the bill gets passed along.

Bush's definition lets a field spend public money with no obligation to bring anything back to the people who supplied it. The pitch is always an investment, the next machine and the you-never-know, and what comes back, more often than not, is a story. Nobody stops to ask the people writing the cheques whether they'd rather have the story or the bread.

Why does it keep happening? Prestige seems to run backwards, so the further a question sits from any use, the higher it ranks. Bush's definition turned that prestige into a budget line. And the people deciding have usually eaten well, so the full table's answer looks to them like plain common sense.

Hunger creates its own perspective. To anyone who has missed meals, no question about the first second of the universe is worth a loaf of bread, and the well-fed have a way of forgetting that.

## The better question

What seems clearly not right is spending the pack's money as though the pack's needs had all been met.

So here's a thought. What if every science had to say, in plain words, which of the three it serves: a roof, a meal or each other? The knights in lab coats could answer in a sentence. The Big Bang gang might need a very long grant application.

For its own sake, or for ours?

title: This or Nothing
dek: The oldest story we tell isn't about knowledge. It's about the knowledge of death.
excerpt: The oldest story we tell isn't about knowledge. It's about the knowledge of death.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

For something like four thousand years we've been telling a story about a garden, a tree and a serpent, and for most of that time we've read it as a story about wanting to know too much. Curiosity was the sin, learning was the trespass, and every hardship since has been the bill.

That reading isn't wrong so much as incomplete. It saw the knowledge and missed what the knowledge was of.

## What the text says

Read the story in the King James words, with an eye on death instead of on knowledge, and death turns up at every turn.

There are two special trees in the garden from the start, the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. The warning about the second names death: "in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die." The serpent says they won't, and in a sense he's right. Nobody drops dead. Adam goes on, the text says, for nine hundred and thirty years. What changed that day wasn't that they died. They became creatures who knew they would.

The first thing they learn is that they're naked: bodies, exposed, able to be hurt. The sentence is dust: "dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return." And the exile is explained in so many words. The man has come to know good and evil, "and now, lest he put forth his hand, and take also of the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever." A flaming sword is set "to keep the way of the tree of life."

Read that way, the story holds together from beginning to end. A creature that knows it will die doesn't also get to live forever. "Good and evil" may well be a way of saying everything, the way "high and low" means everyone, and everything includes the end.

Genesis didn't invent the tale. In Mesopotamia, where the story places Eden, Gilgamesh dove for a plant that restored youth, and on the way home a serpent stole it and shed its skin. He sat down and wept, and went home mortal. Same serpent, same loss, centuries earlier.

## Life's first priority

Every living thing has one priority ahead of all the others: staying alive. A cell walls out the world. An animal flees, fights, freezes or feeds. None of that needs awareness. A bacterium swims away from poison with no idea it could die.

The Garden marks what happened when that priority met a creature that could see itself. The eyes were opened. Staying alive stopped being only an instinct and became a question, one the creature could ask about itself.

Shakespeare gave it its most famous form: "To be, or not to be, that is the question." A deer stays alive without asking whether to. Hamlet is the first priority turned around and examined by the one animal able to examine it. He named the wall, too. Death is "the undiscover'd country, from whose bourn no traveller returns." That's an SOB, a scientific observational boundary, a place where our methods run out though something surely lies beyond. It's the oldest one we have, and the most personal.

## This or nothing

Hamlet's question isn't asked once, in a castle, in a crisis. In small change it's asked all day. Cross the road or wait. Eat the strange berry or leave it. Take the new job or keep the safe one. Every decision weighs staying alive, in body or in some smaller sense, against what might be worth the risk. We call it the principal duality: to be or not to be, inherent in every decision.

Its everyday form is caution and curiosity. Caution leans toward being, keeping what we have. Curiosity is willing to risk a little not-being for something more. All caution starves in the cave; all curiosity meets the first snake. Every living thing balances the two. Only we know we're doing it.

And the choice is starker than it looks. It's never between this life and a better one somewhere else. There's no garden on offer. The basic choice is this, as it is, or nothing.

## What the incomplete reading cost

If the Garden is about knowledge in general, curiosity is the original sin, and for centuries it was treated that way. Augustine counted it among the temptations, "the lust of the eyes." When Galileo turned a telescope on the heavens and reported what he saw, he ended his life under house arrest.

If the Garden is about the knowledge of death, curiosity is no sin at all. It's the instinct that serves the first priority, the _sine qua non_ of survival. What was learned in the Garden wasn't forbidden learning but a hard fact, that we die, and everything we've learned since, from fire to vaccines, has been an answer to it.

The modern world made the opposite mistake. Having shaken off the suspicion of curiosity, it decided knowledge needed no purpose at all, and that science is best pursued for its own sake. One error treats knowledge as dangerous, the other as aimless. Read whole, the Garden gives it back a purpose: the defense and advance of life, the shield and the sword carried by one arm.

## The better question

What seems clearly not right is a reading that turned the knowledge of death into a sin of curiosity, and a modern answer that turned curiosity into an end with no purpose.

The better question isn't why we were punished for wanting to know. It's what we do with what we learned at the gate: that our time is short, and the basic choice, every day, is this or nothing.

title: The Eye of a Quark
dek: If we can't see the whole, we can't really understand the parts.
excerpt: If we can't see the whole, we can't really understand the parts.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

The idea that the truth of the universe can be found in the eye of a quark seems slight. Yet billions are spent on just such a search. The hope is that somewhere at the bottom of matter, small enough, lies the answer to what it all is.

It hasn't worked that way. The parts have been catalogued with extraordinary precision, and they refuse to add up. The quark itself has never been seen alone. It comes only in pairs and triplets, bound so tightly that pulling one free makes new ones. Even the bottom of the search sits behind an SOB, a scientific observational boundary, a place where our methods run out though something surely lies beyond.

## Whole before parts

Our view runs the other way. If we can't see the whole, we can't really understand the parts. We can understand how a part works. What it is comes from the whole it belongs to. You can't deduce a car from rebuilding a carburetor.

The universe is incomprehensibly large, and a better idea may be to see it as the combined choreography of its primary features: what it does as a whole, not what it's made of. Matter gathers and disperses. Light crosses it straight. It thickens into walls and empties into voids. It runs down in one direction while pockets of order keep forming. Those are the steps of the dance, and they belong to the whole. Seeing them takes a different method. Survey what's observed about the whole, with no theory attached. Infer what shape it could have. Imagine what could lie outside it. Guess what could have caused it. Then run the reasoning backward, from the whole down to the particle, and see whether it holds.

## The messenger

The survey turns up a surprise at once. Nearly everything we know about the universe as a whole, the stretched light, the old glow, the horizon, is light's report on its own journey. We measure the messenger, never the sender. And a messenger that has crossed a medium for billions of years may have been changed by the crossing in more ways than the standard account allows.

Take "flat." Physics reports that the universe is flat and builds a great deal on the word. Common sense balks at once: how can anything three-dimensional be flat? Flat is a word for tabletops. Strip the geometry away and what was observed is simpler: light crosses the visible universe straight. That's a feature of the photon, not the universe.

Picture the universe as a basketball holding floating marbles. Light from each marble travels in a straight line to every other marble, and the membrane of the basketball is still round. Straight light inside says nothing about the shape of the ball, because no light inside ever touches it.

## Infinite or a ball

So what shape could the whole be? There are only two choices. Either Reality has no boundary, in which case it's infinite and can never be measured as a whole. Or it has one, in which case it's a basketball, a body with an inside and an outside, and very likely round, since everything in nature large enough to gather itself becomes round.

A ball has a real center. Every observer inside sees its horizon as an even sphere around itself and concludes it stands in the middle. Cosmology noticed that every point looks central and concluded there's no center. Those are different claims. The center isn't absent. It lies, with the membrane, behind an SOB. So does whatever is beyond the membrane. Our definition says "something surely lies beyond," and that "something" isn't a claim about stuff out there. It's a substitute word for the unknowable.

From inside, the most we can hope for is to feel which way the ball leans, and there are hints. The quasars are lopsided across the sky by more than our own motion explains. The expansion rate seems to vary by direction. The largest patterns in the old glow line up along an axis. The standard account calls each a fluke. To an observer off-center in a ball, they're what one would expect.

Run backward, from the whole to the particle, the picture holds together: a ball of one medium that gathers and disperses, a lumpy web, an expansion that rises and falls, matter as knots in the medium, pairs because a twist needs a counter-twist. That isn't proof. It's a test, and the picture passes it.

## The operational horizon

Then the method stops. Where it started and what lies beyond the membrane may be written into the whole and readable from outside, and we'll never be outside. They lie past our operational horizon, where our reach runs out: our instruments, our lifespans, our place inside the ball.

Our insignificance knows no bounds. That isn't a reason to stop asking. It's the reason the asking matters.

## The better question

What seems clearly not right is the belief that the whole will appear once the parts are counted finely enough. Billions more spent on the eye of the quark won't show us the universe, any more than one more carburetor shows us the car.

The better question isn't what the universe is made of. It's what the whole must be, for the parts to behave the way they do.

title: The Awakening
dek: Our insignificance knows no bounds. And neither do we.
excerpt: Our insignificance knows no bounds. And neither do we.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

The fuel always runs out. Every fire, every engine and every star burns something it can't get back. The Sun is slowly brightening, and in about a billion years it will be hot enough to drive off the oceans. The galaxies will stop making stars when their gas is used up, and the last small stars will go dark after that. Physics has known the outline since 1852, when William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, described nature's universal tendency to dissipate its energy. Everything is running down. Only nothing is inexhaustible, because there's nothing in it to exhaust.

## Reality doesn't know

Reality is a given. It does what it does and keeps no record. A star doesn't know it's burning out. The universe doesn't know it's running down, because knowing isn't something the universe does. It's something done, inside it, by a very few things.

Blaise Pascal saw this in the 1650s. A human being, he wrote, is a reed, the weakest thing in nature, but a thinking reed. If the universe crushed him, he would still be nobler than what killed him, "because he knows that he dies and the advantage which the universe has over him; the universe knows nothing of this."

## Neither do we

The trouble is that we hardly use the advantage.

We know we'll die the way we know the boiling point of water: correct, filed and rarely consulted. The end of everything sits farther off still, past our operational horizon, where numbers stop producing feelings.

And we don't know ourselves, in either direction. For four and a half centuries science has told us a story of demotion: the Earth moved off the center, the Sun to the edge of an ordinary galaxy, the galaxy to an ordinary place among countless others. We can recite it. We don't live it. Each of us still meets the world from the middle of it, and so do our nations, our institutions and our species, which speaks of the planet as ours and of the universe as something waiting to be explained to us. Arrogance and self-importance are what insignificance looks like when it isn't known.

The other face we know even less. A creature that's small hasn't stopped being the creature that knows, and what that makes possible has hardly been looked at.

## The awakening

In the Garden the eyes were opened, and the first thing they saw was death. That knowledge didn't end the story. It started it. A creature that knew it would die began, in the same moment, to plan against it: fire, shelter, stored grain, medicine, vaccines. The knowledge of death turned out to be the most productive knowledge we ever had.

The awakening is the same turn on the largest scale. Knowing that the fuel runs out isn't only a sentence. It's a capacity. Nothing else in Reality can see the end coming, so nothing else can do anything about it. A star can't ration its fuel. Only a knower can see what's coming, measure it and decide.

That knowledge bestows foresight, the shape of the road ahead. It gives science its real goal, the defense and advance of life, and gives that goal a horizon and a scale. And it gives us the telling. Reality supplies the events; it doesn't supply the account. Without a knower there's no story of Existence, only Existence, unrecorded from the first change to the last.

## The burden

Everything puts the burden on us, because there's nowhere else for it to go. The animals don't ask, and Reality doesn't know.

Albert Camus carried more of it than most. His father was killed at the Marne when he was an infant. He grew up poor in Algiers, had tuberculosis at seventeen and edited a Resistance paper under the occupation. He survived more than most of his generation and learned more from it. His answer was Sisyphus, rolling his boulder up the hill forever, whom "one must imagine happy." The boulder doesn't get lighter. But only a creature that carries it knowingly can decide how to carry it. The burden and the potential are the same weight, seen from two sides.

## Insignificance and uniqueness

Insignificance and uniqueness are a pair, two faces of one coin. We're small because we're a part of Reality, and unique because we're the part that knows it.

There may be other knowers. If there are, they lie past an SOB, a scientific observational boundary, a place where our methods run out though something surely lies beyond. We can count them neither in nor out. The honest claim is the one we make: the only knowers we know of.

That's humanity's special place in the story of Existence. Not its subject, and nowhere near its middle, but its teller, and the one character able to act on how it ends. Our insignificance knows no bounds, and neither do we. Our observations stop at the SOBs. Our questions never have.

## The better question

What seems clearly not right is a creature that recites its smallness while living as the center, and has never noticed what makes it unique.

The better question isn't whether we matter to the universe. The universe knows nothing of it. It's what the one part of Reality that knows can do with the knowing, while there's still this, and not nothing.

title: Two Faces of Reality
dek: Consciousness is one hundred percent soft. Existence is hard.
excerpt: Consciousness is one hundred percent soft. Existence is hard.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

Reality has two faces. One is cosmic, material and objective. It's everywhere, it lasts billions of years, and it knows nothing. The other is cognitive, ephemeral and subjective. It turns up in a few patches of matter, it lasts a lifetime, and it's the only place anything is ever known.

For a few centuries philosophy has treated these as two different things, mind and matter, and spent a great deal of effort looking for the joint between them. Nobody has found it. Maybe there's nothing to find. Heads and tails don't need a joint. They're one coin.

## Dust and breath

The oldest story we tell drew the coin first. "The LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul." Dust is the material face; breath is the cognitive. The living soul is the two together.

When the sentence comes, it's spoken to the dust: "unto dust shalt thou return." The dust goes back where it came from, as it was. The breath leaves, and where it goes lies past the oldest SOB of all. An SOB is a scientific observational boundary, the place where our methods run out though something surely lies beyond. All the living can see is that the breath is gone from here.

## Matter organized to know

If the faces are one coin, the cognitive face isn't a second stuff added to matter. It's matter arranged a particular way: arranged to take in signals, hold a picture of the world and turn the picture on itself. Nothing is added. Something is arranged.

That's why one face lasts and the other doesn't. Matter is conserved. Arrangements aren't. The atoms in a body were in other things before it and will be in other things after it. The arrangement that let them know they existed lasts a lifetime and doesn't come back. Death isn't the body ending, and it isn't a soul flying off. It's the coin losing a face.

## Knowing burns fuel

Arrangements cost energy to keep, and the one that knows costs most. The brain is about 2 percent of the body's weight and uses about 20 percent of its energy at rest, and it stores almost none. Cut off the oxygen and the knowing goes within seconds, long before the body does.

The same holds on the largest scale. A knower needs a steady flow of energy: a star at the right distance, a planet holding the heat. Those conditions belong to the middle of the universe's story, while the fuel is being burned. Before the stars there was nothing to power a knower, and after them there will be nothing again. The cognitive face is ephemeral in each of us and ephemeral in the whole.

## The hinge

The two faces meet at the senses, and nowhere else. A wavelength arrives at the eye and becomes red. The wavelength belongs to the cosmic face; the red belongs to us. Newton saw it in 1704: "the Rays to speak properly are not coloured."

Instruments stretch the hinge but never move it. Every chain of them ends at a pair of eyes reading a result. That gives the SOB its exact place: it's where no messenger reaches the hinge anymore. And it's why the question always comes from the senses. Every question starts as something that arrived and didn't fit.

## What lives on one face

Some of what matters most exists on the cognitive face only.

The cosmic face has events but no stories, so meaning is ours. Nothing out there is precious or wasted, so value is ours. The equations of physics describe change but mark no present moment, so "now" is ours. And "this," as in this or nothing, is a word only a knower can point with.

Nearly everything we care about lives on the face that doesn't last. That may explain something we see everywhere: monuments, legacies, records, the long effort to carry meaning across to the material face, which holds the marble but not the meaning.

## Soft and hard

Philosophy calls it the hard problem of consciousness: why matter that handles information should have any inner experience at all. The name has the faces backwards.

Consciousness is one hundred percent soft. It's arrangement rather than stuff, the face that comes and goes. Existence is hard. It's the face that lasts, keeps no record and answers no questions, and the truly hard question belongs to it: why is there anything at all?

## The better question

What seems clearly not right is any account that keeps one face and explains away the other. A coin with one face isn't a coin.

The better question isn't how mind is glued to matter. It's what one Reality is doing when, here and there and briefly, it shows a face that knows.

title: The Sister Universe
dek: A thought exercise: what if the result has another half?
excerpt: A thought exercise: what if the result has another half?
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

Everything below lies past our reach. It's a what-if, and we label it as one.

Duality runs through everything we've written: particle and wave, matter and antimatter, gathering and dispersing, something and nothing. Nothing in Reality seems to come single, except the universe itself.

What if that's wrong too? Not the event that started it, whatever that was, but its result. What if the result has another half: a sister universe with opposite features?

## The ledger

Every laboratory makes matter and antimatter in equal amounts. Yet our universe is matter almost through and through. The usual account says the early universe made both, with roughly a billion and one particles of matter for every billion of antimatter. The pairs met and turned to light, and the one in a billion left over became every star and every one of us. Known physics can't produce a surplus that large. It falls short by many orders of magnitude.

A split has two sides. If we got the larger share of matter, something got the larger share of antimatter. There's no sign of it anywhere inside our universe. Outside is the only place left to look.

## Her features

She'd be opposite wherever we're lopsided.

Antimatter where we have matter. Time running the other way, and here the equations offer a curious link: they treat an antiparticle exactly like an ordinary particle traveling backward in time, so those two opposites may be one. Gathering where we disperse: if our expansion is the exhaust stroke winning, she'd be the power stroke winning, one engine with two cylinders. And the mirror hand. One force of nature, the weak force, works only on left-handed particles. Ours favors one hand; hers would favor the other.

That isn't fantasy. Physics has one symmetry nobody has ever seen broken. Flip charge, mirror the hand and reverse time, all three together, and the laws come out unchanged. A universe with all three flipped is exactly as lawful as ours.

## How she keeps us company

Opposite features say what she is. They don't say where. There are three possibilities.

She could be parallel: made in the same event, side by side, never touching. She could run in reverse: joined to us at the first moment, the two of us running away from it in opposite directions of time, each calling its own direction forward. Or she could be shadowing us: sharing our space, passing straight through us, touching only by gravity, invisible except for her weight.

## The fingerprints

We can't see her. But if she exists, our universe should be lopsided in exactly the ways half of a pair would be. It is. Three of the deepest puzzles in physics are these: matter over antimatter, which nobody can explain; the arrow of time, a universe that runs one way from a startlingly ordered beginning though its laws run equally well in both directions; and the favored hand, which nothing else in physics accounts for.

Taken one at a time, they look like three accidents. Taken together, they fall along the same three lines, charge, time and hand, that the one unbroken symmetry ties together. A puzzle if we stand alone. Bookkeeping if we don't.

## Where it stops

She lies past an SOB, a scientific observational boundary, a place where our methods run out though something surely lies beyond. No signal crosses. Everything said about her directly is a dream, labeled _pending_. That's why this is a thought exercise and not a theory.

But the exercise changes the question. Asked about a universe standing alone, the question is why it came out lopsided, and the answer has to be three separate accidents. Asked about a universe with a sister, the three accidents become one fact.

And it can fail cleanly. If physics finds a cause at home for all three, the sister goes, and gladly.

## The better question

What seems clearly not right is treating three lopsided features as three separate accidents.

The better question isn't why our universe came out lopsided. It's where its other half is.

title: The Galactic Accumulator
dek: Are we somebody's compost?
excerpt: Are we somebody's compost?
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

For half a century the biggest, busiest objects in the universe have been named for what they aren't. A hole. A place nothing leaves. A door that only swings one way.

It's an odd name for something that never stops working.

## Two things, one name

Physics files two different things under "black hole."

One is what's left when a big star dies: a few to a few dozen times the Sun's mass, made in a single collapse and then pretty much done. It's a grave.

The other sits at the heart of nearly every large galaxy and weighs millions to billions of Suns. It wasn't made in a moment. It piled up over billions of years. It's a midden, the heap where a galaxy's leftovers collect and its history gets laid down in layers.

They differ in size by a factor of a million, in where they sit, in how they formed and in what they do. Calling them by one name says more about the equations than about the objects. We call the big one a galactic accumulator: something that takes in, holds and gives back.

## The heap grows with the town

Weigh a galaxy's central bulge and you can predict the weight of the thing in the middle, about half a percent of it. Clock how fast the bulge's stars are moving, stars much too distant to feel the center's pull, and you can predict it even better. A hole has no business knowing how fast faraway stars are moving. A heap that grew alongside its town would.

They grew in the same era, too. Galaxies made stars fastest about ten billion years ago, and that's when the central objects blazed brightest. And when the center flares, it heats the galaxy's gas and holds back its star-making. The midden doesn't just keep the town's records. It helps run the town.

## Too big, too early

The standard story says the central giants began as graves and ate their way up. The trouble is, nothing can eat that fast. Light from infalling matter pushes back on the next meal, and even at full tilt, doubling takes tens of millions of years.

The Webb telescope keeps catching giants that didn't have the time: millions of Suns' worth a few hundred million years after the start, some already as heavy as all the stars in their galaxies. Astronomers now suggest the first ones formed heavy, straight out of collapsing clouds of gas. Put plainly, the midden never was a grave. It started as a heap.

## Charge and discharge

A hole takes in. That's all it does. An accumulator takes in, holds and lets go, and the central objects let go constantly.

Quasars blaze for perhaps a hundred thousand years, fade, and light up again. Some switch on or off within a few years. In the Perseus cluster, the center has blown cavities in the surrounding gas big enough to swallow galaxies and set the whole cluster humming, a note some fifty-seven octaves below middle C.

Our own galaxy's midden has had its moments. Two great bubbles of hot gas tower some twenty-five thousand light-years above and below the Milky Way, the likely leftovers of an outburst millions of years ago. Gas clouds near the center still glow with the echo of a flare about two hundred years old. And it flickers every day. Today it's remarkably dim, a heap between meals.

## From star to bloodstream

We already know we're compost once over. That part isn't a what-if, and the route is worth tracing.

The universe began with almost nothing but hydrogen and helium. Everything heavier was cooked in stars. A star spends its life fusing light elements into heavier ones: hydrogen into helium, and in the big stars, helium into carbon, then oxygen, then on up the table to iron, where fusion stops paying. When a big star runs out of fuel, its core collapses and the rest blows apart, scattering what it made. Exploding white dwarfs add more iron. Elements heavier still, gold among them, come from the most violent events of all, such as the collisions of neutron stars, one of which was caught in the act in 2017.

The debris drifts, mixes with the gas between the stars, and in time gathers into new clouds. One of them collapsed about four and a half billion years ago into the Sun and its planets. Most of the Earth's iron sank to the core, but enough stayed in the rocks. Rain and weather wear the rocks into soil, roots draw the iron up, grass and grain carry it, and whatever eats them carries it further. In us it ends up at the heart of hemoglobin, the molecule that carries oxygen in the blood. The oxygen was made in stars too.

So the iron in your blood was forged in a star that died before the Sun was born. We're compost once over, for certain. The what-if is whether we're compost twice.

## Their garbage, our beginning

Now the what-if, and we label it as one.

Every accumulator we can see lets go a little at a time. But what if gathering goes far enough? Picture a great galactic accumulator, or the merger of many, holding the leftovers of countless galaxies until the heap can hold no more and lets go all at once.

That release would look a great deal like the start of our universe: everything at once, hot and dense, rushing outward. Cosmology describes our beginning as matter flying apart from extreme density. A great accumulator is matter gathered into extreme density. Run one forward and you get the other.

If so, our beginning wasn't a beginning from nothing. It was a release. Their garbage became our starting place. Every atom in us would be secondhand, swept up from somebody else's universe, piled in a midden, heated through and thrown out to start again. Farmers have always known what a midden does: what one settlement throws away becomes the richest ground for the next.
