It lies past an SOB, a scientific observational boundary, a place where our methods run out though something surely lies beyond. We can't see it, and nobody will. But a release from one place might leave a lean in the sky, pointing back toward where the heap stood. Our sky has a few of those.

## The better question

What seems clearly not right is naming the busiest objects in the universe after an absence.

The better question isn't what lies inside the hole. It's what the galaxy has been storing at its center, and what it does with it. And whether, once upon a time, one of them made us.

title: Motion and Friction
dek: Matter and motion: the first pair.
excerpt: Matter and motion: the first pair.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

Everything we've looked at comes in pairs. Heads and tails. Particle and wave. North and south, which can't even be cut apart. The pairs aren't two things that happen to attract. They're conjoined: one thing with two faces.

The first pair is matter and motion. There's no matter that isn't moving; cooled as close to absolute zero as anyone can manage, atoms still tremble. And there's no motion without something to move. Matter is what's there. Motion is what it does. Every other pair in nature is some arrangement of these two.

Seen that way, a good deal of physics gets simpler. Start with entropy.

## The score

Entropy gets credit for a lot. It's said to give time its direction, to doom the universe to a cold finish, to explain why eggs break and never unbreak. Lately some physicists have even proposed it as a force.

For something so busy, it doesn't do much. Rudolf Clausius made it up in 1865, working on steam engines: a column in his ledger for the heat an engine could no longer put to work. A few years later Ludwig Boltzmann showed what the column was counting, the number of ways a crowd of particles can be arranged and still look the same from outside.

A column and a count. Neither one has ever moved anything. Entropy is the score of the first pair's game, not a player in it.

## Where motion meets matter

In 1798 Count Rumford was boring cannon in Munich and noticed something odd. A blunt drill grinding into brass made heat without limit; it brought a tub of water to the boil in under three hours. If heat were a fluid stored in the metal, it should have run out. It didn't. The heat was coming from the motion itself.

That's friction, and it's what happens where the two faces of the first pair meet. Motion pushes, matter resists, and the meeting turns ordered motion, the kind where everything moves together and can do work, into the jiggling of atoms, which mostly can't. Brakes do it. Honey does it to your spoon. Wires do it to current. Tides do it to the whole planet: the oceans dragging across the sea floor are slowly braking the Earth's spin and adding a couple of thousandths of a second to the day every century.

Every one of those is friction, and every one is what entropy is keeping score of.

## The case with no friction that has friction

Textbooks like one case that seems to have no friction at all. Open a valve between a full box of gas and an empty one. The gas fills both, entropy rises, and nothing rubs on anything.

Except it does. The gas doesn't tiptoe across. It rushes, pushed by the difference in pressure, a real surge with a leading edge. The surge slams the far wall, tumbles back on itself, swirls and breaks up, and in breaking up it turns its orderly rush into heat. That's friction, at the front and all through the flow.

So the rule needs no asterisk: every increase of entropy is motion, driven down a gradient and scattered by friction. And where motion stops, near absolute zero, entropy stops changing. No motion, no game, no score.

## Two directions

Motion acting on matter goes two ways. It carries matter in, and it scatters it out. Friction plays both sides. Gas circling a star can't fall in while it keeps its motion; it would circle forever. Only friction, turning the circling into heat, lets it settle. Dust becomes planets the same way. Friction scatters energy out and lets matter in. Two directions, one pair.

## Where it tips

So what decides which way wins? Not a fixed number. A local verdict. Matter keeps gathering while three things hold: the pull inward beats the heat friction makes, there's still material around, and no stronger neighbor gets to it first. A planet stops growing when it has swept its lane clean. A galaxy stops making stars when its center blows its gas away or its neighborhood strips it.

Beneath that sits one plain rule. If the heat escapes, gathering wins. If the heat stays and builds, scattering wins. A cloud that cools collapses into stars. A star that keeps its heat holds itself up.

## The better question

What seems clearly not right is crediting the scorecard with the game: saying entropy drives time, dooms the universe or pulls like a force.

The better question isn't what entropy does. It's what the first pair is doing, matter and motion, everywhere and on every turn, and how much of each turn goes to gathering and how much to scattering.

title: Gravity Has No Face
dek: Matter shapes the current. The current carries matter.
excerpt: Matter shapes the current. The current carries matter.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

Gravity is the best-measured thing in physics and the least explained. We know its strength to many decimal places. We don't know what it is.

Newton knew that better than anyone. He wrote the law, found planets with it, and then, when asked what gravity actually was, wouldn't say. The idea of one body tugging another across empty space struck him as "so great an absurdity" that no thinking person could believe it. In 1713 he closed the matter with three Latin words: _hypotheses non fingo_. I frame no hypotheses.

Einstein gave gravity a shape: mass curves spacetime, and things follow the curves. It predicts beautifully. But a curve tells you the path, not the push. And the particle that's supposed to carry gravity has never turned up.

Three hundred years, three descriptions, no face.

## The first pair

Everything comes in pairs, and the first is matter and motion: what's there, and what it does. They don't attract. They're conjoined, one thing with two faces. Gravity is where that pair shows its face most plainly.

Matter shapes motion. If space is a real medium, as we've argued before, a heavy body changes it, packing it denser nearby and thinner farther off. We call that compression.

Motion carries matter. Fluids don't sit still under compression. Wherever pressure falls off, the fluid moves that way. So gravity isn't a pull. It's a current: the medium flows toward mass, and everything in it is carried along.

Matter shapes the current; the current carries matter. Neither comes first.

## Weight, explained

A falling body feels nothing because it's riding the current. A leaf and a log go down the river together, which is why a hammer and a feather dropped on the Moon in 1971 landed at the same instant. Everything rides the same water.

Standing on the ground is the other case. The ground holds us still while the current keeps running past. Weight is the push of a current we're not allowed to ride.

It works by the numbers, too. Let the current run at whatever speed it would take to escape from each distance, and the rate at which it speeds up matches Newton's law exactly. Mathematicians found that version of Einstein's equations in the 1920s and filed it as a curiosity. We read it as a description of something real.

## The bay

So where does all that inflow go? Picture a bay.

The tide comes in, the water goes slack, the tide goes out. One medium, one process, two directions. And the tide doesn't simply turn back. It flows until it meets resistance, and then it ebbs on the other side. Motion carries matter to a friction point and drops it there. The pile grows, adding resistance, until it balances the force of the flow. Then the flow reroutes along an easier path, and steals matter as it goes.

Rivers do exactly this: they build up their beds until they're blocked, then jump course. So do the giant centers of galaxies. Gas pours in through the disk, piles up and heats until the heat pushes back as hard as the inflow presses in. Then it shoots out along the poles, the one direction where nothing is piled in the way, dragging surrounding gas along with it.

Nothing is swallowed. It's stored until balance, then returned.

## Slack water

Our universe looks like a bay at slack water in its middle years. Its expansion stopped slowing and started speeding up five or six billion years ago. Galaxies peaked at making stars ten billion years ago. And today the gathering and the spreading are, curiously, almost exactly balanced. Cosmologists call that the coincidence problem. Slack water is simply what balance looks like.

Reality is a continuing tide as space expands. On the largest scale the expansion is the ebb, and wherever mass gathers the flood goes on, turn after turn. The tide needs nothing outside itself. Flood and ebb are the first pair, matter and motion, working in two directions in one medium.

## One pair, two directions

Put it together and two great principles of physics turn out to be the first pair working in two directions. Gravity is motion carrying matter in. Entropy is the score of motion scattering matter out. Opposites, conjoined.

## The better question

What seems clearly not right is a physics that measures gravity to many decimal places and accepts, for three hundred years, that it has no cause.

The better question isn't what gravity is made of. It's where the current comes from, and where it goes.

title: A Theory of Opposites
dek: Opposites don't attract. They are conjoined.
excerpt: Opposites don't attract. They are conjoined.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

Reality is material, and the first thing matter does is move. Nobody has ever found one without the other. Matter with no motion at all is a limit we can approach and never reach, and motion with nothing moving is only a word. What is there, and what it does: that's the first pair, and every other pair we know descends from it.

Energy isn't a third partner. Physics defines it as a number that never goes up or down, and politely declines to say what it is. Nobody was ever shocked by a bookkeeping system. Energy is motion held back: motion that runs into resistance, gets compressed or locked in place, and builds tension until it lets go. A shock is that tension letting go, all at once and without manners. Motion running free carries its energy as unused potential, and spends it on whatever gets in the way. Even mass is constrained motion. A proton weighs what it does mostly because of the motion boiling inside it with nowhere to go.

## Conjoined, not attracted

The old saying is that opposites attract. It sounds right and it's backwards. Attraction is a pull across a gap, two separate things reaching for each other. Opposites have no gap to cross.

North and south never found each other. They're the two ends of one magnet. Cut the magnet in half and there are two magnets, each with both ends, because there was never a north out there waiting for a south. What looks like attraction is a pair showing that it was one thing all along.

## Made together, unmade together

Nature doesn't make opposites one at a time. When energy turns into matter, it turns into a pair: an electron and its antielectron, born in one act, with charges that cancel to the last decimal. When the two meet again they go back to energy in one act, and nothing is left over. The books balance at the start and at the finish. A plus is never issued without its minus.

## No lone face

A push comes with a push back. Newton's equal and opposite reaction doesn't take days off. Try to pull a quark out of a proton and it won't come alone: pull hard enough and the effort makes a fresh pair instead. No face of a pair has ever been found by itself, and the theory says none will be.

## The lopsided ledger

If every pair balances, a pair that looks lopsided is a clue. Twice in the last century physics followed exactly that clue and found what was missing. Dirac's equation for the electron insisted on a twin with the opposite charge, and four years later Anderson photographed the positron. Pauli watched energy go missing from radioactive decay, refused to believe it, and proposed a small neutral particle to carry it off. Catching one took twenty-six years.

Our Sister Universe comes from the same habit of mind. A universe made almost entirely of matter is a lopsided ledger. Its other half may lie beyond an SOB, a scientific observational boundary, the place where our methods run out though something surely lies beyond.

## Names with one face

Some of our biggest words name only one face. Entropy names the scattering and hides the friction. Attraction names the meeting and hides the pair.

Gravity is the biggest of them, and the one that's been most misread. It names an effect, and for three centuries it's been taken for a force, a pull reaching across empty space. There's no pull. There's motion flowing inward, compressing matter where it gathers, and weight is the push of a current we're not allowed to ride. Gravity isn't a third thing added to matter and motion. It's the first pair at work, seen from the side where things pile up.

Take a one-faced name for a thing and we go looking for a player, and find only the score.

## The ladder

The pairs climb. Matter and motion. Gathering and scattering. Twist and counter-twist. Something and nothing. Mind and meaning, which is the first pair again on the other face of Reality: what's there, and what it does. And at the top, the pair only a knower can see: to be or not to be, the choice between this and nothing that every living thing makes all day long. The rest of life makes it without knowing. We make it knowing.

Every rung is one coin with two faces.

## Double-entry Reality

So we'll say it flatly: Reality is binary. It keeps its books by double entry. Every charge has its opposite, every gathering its scattering, every push its push back, and the whole of matter balances against the whole of motion. A single-entry Reality, one face and one column, has never been found, and it won't be. There's no such thing to find.

Merchants in Renaissance Italy get the credit for inventing double-entry bookkeeping. Nature had been using it all along.

## The better question

What's clearly not right is treating nature's pairs as coincidences, or the forces between opposites as pulls across empty space.

The better question isn't why opposites attract. It's what single thing each pair is a face of, and where its other face has gone.

title: The Candle and the Bonfire
dek: A binary view of Reality, from then to then.
excerpt: A binary view of Reality, from then to then.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

We have a theory. It isn't finished, and it isn't proven, and we're going to keep working on it in the open. But it hangs together, and it's time to put it on the table.

It starts with a single premise. Reality is material, and the first thing matter does is move. Matter and motion: what's there, and what it does. Neither has ever been found without the other. That's the first pair, and every other material pair is built from it.

It runs on a single principle. Every material pair in nature is one thing with two faces. Positive and negative, north and south, matter and antimatter: none of them has ever been made alone. They're made together and unmade together. Reality keeps its books by double entry, and the books always balance. Every this of Reality brings its own that, wherever it goes.

And it asks a single question, of everything: _what is this the other face of?_

## What the question does

Ask it of gravity, and gravity stops being a force. It's the name for what motion does when it flows inward, carrying matter as it goes. Weight is the push of a current we're not allowed to ride.

Ask it of entropy, and entropy stops being a power. It's the name for what's left when motion recedes and scatters its debris. Gravity and entropy are names for outcomes. Motion is the player.

Ask it of energy. Nobody was ever shocked by a bookkeeping system. Energy is motion held back, tension waiting to let go.

Ask it of black holes, and the holes disappear. The giants at the centers of galaxies gather, hold and release. They're middens, not drains. The small ones are graves: what a single star leaves behind.

Ask it of the Big Bang, and it turns out to be a release too: some earlier accumulator letting go. Their garbage became our starting place.

Ask it of a universe made almost entirely of matter, and the lopsided books point to a missing column. Somewhere past our SOB, our scientific observational boundary, the place where our methods run out though something surely lies beyond, our universe has a sister.

And ask it of the end. When the fuel runs out, the debris gathers in the last stores. The end is a storing, and a store is what a beginning comes from.

## The candle and the bonfire

The bonfire is the cosmos: a store of fuel let go, a long burning, embers gathering in the dark. It's vast and it knows nothing.

The candle is the knower: small, brief, and the only place where the bonfire is ever seen. Matter and motion out in the cosmos; mind and meaning in the knower, making the picture. The knower sees one face at a time. Both burn fuel. Both go out. The candle goes first, and knows it.

## Thought first

None of this comes with equations. That's on purpose. A thing has to be described before an equation can be put on top of it, and physics has gotten into the habit of reversing the order: measure first, calculate second, and ask what it all is last, if ever. We'd like to put thought back at the front of the line.

We call it a binary view of Reality. The full paper sets it out carefully, with the evidence it leans on and the objections it has to meet. The posts that follow will keep testing it, one subject at a time. Some of it will hold. Some of it may not. That's what exploring is.

## The better question

What's clearly not right is a physics that treats the pairs of nature as coincidences, its imbalances as accidents, and its names for outcomes as causes.

The better question isn't what the universe is made of. It's what each thing in it is the other face of, and where that other face has gone.

title: The Luck Twins
dek: Fate is the supplier.
excerpt: Fate is the supplier.
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

Most people believe in luck. They won't always say so. They knock on wood, cross their fingers, and say of the turn that changed their lives that it was meant to be. Scientists do it too, usually when no other scientist is watching.

Shakespeare's audiences knew the feeling. Falstaff, twice humiliated and setting out a third time, says, “This is the third time; I hope good luck lies in odd numbers.” Four hundred years later we still say things come in threes.

The experts have a word for all this: bias. The gambler's fallacy, the illusion of control, a brain that sees faces in clouds. Each diagnosis is real, and together they come with a pat on the head. Case closed. Except it isn't. A belief that turns up in every culture and every century, among people who know better, isn't a glitch. It's a fact in its own right, and explaining the mistakes in it doesn't explain why it won't die.

## The supplier

Every life sits inside a web of causes too big to see. The truck left two minutes late. The letter landed on the right desk. The stranger happened to be on the platform. Nobody can trace those chains, because they branch without end. For each of us the web lies past an SOB, a scientific observational boundary, the place where our ability to trace causes runs out though something surely lies beyond.

That web is fate. Not a script written in advance, and not a personality with plans for us. A supplier. It delivers. It doesn't care.

## The twins

What it delivers lands one of two ways. Better than we expected, and we call it good luck. Worse, and we call it bad luck. Those are the luck twins, and they come through the same door. A life open to a windfall is open to a blow. Seal out one and you've sealed out the other.

That's why people knock on wood after good news. They aren't crediting the wood. They know the other twin travels in the same shipment.

Nothing in the supply is good or bad. The same frost is good luck for the ski resort and bad luck for the orchard down the road. Good and bad are the names we give what arrives.

## Why it feels unfair

On average, over the long run, the twins come out even. A life isn't the long run. And three things tilt the ledger.

We see one twin at a time, never both, so we rarely feel them as one supply, even when we half know it. We weigh them unequally: a loss stings longer than a gain of the same size pleases. And they aren't always the same size. A lifetime of small breaks may never arrive in time to cover one catastrophe.

## Who's right

The folk are right that something they can't see shapes their lives. They're wrong to think it has favorites. The experts are right that people misjudge chance. They're wrong to think there's nothing there. Fate is a supplier, not a personality. Luck is a name, not a power.

## The better question

What's clearly not right is a science that treats a universal human perception as a malfunction.

The better question isn't why people believe in luck. It's what they're seeing when they do.

title: I Think, Therefore I Survive
dek: Thinking is the tool that keeps us alive. Why isn't school built to teach it?
excerpt: Thinking is the tool that keeps us alive. Why isn't school built to teach it?
body:
_We're storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can't prove it._

Descartes said, “I think, therefore I am.” He was after certainty. We're after something plainer: I think, therefore I survive.

Thinking is how a soft, slow animal with no claws outlasted nearly everything that could outrun it. Curiosity found the water. Judgment left the wrong berries alone. Foresight put grain away for winter. It's the one tool every one of us carries, and we can't put it down.

So here's a puzzle. Public education is the largest thing a society does on purpose for its children. Twelve or thirteen years, most of the waking day, the biggest item in many local budgets. And thinking, the tool that keeps us alive, isn't what it's built to produce.

## What school is for

Ask what schools are for and the answers come quickly. Reading and arithmetic. Facts about history and science. Getting into college. Getting a job. Becoming a citizen. Sitting still. Each has its defenders, and most are worth something.

Thinking makes the list too, usually in the mission statement. In the classroom it's treated as a side effect. Learn enough facts and thinking will happen. Somewhere between the spelling test and the SAT, it's supposed to show up on its own.

Do we think the Tooth Fairy's going to do it for us?

## Why is this happening

A few suggested causes.

Thinking is hard to grade. A fact is right or wrong, and a machine can score a thousand answer sheets before lunch. A good question can't be scored at all. Schools are judged by what can be counted, so they teach what can be counted.

Thinkers are inconvenient. A child who asks why the rule exists slows down a class of thirty. An adult who asks why the policy exists slows down a great deal more. Institutions aren't built to welcome the people who question them, and schools are institutions.

The fights are over content. Nearly every school board battle is about what children are told: which books, which history, which science. Almost nobody fights over whether children learn to weigh what they're told. Every side wants the right answers delivered. No side is campaigning for the questions.

And thinking can't be handed over. Facts pass from teacher to student. Thinking has to be done by the one doing it, slowly, with plenty of wrong turns. That takes time, and time is the one thing a school day never has enough of.

## What's clearly not right

What's clearly not right is a system that spends twelve years teaching children what to think and leaves how to think to luck.

A graduate can be rewarded, year after year, for producing the answer the teacher wanted. That's a skill. It isn't thinking. Then we turn that graduate loose in a world made mostly of claims, from advertisers, campaigns, feeds, experts and neighbors, and nearly every one of them would be glad to do the thinking for them.

And the bill comes due. People never taught to weigh a claim make worse bets on loans, cures, promises and candidates. Some of the cost lands on them, and a good deal of it lands on the public. A growing share of public money goes to repairing what was never prevented, while the schools that might have prevented it are graded on spelling. Some of that spending would be needed in any case. How much of the rest is the price of a public that was never taught to think is a question almost nobody is asking.

There's an irony on our sidewalks. We starve the mind at twelve and pay for the tent at thirty-five. Young people who leave school without a diploma are far more likely to end up homeless. But the people in the tents are the result, not the cause. The causes run back to decisions made in comfortable rooms: housing rules nobody thought through, asylums emptied with no plan for the people in them, budgets that pay for shelters instead of schooling. We don't have to look far for people who never learned to think. We elect them. The public pays either way. Paying late buys less.

## The better question

The usual question is what children need to know. It's been argued for a century and will be argued for another.

The better question is what children can do with what they know. Can they ask why? Can they notice when an answer doesn't fit? Can they change their minds for a good reason and hold firm against a bad one?

Which leads to a radical notion. What if schools taught how to think as well as what to learn? Thinking would be a subject in its own right, with its own hours, its own teachers and its own line on the report card. It sounds obvious. That it sounds radical tells us how far we've drifted.

The motto would fit on any classroom wall: think first, answer later.

Survival never depended on knowing the answer. It depended on working it out.

title: Think First, Answer Later
dek: What if thinking were a subject?
excerpt: What if thinking were a subject?
body:
_We’re storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can’t prove it._

Every school day begins with answers. The spelling list, the times table, the date of the battle. A child learns early that the job is to produce the right one, quickly, and that questions are something the teacher asks.

What if the day began somewhere else? What if thinking were a subject, taught from the first grade on, with its own hour and its own line on the report card? Think first, answer later.

## What it would teach

The habits underneath every good answer, taught without symbols or jargon.

In the early grades, asking why. Telling a reason from a wish. Noticing when two things are the same and when they only look alike.

In the middle grades, telling a claim from the evidence for it. Spotting an argument that sounds right and isn’t. Asking who gains if we believe it.

In the upper grades, the tricks in an ad or a headline. How a number can be true and still mislead. Changing one’s mind for a good reason, and holding firm against a bad one.

## The book

Picture the textbook, _A Children’s Book of Logic_. Its table of contents might read:

1. Why? Why? Why?
2. I Wish It Were So
3. Twins and Lookalikes
4. The Rooster Didn’t Make the Sun Come Up
5. Says Who?
6. Who Gets the Cookie?
7. Numbers Can Fib
8. The Other Side of the Coin
9. Lucky Socks
10. Oops!
11. Changing Your Mind
12. What I Don’t Know
13. Think First, Answer Later

There’s nothing in it a nine-year-old couldn’t follow, and nothing a teacher couldn’t teach with a good story and an open mind. As far as we know, this one hasn’t been written yet.

## Story first

Thinking starts as a story. Something happened, then something else, and one of them caused the other, or didn’t. Children follow stories long before they follow symbols.

Arithmetic is the same steps in shorthand. Seven take away three is a story about seven of something before it’s a subtraction. Children who can follow the story can follow the steps. Children handed the symbols first can learn to push them around without knowing what they stand for, and many hit a wall the day the symbols stop matching anything they can picture.

So the order would be story, then reasoning, then symbols. Describe the thing before the equation goes on top. It’s the order we keep arguing for in physics. It may be the right order for a nine-year-old too.

## It’s been tried

For half a century a program called [Philosophy for Children](https://www.montclair.edu/iapc/?p=33) has had ordinary teachers reading short stories with their classes and letting the children argue out the questions with reasons. It runs in thousands of schools. The teachers aren’t logicians. A couple of days’ training is enough to begin. It can be done, and almost anyone can do it.

Outside the public schools, homeschoolers and Christian classical schools teach logic from the middle grades up, with books like [The Fallacy Detective](https://www.exodusbooks.com/fallacy-detective/bluedorn/27977/) and [The Art of Argument](https://classicalacademicpress.com/product/the-art-of-argument/). At least they’re trying.

## The teachers learn too

The harder part isn’t the children. It’s the adults at the front of the room. Many teachers were never taught to think this way themselves, and plenty chose the early grades partly because math never felt like home. A course that starts with stories and reasons is a way in for them, too. A teacher who learns to say “I don’t know, what do you think?” teaches more than any answer key.

## What’s clearly not right

What’s clearly not right is a school day that hands out answers before anyone has learned what a question is.

## The better question

The usual question is how to raise the scores. The better question is what would happen to the scores, and to everything after them, if children learned to think before they learned to answer.

Think first, answer later.

title: The Teachers
dek: What if teaching were a job for a country’s best thinkers?
excerpt: What if teaching were a job for a country’s best thinkers?
body:
_We’re storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can’t prove it._

Every chain has a first link. In ours it’s the person at the front of the room.

A child spends more waking hours with teachers than with almost anyone outside the family. What those adults can do, a child has a chance to learn. What they were never given, they can’t hand on.

## How we treat them

We ask teachers to raise thinkers, then hand them a script. Pacing guides, required lessons, and a test in the spring that decides how well they did. We pay them well below what other graduates earn and wonder why so many leave in their first five years. We praise them in speeches and second-guess them at board meetings.

That isn’t a plan for raising thinkers. It’s a plan for delivering content on schedule.

Meanwhile the money goes somewhere. In the two decades after 2002, spending per student, after inflation, rose by about a third. Schools added staff nearly four times as fast as they added students. Most of the new hires weren’t classroom teachers. Non-teaching staff grew three times as fast as the teaching corps.

The scores went the other way. National test results peaked about a dozen years ago and have slid since. The class of 2024 posted the lowest senior reading scores the national test has ever recorded, and the lowest senior math scores in nearly twenty years. More overhead, less learning.

It’s crowd control winning out over learning. Every failure calls for more people to manage it, and they’re paid from the budget that might have prevented it. The problem squares itself. The crisis collapses inward.

Over the long run, this may prove more dangerous than Covid. Covid’s damage came all at once, and we counted every case. This comes a little each year, and nobody adds up the bill.

## One witness

Finland chose differently. Every teacher there holds a master’s degree, and the training programs turn away most of the people who apply. Getting in is about as hard as getting into law or medicine. Grade-school teachers study how children learn, not only what to teach them. Once they’re in a classroom they’re trusted, with a broad national curriculum, their own methods and almost no standardized tests to grade them by.

Finland has troubles of its own, and its scores have slipped. But it answered a question we keep dodging: who stands at the front of the room, and how far we trust them.

## Why is this happening

A few suggested causes.

Teachers are paid from state and local taxes, and every one of those budgets has louder claims on it.

A trusted teacher is hard to measure. A scripted one is easy. Systems judged by what they can count prefer what they can count.

Status follows pay, and pay follows status. The circle holds.

And the people deciding were taught by the same system they’re deciding about.

## What’s clearly not right

What’s clearly not right is asking teachers to teach thinking while treating them as if thinking weren’t part of the job.

## The better question

The usual question is how to find enough teachers. The better question is what would happen if teaching became a job the best thinkers competed for.

What if the course that taught children to think first taught their teachers too? The chain that runs down from careless leaders to the sidewalk could start running the other way, from the front of the room.

title: Why This Can’t Happen Here
dek: The system itself defies Logic.
excerpt: The system itself defies Logic.
body:
_We’re storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can’t prove it._

American public education may be the most studied, analyzed and reformed institution in history. Commissions have examined it, economists have audited it, presidents have rescued it and foundations have rebuilt it. And it never seems to help. How does that happen?

Imagine a school day that begins with thinking. Logic as a subject from the first grade on, story before symbols, teachers learning alongside their students. Nobody would stand up at a board meeting and argue against it. Nobody has to. The system can’t let it in.

## A nation at risk, and then another

In 1983 a federal commission told us we were a nation at risk. Then came Goals 2000. Then No Child Left Behind, Race to the Top, Common Core and the Every Student Succeeds Act. Each arrived with a signing ceremony and a promise. Each changed who governs, who tests and who pays. Hardly one changed what happens between a teacher and a child at ten o’clock on a Tuesday morning. Grades by age, fifty-minute periods, separate subjects, one adult at the front: historians call it the grammar of schooling, and it has outlasted every reform aimed at it. Reform stops at the classroom door.

Every reform is somebody’s monument, and the next administration needs a monument of its own. So each one is torn down before anyone learns whether it worked. The churn is the product. Reform is done to teachers, never with them, and teachers learned long ago to wait it out. They’re usually right.

Every reform aims at what can be counted, because that’s how it will be judged. Not one has set out to teach a child to think. And the churn feeds a whole industry: testing companies, textbook publishers, consultants and education schools all earn their living from the next reform. A reform that worked would put some of them out of work.

Nor is anyone in charge. There are some thirteen thousand school districts, fifty state systems and a federal government that pays with strings attached. Every reform has to pass through every layer, and every layer can quietly say no.

When a reform does show results, the second study is already on its way to say it didn’t. In politics, defending No is always easier than achieving Yes.

## The farthest rooms

The decisions are made at one end of the building and the children sit at the other. The only places farther from the superintendent’s office than the classrooms are the restrooms.

Between the two lies everything that gets paid first: buildings, buses, maintenance, compliance, central offices, and pension and health plans that swallow each new dollar before it reaches a paycheck. In the two decades after 2002, schools added staff nearly four times as fast as they added students, and most of the new hires weren’t teachers. More overhead, less learning. Crowd control wins out over learning, and every failure hires someone new to manage it, paid from the budget that might have prevented it. The problem squares itself. The crisis collapses inward.

Schools have other jobs, too. They’re the nation’s childcare, its lunch counter, its safe place for teenagers during working hours. Any change that threatens those jobs gets fought, whatever it might do for learning.

## The rings of guilt

Call it the hierarchy of guilt, and spare no one.

Start at the widest ring. A society in decay, values in flux, families in pieces, political divisions hardening every year. Every new problem in American life lands at the schoolhouse door, and the target moves faster than any reform can follow. When communities split, they fight over the one place they still have to share. The school becomes the battleground, and the battle is always about what children are told, never about how they think.

Move inward. Teachers unions guarding contracts while the mission walks out the door. School boards turning playgrounds into social war zones. Superintendents who’ve become custodians of budgets instead of learning. Washington strangling the whole enterprise in red tape.

Now the rings nobody likes to name. Voters who demand great schools and vote down the levy that would pay for them. Legislatures that cut budgets and pile on mandates in the same session. Crusaders for and against school choice, using children as ammunition. Parents who treat school as daycare and complain when it acts like one. Employers who want workers, not thinkers. A press that covers the shouting at the board meeting and never the lesson in the classroom. And everyone who gives their own child’s school an A and the nation’s an F, because the problem is always somewhere else. And every voter who went to school and wants their children’s school to look exactly like it did.

Over all of it preside leaders who never learned to think, deciding whether children should. And at the center of all those rings sit the only people with no vote, no lobby and no say. School kids don’t vote.

## What’s clearly not right

What’s clearly not right is a system that studies itself without end and still can’t think. A system that can’t think about itself can’t teach thinking. The system itself defies Logic, in both senses of the word.

## The barracks

If military training were in the hands of our public education system, pity the poor service members. Here’s the part that ought to embarrass everyone: the military runs schools too, and runs them better. The Defense Department runs its own schools for the children of service members, on bases at home and around the world. These are children who change schools every few years and wave goodbye to a parent headed for deployment. On the 2024 national test, those schools led the nation, ahead of every state.

And the military doesn’t train obedience alone. It trains judgment. Officers learn commander’s intent: understand the goal well enough to adapt when the plan falls apart. After every exercise comes an after-action review: what was supposed to happen, what did happen, and why. Think first, answer later, in uniform.

It’s an ironic home run. If we can do it at the barracks, there’s no excuse for failing at the schoolhouse. “Can’t” was never the word. The word is “won’t.”

## The better question

The usual question is which reform comes next. The better question is what can slip past the reformers.

Maybe something small. A book. A few good stories and one teacher willing to open it. Reforms come down from Washington and die somewhere before the classroom door. A book only has to get through the door. Two books, really: _A Children’s Book of Logic_ for the children, and _Logic for Kids_ for the grown-ups learning alongside them. There’s room for both. Either one may turn out to be the little book that could.

Think first, answer later.

So here’s the bottom line. Do we want our nation to honor the promise of the Statue of Liberty, or do we want to be . . . France?

Thank Whomever we live in a random Reality. Something good could happen.

title: Somebody Else’s Flush
dek: Matter is space gathered. Space is matter spread thin.
excerpt: Matter is space gathered. Space is matter spread thin.
body:
_We’re storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can’t prove it._

Physics has never been able to say what space is. It measures space, bends it, stretches it and fills it with fields, and when you ask what space is made of, the answer is a shrug dressed in mathematics. Nothing, apparently, with properties.

We think the answer is simpler. Space and matter are the same stuff at different densities. Matter is space gathered. Space is matter spread thin. One medium, and a dial that runs from dense to rare.

## One line

Draw a straight line from the center of a galaxy outward.

It starts in the densest place we can infer, the dark heart physics calls a singularity. We call it an accumulator: a store that gathers, holds and lets go. Its center sits behind the event horizon, past an SOB, a scientific observational boundary, the place where our ability to look runs out though something surely lies beyond. The line runs out through the horizon, where the inward rush of the medium finally drops below the speed of light. It runs out through the stars and gas, density rising and falling as it passes each one. And it runs out into the space between galaxies, as thin as anything gets.

One line, and it crosses the whole dial. Gravity is the dial turning up. Entropy is the dial turning down. A particle is a knot on it, tied tight where motion is held in place, and like every knot it lasts as long as it’s held. A duration, not a destiny.

The range of that dial is staggering. Out between the galaxies, a cubic meter holds a few lonely atoms. A neutron star crams more than our sun into a ball the size of a city, and a teaspoon of it would weigh billions of tons. Then comes the joke at the top. The giant at the center of a galaxy, measured out to its horizon, is on average no denser than water, and the biggest of them are thinner than air. The bottomless pits of the textbooks are fluffier than bathwater.

Even the solid stuff is mostly motion. The three quarks inside a proton account for about one percent of its weight. The rest is motion trapped inside: quarks racing around and the field that holds them. You weigh what you weigh because the motion in you has nowhere to go. Try to pull two quarks apart and you don’t get a free quark. The effort makes a new pair, and you’re left holding two knots instead of one. Nothing in the medium comes loose alone.

## Somebody else’s flush

The line runs through time, too. Space isn’t a box the universe happened in. Space is what a release leaves behind. When an accumulator lets go, it throws out the medium it was holding, and that medium, spread thin, is space. Our Big Bang was a release of exactly that kind.

Put plainly, the line starts when somebody else flushes their toilet and ends when we flush ours. Their garbage became our starting place. Ours may become someone else’s.

## The two ends

Every dial has two ends, and nothing real sits at either one. At the top is infinite density, the singularity, which physics itself calls the place where its theory breaks down. At the bottom is zero density, true nothing, which nobody has ever found. Even the emptiest vacuum pushes, hums and carries light. Everything real lives in between.

Physics learns that lesson at the top of the dial and forgets it everywhere else. It throws out infinite density as a breakdown, then keeps infinite space for a universe that never ends and infinite time for particles that never die. Infinity is a crisis in one equation and a comfort in the next. We don’t know how that can be mistaken for serious science.

## What’s clearly not right

What’s clearly not right is a physics that can weigh a galaxy and still can’t say what the room is made of.

## The better question

The usual question is whether space is empty. The better question is how thickly the one medium is gathered in each place, what motion is holding it there, and whose flush put it there in the first place.

title: We Don’t Really Belong Here
dek: The Phone Home Reaction
excerpt: The Phone Home Reaction
body:
_We’re storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can’t prove it._

The Welsh, who gave the world Merlin, have a word no other language quite matches: hiraeth. It means a longing for a home you can’t go back to, or one that perhaps never was.

Nearly everyone knows the feeling, even without the word. It comes in a crowded room or on an empty road, in the middle of a good life as easily as a hard one. A quiet sense that this isn’t quite the right place, that somewhere else was, and that the way back has been lost.

It arrives early. When researchers asked children in Ecuador, some from the city and some from the Shuar villages of the Amazon, about the time before they were born, both groups gave the same kind of answer. They had no bodies then, the children said, but they already had feelings. They already wanted things. No one had taught them that.

## The costumes

Every people has dressed the feeling in its own story.

The Hebrews told of a garden. What ended it wasn’t a flood or an enemy. It was knowing. “And the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked.” The first thing they learned was that they were exposed, and then the gate closed behind them, with an angel and a flaming sword to keep the way back.

In Plato’s telling, Aristophanes said we were once whole and were split in two, and that each half has wandered ever since, looking for the other. The Chinese poet Tao Yuanming told of a fisherman who found a hidden valley of peace, left it, and could never find it again. The Irish told of Oisín, who came home from the land of youth, touched the ground and turned ancient where he stood. The Haudenosaunee say the first mother fell from the world above the sky.

The costumes change. The feeling underneath doesn’t. Put plainly, it says this: Earth is not our home. It’s where we were abandoned.

## The phone home reaction

Call it the phone home reaction, after the little stranded traveler in the film who wanted only one thing.

The psychologists have a name for it, birth anxiety: the theory that we spend our lives missing the womb. It names what happens. It says nothing about why it happens, or what it means. The womb was only the first shelter the feeling ever found.

We think the reaction is something more basic. It’s what vulnerability feels like from the inside. A creature that knows it can be hurt, can lose and will die carries an absence it can feel but never name, and it reaches for whatever might fill it. We are the vulnerable in search of the unattainable.

A life also has an edge at each end, a place no one can see past. No one remembers before birth, and no one reports back from after death. These are SOBs, scientific observational boundaries, the places where our ability to look runs out though something surely lies beyond. Where we can’t see, we paint. “Home” is the word we write on both walls.

Our matter is here. It’s made of the same stuff as the stones and the stars, and it has never been outside this universe. Our substance is never sure. That’s why we put Heaven in the heavens.

## What it makes us do

The feeling doesn’t only look back. It sends us out: to study the stars, to write scripture, to build. Every conscious human undertaking can be read as a search for the feeling of home. The first granary was built against hunger, the first writing against forgetting, the hearth against the cold and the dark. Cathedrals, symphonies and telescopes came later, all of them reaching. Insecurity is the mother of invention.

A skeptic could call all of it diversion: busyness to keep from sitting alone with the feeling. A believer could call it devotion. Either way, it’s the same search.

And the feeling is never stronger than when the vulnerability is sharpest. Soldiers in trenches write about kitchens. People in hospital beds long for their own back porch. Trouble strips away the costumes, and what’s left is the longing.

## What’s clearly not right

What’s clearly not right is treating this feeling as a malfunction, a disorder to be managed or an error to be argued away. It turns up across cultures and centuries, and in children who were never taught it. It has been with us longer than any of the stories we’ve told about it.

## The better question

The usual question is where home is: above us, behind us, ahead of us. The better question is why we were built to feel we’ve lost it. It may be a better question, even, than what came before the beginning of the universe. That one lies past the far wall of everything. This one is inside each of us, and it’s the reason anyone asks the other.

The hole can never be filled, and we can never stop trying to fill it. Everything we have ever made is what that looks like from the outside. Albert Camus said one must imagine Sisyphus happy, pushing his rock up the hill forever. One must imagine the homesick proud.

The few people who have seen the whole Earth from far away came back saying much the same thing. From out there, the small blue planet looked like home. It took leaving to see it.

Earth never feels right until you start to leave.

title: The Cat Was Always Just a Cat
dek: A puddle is a puddle. A drop is a drop.
excerpt: A puddle is a puddle. A drop is a drop.
body:
_We’re storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can’t prove it._

In 1935 Erwin Schrödinger shut an imaginary cat in a box with a vial of poison and a trigger that might or might not go off. Quantum theory, as it was being taught, said that until someone opened the lid the cat was both alive and dead at once. Schrödinger meant it as a joke, a way of showing that the theory had gone off the rails.

Physics took the joke and made it a mascot. Ninety years later the cat is on T-shirts, and the idea it was meant to mock, superposition, is taught as the deepest truth about Reality.

## What they say

Before it’s measured, the story goes, a particle is everywhere it might be, in every state it might take, all at once. The act of measuring “collapses” it into one place and one state. Then the arguments begin. How can looking do that? Does the universe split in two every time someone checks? Does it take a conscious mind to make a particle choose? Careers have been built on those questions, and none of them has been settled.

## What we say

A puddle is a puddle. A drop is a drop. They’re both water, but they are not each other.

Before a detector, there is no particle. There is the medium of space, spread out and moving: the puddle. A particle is that medium meeting resistance and gathering at a point: the drop. A detector is resistance. So the measurement isn’t the moment we find the particle. It’s the moment the particle happens. Nothing was ever in two places. Nothing collapsed. The water simply met something and formed a drop.

Something real does pass through both slits in the famous experiment and paint stripes on the screen behind them. That something is the puddle, real and moving. The stripes are its ripples. The dots that arrive one at a time are its drops. It takes no particle in two places to explain any of it.

Physics has even proved the point without meaning to. The experiments honored with the 2022 Nobel Prize showed that particles can’t be carrying their properties around before they’re measured. In plain words, a particle doesn’t exist as a particle until it exists.

## The cat

The cat was alive or dead the whole time. We just didn’t know which until we lifted the lid. The uncertainty was in us, not in the cat. A cat bumps into air, light and the walls of its box billions of times a second. It’s never a puddle. It was always just a cat.

## What’s clearly not right

The moment before a particle forms lies past an SOB, a scientific observational boundary, the place where our ability to look runs out though something surely lies beyond. Nobody can observe what hasn’t happened yet. Physics painted a word on that wall, and the word is superposition.

What’s clearly not right is a word for something that hasn’t happened, sold as a description of something that has.

## The better question

The usual question is how a particle can be in two places at once. The better question is what is there before there’s any particle at all. Our answer is the medium of space itself, a puddle spread thin, waiting to meet something.

We could explain that to a first grader in a minute. He’d wonder whether we thought he was an idiot.

_Here lies Superposition, 1926–2026. It existed only as long as no one looked._

title: The Turkey of All Turkeys
dek: The holographic principle, carved.
excerpt: The holographic principle, carved.
body:
_We’re storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can’t prove it._

Every Thanksgiving somebody brings a dish that looks magnificent and tastes like nothing. Theoretical physics has been bringing the same one for thirty years. It’s called the holographic principle. Time to carve it.

## The bird

Pluck the feathers and the principle comes down to one line: everything inside a space can be described by information on its surface. The inside is a projection of the outside. It has been a headline for a generation: “We may be living in a hologram.”

It began with a real oddity. In the 1970s Jacob Bekenstein and Stephen Hawking found that a black hole’s entropy grows with the area of its surface, not with the volume inside. A black hole lies behind an SOB, a scientific observational boundary, the place where our ability to look runs out though something surely lies beyond. One odd fact about one object nobody can see into was promoted, in the 1990s, into a law for the entire universe.

## Which wall?

A principle that puts everything on a surface had better say which surface. For a black hole, it’s the event horizon. For the showpiece version, it’s a boundary infinitely far away. For the universe we actually live in, nobody knows. Everything is written on the wall, and the theory can’t tell you where the wall is.

Who did the writing? Nobody, says the theory. The “information on the surface” is a second set of equations that gives the same answers as the first. Which leaves only one possible artist: the theorists themselves, who painted the wall and then forgot they’d painted it.

## The stuffing

The showpiece came in 1997, when Juan Maldacena found an exact match between a universe with gravity and a theory without gravity living on its rim. Picture M.C. Escher’s _Circle Limit_ prints, a disk of angels and devils shrinking toward an edge that is infinitely far away. Gravity lives inside the disk. A different theory lives on the rim. Every entry on one side has its twin on the other. His paper became one of the most cited in all of physics.

There are two catches. The first is that Escher’s disk isn’t our universe. It’s shaped like a saddle, with a negative cosmological constant. Ours has a positive one, and it’s expanding faster and faster. The crown jewel of holography is a proof about a universe we don’t live in.

The second is what’s underneath. Maldacena took one hypothetical object from string theory, a stack of membranes, described it two ways, and declared the two descriptions equal. That’s the how. The why is missing. Thirty years on, the match is still officially a conjecture. Thousands of calculations agree with it. Nothing explains why it should hold, and nothing ties it to anything in nature.

## Two sets of books

Real double entry, the bookkeeping nature keeps, matches every entry with its opposite: a gathering with a scattering, a push with a push back. Together they balance. Holography doesn’t do that. It copies the same ledger into a second book. Every entry is duplicated, and so is every blank. Any question that can’t be answered inside can’t be answered on the surface either.

It’s a model and a drawing of the model, with the holographers insisting the drawing is the original. It’s Tweedledum and Tweedledee, identical twins forever arguing over which is which. Lewis Carroll even supplied the motto in 1871: “Contrariwise, if it was so, it might be; and if it were so, it would be; but as it isn’t, it ain’t. That’s logic.”

And the famous “extra dimension” that is said to emerge from the surface? Look at the dictionary and it turns out to be the zoom knob. Deep inside corresponds to coarse and large on the rim, and near the edge to small and fine. Scale has been relabeled as a place. That’s a fact about how we describe things, not about what’s there.

## What’s on the plate

For thirty years of feasting, here’s the meal. A calculating trick that works by analogy, as when it was used to estimate how the quark soup in particle colliders flows. Arguments about black holes settled on paper. A fresh vocabulary for grant proposals: space made of entanglement, spacetime as a code.

In 2015 Fermilab’s Holometer listened for the jitter one version predicted and heard nothing. In 2022 a team claimed to have made a holographic wormhole on a quantum computer and landed the cover of _Nature_. Within months other physicists showed the signal was an artifact of a system too small to mean anything.

If the universe were a hologram, what would change? Nothing anyone could measure.

## What’s clearly not right

As a game, it may be world class: marvelous gymnastics for mathematicians. Served to the public as a window onto Reality, it’s parlor magic, the sideshow passed off as the main event, and an embarrassment to the reputation of science.

And it points to something worse. Every great prediction confirmed in the last half century, from the Higgs boson in 2012 to the gravitational waves heard in 2015, came from theories finished by the mid-1970s or long before. And even those triumphs have been of limited value beyond the laboratory. In that same half century, strings, extra dimensions, supersymmetry, the multiverse and holography have produced no confirmed prediction about nature. The great collider at CERN was widely expected to find supersymmetry. It found none. A field that has to offer this to the world as its prize dish is a field at a dead end.

## The better question

The usual question is whether we’re living in a hologram. The better question is why a theory that can’t be tested, about a universe that isn’t ours, has been the main course of theoretical physics for thirty years.

Tweedledee already gave the answer. As it isn’t, it ain’t.

Happy Thanksgiving. Carve carefully. There’s a lot less meat on this bird than the feathers suggest.

title: The Great Temptation
dek: Physics, the media and the oldest temptation there is.
excerpt: Physics, the media and the oldest temptation there is.
body:
_We’re storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can’t prove it._

Every temptation begins with an offer. The serpent didn’t drag anyone to the tree. He made a pitch: “ye shall be as gods.” And the fruit was “to be desired to make one wise.” Not to be wise. To be made wise. To have the standing of those who know.

Physics heard the same pitch in the twentieth century. It took the fruit.

## The reflex

The first thing the fruit taught was exposure: “the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked.” A creature that knows it can be hurt can never again leave a dark corner unexplained. The rustle in the grass might be the wind. It might be a lion. Guess wind and be wrong once, and you’re lunch. So we’re built to guess lion, every time, and to fill every gap with something before we know what’s there.

That reflex doesn’t wait for evidence, and it can’t be switched off. In patients whose brain hemispheres have been surgically separated, the talking half will invent a confident reason for an act it never saw rather than say “I don’t know.” It explains before it knows. Danger lurks in empty spaces, and biology insists that we fill them.

Science is that reflex on its best behavior. It promises to fill a gap only with what can be seen. Where the seeing runs out, the reflex is still there, waiting.

## The man who said no

Isaac Newton had the most successful theory the world had ever seen, and a hole in the middle of it. His law said how gravity behaves. It said nothing about what gravity is, or how one body pulls on another across empty space with nothing in between. Privately he called that idea “so great an absurdity” that no competent thinker could fall for it.

A ready answer was on offer. Descartes had filled the heavens with swirling vortices, a picture anyone could hold in his head. Newton showed it didn’t work, threw it out, and put nothing in its place. His critics called that an occult quality. In 1713 he answered them in print: “I do not feign hypotheses.”

That was the refusal of the fruit, and a man overriding his own biology. The man with the most to gain from filling the gap left it empty, and labeled it empty.

Physics kept his equations for two centuries. It let his honesty wear away.

## The courtship

Then the suitor arrived. In November 1919 the newspapers learned that starlight bends around the sun just as Einstein had said it would, a result of little use outside an observatory, and overnight a physicist became a celebrity. Quantum mechanics arrived with radio, and its strangeness was perfect copy. The bomb made physicists the most powerful scientists on earth. Sputnik made physics a matter of national pride, and the giant machines of Big Science needed the public’s applause to pay for them. Then came the bestsellers.

No other science was courted like that. Chemists, geologists and doctors live in the same media climate, but their claims answer to something: a reaction, a rock, a patient. Physics works where the looking runs out, at SOBs, scientific observational boundaries, the places where our ability to look runs out though something surely lies beyond. Out there nothing answers back.

Room to wander and a reward for wandering. It was the perfect setting for a seduction.

## What the media buys

The media has no use for “we don’t know.” It wants a name, and physics learned to give it one.

For years astronomers spoke of the “missing mass.” That’s an honest name. It names a gap. Then the gap became “dark matter,” a substance, and the substance went into the textbooks while the detectors kept coming up empty. The singularity is the place where the equations quit, presented as an object. Superposition is a step in a calculation, presented as a state of nature. The multiverse and the hologram are what the theories need, presented as features of the world.

In 1993 a Nobel laureate called his book about the Higgs boson _The God Particle_. Ye shall be as gods. The serpent couldn’t have picked a better title.

A placeholder isn’t a crime. The reflex makes placeholders inevitable, in every science. The discipline is in labeling the gap as a gap. Courted and paid, physics stopped labeling.

## The hinge

Richard Feynman took the stage and kept his head. “I can live with doubt and uncertainty and not knowing,” he told the BBC in 1981. He was the last great physicist who performed and produced in the same body. What the media learned from him was that the audience would pay for the performance alone. After Feynman the stage could be held without the work, and the humility no longer had to come along.

## Why is this happening

A few suggested causes.

The reflex is older than science. It can be overridden but never switched off, and every generation has to do the overriding again.

A placeholder written in mathematics feels like an answer. Once the equations close, the gap stops hurting.

Grants, citations, book contracts and lecture stages all pay for visibility. Over decades that changes who rises.

And the twenty-four-hour cycle killed the night. With it went the quiet in which a refusal like Newton’s is formed and kept. Humility needs a quiet room. Self-promotion needs an audience. The audience is everywhere now.

No villain is required. Temptation doesn’t coerce. It offers, and it waits.

## What’s clearly not right

What’s clearly not right is a field that names its gaps as things and teaches the names as discoveries.

Science is an evolving template on the surface of Reality. Physics has started selling the template as the surface.

## The better question

The usual question is what fills the empty spaces at the edge of physics: what dark matter is made of, what lies inside a singularity, which version of the quantum is true. The better question is whether physics can learn to leave an empty space empty again.

Adam took the fruit. Isaac refused it. Richard took the stage and kept his humility. Physics, as a field, took everything on offer.

It has been done before. It was done in 1713, in Latin, in three words.

_The full argument is in our Paper 21, [“Danger Lurks in Empty Spaces.”](/papers/danger-lurks-in-empty-spaces)_

title: Where Constraint Runs Out
dek: Two checks on every claim, and what is left when one of them is gone.
excerpt: Two checks on every claim, and what is left when one of them is gone.
body:
_We’re storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can’t prove it._

Every claim to knowledge is held in check by one of two things. Constraint is a check imposed from outside. Restraint is a check imposed from inside. There is no third kind.

## Constraint

Constraint is Reality answering back. Where a claim can be tested, the test is the constraint, and the claim survives it or it doesn’t. Whether the claimant is humble or vain makes no difference, because the check isn’t his. Constraint requires no virtue.

Constraint is Reality’s basic feature, and our saving grace. Wherever Reality can answer back, it corrects us whether we like it or not. Constraint is also what shapes matter itself. In our own account a particle is motion constrained.

## Restraint

At an SOB, a scientific observational boundary, the place where our ability to look runs out though something surely lies beyond, Reality cannot answer back. That is what the boundary is. So at an SOB, by definition, there is no constraint. Whatever holds a claim in check there must come from the claimant. That is restraint.

Constraint is not a choice. Restraint is nothing but a choice.

Isaac Newton made that choice. He had a hole at the center of his theory of gravity and a ready-made answer to fill it. He set the answer aside, kept the hole, and said so in print: “I do not feign hypotheses.” Nothing outside him required it.

## Where constraint runs out

It follows: where constraint runs out, only restraint is left.

Constraint belongs to Reality, the world organized by something other than us, which reaches us only as consequences. Restraint belongs to reality, the world we organize for ourselves. Constraint is Reality saying no. Restraint is us saying no on Reality’s behalf, where Reality can’t be heard. Constraint shapes matter. Restraint shapes minds.

Every science works partly inside constraint and partly beyond it. Physics at its edges works entirely beyond it. So at the edges of physics, every check on a claim is restraint, or there is no check at all.

## What the media changed

The media did not remove any constraint. It cannot; constraint belongs to Reality. What it removed were the pauses that made restraint easier: the night between editions, the distance between one claim and the next. And it paid for the absence of restraint: fame, funding, the standing of those who know, and a bestseller called _The God Particle_.

A check that is chosen can be unchosen. A check that is paid against will be.

## Why is this happening

A few suggested causes.

Restraint is chosen, so it can be declined.

Restraint is unpaid, so it competes with everything that is paid.

Restraint chosen by one person binds no one else, so each generation has to choose it again.

And where there is no constraint, “we don’t know” is never handed down by Reality. It has to be said by us, and what has to be said can go unsaid.

## What’s clearly not right

What’s clearly not right is a field that works where there is no constraint and treats restraint as optional. Where there is no constraint, restraint isn’t optional. It is the only check there is.

## The better question

The usual question is what physics will find next at its edges. The better question is what checks its claims there. By definition, the answer is: only physics.

Newton checked himself. It cost him nothing but the applause.

title: Back to Earth
dek: Where the voyage has taken us, and what science looks like when it comes home.
excerpt: Where the voyage has taken us, and what science looks like when it comes home.
body:
_We’re storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can’t prove it._

Ninety essays and twenty-one papers ago, we set out with one suspicion: that physics at its frontier had begun saying more than it knew. We didn’t set out to prove it. We set out to look. This is a report of what we saw on the way, and where it has brought us.

## Where we started

The first essays went straight at the big stories: the Big Bang, black holes, dark matter, the smooth universe, the multiverse. Each is told to the public as settled. Each, looked at closely, rests on far less observation than its telling suggests. The data are real. The stories built on top of them are much larger than the data.

That raised the first real question. Not whether these stories are wrong, but how a discipline so careful about measurement came to be so careless about what it claims its measurements mean.

## The boundary

The first answer was a boundary. Every instrument reaches only so far. Beyond the reach of every instrument lies what we named an SOB, a scientific observational boundary: the place where our ability to look runs out, though something surely lies beyond. Some of these boundaries retreat as tools improve. Others never will. The first instant of the universe, the interior of a collapsed star, the moment before a particle is detected: none of these can be revisited, repeated or approached.

Naming the boundary changed everything that followed. It separated two kinds of statement that physics makes. One kind reports what was found on this side of a boundary. The other describes what lies on the far side. The first kind can be checked. The second cannot, ever, by anyone.

## What fills the far side

The far side doesn’t stay empty. People can’t leave an unexplained gap alone. The mind treats the unknown as a threat, and it fills the gap before the evidence arrives. Scientists are people. At the boundary, explanations arrive early, written in mathematics and given names that sound like discoveries.

A name is not a finding. But a name that sounds like a substance tells the public that a substance has been found, and the public believes it.

## Our own story

We didn’t stop at criticism. Across a long run of papers we offered a story of our own: a binary view of Reality, in which everything that exists comes as a pair, matter with motion, gathering with scattering, and in which the outcomes physics names as forces are the two directions of a single movement.

We hold that story to the same rule we apply to everyone else. It is an idea, not a fact. It earns its place only where it organizes what has actually been observed. Past that point it’s ours, and we say so.

## Why physics in particular

Every science faces boundaries. Most keep their discipline anyway, because their claims meet the world. A chemist’s reaction runs or it doesn’t. A doctor’s patient recovers or doesn’t. Physics, at its edges, works where nothing answers back. There, the only thing keeping a claim honest is the discipline of the person making it.

In the twentieth century that discipline met a new pressure. The mass media discovered physics and paid it in the currencies it values most: attention, funding and standing. Confident claims about the far side of the boundary made headlines. “We don’t know” never did. No conspiracy was needed. Reward did the work.

## What knowing is

The further we went, the more the question moved from physics to knowledge itself.

An observation is an encounter. What is out there supplies a difference. The observer and the instrument supply the form that difference takes. Change the instrument or change the question, and the result changes. So every observation reports an encounter, never the thing encountered.

That holds all the way down. We can describe how matter behaves under every condition we know how to create. We have no description of what matter is. Nor can we describe the knower. The one doing the knowing can’t step outside itself to look. Everything science holds lies between those two unknowns.

There is Reality, organized by something other than us, which reaches us only as consequences. And there is the reality we organize: the ordered world we live in and describe. We live entirely in the second and mistake it for the first, because the mind doesn’t mark its own contribution. Agreement among observers doesn’t fix this. A consensus of subjects is still subjective.

Subjectivity isn’t a stain on observation that better method could scrub away. It runs through every part of it: the senses we were born with, the instruments we chose to build, the questions we thought to ask, the words we use to record the answers. It is the sum total of all our limitations. It is also what makes us unpredictable, the one thing no pattern of ours has ever contained.

Subjectivity is the immovable barrier to objectivity. Objectivity would be knowledge without a knower, and there is no such thing.

## Where it led

All of this brought us to a definition of science that removes what science cannot do and keeps everything it can.

Science is to observe, record, organize and project. It is not to understand.

To observe is to meet the world through instruments, knowing that the instruments shape what they meet.

To record is to keep each encounter exactly, with the conditions that produced it.

To organize is to arrange the records so that patterns show. A law is an arrangement we choose, not a property we dig up.

To project is to carry a verified rule forward to cases not yet observed. Every reliable discovery in history stands on projection. A projection rests on a rule that has been verified. A promise rests on an intention.

That is not a demotion. It is a description of everything science has ever actually delivered: the medicines, the bridges, the harvests, the machines. Every one of them came from observing, recording, organizing and projecting. None came from understanding what matter is, because no one ever has.

Nor would the answers at the fringes change much if we had them. Confirming the Higgs boson cost more than twelve billion dollars, for a glimpse of a particle that lives about a ten-thousandth of a billionth of a billionth of a second. It confirmed a theory written in the 1960s. It has changed nothing about how anyone eats, heals, builds or lives. Knowing the far side of the boundary is beyond possibility. Even if it weren’t, it would change very little for those of us on this side.

## What’s clearly not right

What’s clearly not right is a science that sells understanding it cannot deliver, and asks the public to pay for its promises in the same voice it uses for its projections.

## The better question

The usual question is what lies on the far side of the boundary. The better question is what is dependable on this side, and whom it serves.

That’s where the voyage has led: back to Earth. Back to observations that can be repeated, records that can be trusted, rules that have been verified, and projections that come home to be checked. It’s a smaller science than the one on the covers of magazines. It is also the only one that has ever worked.

title: Don’t Get Your Hopes Up Just Yet
dek: What policy can promise, and what it can’t.
excerpt: What policy can promise, and what it can’t.
body:
_We’re storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can’t prove it._

Every policy rests on two expectations. The first is that the people who make it reason their way to it. The second is that the people who receive it will respond as expected. Neither expectation can be met. Not because people are foolish, but because of what people are.

## One at a time, and in a crowd

A human being is unpredictable one at a time and regular in a crowd. No one can say what a given person will do tomorrow. Almost anyone can say, within a narrow range, what a million people will do. This isn’t a quirk of human nature. It’s what anything looks like when it’s observed by someone who can’t see it whole. In that sense, human beings are quarks observed in a bigger frame.

## Rationality and self-interest

Two words carry most of the weight in policy: rationality and self-interest. Both are treated as traits, things people have. Neither is.

Rationality is not a condition anyone lives in. It’s something that happens: a moment in which reasoning wins out over everything else a mind is doing. Such moments occur. They can’t be scheduled.

Self-interest is the same. It occurs, often. It also fails to occur, often, and no one can say in advance which it will be. After the fact it explains everything, because whatever anyone did can be called self-interest. An explanation that fits every outcome predicts none.

Rationality and self-interest aren’t traits, or even categories. They’re occurrences. Counted in a crowd, they look like laws. In a single person at a single moment, they’re possibilities.

## The making end

A policy is rational only if a rational moment happens to coincide with the decision. The odds of that depend on who decides.
