Committees are never rational. No one owns the decision, so no one’s discipline is engaged, and what emerges is a negotiated average of many occurrences. An average of occurrences isn’t reason. It’s arithmetic.

Teams can be rational, within limits. A team shares one goal and answers to one result it can check, and the result keeps it honest up to a point.

Individuals can be rational if they try very hard. One person can own a decision and check himself. That check is always possible and never guaranteed.

Rationality rises with responsibility. Policy is almost always made by committee, so it begins with the worst odds of the three.

## The receiving end

A policy’s outcome is the sum of millions of occurrences, each one unpredictable. The sum can be estimated from the past. But the people receiving a policy respond to the policy itself, and their response changes the very regularities the policy was built on. The moment a pattern is leaned on, it shifts. So an outcome isn’t merely hard to predict. It’s unpredictable by definition.

## Direction, not destination

What, then, can a policy do? It can change the odds. It can make some moves a little more likely and others a little less. It can’t choose where any single path ends. Run long enough, a system governed by odds forgets where it started. It’s the odds that decide where it settles, not the intentions of whoever set it going.

Policy is an element of direction, not outcome: an intention, not a prediction.

And time alters the frame, not the picture. A policy can change the circumstances people act in. It can’t change the people.

## Why is this happening

A few suggested causes.

A promised outcome wins votes. A tilted probability doesn’t.

Committees spread the blame, so no one pays for a failed prediction.

Statistics about crowds are easy to mistake for facts about persons.

And everyone wants to believe that someone is in control.

## What’s clearly not right

What’s clearly not right is policy sold as rational design with predictable results: an intention dressed as a prediction, decided by a committee, and judged by outcomes no one could have delivered.

## The better question

The usual question is what a policy will achieve. The better question is which way it tilts the odds, how soon the tilt will show in the records, and how easily it can be undone if the tilt turns out wrong.

Hope, by all means, for a direction. Just don’t get your hopes up for a destination.

title: The Road So Far
dek: From the garden to the last question.
excerpt: From the garden to the last question.
body:
_We’re storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can’t prove it._

## 1. The garden: exposure and the reflex

It begins where every human story begins. The fruit of the tree did not give knowledge of the world. It gave knowledge of exposure: “the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked.” A creature that knows it can be hurt can never again leave a dark corner unexplained.

So we carry a reflex. It fills every empty space before it knows what is there, because for a creature outside the garden an empty space is where the danger hides. It cannot be switched off, only overridden. Myth was its first answer. Science is its disciplined answer. Where observation runs out, at the SOBs, the scientific observational boundaries, the places where our ability to look runs out though something surely lies beyond, the reflex returns and paints a word on the wall. We call the word a placeholder.

## 2. Physics: the temptation and the corruption

Every science carries the reflex, and most keep their discipline with little strain, because their claims answer to something: a reaction, a rock, a patient. Physics works where nothing answers back. It has the widest empty spaces in science.

In the twentieth century physics was courted by the media as no other science was: Einstein’s fame in 1919, quantum strangeness on the radio, the bomb, Sputnik, Big Science, the bestsellers. The media made the serpent’s offer: “ye shall be as gods,” to be made wise, to have the standing of those who know. Newton had refused that offer in 1713, when he left the hole at the center of his own theory empty and said so: “I do not feign hypotheses.” Feynman took the stage and kept his humility. The field as a whole took everything on offer.

The result is a field that names its gaps as things. “Missing mass” became “dark matter.” The difference is the difference between two sentences: “We’re searching for dark matter” and “We’re trying to figure out what’s wrong with our model.” The first assumes the answer and treats every empty detector as a reason to look harder. The second places the fault where the evidence points, in the account. The media buys the first sentence. It has no use for the second.

## 3. What science actually holds

Strip away the promises and look at the holdings. All science actually possesses is a catalog of replicable reactions to common influences. Every “fundamental property” in it is a reaction: mass is how a thing resists a push, charge is how it answers a field. A property is how a thing reacts to pressure.

The catalog is real and earned. The discoveries are real. The promises are empty: the fundamental nature of things, the theory of everything. The method returns only reactions, and the thing sought is not a reaction. You can’t find the Easter egg if you don’t know what an egg is. And no one knows what Everything is.

At its edges, then, physics takes public money in exchange for promises its own method cannot keep. Need to Know has to be more than a phrase: reliable data from material observation, for a worthwhile purpose.

## 4. Matter: the faces we ask for

Matter presents features relative to scale and framework. A molecule of water is not wet. Light is a wave to one apparatus and a particle to another. Like clay, matter takes the shape of the question pressed into it, endless shapes in principle, few in practice, and the clay answers back.

Matter cannot be nothing, so it is something, and anything that is something has an identity of its own. That identity lies beyond our functional horizon. Matter only shows the faces we ask for.

The same is true of the image. The object supplies differences; the receptor supplies the face. Color, edges, depth and meaning are ours. We observe what we can observe, not what is being observed.

## 5. Two realities

There are two realities. One is organized by something else: Reality, the clay, which we meet only through its consequences. The other is organized by us: reality, the cosmos, the Universe with a beginning and a story. We author the Universe. We do not author Reality.

We live only in our own, and we think we see both, because the brain does not label its work. It hands over the finished picture as if it came straight from outside. The wall is a _trompe-l’œil_: painted so well that it looks like an open window.

Different eyes organize different small realities from the same Reality: the bee’s ultraviolet flower, the bat’s echoes. They observe simultaneously, not similarly, and no comparison leads back to Reality, because every comparison is made from inside one organizer. Our knowledge is privileged to us and no other.

## 6. The Subject: the miracle and its hunger

At the center of everything is the Subject. Without the Subject there is no sentence, just words: Reality may exist unobserved, but it means nothing unobserved. Nothing is provably anything without an observer who proves it. The gap between what provably exists and what exists is ontology.

The universe appears to us to be predictable, because we built our catalog from what repeats. The universe is a vast collection of debris that does not include awareness, except in a few places where the debris woke up. The Subject is the astonishing miracle: the one thing met from the inside, the one thing that organizes a small reality, the one thing no prediction contains.

The Subject has two faces. One is the knower, who writes the sentence. The other is the one who wants to be known, and that face is where the media feeds. The old stories knew it. Fama, in Virgil, is the winged rumor who grows as she goes, with a tongue for every feather, fond of the false as of the true. Narcissus wastes away at the pool, fed by his own reflection, with Echo able only to repeat. The Sirens promise knowledge, “we know all that happens on the earth,” and their meadow is piled with bones. The crew, ears stopped with wax, row past untouched. The danger is only for the few who want to hear. Odysseus survives by being bound to the mast, which is Newton’s refusal in Greek.

This is not an indictment of the many. It is a description of the few, and of the voice that feeds on them.

## 7. The last question

We cannot describe the core nature of matter, and we cannot describe the core nature of knowledge. Two SOBs face each other, and everything we have lies between them, in the record of their meeting.

Broadly defined, that leaves the last question: What are we, and what is that? Neither religion nor physics had an ontological answer; each had a placeholder dressed as one. Neither will we. But by knowing the right question and how to ask it, we can be a drop in the pond.

## The center

The Subject, with two faces: the knower, who is the miracle, and the one who wants to be known, who is the vulnerability. Every thread above runs through one or the other. Much ado about noting.

_Science is an evolving template on the surface of Reality._
